en: Sūtrasthāna, Chapter Four:
Pippalī, dīpyaka, and likewise mūṣikakarṇikā; the tender leaves of bilva, white haridrā, and madhuka.
1.4.2 These, when properly combined, destroy leprosy (kuṣṭha) through internal consumption and external application: the bile of cows, the bile of dogs, bottle gourd (alābū), and kaṭukā;
1.4.3 likewise, one should apply as an ointment nimba, nata, and sugar; and the roots of yātuṇḍa, maṇḍalī, dvīpa, and eḍagaja.
1.4.3–4 One should likewise apply a plaster consisting of *surādanī*, *sugandhā*, *suvarṇapuṣpī*, *kaṭukā*, *śyāmā*, and *tejovatī*.
1.4.5 They know that *trivṛt*, *sañjātaka*, and *kuṣṭha* constitute a purifying treatment (*saṃśodhana*). One should also take *āragvadha*, *bhārgī*, *aśvagandhā*, and *gavādanī*.
1.4.6 One should likewise prepare fine powders of *śvetā* and *jyotiṣmatī*. That powder should be well-saturated seven times with the bile of cows.

This should be administered with mustard oil and rock salt according to the proper method, for one whose bodily humors have been removed from the heart and who eats a moderate amount of curd and rice.

1.4.8 This body-ointment is prescribed for the destruction of worms and skin diseases (kuṣṭha). Gavedhuka and makūṣṭha, boiled in a decoction of khadira— 1.4.9 both of these should also be applied for the alleviation of kuṣṭha in those afflicted by it. Furthermore, the juices of trees that destroy itching are beneficial for those with kuṣṭha.
For ointments and affusions, however, the khadira tree is praised. One should drink a decoction of khadira water and subsist on khadira water.
1.4.11 One should mostly use a vessel made of *khadira* wood for the purpose of water; both the *dhava* and *rohītaka*, which are great trees possessing heartwood, [are also suitable].
1.4.12 So too are the *śiṃśupā*, the *aśvakarṇa*, the *khadira*, and the *bilva*; as well as the *kadalī*, the *muṣkaka*, the *hiṃsrā*, and the fruit of the *bhadrodumbarikā*.
Cow’s urine used as a wash is also effective for leprosy when combined with these [other substances]: the resin of *sāla* and *aśvakarṇa*, and the resin of *kuliśa*.
1.4.14 These [remedies] shall be the alleviators of the ulcers caused by kuṣṭha. I shall now describe the treatment for puṇḍarīka that destroys the disease.
1.4.15 [One should use] āvartā, the root of śālmali, malayū, kāñcanakṣīrī, the root of bhadrodumbarikā, and the fruits of āvalguja.
At night, having crushed *dantī*, *citraka*, *pāṭhā*, and the two types of *haridrā* with a mechanical press, one should likewise combine them with cow’s urine.
1.4.17 When one-eighth of that has remained, it should be prepared and well-refined; the person afflicted with vitiligo (śvitrī) should drink it upon rising at dawn and then drink cold water.
1.4.18 One should protect it from all sides and place it in the sun; for the humors (doṣas), oppressed by the medicine, remain situated within the skin.
Within the circles, they produce eruptions by means of the sun's rays. Once the eruptions have arisen, one should then seat the patient in the shade.

1.4.20 Having washed [the area] with cold water, one should feed them a meal of meat broth; then they become agitated like clouds filled with rainwater. 1.4.21 Then one should cause pain with the point of a needle or a sharp thorn, using the heartwood of sandalwood, jujube, and khadira.
Then, with these [herbs] ground with water and combined with ghee and honey, [the physician should apply them] upon the leaves of a lotus pond for the sake of the embodied being lying there.
1.4.23 Then one should apply an ointment to the eruptions that have been sprinkled with cold water; the physician should also grind the bark of milky trees.
1.4.24 With the decoctions and pastes of these, he should sprinkle and smear the area; furthermore, he should provide the seeds of the date palm and the navel of a conch shell.
One should dust the discharging [wound] with a fine powder made from añjana, tagara, patra, gairika, and blue utpala.

1.4.26 For the purpose of softening the skin, the physician should administer a single dose of grape juice mixed with honey, along with food, massage, and anointing, according to the previously mentioned procedure.

1.4.27 By following this method for those suffering from kuṣṭha, they shall thereafter become healthy. A wise person should not neglect the disease, for the body is as vulnerable as a house on fire; one must hasten to pacify it.
1.4.27–28 Just as a tree grows steadily and easily when it is alone, so too, having entered the body, disease indeed increases. 1.4.28

1.4.29 Therefore, a wise physician, protecting the patient from great force, should destroy diseases while they are still in the stage of *upacaya* (accumulation) in an embodied being whose [doshas] have not yet been exhausted. 1.4.30 An *avapīḍa* (nasal drop) should be administered every three days; likewise, one should induce emesis after a fortnight or a month, and purgation when a full season has passed; venesection is prescribed [after a full year].

*Śyāmāka* grains, *makuṣṭha*, and chickpeas (*caṇaka*) are beneficial for those suffering from skin diseases (*kuṣṭha*). Indeed, for those who subsist in this manner, the skin disease is pacified. Thus spoke the venerable Ātreya. Thus ends the fourth chapter in the Bheḷa-saṃhitā. The Fifth Chapter: Now we shall explain the chapter on overeating (*atyāśitīya*). Thus said the venerable Ātreya. 1.4.31

1.5.1 Furthermore, when food has been properly eaten, drunk, and chewed, the strength of a living being is nourished immediately, like a fire by fuel. 1.5.2 By that very same food, if consumed in excess, diseases born of the body increase, as the digestive fire of the body is also impaired.
1.5.2–3 However, the physician should know that lightness of food is of two kinds; likewise, listen as the two kinds of heaviness in what has been eaten are being described.

1.5.4 Some food is light by measure (*mātrā-laghu*), while some is known to be light by substance (*dravya-laghu*). Likewise, there may be that which is heavy by measure (*mātrā-guru*) and similarly heavy by substance (*dravya-guru*).
1.5.5 Ancient *śāli* rice, mung beans (*mudga*), rabbit, partridge, quail, and whatever else is of this nature—that substance is considered light.
1.5.5–6 Meat from domestic, marshy, and aquatic animals; curd; ground sesame; and whatever other substance is of such a nature—that is traditionally known as "heavy" (guru).
1.5.7 In this regard, physicians regard even a heavy substance as light when a person eats it in the proper measure.
1.5.8 Even rice and other grains that are naturally very light become clearly heavy when eaten in excess by someone.
The expert should recognize that food as light which, through proper method, allows one to achieve full satiety even with a small quantity of substance; such food is exclusively wholesome and light.
1.5.10 If even by reasoning one reaches satiety with a substance that is not light, I declare such food here to be indeed heavy.
1.5.11 Therefore, one should always seek light food when consuming heavy substances, whether it provides one-third of fullness or even half-fullness.
Even if one consumes a light substance in excessive measure, that light substance, through such over-indulgence, becomes heavy within the digestive tract.

1.5.13 A physician who understands the relative heaviness and lightness [of substances] increases the life-force of men; therefore, one should understand the heaviness and lightness of substances in this manner. 1.5.14 In this very way, a person is nourished by wholesome food and is depleted by unwholesome food, as well as by the vitiated *vāta* and other [humors].

In a healthy person, the bodily constituents (dhātus), such as blood and the rest, increase through food; however, in a diseased person, even food that is consumed results in the aggravation of the humors (doṣas).
1.5.16 Just as a seed perishes in the earth due to unseasonable rain, yet thrives through rain at the proper time, so too do embodied beings [flourish] with the vital essences (rasas).
1.5.17 And he who is always noble, whose mind is unwaveringly happy, who delights in light food and drink, and who remains far removed from even habitual transgressions;
Having bathed, one should be anointed with unguents, wear a garland, have cleansed teeth, and be well-adorned. For dharma, truthfulness, and non-violence are generally dependent upon food.

1.5.19 One should induce emesis for diseases caused by *śleṣman* (phlegm), and administer purgation for those caused by *pitta*. One should administer non-unctuous enemas (*nirūha*) for diseases caused by *vāta*, and perform bloodletting for those born of blood (*rakta*).
1.5.20 One should eat red *śāli* rice, green gram (*mudga*), or alternatively *ṣaṣṭika* rice, well-steamed and in proper measure, combined with ghee and rock salt (*saindhava*).
One should drink a soup of slightly crushed pippala fruits mixed with a little honey, along with a small amount of salt, and also half-boiled milk.

1.5.22 One should always consume scattered birds (viṣkira), birds that strike with their beaks (pratuda), goats, wild animals and birds from arid lands (jāṅgala), and whatever else is pungent in digestion when eaten.
1.5.23 One should not walk on ploughed land, uneven ground, or among thorns; one should not enter dense thickets, approach another's wife, or go near rivers filled with water.
One should avoid quarreling, anger, and wandering about at night; one should not stay near an elephant or a horse wet with water.
1.5.25 One should never associate with those who engage in malicious gossip, those addicted to intoxicants, those who are hostile toward men, barbarians, or those of deceitful intellect.
1.5.26 One should not touch any reptiles or small-footed creatures; one should avoid buffaloes, gayals, rhinoceroses, tigers, and lions.

1.5.26–27 One should not climb trees, nor run through houses during rain or when water is difficult to cross. One should not go against the direction of cows, nor walk between them, nor ahead of them.

1.5.28 One should not ascend Mount Himavat when it has just rained, nor should one consume ghee or warm water; this is the highest state of health. Thus said the venerable Ātreya. Thus ends the fifth chapter in the Bhela [Saṃhitā]. The Sixth Chapter. Now we shall expound the section on "Not Suppressing Natural Urges," so said the venerable Ātreya. 1.6.1 A wise person should not suppress the natural urges that have arisen for urine or feces, nor those of wind (vāta), bile (pitta), semen (śukla), or phlegm (kapha).
1.6.1–2 One should not suppress the onset of the urges of belching, vomiting, yawning, sneezing, tears, sleep, and so forth. 1.6.2

1.6.3 For these [factors] produce diseases; if they are suppressed, they destroy life. Yet, when they have not reached their destination and are instead provoked, they produce these very same [conditions].

1.6.4 From the suppression of flatus, urine, and feces, the *vāyu* (wind) and other humors become aggravated; likewise, from the suppression of semen, there arise gravel (*śarkarā*) and urinary stones (*aśmarī*).
1.6.4–5 Furthermore, there may arise skin diseases, fever, or swelling of the limbs and so forth, due to the suppression and agitation of vomiting, bile, and phlegm. 1.6.5
1.6.6 Blindness results from suppressing yawning and the like; timira (loss of vision) from suppressing tears; and headache arises from suppressing sneezing, belching, sleep, and so forth.
1.6.7 Therefore, one should indeed void urine and feces immediately upon rising. The things that must not be suppressed have been stated; now learn those that ought to be suppressed.
1.6.7–8 A wise man should likewise restrain the impulse that arises from greed, delusion, and fear; from thirst and anxiety; from intoxication and pride; and even from valor.

1.6.9 Indeed, for one who maintains this [practice], his strength and lifespan increase. Facing north in a pure place, or facing east, with his head uncovered, 1.6.10 he should perform the necessary [ritual] worship; and once it is completed, he should touch water. Then, having performed the purification, the person should consume the tooth-cleansing twig.
1.6.10–11 Dhava, palāśa, nyagrodha, or even naktamāla; śirīṣa, karavīra, jātī, and arjuna.

1.6.12 Punarvasu has declared that among these, the tooth-stick (*dantadhavana*) is the best; having been chewed and split apart, it cleanses the gums without causing injury. 1.6.13 It cleanses his mouth of both *pitta* and *kapha*, and the brushing of the teeth brings about the pacification of *vāta-rakta* and other disorders.
One should hold each of these as a mouthful (kavalagraha) in successive order: a paste of Musta with Triphalā, honey, oil, and lukewarm water.

1.6.15 The vitiated *vāta*, *pitta*, and *kapha* are pacified by the use of gargles (*kavalagraha*). Madhūka [gargle] destroys excessive salivation (*upadeha*), clarifies the voice, and purifies the blood. 1.6.16 Oil prepared with *dantī* and fragrant substances (*surabhi*) removes excessive secretions (*abhiṣyanda*). It heals wounds in the mouth and checks the sloughing of oral tissues.
Therefore, massage of the sense organs brings liberation from heavy afflictions; it pacifies skin disorders, is strengthening, and clarifies vāta and rakta.
1.6.18 By transcending worldly desires and by causing the falling of chariots, horses, and elephants, [this practice] destroys pain and fatigue caused by blows from staffs and fists.
1.6.19 Anointing (abhyanga) clarifies the skin; massage (utsādana) pacifies exhaustion; pouring water over the body (avasecana) produces exhilaration, stability, and destroys impurities.
Anointing brings refreshment and destroys itching; it is clarifying for the eyes, cooling, and cataracts (timira) are eliminated.

1.6.21 From the use of oil for nasal administration (*nasya*), one attains strength of the body, hair, and sense organs; clarity of voice and complexion is restored, and gray hairs are eliminated. 1.6.22 Having been well-anointed and thoroughly massaged according to one's strength, and having bathed with water appropriate to the season, one should thereafter apply ointment.

After the head has been adorned [with ornaments], one should then administer nasal medication (nasya). Thereafter, for one whose morbid humors (doṣas) have been purified, one should prescribe medicinal smoke (dhūma).
Kuṭannaṭa, elā, hrībera, dhyāmaka, agaru, candana, kālānusāryā, nalada, pṛthvīkā, and guggulu; tālīsa,
padmaka, musta, priyaṅgu, hareṇukā, haridrā, sugandhā, saralā, and devadāru.
One should collect *śrīveṣṭaka*, resin of *sarja*, and *coraka*. Then, having moistened the mouth with clarified butter (*sarpiḥ*), one should inhale this smoke.
1.6.27 A smoking wick (dhūmavarti) is recommended as being eight fingers in length, or twelve fingers, or six fingers in measure.
1.6.28 Furthermore, a smoking pipe (dhūmanetra) made of gold, silver, copper, or ivory, or even one made of the heartwood of trees, is recommended.

One should administer smoke through the nostrils four or five times; when practiced correctly, smoke promotes the downward movement of wind (vāta), draws out phlegm (śleṣman), and bestows strength as well as clarity of vision.
1.6.30 There are eight times for smoking, at the end of which it is highly recommended: immediately upon rising from bed, after cleansing the teeth,
1.6.31 after returning from water-sports, likewise after eating a meal, after the conclusion of sneezing, defecation, or sexual intercourse, and likewise after vomiting.
1.6.31–32 Now hear the individual benefits produced by the inhalation of smoke; I shall describe them for one who has just risen from bed, in their proper order. 1.6.32

1.6.33 It destroys the accumulated *kapha* of a person and awakens the six sense organs; moreover, when one has been awakened, the smoke acts as a downward regulator of the wind (*vāta*). 1.6.34 Following the cleansing of the teeth, it properly eliminates diseases, removes loosened phlegm, and produces a fragrant and clear mouth.
Smoke also dispels those diseases in the mouth that cause the wasting away of the gums and teeth, as well as disorders such as cough and others.
1.6.36 Smoke quickly dispels headaches arising from playing in water, as well as earache and catarrh.
1.6.37 Smoke pacifies the disorders of wind, bile, and phlegm that have been provoked by eating; it effects purification of the head and even stabilizes the food that has been consumed.
But the wind that has entered the channels, impelled by sneezing, pervades all the passages; it is then driven upward by the smoke. (1.6.38)

1.6.39 When the vāyu, agitated by the act of straining for feces (varcas), reaches the throat, the head, and the top of the skull, it causes the vital breaths (prāṇas) to distend; or else, it is expelled along with smoke.
1.6.40 When the vāyu has entered the white channel (śukla-srotas), it moves only upwards. It indeed produces terrible diseases; one should treat that [condition] by inducing the expulsion of smoke.

These [factors], beginning with the presiding deities of diseases and including vomiting and locations, have been declared as causes of illness; for their pacification, the administration of medicinal smoke (dhūma) is recommended.

1.6.42 When the humors have been expelled, the Vāyu (wind), moving through the empty locations, becomes aggravated upon reaching the head; one should treat that with the inhalation of smoke. 1.6.43 A man who drinks water before eating becomes emaciated; however, for one who drinks in the middle of the meal, the food is not displaced [and is properly digested].
Furthermore,
he who drinks water after having eaten— then that food, being followed by the liquid, attains a state of equilibrium. (1.6.44)
1.6.45 One should warm one's hands over a fire until they become free of moisture; then one should walk a hundred paces. For one who eats food in this manner descends to a lower state.
1.6.46 A wise person, even if he desires to be free from leprosy, should not eat curd at night, nor ghee, nor honey. How much less so if he wishes to avoid throat diseases?

1.6.46–47: A living being who desires to ward off the onset of disease should not touch food that has been thrown into water, nor should he eat stale food, nor should he eat while suffering from indigestion.
1.6.48 Wearing sandals, as well as carrying a staff, an umbrella, and a fan, he should avoid all obstacles and wander about until he is weary.
1.6.49 Constantly worshipping ascetics, the ancestors, the gods, and Brahmins according to the prescribed rule with a concentrated mind, a man shall live for a hundred years.
For when the wind (vāta) is obstructed, it causes colic and produces disorders of the urine; furthermore, when its force is obstructed, it may produce cough, catarrh, wasting, and dyspnea. (1.6.50)

1.6.51: Excessive retention of feces causes obstruction of semen and leads to impotence. Therefore, a man who desires a long life in this world should not suppress his natural urges. Thus said the venerable Ātreya. This concludes the sixth chapter of the Bheḷa-saṃhitā. The Seventh Chapter: Now, therefore, we shall expound the section on the commencement of sexual intercourse. Thus said the venerable Ātreya. 1.7.1: Indeed, all the sense organs decay as one grows old. Therefore, at every stage of life, one should approach a woman at the appropriate time.

1.7.1–2 However, one whose strength has not been replenished should not approach women; he should not engage in intercourse through non-vaginal orifices, and he should avoid animals of non-human species.

1.7.3 One should not suppress a natural urge; having gone [to water], one should touch cold water. However, one should not engage in sexual intercourse when fatigued, nor when hungry, nor when distressed, nor when turbid with passion. 1.7.4 Nor should one do so when emaciated, nor when overfed, nor when dejected. A youth who always speaks measuredly and eats unctuous food may practice this.

One who has very abundant and fertile semen, and who observes the rules for sleeping and eating according to the season; [he should avoid] a woman who is exhausted, near her time of delivery, diseased, soiled, or emaciated.

1.7.6 One should avoid a woman who has a deformity, one who desires another man, and one whose womb is putrid. For the strength, health, longevity, physical form, and vital energy of embodied beings— 1.7.7—all these perish by approaching such a woman, as if one had encountered untimely old age. Therefore, a man should engage in sexual intercourse at the proper time, during every fertile season.
In the rainy season, [one should wait] for nine nights; in autumn, for ten nights; in the summer season, for five days; and likewise in the cold season, for seven days.

1.7.9 During the spring, one should practice [sexual union] every fortnight; however, during the summer, one should do so month by month. In the final month of the heat season, one must avoid sexual intercourse entirely.
1.7.10 Alternatively, if one is endowed with youth, enthusiasm, strength, and passion, having bathed in cool water and being adorned with pleasant garlands and unguents, [one may act as desired].

One who is not devoted to excessive physical exertion, who consumes milk, meat, and ghee, and who wears pleasing garlands and garments and is adorned with pleasing ornaments— [should be attended by such women].
1.7.12 Women who are endowed with a charming youthfulness, who are beloved and follow after pleasant conversation, and who are joyful at all times—one may approach them with half of one’s capacity.
1.7.13 One should avoid the fourteenth, the fifteenth, and the eighth lunar days. One should drink milk and ghee daily; this is beneficial and promotes longevity.
1.7.13–14 Indeed, this promotes strength and complexion, as well as health; a person should have their hair and nails trimmed three times a month.

1.7.15 One should always wear medicinal herbs and auspicious amulets; one should also recite the eternal mantras proclaimed by Brahmā. 1.7.16 May Vāyu take back from my body today whatever breaths have departed; may Indra take away my strength, and may the Waters grant us auspiciousness.

Having thus consumed the mantra and the *ārṣa* [substance], and having gone to women, one who recites [the mantra] or touches water—his lifespan shall not diminish. Thus said the Blessed Ātreya. Thus ends the seventh chapter in the Bheḷa [Saṃhitā]. Chapter Eight: Now, therefore, we shall explain the chapter on "Eating in Moderation" (*mātrāśitīya*). Thus said the Blessed Ātreya. 1.7.17
1.8.1 One should eat in measured portions, eat only well-cooked food, carry a staff, and walk a limited distance; having eaten according to the season, a person should inhale this smoke.
1.8.2 One should drink a preparation of *kaiḍarya*, *śatapuṣpā*, *tālīsa*, *aguru*, *guggulu*, *priyaṅgu*, and *cakṣuṣya*, mixed with clarified butter (*sarpiṣ*) for lubrication.
The wind (vāyu) impelled by food remains in the head from the abdominal cavity; it is cleared by smoking, and the phlegm (kapha) departs from the eyes.

1.8.4 A living being who has already eaten should not consume rice, flattened grains (pṛthuka), or any other foods made of flour, nor sesame seeds; one should eat only in moderation when truly hungry.
1.8.5 One should not undergo exhaustion by traveling on a journey, nor should one suppress any natural urges; even by setting aside all other duties, one’s lifespan will not diminish in this way.
One should avoid uneven and painful postures as well as dangling the feet; one must always protect the body from winds by avoiding improper sitting positions.
1.8.7 Sitting too long, standing too long, and excessive walking; sleeping too much, not sleeping at all, and likewise speaking excessively;
1.8.8 And whatever else a man does to an extreme degree through his physical activities—all this the physicians declare to be detrimental to longevity.
A person who maintains balance in standing, sitting, and walking, as well as in lying down, eating, speaking, and moving about, lives for a long time.

1.8.10 One should always resort to a windless place where the breeze is pleasant; a windless environment is beneficial for longevity and health at all times. 1.8.11 One should not perform work in the heat of the sun without protecting one's head; likewise, except during the summer, one should never expose oneself to the morning dew.

One should administer non-unctuous enemas (anuvāsana) during the autumn, spring, and rainy seasons; furthermore, one should always cause them to be administered for those diseases that are curable by enema.
1.8.13 One should neither eat nor lie down during the transitions between sleep and waking. One should not wander alone at night, nor enter an empty house.
1.8.14 One should avoid crossroads and not dwell for long on a mountain. At night, one should likewise avoid the roots of trees and the wives of others.
Observing an ill-omened king, the ruin of subjects, a forest fire, quarrels among men, or those who are intoxicated or insane, one should avoid them from afar.
1.8.16 One should not serve an enemy, nor should one cross a river by means of one's arms; one should avoid elephants, horses, cattle, and serpents from a distance.
1.8.17 Diabetes mellitus, consumption, thirst, and afflictions such as wind-diseases do not arise from the drinking of wine; therefore, one should drink it according to the prescribed rules.
One should drink four months' worth of boiled water in the prescribed dose, starting from the month of Śrāvaṇa; for the remaining eight months, one may drink as desired.
1.8.19 One should eat the *āmalaka* fruit on an empty stomach, as well as the *harītakī* after eating; and one should also eat the *vibhītaka* at the conclusion of a meal.

1.8.20 Due to its astringent quality, the *āmalaka* properly conquers phlegm (*śleṣman*); due to its sour quality, it conquers wind (*māruta*); and due to its sweet quality, it conquers bile (*pitta*).
Due to its heating nature, the pitta, having become concentrated in its seat, returns [to its place] in an instant; therefore, after eating, a person should consume *abhayā*. 1.8.21.
1.8.22 However, the transformation of food increases bile and phlegm; therefore, one who desires the equilibrium of these two should consume *vibhītaka*.
1.8.23 Having performed the morning rites, one should bathe in waters pleasant for the season; being healthy, pure in conduct, and established in the path of virtuous behavior.
1.8.23–24 A wise person, protecting his own life, should never void urine or excrement in water, nor should he spit therein. 1.8.24
1.8.25 A wise man should not swallow his food unevenly, nor should he eat with his neck twisted; sitting straight, he should take up his food.
1.8.26 He should attend upon his mother, father, wife, and teacher; and by the practice of respectful salutation, he shall increase his own lifespan.
One should never associate with those who act against the interests of the king, those who are hostile toward him, those who follow unrighteous paths, or those who are untruthful. (1.8.26–27)

1.8.28 "This too they call health: blessed, worthy of honor, and bringing fame; a conduct practiced by the virtuous in the past, approved by Ātreya. Thus spoke the Blessed Ātreya. Thus ends the eighth chapter in the Bheḷa [Saṃhitā]. The Ninth Chapter. Now, therefore, we shall expound the chapter on the physician’s victory through the four pillars. Thus said the Blessed Ātreya. 1.9.1 For medicine with its four pillars renders the patient free from disease; it unites the physician with glory and also bestows wealth upon him.
1.9.1–2 Therefore, I shall describe the excellence of the medicinal formulation, the physician, the patient, and the attendant, which brings about success.
1.9.3 Just as a handful of dust thrown against the wind perishes, so too does [the treatment] come to ruin, except for that performed by a physician.
1.9.4 Just as rain poured down upon a flowing river, in a place of chasms, or on dry land perishes, so do treatments that are poorly administered.
Just as a virtuous archer, properly equipped and sword in hand, causes agitation among his enemies and slays them while protecting his own, so too does he strike down his foes.

1.9.6 Thus, a physician who is supported by his [four] quarters and by medicines protects himself from infamy and also subdues the disease. 1.9.7 "He succeeds when he provides treatment"—this is the teaching of Ātreya; however, Bhadraśaunaka has declared that he may succeed even without providing treatment.

Since a [medical] procedure is seen to be fruitless when accompanied by a physician who possesses [all] the qualities, as well as a patient, drugs, and attendants, it is never fruitless in the opposite case.

1.9.9 Therefore, success is not certain in the four-pillared system of medicine; yet Ātreya does not agree with this view of Śaunaka. 1.9.10 For success attends one who treats [the patient], provided they are endowed with excellence of character, enthusiasm, and strength; it would not occur through a multitude of diseases, nor indeed for one who does not treat at all.
He would become discolored and weak, afflicted by diseases, or even incapacitated, like a patient treated by ignorant physicians. (1.9.11)

1.9.12 That is not success which, having been seen, one does not pursue; therefore, a wise physician should seek the success of those who possess knowledge. 1.9.13 In that regard, first learn from me the foot [of the treatment] and the medicine: space, wind, fire, water, and earth as the fifth here.

One should discern all [the elements] as having successively increasing qualities according to their respective order; among them, those which are the qualities of the primary elements (bhūtaguṇa) demonstrate their distinct individual natures.

1.9.15 Through their mutual combination, these qualities reside only in substances. Holes (sauṣirya) and roughness (raukṣya) are the characteristics of space (ākāśa), and they are of the nature of wind (vāyu). 1.9.16 Heat (auṣṇya) belongs to fire (agni), coldness (śaitya) to water (āpas), and hardness (kharatva) is the quality of earth (pārthiva). Whichever substance this characteristic appears in, it is specifically identified by that mark.

Whatever substance belongs to a particular element is considered to have that element as its essence. In this regard, porosity, lightness, and medicinal action are also of the nature of space (khātmaka).

1.9.18 Roughness, distinctness, and dryness are of the nature of wind (anila); oiliness, moisture, coldness, and softness are born of water (vārija). 1.9.19 Sliminess, heaviness, form, stability, and smell are of the earth (pārthiva). Whatever substance is endowed with these qualities of the elements is composed of that very element.
Endowed there with all the qualities consisting of the five elements— [namely] taste, smell, and likewise the forests in every dwelling— (1.9.20)
1.9.21 Cold water and warm water, as well as chariots dear to the King of Cedi, the state of having equipment ready for use, and a collection of roots, bark, and fruits; 1.9.22 Furthermore,
the fragrance of the roots and other parts, as well as their auspicious texture, and their form being neither deficient nor excessive, are praised.
1.9.22–23: On dry land, in low-lying areas, on sandy banks, and among stones, a vein that is excessively perforated, or one that runs obliquely, is censured.

1.9.24 It should be understood that in medical treatment, the first [type of] physician is one who possesses the medicine necessary for immediate recovery and who does not obstruct the course of therapy.
1.9.25 The second type should be one who listens attentively; his individual qualities are that he is strong, dexterous, skillful, pleasant in speech, and free from contemptuousness.
He should be brave, non-opposing, devoted, and a storyteller of varied tales; he should also be wise, attentive, and act in accordance with the scriptures.

1.9.27 Furthermore, one should not be overly obstructive regarding any medicinal procedures; one who endures hardship, is obedient, and possesses the appropriate qualities is highly praised. 1.9.28 And the third type of patient is praised: one who hopes for truth, possesses the [proper] characteristics, is self-possessed, grateful, and of good disposition.
One who accepts the medicine and does not conceal his diseases; one who is firmly devoted, free from malice, and who does not despond—[he is a worthy recipient]. (1.9.28–29)

1.9.30 One who is not contrary in any respect and does not overstep the prescribed treatment—one endowed with these qualities should be known as a patient who is curable. 1.9.31 The physician is the fourth limb [of therapy], being proficient in both the aphorisms and their meaning; he is free from disease, experienced in practice, and skilled in completed procedures.
He is a performer who is bold, patient, and possessed of quick wit; he is intelligent, skilled in reasoning, and endowed with heroism, generosity, and strength.
1.9.33 One who is free from arrogance, vigilant, always having his senses restrained, vigorous, knowledgeable in medicinal herbs, and an expert in the application of place and time;
1.9.34 A physician endowed with such qualities shall constitute the fourth foot [of treatment]. Furthermore, the physician, the medicine, and the patient themselves must be attentive to one another.
Through the combination of their mutual qualities, these [factors] become the causes of success; yet through their deficiency, they become the increasers of disease.
1.9.36 Therefore, the accomplishment of medical treatment is sought through these four pillars, just as for a cook, the vessel, fuel, and fire are the causes for cooking.
1.9.37 Just as for a victor in battle, the ground, the army, and weapons are essential, so too the patient and the other factors are designated as the causes for successful treatment.

Just as clay, the staff, the wheel, the string, and other such tools do not produce their qualities without a potter, so too the three components [of medicine] do not function without a physician. Therefore, one should know that the physician is the primary cause in medical treatment. Thus spoke the Blessed Ātreya. This concludes the ninth chapter in the Bheḷa-saṃhitā. The Tenth Chapter. Now, therefore, we shall expound the chapter on the disorders caused by undigested matter (*āmapradoṣīya*). Thus said the Blessed Ātreya. 1.9.38.
1.10.1 Now he says: from oil, from flour-based foods, from *kṛsara*, or even from milk-rice; from incompatible foods, from undigested food, from lotus tubers, or from dried vegetables;
1.10.2 from shame, grief, anger, passion, envy, greed, agitation, or even fear; or from other such causes, or by staying awake at night—
Furthermore, by means of an unsuitable bed, the bodily fire of a living being is extinguished; his limbs cramp, and his waist and back ache.

1.10.4 Pain arises in his calves and fever is produced in him; likewise, the head of this embodied being becomes heavy, as do the eyes. 1.10.5 Accompanied by eructation and a burning sensation, phlegm and bile are discharged; his heart feels numb, and his abdomen is as if distended.
Like a full, unburdened leather bag, it is agitated by the accumulation of the humors; it repeatedly vomits and also brings on fainting.
1.10.7 He does not feel thirst, yet his mouth becomes parched; his voice becomes altered, and his throat feels as if it has become dry and swollen.
1.10.8 I believe his [internal] organs are scorched and no faith arises in him, when his wind (vāyu), bile (pitta), and phlegm (śleṣman) have all risen up together.
Combined with undigested matter (āmaya), it flows out with a residue; thus, it is repeatedly discharged through both of those channels.

When kapha and pitta have been diminished and vāta has indeed become aggravated, once the digestive tract (koṣṭha) is purified and the morbid humors (doṣa) have been removed, the wind (māruta) moves through the empty body. Unattached, it wanders here and there in a single location, entering the groins, the heart, the navel, the bladder, and the vital points (marmāṇi).
"Having stolen away consciousness, it repeatedly renders one unconscious; one should observe this characteristic of the *āma* stage exactly as it is.
1.10.13 Hereafter, I shall describe the signs of digested food: when the belch is sweet at first and sour in the middle,
1.10.14 and subsequently becomes pungent as well, yet free from burning, and lightness is observed in the body and the mouth is pure and clear.
It makes the wind (vāta) straight, whether upwards or downwards; he becomes fit to eat at a śrāddha ceremony, and his other pain is pacified.

1.10.16 One should recognize food as digested in embodied beings by these signs. In the case of undigested food (*āma*), one should employ fasting (*laṅghana*); thereafter, digestive (*pācanīya*) measures should be applied.

1.10.17 Alternatively, one should subsequently treat the patient with dietary regimens such as gruels (*yavāgū*). A decoction of *śuṇṭhī*, *prativiṣā*, and *mustā* serves as a digestive for undigested matter.

A decoction made from equal parts of *śuṇṭhī* (ginger), *nīraka* (coriander), and *dhānyaka* (coriander) stimulates the appetite. [Likewise, a decoction of] *musta*, *hiṅgu*, *trikaṭuka*, *pāṭhā*, *vatsā*, and *harītakī* [is beneficial].
1.10.19 Powdered *prativiṣā*, *citraka*, and *amanāśana*, combined with *pippalī*, ginger, and alkali (*kṣāra*), and mixed with warm water;

1.10.20 Fomentation (*svedana*) and the kapha-reducing suppository (*varti*) are indicated for colic (*śūla*) and stiffening of the limbs. A fruit-suppository (*phalavarti*) made of house-soot (*agāradhūma*), *pippalī*, *madana*, and black mustard (*rājasarṣapa*), ground with cow’s urine and mixed with jaggery (*guḍa*), is highly recommended. Thus spoke the venerable Ātreya. This concludes the tenth chapter in the Bheḷa-saṃhitā. The Eleventh Chapter: Now, therefore, we shall explain the chapter on "Lying Down on a Level Bed" (*samaśayanaparighanīya*). Thus said the venerable Ātreya.
Food, which is consumed by living beings in four ways, undergoes digestion within the body in two ways, known as the *rasa* (nutrient essence) and *mala* (waste).

1.11.2 Furthermore, waste matter exits in the form of sweat, urine, and feces; from the digestion of food, the *tejas* (heat) of men produces the nutrient essence (*rasa*). 1.11.3 From the nutrient essence comes blood, from that flesh, from flesh fat, and from that bone; from the bone comes marrow, from that semen, and from semen the formation of the embryo occurs.

1.11.3–4 In this manner, the constituent element (dhātu) proceeds from the preceding to the succeeding one in due order; when the food, having been consumed as appropriate nourishment, has again attained the state of rasa.

1.11.5 One should not cause diseases arising from the corruption of the *rasa* (nutrient fluid) in a person with a stimulated digestive fire (*dīptāgni*); at that time, it undergoes transformation and attains the nature of blood and the other tissues.

1.11.6 Then, it produces diseases in whichever tissue (*dhātu*) it becomes corrupted; namely, cholera (*viṣūcikā*), indigestion with diarrhea (*sālasaka*), burning sensations due to *pitta*, and *vilambikā* (intestinal torpor).
Anyedyuṣka, satataka, tṛtīyaka, caturthaka; pitta, lohitapitta, raktārśas, and pralepaka.

1.11.8 They know those diseases such as *vipādikā* (cracking of the feet) to be born from the corruption of the *rasa* (plasma). *Kacchū* (scabies), *carmadala* (eczema), *pāmā* (ringworm), *carmakīla* (warts), and *vicarcikā* (psoriasis);

1.11.9 They know *vyaṅga* (freckles), *visarpa* (erysipelas), and *kuṣṭha* (leprosy/dermatoses) to be born from the corruption of the blood (*rakta*). [They also include] *māṃsakīla* (flesh-warts), *arbuda* (tumors), *gaṇḍa* (goiters/swellings), *ajakā* (cysts), and *jālulāni* (? (webbed fingers/toes).

They know that *pūtimāṃsa* (foul-smelling flesh) and *alajī* (boils) arise from the corruption of the flesh. [These conditions involve] foul odor, perspiration, swelling, thirst, and excessive sleepiness.

1.11.11 They know that there are twenty types of *prameha* (urinary disorders) arising from the vitiation of fat (*medas*). [They also know] diseases of the teeth, and the falling out of nails, beard, hair, and body hair. 1.11.12 Likewise, they know the excessive growth of bones as arising from the vitiation of bone (*asthi*). [They also know] burning sensations (*vidāha*), intoxication (*mada*), insanity (*unmāda*), and apatanaka (convulsions).

They know that darkness of vision and fainting arise from the corruption of the marrow. Semen [discharged] separately as alkaline, fiery, madder-colored, blue, or turmeric-colored [indicates specific defects].

1.11.14 They know that a person who has an ash-colored urine and suffers from white [discharges] is afflicted by *śukla-vyāpatti*. Or, if a man has a woman’s voice, or a woman has a man’s voice, [it is likewise a sign of affliction].

1.11.15 Or even the miscarriage of an immature fetus—these they know to arise from fetal complications. Thus, these diseases of humans are born of undigested matter (*āma*) and consist of incompatible or excessive eating. One should avoid incompatible food; this is the highest health. So said the venerable Ātreya. Thus ends the eleventh chapter in the Bheḷa [Saṃhitā]. The Twelfth Chapter. Now, therefore, we shall expound the *Ātreyakhaṇḍakāpyīya* [chapter]. So said the venerable Ātreya. 1.11.15
1.12.1 Ātreya, Khaṇḍakāpya, Maitreya, and other brahmins of similar standing, held a discussion on the enumeration of tastes in the Caitraratha forest.

1.12.2 Therein, one [teacher] declared that there is only one taste because of the commonality of all tastes; others spoke of two, based on suitability and unsuitability, and three, based on their locations.
"Sweet, non-sweet, soft, and non-soft—thus there are four; others say there are five according to the division of the great elements. (1.12.3)

1.12.4 One should understand this very point as it has been stated: for the aforementioned reason, they may speak of either six or seven [flavors], according to their particular preference. 1.12.5 Sweet, salty, sour, astringent, pungent, bitter, and alkaline—one should employ these seven flavors without exceeding them.
1.12.5–6 By excessive indulgence in tastes, a person may meet with immediate death; furthermore, diseases arising from attachment to tastes will afflict him.

1.12.7 The *vṛtta*, *rohita*, *rājī*, *vṛttākṣa*, and *śakalī* fish, as well as the fish named *cilicima*, frequent the banks of the water. 1.12.8 One should avoid that *cilicima* fish alone, but may eat the others with milk; however, if eaten with milk, it causes the blood to become severely vitiated.
It brings about diseases arising from the derangement of blood as well as death; one should avoid eating the porcupine and the boar together with milk.

1.12.10 One who subsists on wild roots and fruits is incompatible with such [milk]. If one were to eat it with milk, however, one would meet immediate death. 1.12.11 Diseases may also afflict him, such as scrofula, skin diseases, and throat-obstructions. One should not eat *likuca* fruit even with honey or cow's bile.
1.12.11–12 He may go about eating [anything], even deafness, blindness, or death; however, he must not eat pigeons fried with mustard seeds with milk. 1.12.12

1.12.13 Indeed, one may likewise incur diseases arising from the corruption of the marrow; however, one bitten by a serpent is cured by milk when prepared with such [medicinal] substances. 1.12.14 If worm-born diseases appear in him, he may still survive, provided that both the woman and the man here consume wholesome, well-digested, and moderate food.
Furthermore,
the two embryos shall indeed not turn away from each other; moreover, he becomes strong, possessed of a fine complexion, and endowed with keen vision.
Those who act contrary to this reach the opposite result in this world: for one who eats when there is indigestion, and for one who fasts when the food has been digested.

1.12.17 Thus, having encountered such terrible diseases through both [causes], a man should therefore consume all tastes in moderation, when they are wholesome, non-contradictory, and digested, by one whose bodily constituents (*dhātu*) are well-maintained through proper application. So said the Blessed Ātreya. Thus ends the twelfth chapter in the Bheḷa-saṃhitā. The Thirteenth Chapter: Now, therefore, we shall expound the "Classification of Regions" (*janapadavibhaktīya*). So said the Blessed Ātreya. 1.12.17
1.13.1 When asked by Gurdālubhakin, Punarvasu explained: "In which country do which diseases prevail?

1.13.2 "The people of the East (Prācyas), who constantly eat fish and rice, are prone to disorders of phlegm and bile (*kapha-pitta*). Elephantiasis (*ślīpada*) and goiters (*galagaṇḍa*) are generally observed among them."
In the southern direction, people generally suffer from leprosy because they eat fish found in river waters as well as those born in the ocean.
1.13.4 Those who consume lentils, barley, wheat, sesame, and koddāla pulse suffer most from hemorrhoids; for that reason, they are said to be born from Kāmbhoja.

1.13.5 Those who desire meat, wine, and women, and who delight in acts of violence, are seen most frequently to suffer from pulmonary consumption (rājayakṣman) due to their fondness for the land of Prācya.
For the Bāhlīkas generally consume foods that are sharp and hot, as well as meats that cause secretions and water-based drinks.

1.13.7 Furthermore, because the mountain valleys are naturally and constantly damp, the disease *balāsaka* (phlegm-related ailments) generally prevails in the Bāhlīka regions. 1.13.8 When it does not rain during the rainy season, or when it rains during the winter, the "death-bringer" (*janamāra*) epidemic breaks out due to this seasonal disorder.
There,
fasting, steadfast, and devoted to saluting Brahmins, as well as intent upon mantras and medicinal herbs, one is released from people from afar.

1.13.10 At the end of the rainy season, due to the heat of the sun, the pitta is suddenly provoked; by this means, fever generally occurs in embodied beings during autumn. 1.13.11 Among quadrupeds, there is that called *cāraṇa* in cattle and among wild beasts; among fish, there is *indrajāla*; and among birds, there is *pramīlaka*.
1.13.11–12 The *citrakasa* among all grains, and *dava* among roots and fruits, as well as *pākala* among elephants, is designated as "fever" (*jvara*).

1.13.13 Thus, *utkarṇaka* resides among horses, and *tejas* resides in all fevers; for this [fever] dwells everywhere, and it is called the Ender (*antaka*). 1.13.14 One should quickly pacify that manifest fever, which has the appearance of smoke, when the wind blows excessively, having carried along an unwholesome odor.
Among mortals, there occurs a common form of catarrh (pratiśyāya), and likewise, a carbuncle known as batālikā arises upon it.

One should treat [the patient] with haste if [the disease] has spread to the armpits, the roots of the thighs, the palms and soles of the feet, the throat, the ears, the bladder, or even the heart; for if it increases further, it kills the man. Arising from pitta and śleṣman, it is intensified by vāta and blood.

1.13.17–18: "They call her *batālikā*; one who exerts effort therein lives. Thus has everything been correctly explained, including whatever was requested, as a series of questions in due order from the inquiring sages. So said the Blessed Ātreya. Thus ends the thirteenth chapter in the Bheḷa [Saṃhitā]. Chapter Fourteen: Now, therefore, we shall expound the *Cikitsāprābhṛtīya* (The Section on Therapeutics). So said the Blessed Ātreya. 1.13.18

1.14.1 A learned physician, well-versed in therapeutics, should know the procedure for purification; however, he must not administer *dhāmārgava* unless the patient has been previously prepared with oleation (*sneha*) and sudation (*sveda*). 1.14.2 For if one who has drunk a purgative subsequently consumes astringent decoctions (*kaṣāya*), those substances will then take away his life, just as fire consumes its fuel.
Just as dry wood that has not been softened would break when being bent, so too does purgation fail if it is administered without the preliminary preparation of oleation and sudation.

1.14.4 However, once the patient has undergone oleation and sudation and has been induced to vomit, the physician should first administer an enema (āsthāpana) for the successful accomplishment of the purgative therapy.

1.14.5 Furthermore, one should scrape [the tongue] if the purgative medicine does not digest or if the patient is dry; moreover, one should avoid medicinal herbs that have lost their potency or those administered in deficient doses.
For medicine that is excessive takes away the life of embodied beings; therefore, one should know the proper time, strength, dose, and season for purgation.

1.14.7 Just as when the flowers, leaves, and fruits of a tree have withered, others grow in their place, so it is with a disease that has not been expelled. 1.14.8 Just as when the root of a tree is covered [with soil], its tip withers— of this there is no doubt— so too, when purgation is performed, the disease of embodied beings is pacified.
One should not consume water, gruel, fish, meat, sesame seeds, heavy food, or substances that are oily or nourishing.

1.14.10 But he who, having drunk a drastic purgative while his anus is parched, eats solid food with meat broth— 1.14.11 Just as water flows down from high ground toward a low-lying place, so do the morbid humors (doṣas) enter the abdomen from all sides in one who has been lubricated [with oil].
Having been increased by unctuous substances, by the sites of disease, and by tastes; having been softened by sudations and having entered the channels— 1.14.12.

1.14.13 It is a settled conclusion that when all the limbs and the internal cavities of a person are softened by pure medicinal substances, the morbid humors (doṣas) become easily eliminated. 1.14.14 This same principle applies to purgatives, this very same one to emetics, this same principle to non-unctuous enemas (nirūha), and also to the purgation of the head.
1.14.14–15: One who has been excessively oleated or purged, if not treated with meat soups (*yūsa*), even if supported by medicinal drugs, will meet with extreme disaster.
1.14.16 I shall describe another regimen for the use of the wheel (cakriyā) which destroys unborn diseases: one should consume honey during the rainy season and employ clarified butter in the autumn.
1.14.17 One should drink *vāruṇī* liquor mixed with *gaṇḍaka* in the cool season (*śiśira*); however, in spring one should indeed drink *mārdvīka* wine, and in the summer one should employ milk.
*Kalmāṣa* (black-tailed) rice is windy (*vātala*), dry (*rūkṣa*), heavy (*guru*), and causes loose stools (*bhinnavarcas*). It satiates the interior of the head and dries up the phlegm (*śleṣman*).

1.14.19 These [qualities] conquer upward-moving disorders (udāvarta) because of their unctuousness and heaviness; likewise, they overcome the three types of phlegm-born disorders and the *śleṣmannākalās* due to their dryness. 1.14.20 For those who live in this manner—free from disease and mental affliction, and possessing undepressed minds—one shall attain an increase in lifespan. Thus spoke the Blessed Ātreya. Thus ends the fourteenth chapter in the Bheḷa-saṃhitā. The Fifteenth Chapter. Now, therefore, we shall expound the chapter on the "Three Pursuits" (*tisraiṣaṇīya*). So said the Blessed Ātreya.
For a person, there first arises the desire for life; second, the desire for wealth; and then, third, the desire for dharma.

1.15.2 In this regard, a person should first secure the desire for life; for the attainment of dharma, artha, and kāma is achieved through vital breaths that are well-preserved. 1.15.3 Furthermore, the attainment of dharma and the other [aims] is recorded as the supreme human goal (puruṣārtha). Therefore, one should indeed protect the body with great effort in accordance with the scriptures.
1.15.3–4 A man may then enter upon the second pursuit, the desire for wealth; there is nothing more wretched than this, namely, living without wealth.

1.15.5 Therefore, a wise man, having balanced his desire for dharma with his need for wealth, should acquire riches so that he may cast off calamities such as fever and disease. 1.15.6 A human being should then enter upon the third pursuit, that of dharma; for by means of it, one must certainly attain the highest state upon the dissolution of the body.

Therefore, a wise person should practice dharma without obstructing the vital breaths (*prāṇa*) and other functions; for the attainment of that [dharma] without obstructing the three aims of life (*trivarga*) is beneficial for a human being.

1.15.8 Thus, these three pursuits (eṣaṇā) have been explained as they are recognized in the world; employing them as described, one rejoices both in this world and in the next. 1.15.9 There are, however, four supports: food, which is of four kinds, as well as strength and impurity, which are produced from them within the body.

The body is the primary seat of the self's impurities, while the self's strength consists of the vital essences; furthermore, diseases arise from their excessive increase, having the nature of wind, bile, and phlegm.

1.15.11 "Disease indeed arises as impurity (mala) when the bodily constituents (dhātus) have reached a state of imbalance; and from impurity, further imbalance ensues. Therefore, one should eliminate that [impurity]. Thus spoke the Blessed Ātreya. Thus ends the fifteenth chapter in the Bheḷa-saṃhitā. Sixteenth Chapter. Now, therefore, we shall explain the section on the proportions of the bodily humors (vātakalākalīya). So said the Blessed Ātreya. 1.16.1 "Which humor is predominant, and which is deficient? What is the truth regarding this?"—placing Kṛṣṇātreya at their head, the great sages engaged in this discussion.
1.16.1–2 Some say that among those [humors], wind (vāta) is predominant; it destroys the others. For as long as wind remains within the body, so long does the embodied being live.

1.16.3 For it is the *vāta* that causes the female's semen (*śukla*) to be discharged into the womb; by that [discharge], the woman becomes barren (*vandhyā*). 1.16.4 Neither women nor men here in this birth are born barren; rather, it is when the *vāta* in the womb is cold or when the reproductive organs are dried up [that sterility occurs].
Whether his senses are fully functional or his senses are impaired, whatever he gazes upon, whatever he blinks, and whatever movement he makes— 1.16.5.
1.16.6 Indeed, eighty diseases arise from the wind (vāta) within living beings. For it is from the wind that the humpbacked, the maimed, the lame, and likewise those with rheumatism are born.
1.16.7 For there are those with missing limbs, those with extra limbs, and others of similar conditions. Such is the state of living beings, and such is the sound of flowing rivers.
The trembling of the earth arises from wind alone; by wind smoke is produced, and from smoke the cloud is born.
From the cloud water is released; from that comes the production of seeds. The falling of meteors, the thundering, and the trembling of the host of stars—all these occur.
(1.16.9) The power of the lightnings and indeed of the winds proceeds from the wind alone. Fire, the lord of the sacred oblations, blazes by means of the wind. (1.16.10)
1.16.10–11 Rivers flow because of him and they inundate the earth; there, the Wind is the preeminent deity, the source of all embodied beings. 1.16.11

1.16.12 When semen is discharged into the womb, it is joined with the qualities by the wind (vāyu); this [wind] may destroy either the bile (pitta) or the phlegm (kapha) of those two. 1.16.13 Having seized [the humors], the provoked wind becomes disordered within the body; thus, one describes the Vyāna, Udāna, and Samāna [vital airs].
1.16.13–14 Due to the many specific distinctions within the body, there is the apāna and the prāṇa; here too, the udāna moves upward, while the vyāna causes expansion in all directions.

1.16.15 The *prāṇa* breath casts down the *apāna*, while the *samāna* sustains and gathers [the elements] within embodied beings. 1.16.16 It is held that the *apāna* wind is distinct from the senses, the mind, and the elemental self (*bhūtātman*). It is designated by the specific name *apāna*.
Drying, moving, and likewise circulating— thus is the wind known among the five elements; it is declared to be the supreme element.

1.16.18 These [functions] are bound to the wind; the wind is everywhere and at all times. It is the wind that effects the discharge of urine, semen, and feces. 1.16.19 Furthermore, through the digestion of what has been eaten, the function of the *apāna* remains. The *prāṇa* nourishes all beings; the *prāṇa* is traditionally known as the life-force (*jīva*).
From the vyāna arises the movement of the body, as well as the closing and opening of the eyes; whatever other upward-moving activity a living being possesses is the function of the udāna.
Sneezing, hiccupping, coughing, labored breathing, as well as speaking— these cause the rectum to distend, as does that which [distends] the entire body in every respect.

1.16.22. "The wind established in these [channels] is designated as *apāna*. For these and other such reasons, those who perceive the true nature of reality observe that for embodied beings, *vāta* (wind) is superior to the [other] elements. Thus spoke the venerable Ātreya. Thus ends the sixteenth chapter in the Bhela [Saṃhitā]. The Seventeenth Chapter. Now, therefore, we shall explain the section on the ten seats of the vital breath (*prāṇa*). Thus said the venerable Ātreya. 1.16.22.

1.17.1 Furthermore, the fourfold food that has been consumed reaches the vital breath (*prāṇa*) in ten ways: through heat, sweat, feces, urine, and likewise through the three [humors] beginning with wind (*vāta*).
1.17.2 Or else, by means of a woman’s breast milk, semen, and blood—thus, by these ten, the vital breath of embodied beings becomes stabilized.

1.17.2–3 One maintains a mode of life like that of the immortals by means of the three— wind, bile, and phlegm. For it is taught that diseases arise from their imbalance, which occurs when there is a lack of equilibrium in food.

1.17.4 One should know that there are two types of physicians for embodied beings here: the wise and the ignorant. Among them, the wise one is he who possesses the technical manuals (*sūtra*) and is proficient in both the manual and its meaning. 1.17.5 [One should know] the five bases of decoctions (*kaṣāya*), the four bases of diet, the four best types of unctuous substances (*sneha*), and likewise the four bases of diseases.
Powders, plasters, various gruels, and eight types of medicinal soups are prescribed; likewise, twelve kinds of wholesome foods and two types of expiatory rites are taught.

1.17.7 Thirty chapters on the application of poultices (upanāha) are taught according to the truth in eight locations; thirty chapters on the Section on General Principles (sūtrasthāna) and thirty on Therapeutics (cikitsā) are likewise stated here. 1.17.8 Eight etiological factors (nidāna) have been declared, and likewise eight sections on specific investigation (vimāna); there are eight chapters on the body (śārīra), wherein the limbs and their subdivisions are described.
Twelve Siddhis have been proclaimed, as well as the Kalpas and the Indriyas; this is declared to be one hundred and twenty, wherein there are sixteen Mūlinīs.

1.17.10 Nineteen chapters on prognostic signs (*ariṣṭa*) are to be known, as well as the three chapters on milky trees (*kṣīriṇī*); from these, one learns of longevity, knowledge [of prognosis], and the treatment for both curable and incurable conditions.

1.17.11 Knowledge of disease is derived from the chapters on etiology (*nidāna*); place and time are understood from the chapters on specific determination (*vimāna*); and from the chapter on the body (*śārīra*), one learns of the collection of elements (*dhātusaṃghāta*), constitution (*prakṛti*), and the suitability of the elements (*dhātusātmyatā*).
Whatever else of this kind has been heard anywhere in the scriptures, the physician indeed understands it; know him to be wise, but understand the ignorant as follows.

1.17.13 He who administers gruel at the time for solid food, broth at the time for soup, meat-soup at the time for meat, and astringents in cases requiring purification; 1.17.14 Or who administers emesis when purgation is indicated, or non-unctuous enema when unctuous enema is indicated— such a person, acting contrary to the rules or otherwise incorrectly, is called ignorant.

1.17.14–15: "One should acquire knowledge through yoga out of a desire to perceive reality; for just as a lamp serves in the darkness, so does the scripture provide illumination therein. Thus said the venerable Ātreya. Thus ends the seventeenth chapter in the Bheḷa [Saṃhitā]. Chapter Eighteen: Now, therefore, we shall expound the section on the preservation of food (*annarakṣīya*). Thus said the venerable Ātreya. 1.17.15
1.18.1 In the land of Gāndhāra, the royal seer Nagnajit, who provides the path to heaven, clasped the feet of Punarvasu Āndrabhāga and questioned him.
1.18.2 "I have no fear from women, nor from weapons, nor from my servants; my only fear is from the administration of poison. In this matter, may you be my refuge."
Thus addressed by that royal sage, the great seer, the best among speakers, imparted to him the specialized knowledge regarding the application of poisons.
1.18.4 Listen as I describe the various signs of food and drink of the four kinds that have been mixed with poison.
1.18.5 It appears as if repulsive, frothy, and distorted in form; it quickly turns white, and flies do not alight upon it.
Furthermore,
if its smoke becomes dark, red, black, or yellow, one who is discerning should know that the food is spoiled.
1.18.7 Those [veins] which are blue, yellow, black, or variegated, shining like a rainbow, and those others that depend upon the drinking vessels, all appear amidst the various liquors.
1.18.8 However, due to the fault of improper ointment (anulepana), his skin becomes thickened; he suffers from total systemic failure, and his flesh even becomes putrid.
1.18.8–9 A garland that has dark flowers, appears withered and blackened, and is strewn with powders as if covered by dust— this is a sign of death.

1.18.10 The body hairs fall out, the scalp becomes inflamed, and the sensation of the beard-brush is painful; moreover, his hair becomes matted. 1.18.11 Malicious collyrium causes pain and itching, the eyes water excessively, and one perceives darkness.
1.18.11–12: In the case of the defect of smoke (dhūma-doṣa), there occurs purgation, excessive pain in the head, a burning sensation, a splitting pain, and an improper perception of odors.

1.18.13 One does not perceive tastes correctly and is churned like a fire-drill; one should recognize all these as the symptoms of smoke. 1.18.14 When the *vāsa* [dosha] is vitiated, the signs are as follows: one feels as if pricked by needles, burns, perspires, faints, and collapses.
If the ornament is defiled, however, burning, perspiration, and itching arise; it causes discoloration of the limbs and itself appears lusterless.
1.18.16 A man who occupies a defective seat may fall down in a state of confusion; his scrotum becomes swollen and painful, and he is unable to rise.
1.18.17 By using a seat that is afflicted by the *doṣas*, his thighs tremble; however, when the bed is afflicted, there is numbness of the limbs and intense itching.
And sweat flows out from all sides through the pores of the skin; being tormented once more, he perceives his bed as being covered with living creatures.
On a fair day it becomes a foul day, and likewise on a foul day it becomes a fair day; and the earth may have its borders corrupted by the influence of a wicked parasol.
(1.18.19) One who has a barber with a disfigured beard causes a discoloration of the complexion; he perspires in the winter and suffers from cold in the summer. (1.18.20)
He trembles and is deeply distressed; his speech is faltering; and his two lips have become pale, discolored, and rough.

1.18.22 When shoes are contaminated, itching arises; likewise, the soles of the feet perspire and experience a tingling sensation. 1.18.23 Furthermore, O King, one should observe these symptoms in one who has drunk poison, or been burned by it, or pierced by a poisoned weapon.
The man experiences a twisting of his limbs; he trembles and suffers pain; his throat quivers, and he repeatedly emits a sound while spitting.
1.18.25 His tongue becomes numb and is pricked as if by needles; he is unable to speak and finds no peace.
1.18.26 The hair at his temples falls out, his nails turn dark, and the thumbs and fingers, along with the soles of his hands and feet, become black.
The body of the embodied one who is afflicted by poison turns pale; he becomes incapable of action, like a chariot broken in battle.

1.18.28 Therefore, a physician who is skilled in the sixteen branches of medicine should perform the treatment; he should be endowed with modesty, of noble birth, knowledgeable in dharma, and possessed of foresight. 1.18.29 And his wealth, properly collected according to rule, should be established in the house—wealth which has been prescribed as beneficial for medical treatments and for the pacification of poisons. Thus spoke the Blessed Ātreya. Thus ends the eighteenth chapter in the Bheḷa-saṃhitā. Nineteenth Chapter. Now, therefore, we shall expound the chapter on the rules regarding blood (vidhi-śoṇitīya). Thus said the Blessed Ātreya.
1.19.1 For one who consumes *vāruṇī* liquor while suffering from blood-born [fever] according to the prescribed rule, it becomes aggravated by the burning sensation and leads to disease.

1.19.2 All intoxicants are detrimental to the eyesight and likewise devoid of manly vigor; they destroy the strength of men and are proclaimed to be non-conducive to longevity. 1.19.3 However, for one who partakes of them with proper moderation, disease does not afflict him; know that when drunk in excess, they are unwholesome, though in that context [of moderation] they are a source of strength.

But one should not drink at night; therefore, a wise person should drink [liquor] with moderation. For this indeed produces strength and complexion, and is the supreme means for bringing about health.

1.19.5 Furthermore, in the drinking of medicated fats (sneha), as well as in the administration of enemas (mātrāvasti), and in the case of alkaline (kṣāra) or saline (lavaṇa) preparations, wine is not prohibited.
1.19.6 There is no nourishing agent (bṛṃhaṇa) such as wine taken together with food. However, one should especially avoid consuming it when it is parched (rūkṣa) or in excessive quantities.
When severely vitiated by vāta and kapha, this [agni] becomes extremely cold; having dried up [the bodily constituents], it indeed impairs the grahaṇī of embodied beings.

1.19.8 For one whose wind, having entered the abdominal cavity, produces intense suffering— whether as upward-moving wind (udāvarta), heart disease, or even wind-tumor (vātagulma)— 1.19.9 Or if the wind is localized throughout all the limbs, it is quickly pacified for one who drinks this [mixture] that is properly prepared and clear.
Wine destroys phlegm and bile, and furthermore breaks up the feces; honey alleviates bile, while Ariṣṭa pacifies the affliction of wind.

1.19.11 Through drinking [these], the bladder is purified and even gravel is broken up; vitality, strength, and virility increase through judicious drinking. 1.19.12 It kindles desire, is delicious, nourishing, and does not cause harm. Therefore, having understood the qualities of drinking, one should practice accordingly. Thus said the Blessed Ātreya. Thus ends the nineteenth chapter in the Bheḷa [Saṃhitā]. The twentieth chapter: Now we shall explain the chapter on the ten roots for the sake of [specific] purposes. Thus said the Blessed Ātreya.
"The *artha*," he says, "is the heart; in it are ten vessels (*dhamanī*). Four go upward, two go crosswise, and four go downward, respectively. (1.20.1)

1.20.2 From those [channels], the root-vessels branch out transversely in many ways. Therefore, one must possess knowledge of their purpose as well as mental application through mindfulness (*smṛti-yoga*). 1.20.3 The nutrient essence (*rasa*) issues forth from the heart and spreads everywhere; it reaches the heart by means of the vessels. Therefore, the vessels have their origin in that [heart].
The vital breaths (*prāṇas*) are situated in the heart like a pericarp within a wheel on a chariot; therefore, one can endure a blow to the vital points (*marmans*) elsewhere, but not to the heart.

The human heart possesses the shape of a lotus (*puṇḍarīka*), a *kumbhikā* flower, and its fruit; it also bears the color of these very same things. Just as a closed lotus blooms during the day at night, so too the heart is considered closed during sleep and open while one is awake.
One should know that water possesses great flavor, and food is indeed a great medicine; therein lies a great ointment, as well as a supreme and great energy.
1.20.8 Water is the source of the tastes; food is traditionally held to be the supreme sustenance. It moistens and then sustains the body of embodied beings once again.

1.20.9 They say that smoke is a portion of the sun, from which the clouds are said to originate. From the clouds comes rain, and from that come foods; therefore, light is the great and supreme [element].

1.20.10 Sweat, tears, urine, foam, and internal impurities, as well as frost and snow-water, are designated as external [impurities]. [The heart... Thus ends the twentieth chapter in the Bheḷa [Saṃhitā]. Chapter Twenty-one ... [those] persons who are to be purged, those to be administered non-unctuous enemas (āsthāpana), and those to be administered unctuous enemas (anuvāsana), as well as all those suffering from diseases of Vāta.
One should dry out those who are excessively unctuous, as well as those with intestinal worms; [this also cures] dryness, stiffness, urinary disorders (prameha), and all diseases of phlegm (kapha).
One should administer emetics to persons suffering from cough caused by phlegm (*kapha*), catarrh (*pratiśyāya*), heart disease, leprosy (*kuṣṭha*), and all diseases arising from phlegm. Indeed,
one should induce purgation for those with leprosy, fevers, eruptive boils (*visphoṭaka*), burning sensations, scabies (*vicarcikā*), and all types of wind disorders (*vātavyādhi*).
A wise physician should employ [this treatment] for diseases of the hips, back, and sides, as well as for abdominal tumors (gulma), convulsions, and all types of vāta disorders.

1.21.5 Indeed, one should apply [this therapy] for abdominal tumors (gulma), urinary retention, abdominal enlargements (udara), epilepsy, skin diseases (kuṣṭha), and all types of wind disorders (vātavyādhi). 1.21.6 One should apply fomentation (sveda) for lockjaw (hanustambha), facial paralysis (āyāma), hemifacial spasm (ardita), pain in the flanks (pārśvaroga), abdominal tumors, and all types of wind disorders.
The wise physician should arrest hemorrhagic disorders (raktapitta), erysipelas (visarpa), burning sensations, eruptive boils (visphoṭaka), and all diseases of the pitta humor.

1.21.8 Thus, one should know that those arising from pitta and kapha are of the nature of the *āmāśaya* (stomach), and one should designate those arising from the *pakvāśaya* (intestines) as diseases of vāta. 1.21.9 One should cause those who are fit for emesis to vomit after examining those whose affliction resides in the *āmāśaya*; likewise, one should administer purgation to those who are fit for it and whose affliction resides in the *pakvāśaya*. Thus spoke the venerable Ātreya. Thus ends the twenty-first chapter in the Bheḷa [Saṃhitā]. Chapter Twenty-Two: Now, therefore, we shall explain the chapter on sudation (*sveda*). Thus said the venerable Ātreya.
They know fomentation therapy (*sveda*) to be of eight kinds: *saṃkara*, *prastara*, *seka*, *nāḍī*, *droṇī*, *jalāni*, *udakoṣṭha*, and *kuṭī*. 1.22.1
1.22.2 Stone, ashes, sand, chaff, dust, and husks; the dung of goats, sheep, and cows; coarse coverings and garments worn in windy places;
1.22.3 Milks, sour liquids, grains, and mountain minerals; all kinds of intoxicants, meats, and salts likewise.

The physician, having observed the strength or weakness [of the patient], should apply sudation according to the prescribed rules, using kāleyaka and aguru, whether for those who are strong or even for those who are weak.

1.22.5 Having covered the men with blankets (*kutha*), woolen cloths (*kambala*), silks (*kauśeya*), *praveṇī* rugs, *ajina* skins, and so forth, as well as garments made from the hair of goats (*kiṭija*) or sheep (*rājīja*), one should cause them to sweat. 1.22.6 Pleasant touch, absence of discoloration, sweating on the limbs, softness of the body, and the emergence of cold [sweat] are the signs of one who has been properly sweated.

Burning sensation due to the provocation of pitta, thirst, fainting, a sense of melting, aversion to sweating, and a redness of the limbs— these are the signs of one who has been excessively fomented.

1.22.8 Tightness, harshness, heaviness, stiffness of the limbs, and the failure of the *marut* (vital wind) to function—these are not the signs of one who has been properly fomented (*svinna*). 1.22.9 If one has not been properly fomented, one should first apply oleation (*snehana*) and then treat with fomentations; for fomentation administered after prior oleation conquers the *māruta*.
For even dry pieces of wood can be made to bend according to the proper method by means of lubrication and sweating; how much more so, then, living men?
1.22.11 When there is excessive sudation, one should especially employ cooling treatments; or else, one should sprinkle [the patient] with cold milk or ghee.

1.22.12 Who would treat with sudations a person who is thirsty, one who is unable [to endure heat], a pregnant woman, one suffering from abdominal diseases, or anyone afflicted by diseases born of pitta?
1.22.12–13 Listen now to each one of those perspirants that were previously mentioned: bilva, agnimantha, śyonāka, kāśmarī, and likewise pāṭalā.

1.22.14 One should cook barley, horse gram (*kuluttha*), and jujube fruits (*kola*) after pouring them into a pot; once they are known to be cooked like barley, one should remove them while they are still pleasantly warm. 1.22.15 Then, for the person who has been anointed according to rule and is ready for sudation, one should gradually cover the entire body or a specific part of the body with these pleasantly warm substances.
Then one should cover it again with silk, skins, and woolen blankets; this is to be known as the *saṅkara* (mixed) type, which is said to be the foremost among the *sveda* (sudation) methods.
1.22.17 The physician should collect these and other substances used for sudation.
1.22.18 Having scattered them upon a bed covered with a mat, he should lay the well-anointed patient there; this is prescribed as the *prastara-sveda* (bed-sudation).
One should sprinkle the patient to be sweated with warm fat, oil, ghee, milk, urine, whey, sour gruel, or fermented rice-water; this is proclaimed as *sekasveda* (sprinkling sudation). 1.22.18–19.

1.22.20–21: Having prepared a tube three cubits long, shaped like an elephant's trunk, and having fitted it to a vessel filled with fermented grain-water (dhānyāmla), one should apply an ointment [to the patient]. Then, having brought that three-cubit tube [close] to the body of the person whose limbs have been well-anointed and whose body is covered, the physician should open the tube.
This is declared to be *nāḍī-sveda* (tube-fomentation), continuing until perspiration occurs. [The tube] should reach down to the neck, be without holes, and likewise long and even.
Having filled a trough with milk-porridge, boiled milk-rice, *kṛsara*, and milk, and having well-anointed the patient suffering from wind-disease (*vāta*),
the physician should have him immerse himself in that comfortably warm liquid until perspiration arises; or alternatively, the physician may use heated vessels or pure water.
Then, once the body has been properly massaged, one should apply water and steam; likewise, [steam] should be applied using such waters in a cauldron that is half-filled.

Having caused the patient to enter, one should apply sudation; this is proclaimed as the *udakoṣṭha* (water-chamber) method. One should have a small hut constructed, well-plastered, with its doors closed and secured.
It should be small in size, pleasant, firm, and its floor covered with stones. Two hearths should be made for it, positioned below and enclosed on the sides.
Having placed two pots there, one should surround them on all sides. When the two pots are heated, the hut also becomes warm by that heat.

Then, a man suffering from diseases of all his limbs should enter that hut, with his body well-anointed with oil, having undergone sudation, and with his eyes covered by a linen cloth. Thereafter, one should cause a beautiful jar of cool water to be brought in there; exhausted, he shall obtain the pleasure of touch through that cool water.

This is to be known as *kuṭisveda* (enclosure fomentation), which immediately eliminates disease. [Avoid] fomentation when one is deficient in digestive fire (*agni*), as well as during hunger, thirst, fear, anger, and sexual intercourse.

1.22.32 Those conditions arising from Vāta and Kapha, as well as those arising from Vāta alone or Kapha alone, should be treated with a windless environment, avoidance of midday heat, and heavy coverings.

1.22.33. Therein, diseases born of *vāta* are [aggravated] by hot, salty, unctuous, and sour things; those of the nature of *kapha* by dried cow-dung, chaff, stones, steam, and charcoal. Those requiring sudation should be treated with both unctuous and dry substances, having ascertained the strength or weakness of the disease. Thus spoke the venerable Ātreya. This concludes the twenty-second chapter in the Bheḷa-saṃhitā. The Twenty-third Chapter. Now, therefore, we shall explain the chapter on hard stools (*gāḍhapurīṣīya*). Thus said the venerable Ātreya. 1.22.33.
1.23.1 Hard, knotted, or dry feces, impelled by Vāta, obstruct his channels and causes swelling in the anus.
1.23.2 That same aggravated Vāta of the person moves upward and settles in the sides, the hips, the back, and the heart.
And by seizing the head as well, it produces many disorders, such as deafness, blindness, and even catarrh.

1.23.4 Now, the wind (anila) displaces either the bile (pitta) or the phlegm (kapha) from their own locations. Consequently, as he runs about, his bodily constituents beginning with the nutrient fluid (rasa) become vitiated by the humors (doṣas).
1.23.5 Thereupon, a powerful fever arises in him, as well as pallor; swelling may occur, and his digestive tract (grahaṇī) becomes severely impaired.
Therefore, for one who has a harsh bowel and very firm stools, one should avoid dry food and should not cause him to undergo excessive depletion.
