1.23.7 One should always provide the person with unctuous, heart-pleasing foods and various kinds of meat, prepared with the broth of *kulattha* beans.
1.23.8 For a man who applies such remedies, disorders caused by *vāta* do not arise, provided he undergoes both non-unctuous enema (*āsthāpana*) and oil-based unctuous enema (*anuvāsana*).
Now,
if there should be a man who is impotent yet desires offspring, and who is likewise of low caste and devoid of merit; 1.23.8–1.23.9.

1.23.10 Now, those who were both stout and lean, as well as those who were considered worthy; likewise, those from a single village, ascetics, and those learned in the Vedas—he did not recognize them. 1.23.11 Those with broken limbs, the delicate, pregnant women, young maidens, the wicked-minded, and those who had arrived—those suffering from coughs and those with excessive bile.

The physician should always cause King Pāṇḍu, Karṇa, and whoever is coughing to drink emetics and purgatives prepared with medicinal decoctions. Thus spoke the venerable Ātreya. Thus ends the twenty-third chapter in the Bheḷa [Saṃhitā]. Chapter Twenty-Five: Now, therefore, we shall explain the section on the divisions of the seasons; so said the venerable Ātreya. 1.23.12
1.25.1 A wise man named Suśruta said to Cāndrabhāga: "Purgation should not be administered by one who is free from disease and desires happiness.
1.25.2 The removal of humors (doṣas) that have not been provoked is not praised; in my view, the displacement of those humors already situated [in the body] leads to the loss of life."

Just as the touch of a venomous snake, fire, or a weapon is [fatal] to one who is healthy, so too is medicine [to such a person]. Therefore, one should not administer it to a healthy person, for medicine is prescribed for the sake of restoring the natural state.

1.25.4 Because the interior of the abdomen cannot be seen, medicine swallowed by a healthy person does not invariably achieve its intended effect; therefore, one should not administer medicine to a healthy person.
1.25.5 Having heard these words, Punarvasu replied: "In this world, a man should administer medicine according to the specific nature of the *doṣas*."

In the case of Vata, one should administer nourishing therapy; in the case of Pitta, purification; in the case of Kapha, emesis is beneficial; and in the case of Sannipata (the combination of all three), purgation is recommended.
1.25.7 The physician should not administer purgation to those who have been withered by wind and sun, nor to men devoted to labor, nor to those exhausted by travel on foot or by carriage.
1.25.8 [One should avoid] oil, black gram, sesame, ghee, treacle, flour-cakes, and sweetmeats; as well as goat, cow, sheep, or buffalo meat, fish, meat-broth, and curd.
In one who overeats, drinks excessively, or constantly sleeps during the day, the terrible humors become provoked; for such a person, purgation is beneficial.

Furthermore: 1.25.10 Medicinal substance administered according to the rules at the proper time, having been lubricated and fomented, and drunk in the correct dose and in a light form, never fails to produce its effect.

1.25.11 One should not practice [this] in excessive measure; rather, one should drink it frequently and gently. However, it should be administered with a decoction (*kaṣāya*), for it is successfully accomplished by means of decoctions.
For just as food taken at the wrong time becomes poison, while at the right time it becomes nectar; so too medicine taken at the wrong time becomes poison, while at the right time it becomes nectar.

1.25.13 Therefore, when the earth is satisfied and becomes covered with flowers, then, at the arrival of the rainy season, one should administer emetics and other such treatments. 1.25.14 When the sun moves through the middle [of the sky] and agitates the bodily constituents (dhātus) of living beings, then, at the arrival of spring, one should administer emetics and other such treatments.
1.25.14–15 Then, it should be given during the rainy season, for that is indeed a pleasant time; for seasons characterized by moderate cold and heat are praised for ritual acts.

In the winter it should be done one way, in the summer it is otherwise; in the rainy season it is yet another way, and on a cloudy day it is different from that. Indeed, at each respective time, the practice must be adjusted accordingly; for the suitability and unsuitability of things for human beings changes from one occasion to another.
However, one should administer unctuous substances for three days when an unctuous purgative is to be given; the unctuous purgative should be drunk neither when it is too cold nor when it is too hot.

In the heat, there is the affliction of thirst, whereas in the cold, it subsides. Furthermore, during the summer, when the bodily constituents (*dhātus*) are scorched, the embodied being suffers from excessive thirst; therefore, one should not administer [cold water] then. Moreover, in the winter, due to its potency, the humors (*doṣas*) have reached a state of severity.
Even then,
one should not administer an unctuous substance at an improper time; for here, a medicinal drug that is hot undergoes transformation due to the lapse of time.

In summer, however, this [semen] becomes dull and restrains its sharpness; therefore, one who carries white [semen] should abstain from sexual intercourse, as it may cause affliction of the bladder, thighs, sacrum, and so forth.
Furthermore, his heart becomes weak and the vital wind (māruta) becomes agitated; for these reasons, he should remain celibate, otherwise he suffers from disorders of bile (paittika).
Facial inflammation, intoxication, fainting, delirium, digestive disorders, confusion, burning sensations, thirst, fever, and a yellowish tint of the face and eyes.
1.25.25 Those disorders of pitta which are proclaimed to arise when [the body] is afflicted by smoke are: vertigo, exhaustion, delusion, intoxication, fainting, and trembling.
1.25.26 Furthermore, when [the smoke] reaches the seat of the rasa, internal heat is known to occur, as well as the ripening of eruptions that are either red or open.
When pitta has reached the location of blood, one should recognize discoloration; when it has reached the location of muscle, perspiration and lassitude arise.

1.25.28 One should know that when [the fever] has reached the fat tissue (*medas*), there is excessive sweating and yellowish urine; when it has reached the bone and marrow (*asthi-majjan*), there is emaciation and discoloration of the nails and teeth.
1.25.29 From a violent struggle, carrying heavy loads, compression, or even from leaping, there may arise heat in the penis and testicles, impotence, or the appearance of semen.
Excessive sexual indulgence causes exhaustion of the mind; so too do fear, agitation, suppression [of natural urges], and the consumption of dry drinks and food.
1.25.31 By these and other such causes, the aggravated *vāyu* (wind) produces disorders known as dyspnea (*śvāsa*), cough (*kāsa*), and constipation (*viṣṭambha*).

1.25.32 [It also causes] piercing pain (*śūla*), trembling (*vepana*), flatulence (*ādhmāna*), pricking pain (*nistoda*), numbness (*suptatā*), as well as cracking (*sphoṭana*), shifting (*ālana*), dryness (*raukṣya*), constriction (*veṣṭana*), and upward displacement (*utkṣepaṇa*).

Drying up, blackish discoloration, and excessive discharge are known as the [preliminary] stages, while separation is considered the final stage. Thus, diseases arising from Vata in the body are said to be of two kinds.

In that context, those who suffer from diseases of all the limbs should be known as *koṣṭhānusārin* (those following the internal channels). Likewise, those suffering from diseases of the wings and the limbs should be known as *sarvāṅgasārin* (those affecting all the limbs).

(1.25.34) All those afflicted by colic, trembling, contractions, and stiffness of the limbs, as well as those seized by *asthigraha* (seizure of the bones), are to be known as *sarvāṅgarogin* (those with diseases of all the limbs). (1.25.35)

Therein, [the channels] are connected by means of the soles of the feet, the big toes, the calves, the knees, the thighs, and the groins; as well as by the anus, the penis, the hips, the back, the female organ, and the uterus.
1.25.37–38: By means of the liver, spleen, flesh, heart, flanks, chest, and the space between the arms; by the neck, cheeks, temples, conch-shell regions (mastoid areas), nose, eyes, and lips;
and by the forehead, ears, and hair-partings—each of these being afflicted by wind (vāta), suffering pain, and becoming impaired—one should recognize those who are diseased in a single limb.

1.25.38–39. Thus has the root cause of diseases been described according to the rules; furthermore, one should observe this basis for each individual disease. So said the Blessed Ātreya. Thus ends the twenty-fifth chapter in the Bheḷa [Saṃhitā]. Chapter Twenty-six. Now, therefore, we shall expound the chapter on the eight types of abdominal enlargements (aṣṭodarīya). So said the Blessed Ātreya. 1.25.39.

1.26.1 Now, one should describe the eight types of abdominal enlargements (*udara*) and the urinary obstructions (*mūtrāghāta*); one should also recognize the six types of cataracts (*kāca*), the loss of vision (*liṅganāśa*), and the various forms of partial blindness (*timira*).

1.26.2 Furthermore, [one should describe] hiccups (*hikkā*) and dyspnea (*śvāsa*), coughs (*kāsa*), graying hair (*khālitya*), and premature baldness (*palita*); diseases of the head (*śiroroga*), tumors (*arbuda*), abdominal lumps (*gulma*), vomiting (*chardi*), and fistula-in-ano (*bhagaṃdara*).
One should specify insanity and diseases of the mouth as the locations for fasting; likewise, one should designate five types of tumors, five types of [skin] diseases, and eight types of leprosy.

1.26.4 Heart diseases, anemia, edemas accompanied by discharge, as well as ocular discharges, adhimantha, and conditions leading to impotence; 1.26.5 Eye diseases, epilepsy, and raktarohiṇikā, as well as thirst and upadaṃśa— one should designate these as the groups of four.
Backache, fever, hemorrhoids, internal hemorrhaging, ulcers, as well as two types of abscesses, three types of carbuncles, and blood disorders.

1.26.7 One should specify seven types of *ślīpada* (elephantiasis), including those caused by semen and skin; twenty types of *prameha* (urinary disorders); the various species of worms; and the twenty disorders of the female reproductive tract (*yonidoṣa*).

1.26.8 Among those, the eight types of abdominal enlargements (*udara*) have already been explained in the section on therapeutics (*cikitsita*). Now, learn from me those diseases that have been described according to their etiology (*nidāna*).
One should diagnose reddish, bluish-yellow, green, white, and blood-red [discharges], as well as cataracts (kāca), loss of vision (liṅganāśa), and various forms of darkness before the eyes (timira).
1.26.10 When vāta, pitta, or even kapha courses through the head, it burns the roots and flows into the channels.
1.26.11 Furthermore, baldness or premature graying occurs in embodied beings in five ways: due to travel, excessive burden, or old age.

One should specify five distinct types of *arbuda*: those born of wind (*vātaja*), those born of bile (*pittaja*), those born of phlegm (*śleṣmaja*), those born of flesh (*māṃsaja*), and the fifth, which is born of fat (*medasa*).

1.26.13 They declare that diseases of the mouth are of five types: those born of wind (vāta), those born of bile (pitta), those born of phlegm (śleṣman), those born of the combination of all three (sannipāta), and the fifth, which is exogenous (āgantuka).

1.26.14 One should likewise recognize fistula-in-ano (bhagandara) as being of five types: camel-necked (uṣṭragrīva), oozing (parisrāvin), conch-spiraled (śambūkāvarta), deviating from its path (unmārga), and having a hundred openings (śatayoni).
One vomits due to wind (vāta), bile (pitta), and phlegm (kapha); the fourth is from disagreeable food, and the fifth is from the combination of all three (sannipāta).
When the heart is obstructed by wind (vāta), bile (pitta), and phlegm (kapha), a person does not consume food that is tasteless or unpalatable.
The physician should recognize the types of vascular nodules (sirā-granthi) as being caused by wind, bile, phlegm, and their combination (sannipāta), with the fifth arising from the tendons (snāyu).
The wise physician should recognize that *abhiṣyanda* (ophthalmia) and *adhimantha* (glaucoma) arise from vāta, pitta, kapha, and their combination (*sannipāta*). 1.26.17–18.
1.26.19 One should point out four causes of impotence: obstruction of semen, debility, as well as the collapse of the penis, and the depletion of semen.
1.26.20 One should recognize that eye diseases in human beings are of four types: those born of wind (vāta), bile (pitta), phlegm (śleṣman), and the combination of all three (sannipāta).
A physician should recognize *upadamśa* (venereal sores) as being of four types in embodied beings, arising from pus, urine, semen, and even from the joining [of sexual organs]. (1.26.21)
1.26.22 A physician should recognize that there are four types of discharges: discharge of blood, discharge of phlegm, likewise discharge of pus, and discharge of watery fluid.

1.26.23 A physician should also recognize that there are four types of thirst: that born of wind, that born of bile, that born of phlegm, and that born of the combination of all three humors (sannipāta).
The physician should recognize *rohiṇikā* as being of four types: arising from vāta, arising from pitta, arising from kapha, and arising from the combination of all three (sannipāta). 1.26.23–24.

1.26.25 A physician should recognize four types of *arman* (pseudomembranes): those consisting of flesh, fat, a spreading membrane, and likewise those consisting of ligaments. 1.26.26 They know there are two types of fever—those characterized by heat and cold—and two types of wounds—those that are endogenous and those that are exogenous. Likewise, they recognize two types of hemorrhoids: dry hemorrhoids and blood-born hemorrhoids.
One should diagnose back diseases as *upakṣārika* and *kṣārin*, as well as external and internal convulsions (*bāhyāyāma* and *antarāyāma*), and likewise *ākṣepaka*.

28. Three types of *alajī* arise from fat (*medas*), ligament (*snāyu*), and muscle (*māṃsa*). Likewise, three types of abscesses (*vidradhi*) are recognized as arising from wind (*vāta*), bile (*pitta*), and phlegm (*kapha*).
Furthermore, there are those caused by wind, bile, phlegm, muscle, fat, and even ligament, which have the appearance of a boar, are red, and resemble the color of bell-metal (*kāṃsya*).
The physician should know that the seventh vital point (marman) of embodied beings is the sirāja; he should also know the seven types of wholesomeness (sātmya), six of which correspond to the tastes.
1.26.31 That which is wholesome for all is said to be the best form of wholesomeness (*sātmya*). [The following are types of skin diseases: *mṛjjā*, *jarāyujā*, *lekhā*, *rūpaka*, and *bahurūpaka*;
1.26.32 *parisarpa* and *visarpa*, as well as those arising on the limbs, those arising in the eyes, *romada*, *rohitā*, and likewise the painful *dāruṇakas*.
Those born from the head, those born from the teeth, those born from phlegm, those residing in the feces, the red ones, the black ones, and likewise the hundred mothers (śatamātṛkā).

1.26.34 One should know that there are these twenty species of worms in embodied beings. Just as a bird, however swift, cannot overtake its own shadow, so too many diseases cannot overcome [the influence of] wind and the other humors. Thus spoke the venerable Ātreya. This concludes the twenty-sixth chapter in the Bheḷa-saṃhitā. The Twenty-seventh Chapter. Now, therefore, we shall explain the rules for food and drink; thus said the venerable Ātreya. 1.26.34

1.27.1 Now, water moistens, and salt causes even [solid] matter to flow; likewise, alkali causes digestion, while milk indeed brings life. 1.27.2 Ghee causes unctuousness, and meat causes growth; beans produce much waste, and curd gives rise to elephantiasis (ślīpada).
Oil clarifies the skin and is suitable for oleation; oil-cake causes exhaustion, while buttermilk even diminishes [the body].

1.27.4 Honey also causes [the humors] to coalesce, while wine causes them to become shattered; moreover, the wind (vāyu) becomes greatly provoked by *hareṇu* and *masūra*. 1.27.5 One should know that radish (*mūlaka*) produces phlegm (*kapha*), while mustard (*sarṣapa*) provokes the wind; garlic (*laśuna*) pacifies the wind and produces both bile (*pitta*) and phlegm.
Asafoetida does not increase phlegm, whereas alkali causes impotence. One should know that everything bitter is non-aphrodisiac, with the exception of *kūlaka*.

1.27.7 All products made from flour (*paiṣṭika*) are non-aphrodisiac, with the exception of those made from barley and wheat. Furthermore, all sour substances other than pomegranate and *āmalaka* increase *pitta*. 1.27.8 One should know that *yavaka*, *dāruna*, *pṛthuka*, *śāli*, and *ṣaṣṭika* [grains] are similar to deer. Likewise, one should designate wild animals and birds from marshy regions (*anūpa*) as being like deer.
Likewise, there are wild animals and birds that are exclusively beneficial. Thus has the food been described in brief; hear it now in detail.
Pippalī, śṛṅgavera, palāṇḍu, laśuna, mūlaka, kṛṣṇagandhā, parṇāsa,
and kālamānaka; likewise surasa, sumukha, caṭaka, and phaṇijjaka— one should know these to be pungent in taste (rasa) and sweet in post-digestive effect (vipāka).
1.27.11–12 Kirātatikta, nimba, ketu, kāśa, kaṭhillaka, kūlaka, along with the tips of vetra, are bitter and sweet in their post-digestive effect.
1.27.13 Plakṣa, kāśmarya, madhuka, parūṣaka, kharjūra, coconut, priyāla, and other such [fruits] are sweet in both taste and post-digestive effect (pāka).
1.27.14 One should know that madhuka, bisa, and whatever else is life-promoting (jīvanīya), as well as various other substances, are sweet in both taste and post-digestive effect.

Basā, kaṭukā, bimbi, and all varieties of sugarcane products— know that these are sweet in both taste and post-digestive effect (pāka), as well as those other things which possess these three qualities.
One should know that the nyaṅku, the carasa, the udvāṅśa, the sṛmara, the rhinoceros, the boar, and other animals from marshy regions are sweet in both taste and post-digestive effect (pāka).
Likewise, one should know the kādamba, the saindhava, the haṃsa, the sārasa, the cetavāraṇa, the kācākṣa, the mallikākṣa, and the puṣkarasāyaka.
And [he saw] the *dīpavepni* and *śarārī* types, those with beautiful faces, the *nandis*, the *maudgalyakas*, the *kālakas*, and those with black tails.

One should know that the *ājñāta* species of *ḍuṇḍubha*, as well as frogs, *chuṭumallikā*, *harṣya*, those beginning with the seven types of *vāra*, and likewise *garbhabhatāsaka*; and all aquatic creatures should be known as sweet in both taste and post-digestive effect (*rasa-pāka*). So too are *priyaṅgu*, *plāṅga*, and the *balākā* birds.
And whatever other aquatic creatures are known to dwell on land or in the sky— crocodiles, porpoises, Vallakī-fish, and tortoises.
One should know other water-born grains as well, sweet in both taste and digestion: *priyaṅgu*, *vinakta*, *nīlikā*, *śāli*, and *ṣaṣṭika*;
likewise *parūṣaka*, *nīvāra*, *kodrava*, and *brahmabhūtika*. This is the class of grain, as well as whatever else is of that same kind.
They know that it is sweet in taste and pungent in its post-digestive effect (vipāka). [One should avoid] mung beans, lentils, chickpeas, horse gram, and peas.

25. They know those [animals]—the *rohī*, *śvadaṃṣṭra*, *anuṣṭra*, *śarabha*, and *mṛgamātṛka*—to be sweet in taste but pungent in their post-digestive effect (*vipāka*). 26. Furthermore, they know other animals that have a sweet flavor to be pungent in their post-digestive effect, such as the *khara*, *aśvatara*, *eṣa*, and whatever other similar wild beasts there may be.
They know those sweet birds— such as the harīta, the stokaka, the pigeon, the parrot, and the śārika— to be sweet in taste but pungent in their post-digestive effect (vipāka).

1.27.28–29: Sparrows, *bhṛṅgarāja* birds, as well as *pippalaka* birds, *godhāputra* birds—these are fried in oil—as well as other pecking birds (*pratudāḥ*) and others that are sweet, one should know these to be pungent in their post-digestive effect (*vipāka*). I shall now describe the after-drinks (*anupāna*) which are beneficial for each of them.

On this day, a decoction cooled with water, as well as water boiled with *hāyana* [grain], should be prescribed as a post-medicine (*anupāna*) for the patient who has consumed the *vārāha* and *khadira* preparations.

One should cause curd and sour gruel to be given as a post-drink (anupāna) with grains; likewise, cool water, *bisa* (lotus stalks), *granthi* (ginger), lotus roots, and fermented liquors (*āsava*). One should cause the meat-juices of aquatic creatures to be given as a post-drink; as well as *triphalā*, *śīdhu* (a type of spirit), *mārdvīka* (grape wine), and the decoction of *kadamba* and jackfruit.

One should separately provide drinks made from the fruits and stalks of the celestial tree (kalpavṛk�sa), jambu, and plakṣa, as well as soups and grain-based drinks made from mung beans and other pulses, as after-drinks.
1.27.34 One should administer the fermented liquors (*āsava*) made from the paste of *bilva* fruits or *kapittha* fruits as a post-drink (*anupāna*) for creatures that dwell in caves.

1.27.35 Furthermore, one should administer the fermented liquors (*āsava*) made from the trunk, branches, and fruits of the *nyagrodhādi* group of plants as a post-drink for birds that scatter their food (*viṣkira*).
1.27.35–36 As a post-drink for *kakubha*, one should also provide *vāruṇī* for those who have undergone oleation; for the four types of unctuous substances, one should administer warm water.

1.27.37–38: Grapes, *kāśmarya*, dates, barley, and *vāṭyā* liquors, as well as a decoction of *aśvagandhā* and the scum of *vāruṇī* wine—this after-drink easily digests food for men, provides relish, removes [impurities], and bestows wholesomeness. Thus spoke the venerable Ātreya. This concludes the twenty-seventh chapter in the Bheḷa-saṃhitā. Chapter Twenty-Eight: Now, therefore, we shall explain the rules for eating; thus said the venerable Ātreya.
Whatever a man eats or consumes according to the prescribed rules, and whatever else he drinks— all that is endowed with the six flavors.

1.28.2 What is wholesome and what is unwholesome is difficult to discern for one lacking understanding; therefore, I shall hereafter explain the food of embodied beings according to their taste and potency.

1.28.3 All varieties of *śāli* rice are sweet and are known to be pungent in their post-digestive effect (*vipāka*). Among them, red *śāli* is the best; because it is not parching, it does not cause excessive scraping of the tissues.
Dīrghaśūka, Mahāśāli, Sugandhi, Śālikāmukha, Kṛṣṇavrīhi, Kāñcanaka, Lopārkṣa, and Śītabhīruka.

1.28.5 Hāyana and Lodhraśāli possess the qualities of Raktaśāli; each preceding one among them is lighter and more wholesome than the following. Furthermore, there is this [distinction]: 1.28.6 Sugandhaka and Gandhavanta intoxicate by their fragrance; moreover, one should know that Cakala is especially superior due to its dryness (raukṣya).
Decoctions (kaṣāya) are slightly superior; the sixty-day rice (ṣaṣṭika) is equal to the śāli rice. Likewise, the pāṭala and vrīhi varieties are greatly defective and very heavy.

1.28.8 Yavakas are always considered unwholesome; they are said to be sweet, with a slightly astringent taste, and are hot in potency. 1.28.9 Koradūṣas, along with vāruṇakas, prasādhikas, kaṅgus, and śyāmākas, are very dry and astringent, and are equal in their tastes.
The uddālaka plants are enumerated as being astringent and sweet in taste; when consumed during the summer, they indeed quickly aggravate the bodily winds (māruta).

1.28.11 Barley, *atiyava*, and wheat are similar in taste; they are sweet and slightly astringent, increase *kapha*, and cause the blood of men to become turbid. 1.28.12 Furthermore, bamboo barley (*veṇuyava*) is very astringent and sweet in taste; when consumed in excess, it aggravates *kapha*, *pitta*, and fat (*medas*).
Black mung beans, large mung beans, green long-lived mung beans, and makuṣṭhaka beans are also said to be astringent and sweet in taste.
1.28.14 Harēṇu, masūra, satīna, as well as āḍhakī and especially kulattha are astringent-sweet in taste.
1.28.15 All salt and alkaline substances are proclaimed to be digestive stimulants (dīpanīya), non-aphrodisiacs (avṛṣya), and beneficial for those who are weak.
Śvadaṃṣṭrā and yāvanāla are known as the two cool alkalis; when these two are applied white, they restore the vision of embodied beings.
Fresh butter is sour, while clarified butter (ghṛta) is indeed considered sweet. All milk causes secretions (is abhiṣyandi), but cow’s milk is superior to them all.
By means of milk, one becomes vigorous and great strength is produced; it is declared that all milk is life-sustaining.
1.28.18–19: All oils are proclaimed to be sweet in both taste and post-digestive effect (pāka). However, understand that specific distinction which belongs to each particular oil.
1.28.20 The oil of *eraṇḍa* and *bilva* is known to be hot in potency and a destroyer of *vāta*. Thus have been described those substances that are hot in potency; whatever else exists is cold.
1.28.21 The oil of *vibhītaka*, however, is astringent and sweet in taste; it is declared to destroy *kapha* and *pitta*, and it is beneficial for the hair of embodied beings.
Likewise, one should understand that the oils extracted from the seeds of the karañja tree are to be known as both bitter and sweet in taste.
1.28.23 Ingudi oil is said to increase pitta and kapha and is bitter; Madhūka oil is astringent and alleviates kapha, pitta, and vāta.
1.28.24 Kaulaka oil is sweet in touch, taste, and post-digestive effect (vipāka); learn from me whatever specific qualities each of these possesses.
A mass of straw is considered extremely heavy, very unwholesome, highly harmful, obstructive to the channels, and easily subject to external damage.

1.28.26 The mushroom produced from cow dung is astringent and sweet in taste; the bamboo mushroom is astringent and aggravates the wind (vāta) in men. 1.28.27 All leafy vegetables are sweet in taste as well as in their post-digestive effect (vipāka); however, learn now which specific qualities belong to each particular one.
1.28.27–28 Alābu (bottle gourd) provokes the bodily wind (*māruta*) in men due to its constipating nature, and it also increases phlegm (*śleṣman*) because of its powerful digestion.
1.28.29 One should know that the *kūṣmāṇḍa* fruit is phlegm-increasing when eaten fresh in the autumn; however, it becomes less harmful when it has been stored for a full year.
1.28.30 One should know that the *khadira* fruit is astringent and sweet and is used for diarrhea; it is bitter, stimulates the digestive fire, and is free from defects for embodied beings.
The bitter group consists of kośātakī, karīra, śatāvarī, and nālikā; the astringent group consists of puṣkara and vartaka.
1.28.32 Vetrāgra, tiktaka, nimba, tilaśāka, and śītikā; kurūṭikā, kunaṭikā, and likewise gandharvahastaka;
1.28.33 as well as nāḍīkalāya and pañcāṅguli—one should know these to be vegetables that are bitter in both taste and post-digestive effect (pāka).
The vegetable of *satīna* is sweet with a slight admixture of bitterness; the vegetable of *kovidāra*, however, is considered equal to the former.

1.28.35 The fruit of the vārtākī is bitter and endowed with pungency; it kindles the digestive fire (grahaṇī) and destroys phlegm (śleṣman). 1.28.36 Kaṭhillaka and bakula are likewise sweet and purify the semen; they destroy drowsiness, wind (vāta), and constant colic (viṣūcikā).
Alambuṣa is pungent and bitter; it aggravates the wind (vāta), breaks up accumulations of phlegm (kapha), and, having caused constipation, it then undergoes digestion.

The *lāṅgaśāka* is sweet, combined with salt, pungent, increases many *doṣas*, and likewise causes the wings [of the eyes] to stiffen. The *svastika* is pungent, digestive, a destroyer of poison, and sweet in taste. The *cillī* is astringent and sweet, while the *cuñcu* is sweet and cooling.
Bhārgī and Māṣa are proclaimed to be sweet in taste; while Mudga-śāka is slightly bitter, Vāstuka is alkaline.

Niṣpāva-vegetable is known to be sweet, as is the Māṣa-vegetable; the Candrārkā-vegetable is sour, while the Gavedhuka is astringent. Tunnaka, Prapunāṭa, Jīvantī, and Suniṣaṇṇaka are sweet and have few defects, and Kuṭiñjaka is likewise.
Fresh piṇḍālu vegetables and tuṇḍikerī fruits are sweet, cause little harm, and possess a blended pungency.

1.28.44 Upodakā is sweet and combined with salt; one should designate this as a vegetable, as well as any other of that same kind. 1.28.45 One should designate the meat of goats, cows, sheep, and boars—as well as that which is remembered as elephant meat—and camel meat as sweet and heavy.
One should know that buffalo meat possesses such qualities; it is slightly astringent, causes secretions (abhiṣyandi), and is sweet and salty in taste.

1.28.47 Kutamāyu, mayūra, gokarṇa, gavaya, guru, sṛmara, camara, nyaṅku, madhu, and rāgu—these are heavy. 1.28.48 Ṛśya, mṛgamātṛ, tuṅga, hariṇī, mṛga, and pārāvata. Thus ends the twenty-eighth chapter in the *Bhela*. Thus the *Sūtrasthāna* in the *Bhelasaṃhitā* is completed. The *Nidānasthāna*. Second Chapter.
From the striking of the chest, fever and cough arise; his voice fails, and he spits up blood.

2.2.2 Or else, even if the creature is helpless, he constantly declines; by these symptoms one should recognize wasting caused by violence. 2.2.3 One should strengthen him only as long as he possesses strength, because in this world, a person's life is dependent upon the presence of strength.
2.2.3–2.2.4 Whether he is in the midst of his teachers, or in an assembly of kings, in a cow-pen, in the midst of women or gambling, on the back of an elephant, or in a chariot; 2.2.4

2.2.5–2.2.6: A person who, out of fear, attachment, shame, or even out of disgust, suppresses feces or urine that have already reached the point of discharge— for him, the *vāyu* (vital air), stirred upward by that suppression, subsequently produces pain in the chest, pain in the sides, and abdominal tumors (*gulma*).
2.2.6–2.2.7 Furthermore, fever and cough arise as causes for the production of a gulma; his voice becomes broken, and he spits out matter that is putrid.

2.2.8 Or else, even an unwilling person is constantly diminished; by these symptoms one should recognize the wasting caused by the suppression [of natural urges]. 2.2.9 A person feels shame for his own sake, or before his teacher or women; therefore, one should not suppress a natural urge that has arisen here for the sake of oneself alone.
2.2.9–2.2.10: When a creature is weak, eats very little, or is emaciated— especially one who eats dry food or excessively indulges in women— [the semen becomes diminished].

2.2.11 Due to the depletion of semen (*śukla*), a person passes urine mixed with blood; moreover, his wind (*vāyu*) rushes into the hollowed-out seminal receptacle (*retaḥsthāna*). 2.2.12 In him who is thus overcome by wind, fever and cough arise; his voice fails, and he spits out blood.
2.2.12–13 Alternatively, even a helpless creature is constantly wasting away. By these symptoms, one should recognize the decline resulting from excessive sexual indulgence.

2.2.14 For the body has pleasure as its root, and pleasure is the fruit of the body. Therefore, one who desires the fruit should, for the sake of that root, enjoy women with propriety. 2.2.15 When that weak person indulges in irregular diet, the bodily constituents (dhātus) of him who eats irregularly fall into a state of imbalance.
Consequently, his food only increases his excrement here; he does not obtain the essence [of the food], just as an embodied being whose body has been corrupted does not obtain the essence.
2.2.17 When the taste has ceased, fever and cough then arise for him; his voice fails, and he spits up blood.
2.2.18 Or else, the helpless person constantly wastes away. By these symptoms, one should recognize wasting caused by irregular eating.
Since a person seeking [well-being] desires flavorful food for the sake of the body, one should therefore consume food with due regard for the body. 2.2.19

2.2.20 Thus, these four seats of wasting diseases have been described to me; having understood them, a man who desires health should avoid them in this world. For the great seer has stated that health depends upon knowledge. Thus spoke the blessed Ātreya. This concludes the second chapter in the *Nidāna* section of the *Bhela Saṃhitā*. **The Third Chapter** Now, therefore, we shall explain the diagnosis of abdominal tumors (*gulma*). So said the blessed Ātreya.

2.3.1 From wind (*vāta*), from bile (*pitta*), from phlegm (*kapha*), from their combination (*nicaya*), and from blood (*lohita*)—these five types of abdominal tumors (*gulma*) arise here. I shall describe their characteristics.
2.3.1–2 When that living being, being of a windy (vātala) nature, partakes of food that increases wind, it runs or leaps, or again, it remains awake at night. 2.3.2

2.3.3 He speaks excessively, laughs loudly, or indulges excessively in women; or he suppresses natural urges, or performs excessive physical labor. 2.3.4 Or, due to falling from a tree, or by forceful vomiting, the Vāyu becomes aggravated in him and reaches the stomach (āmāśaya).
Then, it produces a gulma (abdominal tumor) in the sides, the heart region, or the abdomen; it appears once as large and then again becomes small.

2.3.6 Accompanied by throbbing throughout the entire body, it pierces and causes movement; it produces sensation and even engenders fever. 2.3.7 Seizing the head of the bladder, it remains as if tearing it apart; food becomes poison and reaches the head.
Furthermore, it is clearly seen that [the fetus] appears again and then perishes again; it passes hard excrement with great pain, along with blood-stained urine.

2.3.9 And that man who suffers from a vāta-gulma (abdominal tumor/distension) is seen to have a dark complexion. A person who is naturally prone to pitta and constantly consumes pitta-increasing food, 2.3.10 Or one of impaired intellect who immoderately indulges in such drink— his pitta becomes thus provoked and migrates to the āmāśaya (stomach).
2.3.10–11 Then, it produces a gulma (abdominal tumor) in the sides, the heart, or the abdomen; it is characterized by heat, pain, a burning sensation, and likewise a feeling of fuming.

2.3.12 Constantly heated, it repeatedly discharges red sweat; like a glowing iron ball, it causes burning wherever it reaches. 2.3.13 It produces thirst and fainting, and it spreads even from its location; moreover, extreme pain arises in that very place.
The hairs that had previously grown there fall out from the site occupied by the gulma and do not grow back again as long as the disease has not been pacified.

2.3.15 A man afflicted by a gallbladder disorder (pittagulma) is observed to have a yellowish complexion. When a person who is naturally phlegmatic (śleṣmala) constantly consumes phlegm-inducing food, 2.3.16 and when he is of poor intellect, lacks moderation, and is likewise addicted to sleeping during the day, his phlegm becomes aggravated and enters the stomach (āmāśaya).
Furthermore, it produces a gulma (abdominal tumor) in the sides, the heart, or the abdomen; food does not taste pleasant to him, and what is eaten is not properly digested.
2.3.18 Furthermore, that which is eaten together with phlegm repeatedly rises upward; likewise, the urine, feces, and complexion become white.
2.3.19 And the eyes become white in a gulma arising from phlegm, as does the person who is constantly emaciated by disease or by medicine.
Furthermore, when one whose digestive fire has not yet gained strength consumes substances that increase the *doṣas*, the accumulated *doṣas* produce a severe *gulma*.
2.3.21. In that [sānnipātika type], all symptoms are seen. Now, however, a blood-tumor (lohitagulma) occurs only in women;
it does not occur in men, but I shall describe its characteristics. It occurs shortly after a miscarriage or immediately following childbirth.
Furthermore, due to excessive procreation, or conversely, due to lack of procreation, or from the suppression of the natural discharge, blood becomes congested and distended.

2.3.24 When that [menstrual blood] remains within her, the woman thinks, "I am pregnant. Then, after a period of time, pains arise in her abdomen. 2.3.25 And in the internal cavity, there appears a Gulma or abdominal enlargement, which she likewise thinks is "this is a fetus. This disease, thinking it is a fetus, persists for one year or even many years.
Then she maintains [the fetus] without rupture and somehow keeps it restrained; then, through the passage of time, her two breasts become full of milk.
She becomes emaciated and pale, yet longs for pregnancy cravings; moreover, vomiting, spitting, and drowsiness afflict her.

2.3.28 Furthermore, when blood is vitiated in a *raktagulma*, there may be swelling of the feet. Regarding these five types of *gulma* that have been described, one should know that the one arising from the combination of all [doshas] (*nicaya*) is incurable, while the others are curable with effort. Thus spoke the venerable Ātreya. This concludes the third chapter of the *Nidāna* section in the *Bhela Saṃhitā*. Chapter Four: Now, therefore, we shall explain the diagnosis of cough (*kāsa*). Thus said the venerable Ātreya. 2.3.28

2.4.1 Five types of cough arise here from vāta, pitta, kapha, injury, or even wasting; I shall describe their characteristics. 2.4.2 That person who is naturally prone to vāta and habitually indulges in unwholesome things—who eats dry food, drinks dry liquids, and consumes them in great excess—[develops vāta-cough].
Alternatively, the vitiated vāta, having seized the heart and then reached the upward-moving vessels (dhamanīs), leads to coughing.
2.4.4 Chest pain, pain in the flanks, and stiffness of the back arise; his abdomen distends, and his head feels as if it were being churned excessively.
2.4.5 Due to the impact on the chest, the sides of the embodied person feel as if they are being seized; as he coughs, phlegm accompanied by distress flows forth.
For when a person coughs continuously, the wind (vāta) obstructs the urine; by these symptoms, one should recognize vāta-cough in embodied beings.
2.4.7 When a person who is naturally prone to pitta indulges in unwholesome things— eating, drinking, chewing, or tasting sour substances—
2.4.8 his pitta becomes aggravated; having seized the heart and then reached the upward-moving channels (dhamanīs), it leads to cough.
2.4.8–2.4.9 His chest feels as if it is burning and likewise becomes inflamed; his nose becomes hot, and then both eyes feel as if they are burning.
2.4.10 A person afflicted by pitta-type cough (pittakāsa) may at times spit out blood mixed with bile, or his mouth becomes yellowish.
2.4.11 A person who is naturally of a phlegmatic constitution (śleṣmala), who consumes phlegm-increasing food, drinks sweet liquids, eats sweets, or even chews sweet foods;
Furthermore, one who delights in a lack of physical exercise and indulges in sleeping during the day— his *śleṣman* (phlegm), thus provoked, seizes the heart. 2.4.12

2.4.13 Having ascended the upward-moving channels (dhamanīs), it then leads to coughing; one spits out a knotted, putrid phlegm accompanied by a cough. 2.4.14 A corrupted catarrh (pratiśyāya) arises from a phlegmatic cough (śleṣmakāsa) in one who, having performed a rash act, causes pain to the chest despite being unwounded.
In coughing arising from a chest wound, one spits out blood; and for that person who is excessively attached to women, there occurs a wasting away of the semen.

2.4.16 Due to being overwhelmed by Vāta, the penis feels as if it is being pricked by needles; it passes urine that is mixed with blood, or likewise white and red. 2.4.17 All these types of cough have been described by me according to their symptoms. Having examined them with his intellect, the physician should then administer the treatment. Thus spoke the venerable Ātreya. This concludes the fourth chapter in the Nidāna section of the Bheḷa-saṃhitā. Fifth Chapter: Now, therefore, we shall explain the diagnosis of skin diseases (kuṣṭha). Thus said the venerable Ātreya.
2.4.17–2.5.1 Pippalī and kākamācī with curd and ghee; vātāyu with milk; and mūlaka together with jaggery.
2.5.2 Furthermore, for one who consumes other such incompatible foods, or suppresses vomiting, or indulges in improper associations;
2.5.3 Or for one who eats while not having scraped away the undigested residue (*vidagdha*), or eats pungent (*vidāhin*) food, or drinks water on the road after being fatigued and recently purged.
For a person who eats fish, milk, and nimbu fruits together in one meal, or who habitually consumes such combinations, leprosy (kuṣṭha) arises.

2.5.5 If a person who is naturally of a phlegmatic constitution (śleṣmala) consumes phlegm-increasing food and indulges in sleeping during the day, his phlegm increases. 2.5.6 Once increased, it vitiates his flesh, skin, and blood; consequently, he is afflicted by a skin disorder and suffers from perspiration.
Among those [diseases], skin diseases (kuṣṭha) arise, such as ringworm (dadru), pityriasis (sidhma), and again various circular patches (maṇḍala); I shall describe their characteristics. 2.5.7
2.5.8 One should identify ringworm (dadrū-kuṣṭha) as circular, thick, and resembling pustules in every respect; it is characterized by itching and spreads extensively.
2.5.9 When those [lesions], aggravated by the humors (doṣas), exude a discharge from the bodies of living beings, then they emit a stinging pain, form a sheath, and flow with a slimy secretion.
Those that are clustered, pale-yellow, and covered with mud-like crusts are caused by the skin (tvak). Furthermore, those that are rough and even thin are also [caused by the skin].
2.5.11 One should recognize the *sidhma* types of leprosy; they indeed become thus when the humors (*doṣas*) exude a slimy, honey-colored discharge.
2.5.12 One should know that the *maṇḍala* types of leprosy appear as white, thick, and elevated circular patches on all sides, which persist for a long time in embodied beings.
But when those [pustules] burst, they indeed exude a white discharge; thus one should designate these three types of kuṣṭha as arising from phlegm (śleṣman). 2.5.13

2.5.14 When a person who is naturally prone to wind (vātala) consumes a wind-increasing diet and indulges in wind and heat, his wind (vāta) increases. 2.5.15 Once increased, it vitiates his skin, flesh, and blood; consequently, he is afflicted by a skin disorder and suffers from perspiration.
Because of that [vitiation], when the muscle and blood of a person whose vāta has increased excessively are corrupted, it results in Kapālakuṣṭha; I shall now describe its symptoms.

2.5.17 One should recognize *kapālakuṣṭha* (scaly leprosy) by its rough, reddish, and even circular patches that take a long time to break open in embodied beings. 2.5.18 When a person who is naturally prone to *pitta* constantly consumes *pitta*-increasing food and exposes himself to wind and sun, his *pitta* becomes aggravated.
Then that aggravated [dosha] vitiates his skin, flesh, and blood; consequently, the skin is destroyed by the skin-disease and further becomes covered with sweat.

2.5.20 Thereafter, when the muscle tissue (māṃsa) and blood (śoṇita) are vitiated, or when there is an excessive provocation of pitta, skin diseases (kuṣṭha) arise; I shall now describe their characteristics.
2.5.21 Those circular patches (maṇḍala) here which have the color of a ripe udumbara fruit should be known as audumbara; these are incurable for embodied beings.
When they attain differentiation, those leucoderma (kuṣṭha) patches become indeed maṇḍalīka leprosy. 2.5.22
2.5.23 Furthermore, those circles here which resemble lotuses, a wise person should know that those *puṇḍarīka* [leprosy] types are curable.
2.5.24 When those very *puṇḍarīka* spots undergo a splitting or cracking, one should then designate them as *ṛśyajihva* leprosy.
Those circular patches (maṇḍala) here which are in color like blue lotuses and have tongues shaped like those of a rishya deer— these types of leprosy (kuṣṭha) should be designated as incurable.
2.5.26 When they attain a distinction [in color] that is entirely different from the tongue of a deer, a wise person should then designate them as *kākaṇāni*.
2.5.27 Those circular spots here which have the color of a *kākaṇantikā* berry are called *kākaṇāni*; they are to be rejected for embodied beings.

2.5.27–28 Thus, the diagnosis of *kuṣṭha* has been explained in due order. Having heard this, a wise person here should consume wholesome and well-digested food. So said the Blessed Ātreya. Thus ends the fifth chapter in the *Nidāna* section of the *Bhela*. The Sixth Chapter. Now, therefore, we shall explain the diagnosis of *prameha*. So said the Blessed Ātreya. 2.5.28.

2.6.1 Prameha is to be known as being of two kinds: that which originates from one's constitution (*prakṛti*) and that which is produced by one's own actions (*svakṛta*). I shall describe its characteristics. 2.6.2 Men who have developed prameha—those with smooth limbs, who are soft, unctuous, excessively phlegmatic, and corpulent, and who are accustomed to fish and meat—cry out like bulls.
However, that man who is begotten by parents of such a nature as these, because his body is lax with fat, naturally passes urine [frequently].
2.6.4 For those living in marshy regions, [the diet should consist] of various very unctuous aquatic products, as well as the meat of cows, goats, and sheep, with fresh curd or ghee.

2.6.5 [It should also include] various kinds of molasses, milk, sesamum paste, water-dwelling creatures, and birds; likewise, due to lack of physical exercise, sleeping during the day, and comfortable beds and seats.
2.6.5–2.6.6 By these and other such substances that are unctuous with fat (*medas*), the fat increases; and when the fat has increased, it moistens both the body and the bladder. 2.6.6
2.6.7 When one whose body is constantly moistened by fat consumes food that increases *śleṣman* (phlegm), his provoked *śleṣman* produces ten types of *prameha*. 2.6.8 Namely:
*udakameha*, *piṣṭameha*, and likewise others; I shall describe their characteristics.
In udamehin, one passes urine resembling rock crystal or water; in piṣṭamehin, one passes urine resembling white flour.

2.6.10 The patient suffering from *kāṇḍekṣurasameha* passes urine resembling sugarcane juice; the one suffering from *ikṣurasameha* likewise passes urine like sugarcane juice, while the one suffering from *śuklameha* passes urine that resembles semen or is white in color.
2.6.11 One should recognize these four types of urinary disorders (*meha*) as arising solely from *kapha*. Now hear of those who pass urine when *pitta* is dominant over *śleṣman* (kapha).

2.6.11–12. One should know that the urine of a person suffering from *lavaṇameha* resembles salt water. Likewise, a person with *surāmeha* passes urine that has the appearance of liquor (*surā*). The urine of one with *sāndrameha* is seen to be thick and clear. Thus ends the sixth chapter in the *Nidāna* section of the *Bhela-saṃhitā*. **Chapter Seven** One afflicted by *pitta*-induced insanity constantly engages in singing songs. (2.6.12)
2.7.1 When a person who is naturally of a phlegmatic constitution consumes phlegm-increasing food and indulges in sleeping during the day, his phlegm increases. 2.7.2 Once increased,
it ascends from the heart, seizes the ten vessels, and by obstructing the pathway that carries the mind, it then causes the loss of consciousness.
2.7.2–3 That man, having lost consciousness, performs various movements; he sings and dances in one place, and then laughs and weeps.

2.7.4 A man afflicted by phlegmatic insanity (śleṣmonmāda) stays here alone without people and sleeps like one who is inert; he also strikes terror into those around him. 2.7.5 But he who consumes all these aforementioned things that provoke the humors (doṣas) falls, due to the simultaneous derangement of all three (sannipāta), into an insanity exhibiting all symptoms.
When, due to the loss of wealth, death, or the [death of] a beloved, he then broods, his consciousness fails him because of that brooding.

2.7.7 He thinks of certain things and then speaks of those very same things; one should recognize this fifth [type] as the adventitious insanity (āgantuka-unmāda) of embodied beings. 2.7.8 One should understand all these types of insanity through medical treatment, for one whose consciousness has been lost due to suffering returns again to their natural state.
2.7.8–2.7.9 Thus, the humors born of the body, when they become aggravated within the body, destroy the body itself, just as fire consumes its own source.

2.7.10 Indeed, neither living beings, nor *piśācas*, nor *rākṣasas* harm them; likewise, the gods, being of righteous character, remain neutral toward human beings. 2.7.11 A person who is properly engaged in emesis, purgation, non-unctuous enemas (*nirūha*), and unctuous enemas (*anuvāsana*) shall never suffer from severe diseases or insanity. Thus spoke the Blessed Ātreya. Thus ends the seventh chapter of the *Nidāna-sthāna* in the *Bhela-saṃhitā*. The Eighth Chapter. Now, therefore, we shall explain the diagnosis of epilepsy (*apasmāra*). Thus said the Blessed Ātreya.
Epilepsy (apasmāra) arises here from wind (vāta), from bile (pitta), from phlegm (kapha), and likewise from their combination (sannipāta). I shall describe their symptoms.

2.8.2 When a person who is naturally prone to wind (vātala) consumes a wind-increasing diet and also indulges in physical exercise, his wind becomes aggravated. 2.8.3 Having increased, it seizes the ten vessels above the heart; then, by obstructing the pathway that carries consciousness, it causes the loss of awareness.
Having lost consciousness, he falls down; his teeth grind together, his eyes bulge out, and likewise his eyebrows are cast upward.

2.8.5 If, upon returning, he should say: "I went beyond darkness; and the earth appeared to me as if broken into pieces," 2.8.6 "Then, upward from there, the wind pursues my heart and my excrement"—by these symptoms, one should recognize epilepsy born of Vāta.
For a person who is naturally of a bilious temperament (*pittala*), if they consume bilious food, and if they expose themselves to fire and the sun, their *pitta* increases.

2.8.8 Having seized the ten vessels above the heart, that [wind], having increased, obstructs the path that carries the mind; thereafter, it causes the loss of consciousness. 2.8.9 With his consciousness lost, he falls down, grinds his teeth, rolls his eyes upward, and likewise raises his eyebrows.
2.8.9–10. If, having returned, he should say: "I went beyond darkness; and the white world appears to me as broken into fragments. 2.8.10

2.8.11 Thereafter, in this manner, phlegm (kapha) flows toward the heart and the feces; by these symptoms, one should recognize epilepsy as being of the nature of phlegm. 2.8.12 But he who consumes all of these [substances] that provoke the doshas as described, falls into epilepsy arising from the combination of all three doshas (sannipāta), exhibiting all its symptoms.

2.8.12–13 Thus, when the bodily humors such as wind (anila) and the others have increased due to unwholesome tastes in this world, a living being neither suffers from epilepsy nor is afflicted by malevolent spirits (sattva).
2.8.14 Whenever the *doṣas* increase like the ocean during its phases (*parvan*), at those times he suffers from epilepsy; he does not suffer continuously.
2.8.15 [This applies] to those with fever, consumption, abdominal tumors, coughers, as well as those with leprosy, urinary disorders, insanity, and likewise those with epilepsy.

2.8.15–16: "Thus, eight diagnostic foundations (nidāna) for embodied beings have been taught. I shall now explain the specific measurements (vimāna) correctly and in their proper sequence. So said the Blessed Ātreya. Thus ends the eighth chapter in the Bhela [Saṃhitā]. Thus ends the Section on Diagnosis (Nidānasthāna) in the Bhela Saṃhitā. [The Section on Specific Measurements (Vimānasthāna)] Chapter One: "Now, therefore, we shall expound the specific measurement of tastes (rasavimāna). So said the Blessed Ātreya. 2.8.16
3.1.1 When the six tastes are taken in equal measure, they sustain the body here; otherwise, they produce disorders in embodied beings.
3.1.2 Astringent, bitter, and even pungent are dry, light, stable, and cold; whereas sour and salty are sharp and hot, while the bitter is indeed spreading and expansive.
Cold, unctuous, heavy, strengthening, slimy, and sweet is the taste (rasa). Wind (anila) is known to be astringent, bitter, pungent, cold, and dry.

3.1.4 Pitta is said to be dry, hot, sour, and pungent; whereas kapha is sweet, unctuous, cold, slow, stable, and heavy. 3.1.5 Thus, these qualities are known to have arisen simultaneously with the tastes and the humors (*doṣas*); among them, those that are astringent, pungent, and bitter possess qualities similar to those of vāyu.
They know that pungent, sour, and salty tastes possess qualities identical to pitta; one should know that sweet, salty, and sour tastes are similar to kapha.

3.1.7 Therefore, by the repeated consumption of those [substances], phlegm increases in the body. When accumulated in one place, it attains a state of great magnitude here. 3.1.8 Due to the equilibrium of their qualities, the bodily constituents (dhātus) of humans increase according to their own nature; conversely, they undergo depletion when brought about by tastes that are opposite to them.
3.1.8–3.1.9 Just as fire attains tranquility upon reaching water, [the wind] increases when it encounters astringent, bitter, and pungent substances, and when it is dry by means of dry things. 3.1.9
3.1.10 The Vāta [dosha] is pacified by unctuous substances and by others that are different from them; Pitta increases through pungent, sour, salty, hot, and heating [substances].
3.1.11 It is pacified by cold [substances], for it is specifically by the remaining qualities [that they act]; Kapha also increases by unctuous substances and by sweet and other such [qualities].
It is pacified by dry tastes—bitter, pungent, and astringent—and by those with similar properties. Each one increases by three, because of their mutual similarity.
3.1.13 Furthermore, tastes overcome the bodily humors (doṣas) by virtue of their own specific qualities. Vata does not diminish when combined with oil, because of the oil's unctuousness and heat.
3.1.14 Pitta does not diminish when combined with ghee, because of the ghee’s coldness and sweetness; whereas [Vata] is non-unctuous and astringent due to its dryness and astringent nature.
Phlegm does not persist in the body when combined with honey, nor do the fat and marrow derived from the meat of marshy animals.
3.1.16 Like oil, the juices of leafy vegetables (śāka), birds of the aviṣkira class, and even marrow, destroy the wind (vāta) due to their oily, hot, and heavy qualities.
3.1.17 Like clarified butter (ghṛta), they pacify bile (pitta) because of their cold and sweet nature; this applies as well to any medicinal substance here that is astringent, bitter, or pungent.
That sweet [substance] destroys the phlegm (kapha) of embodied beings due to its contrary qualities; however, one should not consume long pepper (pippalī) or alkali (kṣāra) in excess.

3.1.19 Salt as well—this much, when consumed in excess, leads to disorder; for once it has displaced the *śleṣman*, one would not be able to expel it. 3.1.20 Long pepper (*pippalī*) is sweet in its post-digestive transformation (*vipāka*); therefore, one should not eat it in excess. Consumed in excess, it would cook the body due to its sharp, hot, and pungent nature.
3.1.20–21 One should not desire to eat alkaline or salty food exclusively. A meal should be moderate in quantity, warm, unctuous, wholesome, and delicious.
3.1.22 One should consume that which is non-burning (*avidāhin*) upon digestion; it bestows strength and complexion, is unctuous, hot, and subdues *kapha* and *vāta*.

3.1.23 That which does not cause burning even when taken in large measure brings about suitability (*sātmya*); moreover, being sweet, it nourishes living beings, is non-burning, and is clarifying (*prasādana*).
Furthermore, food that promotes longevity for men is desired when it is digested; one should eat neither while talking nor laughing, neither too quickly nor too slowly.

3.1.25 One should eat with focused attention and oily food, so that the nutrient essence (*rasa*) is produced within the body; just as a kindled fire proceeds vigorously when fed with excellent wood. 3.1.26 In the same way, while the food being digested, the nutrient essence and other constituents are built up. The rainy season nourishes them further, and the winter even causes them to flow.
Furthermore, summer cooks him like another form of transformation. Summer, being intensely hot and pungent, dries up all the bodily constituents (dhātus).
3.1.28 Cold [water] produces steadiness and stability; [it is beneficial for those suffering from] rain-induced disorders and intoxication... Thus said the venerable Ātreya. Chapter Three.
[It is the remedy] for one whose food does not digest, and for whom strength and complexion decline even while eating foods.

3.3.1–2 Even if food that is small in quantity and light is eaten, if it is digested with difficulty and one does not obtain strength or a healthy complexion, such a person is said to have weak digestive fire (durbalāgni).

3.3.3 Sometimes what has been eaten is digested, and sometimes it is not digested; he whose digestive fire is irregular is said to have *viṣamāgni*. 3.3.4 One should know that man to have *samāgni*—wherein balanced *pitta*, *kapha*, and *vāyu* reside—if his food is digested when taken in measured amounts, but is not digested when eaten in excess.

A person who is constitutionally dominated by vāta and pitta possesses a sharp digestive fire; one dominated by vāta has an irregular digestive fire, and a person due to kapha has a sluggish digestive fire.

3.3.6 For one whose digestive fire (*agni*) is either deficient or excessive, the body is quickly abandoned; whereas he whose fire is balanced and whose mind is balanced attains long life. 3.3.7 One with an excessively strong fire (*atyagni*) should be fed with the fatty meats of cattle, buffalo, boar, crabs, fish, and *karkaṭa* shrimp, along with minced meat (*palala*).
3.3.7–3.3.8 One should eat milk-rice (pāyasa) prepared in milk boiled with the meat of a monitor lizard; one should drink curd mixed with ghee and combined with mung bean soup. 3.3.8
3.3.9 Likewise, one should drink the white meat of a tortoise mixed with sesame paste; one should also take jaggery mixed with oil, and whatever else is beneficial for that condition.

3.3.10 For one whose digestive fire is irregular, one should administer emetics and other therapies after first applying oleation. However, for one with weak digestion, the treatment described in the chapter on the impairment of the *grahaṇī* should be followed.
Internal medicinal decoctions for drinking, external applications as ointments, and the procedure for surgical operations—these are considered the three types of medicine.

3.3.12 Sweet, sour, and pungent are known as the three pathways of digestion; the pungent occurs when the food is digested, while the other two occur while it is being digested. 3.3.13 In this context, food and drink are declared to be sweet and sour for disorders born of Vāta, or whenever they are not alleviated by those [other measures].

Then, the physician should administer an unctuous purgative to this patient who has been prepared with oleation; or, if the Vata is located in the lower part of the body, he should treat him with enemas.

3.3.15 Likewise, one should administer bitter and sweet drinks and food in cases of Pitta disorders; however, if these do not bring relief, 3.3.16 one should perform emesis for that patient and purgation of the head according to their strength, for Kapha is said to reside in the upper part [of the body].
One should know that feces, urine, flatus, as well as blood, flesh, and the other [tissues], these six are the bonds within the bodies of embodied beings.

3.3.18 Strength, age, and the body are each considered to be of three kinds—superior, inferior, and middling. One should observe them according to these distinctions. 3.3.19 Diet and lifestyle, when practiced in due order over time and having become naturalized, are said to possess the characteristic of suitability (*sātmya*). Thus spoke the venerable Ātreya. Thus ends the third chapter in the Vimāna-sthāna of the Bheḷa-saṃhitā. The Fourth Chapter: Now, therefore, we shall explain the determination of the nature of diseases (*rogaprakṛtiviniścaya*). Thus spoke the venerable Ātreya.
3.3.19 3.4.1 Having examined by touch, having observed, and having questioned, the physician should investigate the patient; first comes the diagnosis of the disease, and thereafter the treatment.

3.4.2 Having observed the complexion, the shadow, and the bodily build of the patient both before and after the onset of disease, the physician should examine whether they are natural (*prākṛta*) or morbid (*vaikṛta*). 3.4.3 By observing the equilibrium or imbalance of fever, and whether the body is smooth or rough, one should indeed ascertain coldness or heat by means of the hand through touch.
The conduct of the mother and father, the cravings of the fetus, the transformation [of the embryo] over time due to disease, and the discoloration of the feces and urine.

3.4.5 One should understand the premonitory signs, the origin [of the disease], the strength of the body's digestive fire (*agni*), age, constitution (*prakṛti*), the place of birth, and appropriate diet.

3.4.6 One should also recognize physical exercise, habitual practices, suitability (*sātmya*), and the proper and improper quantities of food; furthermore, one should understand whatever else has been mentioned in response to questions that pertains to the same category.
3.4.6–7 Some sages maintain that there is one additional fault here: because the transformation is indistinguishable [from the original], that cause is undesirable. 3.4.7
3.4.8 A man who cannot tolerate dryness is known as having a *vāta* constitution; one who resembles water is of *pitta*, while one who cannot tolerate sweet and sour tastes is due to *kapha*.

3.4.9 For this [constitution] arises from one's own nature (*svabhāva*), being a quality acquired simultaneously with birth; one should understand it as *prakṛti*, and I shall describe its characteristics.
The unmanifest, the Great One (mahat), and the five gross elements— these seven are the primary natures (prakṛtis), as well as inherent nature (svabhāva) and time (kāla).
3.4.11 From them the elements arise, and into them they return; likewise do the sense organs, the objects of the senses, and the five types of cognition.
3.4.12 When a woman, during her fertile period, consumes dry foods, or when she suffers from upward-moving wind (udāvarta), or likewise performs excessive physical exertion here;
Then, when blood vitiated by wind (vāta) situated in the uterus comes into contact with semen of a similar nature,
[the following occurs].

3.4.14 At that time, by means of semen and blood vitiated by Vāta, the embryo indeed first attains a Vāta constitution prior to its own [actual] self. 3.4.15 In this very way, for a woman who engages in intercourse during her fertile period when her [semen and blood] are dominated by Kapha or Pitta, a Ślaiṣmikī (Kapha-type) or Paittikī (Pitta-type) constitution is likewise produced.
Short, quick-tempered, emaciated, and minute; a chatterer, fond of harshness, with stiff limbs and uneven joints; he finds his stability in a group within a group.
3.4.17 One who endures hardship with confidence, is rough-skinned, unstable, has a harsh head, hair, body hair, and limbs, and is quick to grasp—

such a person is known as having a *vāta* constitution. 3.4.18 Furthermore, he who in dreams arrives on a camel or travels through the sky, and whose body feels excessively oily, is a man of *vāta* constitution.

One with flaccid limbs, a foul odor, a violent temperament, haste, and a great appetite; one with wrinkles, gray hair, and baldness; one whose digestion is slow and who is likewise lacking in fortitude.

3.4.20 One of bilious temperament (paittika-prakṛti) has round eyes, is prone to anger, is weak, and has weak senses. He does not relish sour food, eats cold things, has poor offspring, and is fond of coolness. 3.4.21 A man of bilious temperament is of excellent complexion, possesses great intelligence, and likewise sees fire in his dreams; he breathes rapidly and feels refreshed immediately after bathing.
He is very affectionate, with smooth and well-knit limbs; he is fortunate, pleasing to behold, possessed of firm memory, capable of long-term retention, and devoted to steadfast faith.
3.4.23 He is fond of meat, heat, and pungent flavors; he is devoted to women, generous, patient, strong, fortunate, desirous of coolness, and fond of food.
3.4.24 He is known to suffer from chronic and severe diseases; he speaks sparingly, eats little, is far-sighted, possesses great energy, is steadfast, and likewise endures hardships.

He who dreams that he has bathed and that his body, with its hair, teeth, and nails, remains firmly bound and thick with hair, and that he subsequently smells water for a long time, [sees an ill omen].

3.4.26 But the man who endures dryness is of the *śleṣman* (phlegm) constitution; one should recognize a mixed constitution by means of mixed characteristics. 3.4.27 A constitution that has ceased [its dominance] is auspicious; that which is dual-natured is middling; but that which consists of the combination of all three (*sannipāta*) is proclaimed as the lowest. Thus spoke the venerable Ātreya. Thus ends the fourth chapter in the Bheḷa [Saṃhitā]. The Fifth Chapter. Now, therefore, we shall explain the chapter on the symptoms of the diseased; thus said the venerable Ātreya.
One man has a severe illness, both in terms of his physical form and his strength; another man has a mild illness, yet he is not endowed with [the same] degree of courage and other such qualities.

3.5.2 A physician becomes bewildered when a disease appears as heavy as a mountain; for such heavy patients, even a small dose of medicine administered may not burn away all the humors (doṣas) due to its limited potency. Consequently, fainting, vomiting, stiffness, yawning, and heaviness of the limbs occur.
3.5.3 [The medicine] does not completely incinerate all the humors because of its slight brilliance. Fainting, vomiting, rigidity, yawning, and heaviness of the body result.
For him, however, these conditions arise: thirst and a state of constant exhaustion. Mustā, kuṣṭha, the two types of haridrā, pragraha, ativiṣā, and amaya [are the remedies].
3.5.5 One should administer an asthāpana enema using bhallātaka, vayasthā, citraka, and suradāru, combined with cow’s urine.

3.5.6 By this, one brings about the pacification of both those [fevers] for which specific treatments have been prescribed and those for which they have not; as well as āragvadha, saptaparṇa, madana, and svādukaṇṭaka.

The physician should prepare an *āsthāpana* (non-unctuous enema) for the purpose of *āragvadha*, using *śārṅgeṣṭā*, *kaṭukā*, *pāṭhā*, *naktamāla*, and *vatsaka*. The Sixth Chapter. Now, therefore, we shall expound upon the *ṛtuvimāna* (the specific determination of seasons); thus said the venerable Ātreya.

3.6.1 Due to the specific movements of the sun and the revolution of the seasons, the bodily constituents (*dhātavaḥ*) of human beings undergo decrease and increase according to their respective natures.
3.6.2 [This occurs] from drinking newly fallen water that is corrupted by the vapors of the earth, by easterly winds, by contact with thick shadows, and by the turbidity of the ground.

Due to the effects of the summer season and the state of emaciation, when the vital breaths have become weak, the digestive fire of embodied beings reaches a state of mildness during the rainy season.
3.6.4 Thereafter, because the obstructing wind (*viṣṭambha-jīvāyu*) becomes aggravated by [certain factors], one should not consume pungent, sour, or salty tastes during the rainy season.
3.6.5 One should eat aged *śāli* and *ṣaṣṭika* rice with mung bean soup; alternatively, barley and wheat are considered beneficial when wind is active.
One should consume patola, buttermilk, light meat broths of wild animals, water from wells or rainwater, prepared decoctions, and non-unctuous enemas (āsthāpana). 3.6.5–3.6.6.

3.6.7 Because it has not settled, water ripens into acid during the rainy season; therefore, pitta increases, just as it does from acidic foods and drinks. 3.6.8 Due to the heat of the sun and because the pitta produced by medicinal plants has suddenly vanished, the pitta accumulated during the rains becomes aggravated in autumn.
Therefore, in the autumn, one should perform bathing and the application of unguents while they are cool; one should fan oneself with palm-leaf fans and plunge into lakes.
3.6.10 One should also drink parched grain flour (lāja-saktu) with water mixed with sugar and honey, and one should eat aged śāli and ṣaṣṭika rice with mung bean soup.
3.6.11 One should also consume sweet meat juices from wild animals prepared with ghee, as well as the juice of vidārī and sugarcane, grapes, and other similar substances.
3.6.11–12 When the force of the pitta has subsided, one should drink ghee during the autumn season; thus his body is nourished and the remaining doshas are expelled downward. 3.6.12

3.6.13 Because the northwest wind is dry and because the season is likewise cold, the bodily constituents (dhātus) of men attain a state of roughness due to the winter. 3.6.14 Therefore, one should resort to various kinds of unctuous substances and bathing with warm water; thus, through massage, the roughness and harshness are pacified.
3.6.14–15 One should consume aquatic birds, fish, and meat from marshy regions, along with fats, sours, and salts, as well as other items of a similar nature.
3.6.16 The final wind (apāna) is indeed pungent, and water possesses intense coldness. If one eats dry food, the wind excessively dries out the body.
3.6.17 One should wear heavy garments and resort to the sun and fire; for when the body is parched, the strength of a living being is drawn away from it by the heat.
In the winter season, water indeed becomes cold and sweet; therefore, *kapha* is accumulated by means of those [waters] as well as by unctuous foods. 3.6.18
3.6.19 Because the season is also cool, [the phlegm] is not yet broken down; therefore, one should drink *vāruṇī* wine mixed with oil and molasses during the cold season.
3.6.20 And one should eat various kinds of meat in their different forms; for in this way, the accumulated phlegm of embodied beings is dissolved here by the coldness [of the season].
Being touched by the heat of the sun in spring, it attains a state of fluidity; for in spring, the sun reaches the meridian point.
As if the mountains were being consumed by fire, it becomes provoked within the limbs of men; thereafter, the phlegm, having become liquefied, spreads over the heart.

3.6.23 Therefore, vomiting and indigestion are observed at the end of the cold season; for that reason, honey and *mārdvīka* wine are prescribed in spring to subdue *śleṣman*. Thus ends the sixth chapter in the *Bhela-saṃhitā*. With this, the Section on Specific Determination (*Vimānasthāna*) is completed. The Section on the Body (*Śārīrasthāna*). Second Chapter. [The fetus] remains [in the womb]. In the tenth month after birth, once the name and lineage have been honored, [the child is born]. In a young boy whose bodily constituents (*dhātus*) are increasing, semen is not produced until the bones and marrow are fully developed. 3.6.23

4.2.3 When the limbs and sub-limbs have fully developed and the bodily constituents (*dhātu*) have reached their respective roots, semen becomes clearly manifest in the sixteenth year. 4.2.4 Likewise, in an aged person whose bodily constituents have been depleted, the faculties of discernment (*viveka*) no longer function as they did before, due to that depletion.
Thereafter, the man becomes one whose semen is diminished, or he is poorly digested and weak; due to the depletion of all the bodily constituents (*dhātu*), he no longer perceives white [objects].
4.2.6 Blood, flesh, fat, bones, marrow, semen, as well as fire, feces, and urine— one should know that by these [elements],

the embryo is weak beyond the ninety days. 4.2.7 In this world, a woman who is afflicted by wind (*vāta*) or by a defect of the womb (*yonidoṣa*), or one who does not conceive due to food, is not truly barren, nor is she a non-woman.

4.2.7–8 Emesis, purgation, as well as enemas— both unctuous and non-unctuous— should therefore be administered to women; for it is well known that they give birth [only] after these have been performed.

4.2.9 Now, in this regard, there arises a question: Why does one not perceive sound through the nose, nor smell through the mouth, even though space (*kha*) is equally present everywhere? 4.2.10 And why does one not perceive taste through the other [senses], since the portion of the skin (*tvag-bhāga*) is the same for all? Having heard those words, Punarvasu replied:

The sense of smell and its object, odor, belong to the earth; the eye and its object, form, are fiery (taijasa); touch and the organ of touch belong to air; and likewise, the ear and its object, sound, consist of space.

4.2.12 And because the tongue consists of water (the watery element), the sense of taste is likewise composed of water; therefore, by these respective senses, the apprehension of their corresponding objects is traditionally taught through their shared affinity.

4.2.13 For each constituent element (*dhātu*), conjoined with the self (*ātman*), perceives its own respective object. Know this to be due to the connection between the self, the senses, the mind, and the objects. Thus spoke the venerable Ātreya. Thus ends the second chapter of the Bheḷa Saṃhitā. The Third Chapter: Now, therefore, we shall expound the anatomical treatise (*śārīra*) concerning those of different lineages (*asamānagotrīya*). Thus said the venerable Ātreya.
4.2.13–4.3.1 Here, one should approach a woman who is not of the same lineage when she has bathed after her menses; in this way, she gives birth to a son who is wise and free from disease.

4.3.2 Just as grain does not grow properly due to defects in the seed, so too the embryo perishes through the defect of the mother and father. 4.3.3 Therefore, at the proper time [of the fertile period], the husband and wife, consuming wholesome food and nourishment, should engage in union in private, while keeping the All-pervading Lord in mind.

the menstrual discharges may become abnormal even in the absence of pregnancy due to the consumption of unwholesome tastes, from the suppression of natural urges, or again, through a disorder of the female reproductive tract.

4.3.5 When the female reproductive tract (*yoni*) is afflicted by the *doṣas*, the embryo does not take root. This is likewise the case in an external tract (*bāhyayoni*), or one that is constantly discharging (*nirvāhiṇī*). 4.3.6 Furthermore, in whichever tract the wind (*vāyu*) seizes the semen once it has entered, a woman who possesses pure menstrual flow (*śuddhārtava*) will bear an embryo.
When that [embryo] falls away, then the fetus perishes; that indeed is *vātodara* for the woman. Therefore, one should avoid [sexual intercourse] during the [periods of] *ṛtu*.

4.3.8 When the semen (*śukla*) is in excess, a male is born; when the blood (*śoṇita*) is in excess, a female; when the two are equal, a neuter (*napuṃsaka*). Therefore, one should cause the semen to increase.
4.3.9 But when the powerful wind (*vāyu*) divides that *kalala* into two, then twins are produced. This is according to the word of Kṛṣṇa Ātreya.
In that regard, if the white portion predominates, it is a male; if the red portion predominates, it is a female. By this very same method, one should also determine [the gender] among twins.
4.3.11 Furthermore, the wind (vāyu) is powerful within the bodies of horses and boars; having pierced the embryo there, it causes the birth of many offspring.
4.3.12 And when the embryo does not obtain nourishment (rasa) due to the vitiated openings of the vessels, it remains for years like a snake dwelling in an incomplete state.

4.3.12–13 When the fetus has been nourished by the vital essence (*rasa*) and its limbs are fully developed, it is then born at the proper time, emerging from the mother's womb into the open air. 4.3.13
4.3.14 Those twenty disorders of the female reproductive tract (*yonidoṣa*) which have been described by physicians, as well as these and many others, cause the destruction of the fetus in a woman.
4.3.15 Therefore, one should treat these disorders with the desire for a son; indeed, through proper application, there will be purity resembling the fetus of an elephant or a horse.
For when conjoined with wind, space, and the seasons, among the other deities, Jātavedas, having been born within, becomes capable of manifesting his power. (4.3.16)
4.3.17 When, during the fertile period, a woman and a man approach in private with serene minds, then the embryo that is formed is characterized by *sattva*.
4.3.18 When, during the fertile period, a woman and a man approach with extremely agitated minds, then the embryo that is formed is characterized by *rajas*.
When, during the fertile period, a woman and a man approach in private with depressed minds, then a *garbha* (embryo) characterized by *tamas* comes into being.

4.3.20 “The characteristics and the origins—this has been declared as the means by which one should recognize the three types of birth-places of beings, as well as those that are mixed. Thus spoke the Blessed Ātreya. Thus ends the third chapter in the *Śārīra* section of the *Bhela Saṃhitā*. Chapter Four. Now, therefore, we shall expound the *Śārīra* [section] on the accumulation of the person (*puruṣanicaya*). Thus said the Blessed Ātreya. 4.3.20

4.4.1 Indeed, O noble one, this person here arises from *rasa*. His diseases are born of *rasa*. For instance, this person is born of *rasa*, lives by *rasa*, is inflamed by *rasa*, finds his fulfillment in *rasa*, and is sustained by *rasa*. Through the improper use or the wrong use of *rasas*, he incurs their disorders. No one becomes healthy through wrong use, nor through eating undigested or unwholesome food.

4.4.2 Now, a question arises here: who indeed digests food in this body—is it *vāta*, *pitta*, *śleṣman*, or the after-drink (*anupāna*)?
