No, said the venerable Punarvasu Ātreya; for if these were the causes of digestion, then no one here would have a weak digestive fire, since *vāta* and the others would be constantly present, along with the after-drinks. Rather, its heat (*ūṣman*) and fiery essence (*tejas*), residing within the body, digest the food. One should know that these constitute the bodily fire (*kāyāgni*). 4.4.2

4.4.3 Thereupon Bhela said this to Ātreya: "O Blessed One, it is taught that there are five types of bodily cavities (śārīra), distinguished as the ālocaka, rājaka, bhrājaka, sādhaka, and pāvaka. How does this distinction come about for these five designations?"

4.4.4 On this matter, the venerable Ātreya said: Among these, that which is called the "discerning" (*ālocaka*) increases with rain, cold, and heat. It is of two kinds: specific to the eye (*cakṣurvaiśeṣika*) and specific to the intellect (*buddhivaiśeṣika*). That which is called specific to the eye is as follows: having produced the knowledge arising from the contact of the self and the mind, and having fixed the mind upon the mind, it produces a specific visual capacity (*vaiśeṣya*) through the eyes for the sake of perceiving the forms, structures, colors, and sounds of the four classes of beings—those born of moisture, those born of eggs, those born of sprouts, and those born from a womb—including the high and low qualities of flowers, fruits, and leaves. This occurs whether one, two, three, or all of them simultaneously have prostrated themselves [before him]. This is the [specific visual capacity].
4.4.4. The Four Noble Truths: Suffering, its Origin, its Cessation, and the Path.

4.4.5 That which is called *buddhivaiśeṣika* (the specialized faculty of the intellect) is situated in the *śṛṅgāṭaka* (triangular junction) between the eyebrows; it perceives through knowledge extremely subtle objects pertaining to the inner self (*adhyātman*). It reveals the object of knowledge (*jñeya*) and knowledge itself for the sake of the absolute isolation (*kaivalya*) regarding all knowable things. Therefore, having known the object of knowledge through knowledge, one grasps that knowledge. One retains what has been grasped. One reviews what has been retained, remembers what is past, and having attended to the present, desires the future. Furthermore, immediately upon birth, even without being instructed, one craves the mother’s milk. And through application to meditation (*dhyāna*) and withdrawal of the senses (*pratyāhāra*), one produces this excellence of the intellect.

Among these, that which is called *bhrājaka* (the illuminator) is that which brings about the body and its characteristics, demonstrates preeminence, and produces specific manifestations and growths of the head, hands, feet, sides, back, belly, shanks, mouth, nails, eyes, and hair; it is called *bhrājaka* because it causes them to shine (*bhrājayati*).

4.4.7 Due to the predominance of the senses through its sovereign power, or by means of the ego-sense (*ahaṃkāra*) in the state of the intellect (*buddhi*), it projects a desired object from among all objects; that is, it produces passion for one another among all objects of the senses—sight, hearing, smell, taste, touch, speech, hands, feet, anus, and genitals—which are colored by their own inherent natures. Furthermore, having entered the internal seat of bile (*pitta-sthāna*) within the body, it generates passion; thus it is called *rājaka*.

4.4.8 *Sādhaka*: One who, for the sake of the highest good (*viśreyasa*) regarding sounds, touches, smells, objects of desire, and the purposes of gods, ancestors, and seers—both in this world and the next—attains all things and accomplishes them through his own skillful means is called a *sādhaka*. 4.4.9 *Pācaka*: One who digests the various kinds of food—eaten, drunk, licked, and chewed—once their vitality has been extracted, is called a *pācaka*. He who fills and delights the fire of his own desire is [also so called].

And there are verses on this point: That which quickly consumes the food of all embodied beings, having its origin in the downward-moving wind (*apāna*) and alcohol, is declared to be the bodily fire (*kāyāgni*).

4.4.11 The eternal [self] of the living being here is conjoined with that which is characterized by radiance. One should know that the lunar orb (somamaṇḍala) is situated in the center of the body’s navel.
4.4.12 One should know that the solar orb (sūryamaṇḍala) resides within the center of the lunar orb; and like a lamp, the fire (hutāśana) is in its center for human beings.
Just as the sun, stationed in the sky, endowed with splendor and possessed of rays, [digests] the food eaten by an embodied being prepared with various condiments;

4.4.14 Just as [the sun] dries up all the pools and waters, so too does the digestive fire (*jāṭhara*), situated at the navel, clearly [dry up] what has been consumed by embodied beings. 4.4.15 Just as the sun-stone (*sūryakānta*) quickly draws [heat] with its rays, so too does it quickly and thoroughly burn cow dung and wood.
Among beings with large bodies, [the size] is the measure of a barley grain; among beings with small bodies, it is the measure of a minute particle.

4.4.17 Only the vital air (vāyu) remains within worms, insects, and moths; he who can treat that [air] as it perishes, as well as the diseases of embodied beings, is truly a physician of the body through his application of Āyurveda. 4.4.18 He indeed treats the body by means of his mastery of Āyurveda, [addressing] the lymph-chyle (rasa), blood, fat, and even flesh.
When one abstains from food for a long time, he devours all these [beings]; the entire world, both stationary and moving, consists of the nature of Agni and Soma.
4.4.20 All embodied beings consist of Agni and Soma and are of four kinds; all [the elements] are solar, as well as lunar, and likewise consist of Soma.
4.4.21 Therefore, during a great fast, the digestive fire (*jāṭhara-pāvaka*), which is born from water and accompanied by the vital winds (*pavana*), does not consume the intestines of living beings.

4.4.21–22 Just as a lamp, filled with fuel, blazes within the chamber of men when there is water present, so too does sorrow, having taken hold of the treasury of the Ikṣvākus, shine forth while they remain steadfast.

4.4.23 Just as a fire situated in still water remains steady, but not so when the water is moving; likewise, the digestive fire (*agni*) of embodied beings repeatedly attains a state of imbalance (*vaiṣamya*) when the abdominal cavity is repeatedly filled by morbid humors (*vaikṛta*). 4.4.24 That fire must indeed be protected with effort, for its failure is seen to result in harm. It may cause vomiting, diarrhea, or it may lead to various other disorders.

He who dies in this manner has not reached his proper time; for the lifespan of a human being is one hundred years, and one should strive to attain that by following a regimen of light, wholesome food suited to one's digestion.

4.4.26. Regarding this, it is asked: why is it that one suffering from *alasaka* (intestinal obstruction) or *viṣūcikā* (cholera-like gastroenteritis) sometimes becomes free of disease immediately, while another dies instantly? To this, it is said: in the case of a person who is dry (*rūkṣa*), the *vāta*, *pitta*, and *śleṣman* are compressed by overeating; they do not move in their natural downward or upward courses, and being thus provoked, the patient dies immediately. In the case of a person who is unctuous (*snigdha*), the *vāta* and other humors, though compressed by overeating, move in their natural downward or upward courses and discharge themselves toward their respective locations in the body; therefore, by means of them, the patient becomes free of disease immediately.
4.4.26: *ṣaṣṭhyā ākrośe* (The sixth case-affix is used after a word in composition with a word expressing abuse).

4.4.27 Now, what are the ten internal cavities (*antarguhā*) and the ten external qualities (*bahirguṇā*)? They are as follows: the two eyes, the two nostrils, the two ears, the throat, the vessels of the anus, the penis, and the channels of the vital air (*vāyu-srotas*)—these are the ten internal cavities. There are ten arteries (*dhamanī*) attached to the heart. Having proceeded a distance of four finger-breadths from their origin, they become twenty. Thus, these ten arteries become sixty. In this regard, there are three hundred thousand and sixty network-joints (*jāla*) of veins (*sirā*). Just as a tree covered with branches descends everywhere with its fruits and leaves, or as a hide is stretched out with stones [to dry], so too is this [body] spread over with veins. Indeed, at every single pore (*romakūpa*), there is an opening of a vein, through which sweat flows out.

4.4.27–28. Regarding this, it is asked: "Why does this person not suffer from epilepsy continuously? To this it is replied: Just as aquatic creatures appear when rivers appear, or laugh when there is laughter, whenever they encounter the force of the *rasa*, then and there they cause the fit of epilepsy (*apasmāra*). Therefore, they suffer from epilepsy every two days, three days, a fortnight, or at intervals of a month.

4.4.29 Some say that [the patient] is afflicted by a *rakṣas* (demon), but that is incorrect. For if it were so, one would see wounds or other such marks on the person's body; yet this is not the case. If it is argued that he is possessed by a *vetāla*, that too is untenable, for their minds are fixed upon meritorious things (*puṇya*). And even if such a thing were to happen occasionally, therefore that very [condition] should be taught as being afflicted by *rasa* (poison/humor). If it is argued that it is exactly thus, then at the time of the discernment of *rasa*, both the third-day and fourth-day fevers (*tṛtīyaka-caturthaka*) are also seen. Is there no purpose here for [mentioning] these?
4.4.29. *ṣaṣṭhyā ākrośe* (The sixth case-affix is used after a word in the sense of a name of reproach).

4.4.30 Here it is asked: what indeed arises first in this embryo—the hands, the feet, or the anus? Baḍiśa says it is the hands and feet, because the body is established upon them. Śaunaka says it is the anus, because the vital air (vāyu) depends upon it. Khaṇḍakāpya says it is the navel, because the channels (nāḍī) are established there. Parāśara says it is the heart, because it is the root of those things rooted in consciousness. Bharadvāja says it is the head, because the body is rooted in that. Kāśyapa says it is the eyes. "No," said the venerable Punarvasu Ātreya. "Therefore, the *arbuda* (the fetal mass) itself arises first for him. All parts of the body arise therein, having originated from the fat (*sneha*) of the *arbuda*."

4.4.30–31. Here it is asked: Does the embryo, while staying within its mother’s womb, eat or not? To this it is said: It does not eat. For if it were to eat, there would be feces in it from past times, yet such is not the case. How then? A channel is established at the navel; another [channel] from it rests upon the mother’s heart. By means of that, the essence of the mother’s food is conveyed, which nourishes and causes the embryo to grow. Just as small irrigation channels, reaching a field, nourish it, so it is in this case. 4.4.31.

4.4.32. Regarding this, it is asked: "How does the embryo remain in the mother's womb? Śaunaka says, "Upright. Bharadvāja says, "With its head downward. No, says the venerable Punarvasu Ātreya: "If it were to remain upright, it would be a killer of the mother; if it were with its head downward, it would be a killer of itself. How then? It lies crosswise, with all its major and minor limbs bent. [The intended meaning of this passage is not clear from the context. Therefore, Punarvasu Ātreya maintains that its head is what is reached first. For that [head] is the heaviest part of it. Now, indeed, the kidneys and the fat, being heavy, mutually increase one another as they grow.

4.4.32–33. On this point there is a verse: "The heat situated in the *rasa* (nutritive fluid) within this body remains, having grasped the life-force (*jīvana*). Since the person (*puruṣa*) arises from the *rasa*, the *rasa* is called the life-force. Thus spoke the venerable Ātreya. Thus ends the fourth chapter on the body in the Bheḷa [Saṃhitā]. Fifth Chapter. Now, therefore, we shall explain the accumulation of the body (*śarīranicaya*). Thus said the venerable Ātreya. 4.4.33.

4.5.1 In this world, indeed, heat (*tejas*) and body (*śarīra*) exist eternally. There are twelve locations for these two; namely: skin, blood, flesh, fat, bone, marrow, semen, sweat, bile, phlegm, urine, and feces. When these are undisturbed, they are called "well-being. However, when disturbed, the wind (*vāta*), bile (*pitta*), and phlegm (*śleṣman*), being corrupted, produce disorders within the [tastes such as] *rasa* and the rest.

4.5.2 Now, there are four modes of birth (*yoni*). They are as follows: viviparous (*jarāyuja*), oviparous (*aṇḍaja*), soil-born (*udbhijja*), and sweat-born (*svedaja*). Among these, the viviparous are those born from a womb (*jarāyu*), such as cattle, wild animals, humans, and so forth. The oviparous include birds, fish, tortoises, snakes, and the like. The sweat-born include lice, bugs, moths, venomous insects, flies, and so forth. The soil-born, however, consist of grasses, creepers, trees, and forest giants. 4.5.2

4.5.3 Therein, trees possess flowers and fruits; forest giants (*vanaspati*) possess neither flowers nor fruits; creepers (*bīrudh*) possess both flowers and fruits, as well as being flowerless and fruitless; and climbing plants (*latā*) and medicinal herbs (*oṣadhi*) are characterized by the ripening of their fruits. Among these, those with white milky sap are Soma-related; those with red milky sap are Kadrū-related, Vāruṇa-related, or Vāligraha-related. 4.5.3

4.5.4 In this regard, during these three ten-night periods, the male is joined with the *rasa*. When the *rasas* reach the four types of *yoni* properly at the time of the menstrual period (*ṛtukāla*), then the embryo remains unaltered; in the opposite case, there is a deformity.

4.5.5 One should indeed avoid [intercourse during] the first three days of old blood. And what is that "old" [blood]? That which flows for the first three days during the period of menstruation is "old. During those three days, by the onset of conception, the embryo does not remain; or even if it remains, it is not capable of longevity. But when the three days have passed and the old blood has ceased, for a woman who has bathed after purification, on the fourth, sixth, eighth, tenth, and twelfth days, the embryo entering [the womb] becomes male. On the fifth, seventh, ninth, and eleventh days, it is prepared for femininity. This entire movement [of the seed] occurs up to seven nights; beyond this, because the movement has been determined or due to its smallness, there is no further movement.

Indeed, the blood of women dries up their bodies; therefore, they do not see the *rajas*. However, when their bodily constituents (*dhātu*) become fully replenished, they discharge the water-like blood (*vivekajalalohita*) month by month. And that menstrual flow (*ārtava*), having returned to its place of entry, arrives again after a month. 4.5.6.

4.5.7 When that vitiated blood enters its [proper] channel, then *pradara* (menorrhagia) occurs in women. One should treat this condition, which dries up the body, with the same remedies used for *raktapitta* (hemorrhagic disorders).
4.5.8 In a pregnant woman, however, the nutrient essence (*rasa*) is transformed in three ways within the body: into the embryo, into breast milk, and into the [circulating] nutrient essence itself.
4.5.8. The section on the treatment of *vāta-roga* (wind disorders).

4.5.9 Now, indeed, O friends, while the woman is pregnant, the abdomen becomes elongated and remains situated within her middle. When a male is inside, it is thick at its base, well-formed, and without gaps. When both are inside, the abdomen becomes like a trough (*droṇī*). A female staying in the mother’s womb occupies the left side; a male, the right; and a neuter, the middle. When a female is inside, the left eye contracts; when a male, the right; and when a neuter, both contract. She first moves the left foot, first directs the left eye and eyebrow, and generally lies on her left side. Furthermore, when a female is inside, she generally experiences pregnancy-longings (*dauhṛda*) for things associated with women. One should know that in the opposite case, she carries a male.

4.5.9–4.5.10 Now, indeed, in this case, the body of the embryo is produced from six elements (*sthāna*). Namely: from the water-element, the air-element, the fire-element, the earth-element, the space-element, and the taste-element.
4.5.11 This person consists of six elements (*dhātu*). Furthermore, the elements are the five gross elements (*bhūta*) and Brahman as the unmanifest (*avyakta*).

4.5.12 Among these, that which is hard and solid—such as teeth, hair, body hair, nails, mouth, excrement, sinews, and bones, as well as the perception of odor, the nose, the aggregate [of the body], and heaviness—belongs to the earth element. That which is liquid, moist, or soft belongs to the water element (*audaka*).

Now, when two [persons] have come together, if the man first achieves his purpose and the woman afterwards, then a male is born here who resembles him in his major and minor limbs. But where the woman first accomplishes her purpose and the man afterwards, there a female is born who resembles her in her major and minor limbs.

4.5.14 Now, if a man and woman, during the period favorable for conception, consume foods that are parched or wind-increasing (*vātalā*), and suppress their natural urges, the embryo—having been discharged into the blood and other elements vitiated by *vāta*—becomes afflicted with stammering, deafness, nasal speech, or one of the various disorders of *vāta* and *pitta*. In the same way, when the parents engage in intercourse during the fertile period while consuming foods that increase *pitta* and *śleṣman*, the embryo comes into being vitiated by *pitta* and *śleṣman*.
4.5.15 Now, indeed, fourteen groups of sense-faculties enter the embryonic body: seven divine and seven human, which are sustained yet remain imperceptible.

4.5.16 Among them, the divine ones consist of the Brahma-deities, Varuṇas, Gandharvas, Piśācas, Asuras, Mahārājas, and Kāyas. We shall explain these. Therein, one who is endowed with truthfulness, straightforwardness, compassion, patience, self-restraint, and meditation, and who perceives the reality of the inner self—that one should be known as belonging to the Brahma-body.
One who possesses the acquisition of such conduct as this today—know that, O God, he is one whose body is joyful.

4.5.18 One who delights in sacrifice, possesses a passionate disposition, is fond of water, bathes for long periods, has reddish-brown eyes and reddish-brown hair— one should know him to be of the body of Varuṇa.

4.5.19 But he who is fond of dancing, singing, and instrumental music, is constantly engaged in the company of women, and delights in clean clothes, perfumes, garlands, and ointments— one should know him to be of the body of a Gandharva.

But one who is fond of pleasant drinks, meat, and fish, as well as beef, who is loathsome, who terrifies children, and who is excessively prone to sleep—one should know him as having the body of a *piśāca*.
4.5.21 One who first honors his elders but later becomes a hater, fierce, wrathful, and a divider of his kinsmen— one should know him as belonging to the *āsura* body.
4.5.22 But one who is steadfast, heroic, possessed of great enjoyments, great energy, and great sovereignty— one should know him as belonging to the *mahārāja* body.

But human beings, through passion, exist in their entirety—both accompanied by ignorance and alone—with respect to the individual perception, hearing, touch, tasting, and smelling of pleasure and pain. Endowed with these, a living being moves about, blinks, contracts, extends, and experiences that which is to be known.

4.5.24 When he undergoes dissolution, then finally—just as [it is said]: "The internal body goes back to the body itself"—the water goes to the body of water, the wind to the body of wind, the fire to the body of fire, the earth to the body of earth, and space to the body of space. Thus, according to the body, he resorts to the body of the sense-faculties.

4.5.25 And there is a verse on this point: "While the body indeed exists, one element governs another; the mind and the intellect of all beings are established in Brahman. Thus spoke the venerable Ātreya. Thus ends the fifth chapter in the *Śārīra* section of the *Bhela*. The Sixth Chapter. Now, therefore, we shall explain the *khaḍḍikā* [type of] descent of the embryo, as part of the *Śārīra* [section]. Thus said the venerable Ātreya. 4.5.25

4.6.1 "In this world, indeed, O sir, this embryo is born of the mother, born of the father, born of the self, born of suitability (*sātmya*), and born of the essence (*rasa*). Furthermore, there exists a transmigrating being (*sattva*)," so says Ātreya. "No," says Bharadvāja. "This embryo is not born of the mother, not born of the father, not born of the self, not born of suitability, and not born of the essence. Nor does a transmigrating being exist. For if the mother were to produce the son, then women who most intensely desire a son would produce a son by engaging in sexual intercourse, and those desiring a woman would produce a woman.

4.6.1 The Blessed One said: “Ānanda, when a noble disciple possesses four qualities, he is one who has entered the stream, become incapable of falling into states of misery, assured of rightness, and destined for full awakening. What are these four? Here, Ānanda, a noble disciple possesses confirmed confidence in the Buddha thus: ‘The Blessed One is an arahant, perfectly enlightened, accomplished in true knowledge and conduct, fortunate, knower of the worlds, unsurpassed leader of persons to be tamed, teacher of devas and humans, the Buddha, the Blessed One. He possesses confirmed confidence in the Dhamma thus: ‘The Dhamma is well-expounded by the Blessed One, directly visible, immediate, inviting one to come and see, applicable, to be personally realized by the wise. He possesses confirmed confidence in the Saṅgha thus: ‘The Saṅgha of the Blessed One’s disciples is practicing the good way, practicing the straight way, practicing the true way, practicing the proper way; that is, the four pairs of persons, the eight types of individuals—this is the Saṅgha of the Blessed One’s disciples, worthy of gifts, worthy of hospitality, worthy of offerings, worthy of reverential salutation, the unsurpassed field of merit for the world. And he possesses the virtues dear to the noble ones—unbroken, untorn, unblemished, unmottled, freeing, praised by the wise, ungrasped, leading to concentration.”

4.6.2 When the subtle fire and wind enter the embryo along with the life-force (*jīva*), then these two transform the major and minor limbs and cause them to move; they cause them to grow. When those very two depart from the body, then it becomes devoid of wind and devoid of heat—a departed one, a dead one. To this, Bharadvāja says: "Even a dead creature is inflated by wind and dried up by fire. To this, the Blessed Ātreya says: "Or rather, the fire and wind sustain that [embryo] together with the life-force; when those two have departed, the external fire and wind enter [the body]."

4.6.2–3 Furthermore, as for the objection: "If there is indeed a plurality of elements (*bhūta-nānātva*), how could there be one? To this it is replied: That upon which this plurality depends is the unmanifest (*avyakta*), which consists of the collection of the five great elements (*pañca-mahābhūta-saṃgraha*).

4.6.4 As for what was further stated—that if everything were unmanifest (*avyakta*), there would be no modification (*vikāra*)—to this it is replied: The manifest modifications of this [body] are said to arise from the *rasa* (nutritive essence) and be produced by wind (*vāta*), bile (*pitta*), and phlegm (*śleṣman*). For if they are said to be unmanifest, how could those manifest [modifications] be emitted from the unmanifest? Furthermore, how then does that [unmanifest] undergo modification in the body, and how does insanity (*unmāda*) affect the unmanifest mind? This is untenable. Rather, just as the sun, though arisen, does not produce light when obscured by clouds, so too the mind, when the channels of consciousness are hidden by darkness (*tamas*), does not produce memory.

Furthermore, as for what was said—that if this embryo were to descend from the next world, nothing unobserved would be found therein—it is replied to this: first of all, here in this life, he does not remember various cognitions long since cast off, nor even things that were wondrous; how much less, then, could he remember other bodies that have existed in the past, which are distinct states of being?

4.6.6 On this point there is a verse: "That man who, permeated by *tamas*, does not remember [his past], would not remember his former conduct, just as a twice-born man learned in the Vedas remembers his own good deeds. Thus spoke the venerable Ātreya. This concludes the sixth chapter of the *Śārīra* section in the *Bhela Saṃhitā*. The Seventh Chapter: "Now, therefore, we shall expound the *Śārīra* concerning the enumeration of the body," so said the venerable Ātreya. 4.6.6

4.7.1 Indeed, in this body there are six layers of skin (*tvac*). The first is the water-bearing layer; the second is the blood-bearing layer; the third is the substratum for the origin of *sidhma* and *kilāsa*; the fourth is the substratum for the origin of *dadru* and *kuṣṭha*; the fifth is the substratum for the origin of *alajī* and *vidradhi*; but as for the sixth, when it is severed one suffers distress, as if entering into darkness, and it is upon this that malignant eruptions (*duṣṭāruṣka*) arise. 4.7.1

4.7.2 Counting the Bones—There are three hundred and sixty bones (*asthi*), as follows: thirty-two teeth; thirty-two sockets for the teeth (*dantolūkhalāni*); twenty nails (the bones of the fingers and toes of the hands and feet); sixty bones of the fingers and toes of the hands and feet; twenty phalanges of the hands and feet; four bases for the phalanges of the hands and feet; two bones of the heels (*pārṣṇi*); four ankle-bones (*gulpha*) in the feet; two wrist-bones (*maṇika*) in the hands; four bones of the forearms (*aratni*); two bones of the shanks (*jaṅghā*); two knees (*jānu*); two kneecaps (*jānukapālikā*); two thigh-bones (*ūrunala*); two shoulders (*aṃsa*); two shoulder-blades (*aṃsaphalaka*); two collarbones (*akṣaka*); one clavicle (*jatru*); two palates (*tālunī*); two chins (*cibuka*); two hip-blades (*śroṇiphalaka*); one pubic bone (*bhagāsthi*); forty-five vertebrae in the back; fifteen in the neck (*grīvā*); fourteen in the chest (*uras*); twenty-four ribs (*parśukā*) in the sides, and an equal number of costal cartilages (*sthālaka*), and an equal number of costal tubercles (*sthālakārbudaka*); one jaw-bone (*hanvasthi*); two ligaments binding the jaw (*hanubandhana*); one [bone] consisting of the nose, the jaw-joint, the frontal bone (*lalāṭa*); and four cranial bones (*śīrṣakapāla*).

The heart is the single seat of consciousness. There are ten seats of the vital breaths (*prāṇa*), namely: the head, the throat, the heart, the rectum, the navel, the bladder, semen, milk, blood, and flesh.

4.7.4 The fifteen cavities (koṣṭha): namely—the navel, the heart, the kloman, the liver, the spleen, the two kidneys, the bladder, the receptacle for feces, the stomach, the upper rectum, the lower rectum, the small intestine, the large intestine, and the omentum.

4.7.5 There are fifty-six minor parts (*pratyaṅga*), namely: two ankles, two buttocks, two calves, two shanks, two thighs, two hips, one penis, two temples, two groins, two *kukundara* depressions, one bladder, one head, one abdomen, two breasts, two arms, two axillae, one chin, two lips, two gums, two corners of the mouth, one palate, one uvula, two ears, two ear-lobes, two cheeks, two eye-sockets, four eyelids, and two eyes.

4.7.5–4.7.6. The substances of the body: ten handfuls (*añjali*) of water remain in the body when the excreting feces have been eliminated through excessive discharge. Experts state that nine handfuls constitute the essence (*rasa*) derived from the transformation of the previous day’s food; eight handfuls are of blood; seven of feces; four of urine; two of fat; one of marrow; and one handful each for the brain and semen. 4.7.6

4.7.7 Now, a question arises here: by which [path] does this living soul (*jīva*) proceed from one body to another body? Regarding this, the venerable Ātreya said: Some describe its movement as being like that of a leech; that is not correct. In this world, even other incorporeal entities might exist simultaneously in different locations; others also maintain this view. In every case, for this seeker of liberation, this inner self proceeds toward the Supreme. In any event, when this [body] is abandoned, it would be a state of non-attainment until [the next] familiarity is reached. If it is claimed that this is due to its state of abiding, then the same would apply to *karma*, rendering it useless. However, one should know that having promised [to go], he departs for the next world. Or rather, just as the rays of the sun rest upon the earth within its heart, so too, one should observe his movement there as if lingering.
4.7.7. The section on the treatment of diseases of the head and neck.

4.7.8 Now, indeed, there are sixteen internal deities within the person (*puruṣa*). They are as follows: Fire, Earth, Water, Space, Wind, Lightning, Parjanya (the Rain-god), Indra, Gandharva, Death, Āditya (the Sun), the Moon, Tvaṣṭṛ, Viṣṇu, Prajāpati, and Brahmā. One should know them by their functions and by their origin and measure. For here, the function of Fire in the body is heat; that of Earth is the sense of smell; that of Water is moisture, taste, and cognition; that of Wind is touch; that of Space is hearing; that of Parjanya is the grasping of form; that of Lightning is the grasping of speed; that of Indra is strength; that of the Gandharvas is desire; that of Death is anger; that of Āditya is sight; that of the Moon is clarity; that of Tvaṣṭṛ is form; that of Viṣṇu is movement; that of Prajāpati is sexual union; and that of Brahmā is the intellect (*buddhi*).

4.7.8–4.7.9 There, a verse: “Sages of pure vision, through their asceticism, with their defilements stilled, behold all men in the world as they truly are. Thus spoke the Blessed Ātreya. Thus ends the seventh chapter in the *Śārīra* section of the *Bhela Saṃhitā*. **The Eighth Chapter** Now, therefore, we shall expound the *Śārīra* concerning the rules for birth (*jātisūtrīya*). Thus said the Blessed Ātreya. 4.7.9

4.8.1 Now, indeed, O sirs, those women who eat wholesome and light food, who do not habitually suffer from menstrual irregularities, who are free from defects, whose uterine cavities are as they should be, and whose channels are perfectly pure—they are called "fertile" by the experts. They give birth to offspring of desirable form and endowed with intelligence; in the opposite case, the result is the reverse.

4.8.2 And during the fertile period (*ṛtu*), the embryo takes its place. It is just as when seed is sown in a well-plowed field: there, rice is prepared for the state of rice, and barley for the state of barley. In the same way, the semen (*indriya*) released by a lover during the fertile period enters the womb (*garbhāśaya*) in the non-defiled female organ (*yoni*). Just as water caught in a whirlpool flows backward against the current, so too the semen and blood, once poured into the womb like milk, attain oneness with the *udumbara* (the embryo) and, being infused, achieve growth. It is like gold [cast] into many molds, which, having attained unity, reaches perfection.

4.8.2 The Blessed One said: “Monks, there are these four kinds of persons found existing in the world. What four? Here, monks, a certain person dwells contemplating the body in the body, ardent, clearly comprehending, and mindful, having removed covetousness and displeasure regarding the world. This, monks, is called the first kind of person found existing in the world. Furthermore, monks, a certain person dwells contemplating feelings in feelings... consciousness in consciousness... phenomena in phenomena, ardent, clearly comprehending, and mindful, having removed covetousness and displeasure regarding the world. This, monks, is called the fourth kind of person found existing in the world. These, monks, are the four kinds of persons found existing in the world. Thus spoke the Blessed One. Having thus spoken, the Well-Farer, the Teacher, further said this: “One who dwells contemplating the body in the body, Ardent, clearly comprehending, and mindful, Having removed covetousness and displeasure regarding the world— This is called a person by the Buddhas. “Furthermore, one who dwells contemplating feelings in feelings, Consciousness in consciousness, and phenomena in phenomena, Ardent, clearly comprehending, and mindful, Having removed covetousness and displeasure regarding the world— This is called a person by the Buddhas. Thus have I heard. At one time the Blessed One was dwelling at Sāvatthī in Jeta’s Grove, Anāthapiṇḍika’s Park. There the Blessed One addressed the monks: “Monks! “Venerable sir,” those monks replied to the Blessed One. The Blessed One said this: “Monks, there are these four foundations of mindfulness. What four? Here, monks, a monk dwells contemplating the body in the body, ardent, clearly comprehending, and mindful, having removed covetousness and displeasure regarding the world. He dwells contemplating feelings in feelings... consciousness in consciousness... phenomena in phenomena, ardent, clearly comprehending, and mindful, having removed covetousness and displeasure regarding the world. These, monks, are the four foundations of mindfulness. Thus spoke the Blessed One. Having thus spoken, the Well-Farer, the Teacher, further said this: “The body, feelings, consciousness, and phenomena— One should dwell contemplating these within themselves. Ardent, clearly comprehending, and mindful, One should transcend birth and old age.”

4.8.3 If she should desire, "May I give birth to a son who is auspicious and fair-complexioned," she should eat a gruel of barley mixed with ghee for seven nights, provided it remains uncontaminated. Then, being pregnant with longing (*dauhṛdinī*), she should cook milk-rice (*pāyasa*) in the milk of a white cow that has a calf of the same color and eat that very food. She should put on two white garments. She should have a decorated carriage made entirely white. She should show her a bull or a horse. In this way, she will give birth to a fair-complexioned son. "No," said Śaunaka, "for even from that, there may be a tawny complexion. Ātreya said: "What would be the harm? Those born of a tawny-limbed mother are long-lived and free from disease."

4.8.3. The Four Nutriments of Consciousness and Their Cessation What are the four nutriments of consciousness? They are: physical food as nutriment, gross or subtle; contact as the second; mental volition as the third; and consciousness as the fourth. And what is the cessation of these four nutriments of consciousness? It is the cessation of craving, its abandoning, its relinquishment, its release, and its non-arising. This is called the cessation of the four nutriments of consciousness. Furthermore, there is the nutriment of contact. What is the nutriment of contact? There are six classes of contact: eye-contact, ear-contact, nose-contact, tongue-contact, body-contact, and mind-contact. This is called the nutriment of contact. And what is the cessation of this nutriment of contact? It is the cessation of the six bases, its abandoning, its relinquishment, its release, and its non-arising. This is called the cessation of the nutriment of contact. Furthermore, there is the nutriment of mental volition. What is the nutriment of mental volition? There are six classes of mental volition: volition regarding forms, volition regarding sounds, volition regarding odors, volition regarding tastes, volition regarding tangibles, and volition regarding mental phenomena. This is called the nutriment of mental volition. And what is the cessation of this nutriment of mental volition? 4.8.4 If she should desire thus: "May I give birth to a dark-skinned son with red eyes," [or as far as: "In the second month, may I see the flower"], she should have a mash (mandam) prepared from these very same barley grains. For seven nights, she should eat unadulterated boiled rice of red *śāli* paddy mixed with the blood of a red cock. During her pregnancy longings (*dauhṛda*), she should wrap herself in a copper-colored cloth. She should provide a copper bed and seat, or she should show her a red bull or horse. In this way, she gives birth to a dark-skinned son with red eyes.

As long as she sees a flower [during her second menstrual period], one should know that the embryo does not remain; for at that time, those who are pregnant are said to be "without produced essence" (*ajātasārā*). However, if a woman’s womb has produced essence and yet the flower flows out, her embryo either falls away, or it remains for an excessive length of time with its limbs completely dried up.

4.8.6 When the fourth month has arrived, one should consume fresh butter (*navanīta*) with milk. In the fifth month, milk-gruel (*kṣīrayavāgū*); in the sixth, milk-ghee (*kṣīrasarpis*); in the seventh, curd-whey (*dadhyudaśvit*); in the eighth, milk-ghee; and when the ninth month has arrived, an oil enema (*anuvāsa*) should be administered using oil prepared with sweet medicinal herbs [and *kadamba*, *māṣa*, *erā*, *ghata*, and *eta*].
4.8.7 For thus, as this [woman] undergoes monthly transformation, her abdomen, hips, sides, and back become softened; digested feces pass downward, and she gives birth with ease.

4.8.8 But in the seventh month, indeed, the wind, bile, and phlegm—oppressed by the fetus—reach the chest and, being inflamed, produce itching. By that, eruptions (*kikkisāni*) arise on the women's bodies. One should grind the powder of the three myrobalans (*triphalā*) with rabbit blood and smear it upon those eruptions for her.
4.8.8–4.8.9 When the eighth month has indeed arrived, one should have a maternity chamber constructed with its door facing either east or north, using *tinduka*, *palāśa*, and *aśvattha* wood. 4.8.9

4.8.10 Now, in this case, there should be those things previously prepared: two couches made of *bilva* wood, two winnowing baskets, two mortars for rice, a pillow, rice-gruel, clarified butter, oil, and mustard seeds.

4.8.11 Now, when she is about to give birth, one should have her drink barley gruel (*yavāgū*). If the fetus has not yet descended, one should cause her to undergo both the *āvahana* (inducing) and *avahanana* (expelling) procedures. If she should perceive: "My womb has slipped down; the fetus has been released from my heart; my vagina has flowed open," then four attendants with trimmed nails, who provide for her livelihood, should wait upon her daily. [The physician should instruct: "First, let her push gently; afterwards, let her push more forcefully. And she must not, out of foolishness, suppress the onset of the labor pains; for by suppressing the onset of the pains, she brings suffering upon herself along with her son.
4.8.11. The section on the *kṣāra* (alkaline) treatments for hemorrhoids.

4.8.12 If, after she has given birth, the afterbirth (aparā) does not come away, one should have her drink a paste of red rice (*rakta-śālī*) the size of an *akṣa* fruit, prepared with sour gruel or urine. According to this same method, one should prepare a preparation from *dantī*, *dravantī*, *vṛścikālī*, *unarnavā*, and *vanaśīrṣaka*. Likewise, one should fumigate her with any one of the following: *talā*, *umā*, *kālasarpa*, or old *mālā*. If it still does not come away by this procedure, then one should administer an unctuous enema (*anuvāsana*) using the oil of sharp fruits (*tīkṣṇa-phala*). 4.8.12 5.1.0 "Either [the embryo] perishes as soon as it is born, or it dies.
5.1.0 "Certainty: low."
5.1.1 If the embryo is short on one side and broad, yet possesses a beautiful voice, it will live for one month and then perish.
5.1.2 If the head is globular, the jaw is long, and the eyebrows are thick and joined together, such an embryo dies when the second month has arrived.
5.1.2–3 When the signs of a newborn infant are visible within the embryo, such an embryo dies once the third month has arrived. 5.1.3

5.1.4 He who has three dimples (*trikakara*), a pot-shaped head (*ghaṭaśiras*), and a fetus that is well-formed but emits a harsh sound, meets his destruction when the fourth month arrives. 5.1.5 He for whom secondary sexual characteristics (*vyañjana*) appear at the age of sixteen is seen here to have a short lifespan, due to the rapid depletion of the five elements (*pañcadhātu*).
For that man of twenty years in whom the secondary sexual characteristics appear, he attains a long life; there is no doubt about this.

5.1.7 One should declare that child whose body wastes away, whose intellect declines, and who likewise lacks strength and appetite, to be one whose life has departed. 5.1.8 A man in whom goiters and skin eruptions appear at birth will be destroyed by them all once the twenty-eighth year has passed.
If a whirlpool-like mark is seen on the back or the chest accompanied by pain when the fortieth year has passed, it leads to death.

5.1.10 If a whirlpool-like mark is seen on the back, bent in three places, its fruit should be known as follows: she does not give birth to a child who can be established [in life]. 5.1.11 She whose hands have fingers that are neither too thick nor too thin, and whose nails are red; she whose minor limbs are auspicious in their proportions, and she who is exactly fifty years of age.
He who has a broad chest, long arms, and thick knees, and who has long fingers and long nails, lives for sixty years.
5.1.13 A man with a constricted voice, a prominent nose, and a face turned upward, possessing the *ūruka* and *bhadra* qualities, should be known as seventy years of age.
5.1.14 One who possesses the *bhadra* quality both in front and behind, is upright, and speaks kindly, should be known as eighty years of age, according to the words of Kṛṣṇa Ātreya.
He whose forehead, nose, and two ears are each six finger-breadths in measurement shall live for a hundred years.

5.1.16 That man whose head remains unbent and level with his knees, and whose ears reach above his knees, beholds his grandson. 5.1.17 He whose ears are large, broad, hairy, smooth, and thick with hair, attains a hundred years in this world.

"By means of righteousness, truthful speech, service to one's teacher, and the use of elixirs (*rasāyana*), he lives for a long time. Thus said the venerable Ātreya. Thus ends the first chapter in the *Indriya* section of the *Bhela*. Chapter Two:
5.1.18 [continued]

5.2.1 He whose face, eyes, body, as well as hands and feet, appear reddish, will indeed remain healthy. 5.2.2 In those men upon whose heads a powder resembling cow-dung is seen, and for whom intense itching arises when the head is being anointed with oil;
5.2.3 When the hair of an embodied being falls out with its roots withered, and when these symptoms appear, he will indeed become healthy.

5.2.4 His teeth do not chatter and his mouth does not become distorted; he does not speak incoherently either—he indeed shall be restored to health. 5.2.5 He does not toss his limbs about and his voice does not falter; he covers his private parts with his garment—he indeed shall be restored to health.
One whose navel is neither protruding nor depressed, who stands with his body properly aligned, who breathes easily at night— he indeed will be healthy.

5.2.7. His nails are not rough-appearing, nor discolored, nor lusterless; they are clear and possess a fine radiance—he indeed shall remain in good health. 5.2.8. He who, though situated in the sunlight, does not [appear] bright, and whose [eyes] are not reddish—[he is in danger]. [End of] the Third Chapter. 5.3.1. "This palanquin of mine is refined and fastened with lapis lazuli gems"—if one speaks thus in distress, they know him to be one whose life has departed. He does not survive that night if he dreams of such things while his health is impaired.
5.3.1–2 Even when a lamp is burning, he who perceives only darkness, and who would perceive sounds as if they were something unprecedented— he does not exist. 5.3.2

5.3.3 “I am hanging head-downwards; do not turn me over!”—if a man speaks thus, he will not survive beyond seven days. 5.3.4 He whose vital organs feel as if they are being torn apart, who suffers from frequent diarrhea, and who passes foul-smelling, corpse-like, and putrid excrement;
5.3.4–5.3.5 And if that [urine] has the smell of blood or the smell of fish, or if it is black, blue, or discolored, he is said to be one who is about to die. 5.3.5
5.3.6 The man who suffers from honey-like urine, fat-like urine, or ghee-like urine, and the person who passes excessive urine— he is indeed declared to be near death.
5.3.7 When a person urinates drop by drop with pain, his bladder having been ruptured by the wind (vāyu), his life is difficult to preserve.
For that patient lying on his bed from whom many worms emerge from the body, no medicine succeeds.

5.3.9 Having observed these signs of those about to die, a physician who desires to act according to the path [of medicine] should not apply treatment. Thus spoke the Blessed Ātreya. This concludes the third chapter on the sense organs in the Bheḷa-saṃhitā. Chapter Four: 5.4.1 When Vāyu, having seized the heart of the patient, remains there and completely obstructs the channels (dhamanīs), it shall cause him to lose his life instantly.
5.4.1–2 When the wind (vāyu) enters the body of a patient, and there is a discharge from the eyes while lying on the back, he shall immediately lose his life. 5.4.2

5.4.3 When the wind located in the abdominal cavity of a person whose blood and flesh are wasted turns inward, he shall immediately lose his life. 5.4.4 That patient in whom a *vātāṣṭhīlā* (a stone-like mass caused by wind) develops due to wind and does not move elsewhere, he immediately abandons his vital breaths.
He whose two temples are rigid, whose nose appears crooked, and whose eyes are rolled back, abandons his life-breaths immediately.

5.4.6 He in whom cutting pain arises from the stomach (āmāśaya), accompanied by thirst and intense passion, shall lose his life immediately. 5.4.7 He in whom cutting pain arises from the large intestine (pakvāśaya), accompanied by thirst and severe constriction of the throat, shall abandon his life immediately.
5.4.7–8. That embodied being from whose hair-pores blood flows excessively, or who has a hemorrhage from the mouth, shall immediately lose his life.

5.4.9 When the heart of an emaciated embodied being is afflicted by a mass of [pathological] humors, an excruciating pain arises; he instantly abandons his life-breaths. 5.4.10 When the wind (māruta) robs one whose body is wasted of consciousness and obstructs the great channel (mahāsrotas), he instantly abandons his life-breaths.

"The physician should examine the patient who has reached a state of morbid transformation of his constitution (*prakṛtivikṛti*), by means of these aforementioned signs, as well as other similar ones, when the heart of the embodied being is failing. Thus spoke the venerable Ātreya. Thus ends the fourth chapter on the sense organs (*indriya*) in the *Bhela*. **The Fifth Chapter** Now, therefore, we shall expound the chapter concerning the patient with darkened lips (*yasyaśyāvīya*). Thus said the venerable Ātreya. 5.4.11
5.5.1 If both of one's eyes appear dark-brown or greenish, and a disease of the head has arisen, his life has already borne its fruit [is at its end].
5.5.2 If one’s veins are greenish and the pores of the skin are reddish, and he eats foods that are sour, he perishes right there.
5.5.2–3: When the wind (vāta), provoked by anger, enters the stomach (āmāśaya) of a person and seizes the heart, his life has departed.

5.5.4 If one's blood dries up in the limbs, hands, and feet, and if one dances again and again, his life has departed. 5.5.5 If one's testicles, hands, and feet are dry, as is the mouth, and if the complexion becomes parched, his life has departed.
5.5.5–5.5.6: When the jaws, the hands, the feet, the testicles, and the penis of an embodied being are seen [to be protruding], his life has departed.
5.5.7 One whose heart burns should be declared to be on the verge of death; that patient has indeed departed, for his life has gone.
5.5.8 Epilepsy, consumption, leprosy, hemoptysis, abdominal dropsy, abdominal tumors, and diabetes—these are long-standing diseases.
If a long-term patient experiences a loss of strength and flesh, and a deterioration of the voice is observed, his life has departed.

5.5.10 If one’s heart burns, there is colic in the abdominal cavity, and loss of voice, and if one also frequently experiences a burning sensation, his life has departed. 5.5.11 If living beings experience terror and distress, and colic moves within the abdominal cavity, and if one is overcome by hiccup and vomiting, his life has departed.
A mortal who considers a barber to be a blazing fire, water to be fire, and the sun to be the moon— for him, life is difficult to attain. (5.5.12)
5.5.13 Furthermore, he who sees clouds on all sides in the cloudless sky, for him both fair weather and foul weather have passed; his life has departed.
5.5.14 He in whom the bodily fluids do not remain stable, nor the medicinal herbs and the sense faculties, or for whom these are perverted—he does not live.
If the fruit or root of a tree belonging to a person who has been touched by disease is not seen available for medicinal purposes, such a person does not survive.

5.5.16 Having observed these signs of those about to die, the physician should not apply medical treatment out of regard for his reputation. Thus spoke the venerable Ātreya. Thus ends the fifth chapter on the sense organs in the Bheḷa [Saṃhitā]. The sixth chapter: Now we shall explain the chapter on premonitory symptoms (pūrvarūpīya). Thus said the venerable Ātreya. 5.6.1 When the body is red within but appears pale on the outside, that is declared to be a premonitory symptom of a man about to die.
5.6.2 But when the body is red on the outside while appearing pale within, that man is said to have reached the precursor stage of death.

5.6.3 One who is emaciated within yet bloated without, or indeed bloated externally, as well as one who is excessively distended— all these have departed from life. 5.6.4 But he who is constantly feverish, who delights in windless places, and suffers from persistent catarrh, is quickly slain by dyspnea.
5.6.4–5 Whether making loud noises or engaging in incoherent chatter, and laughing excessively, a person emaciated by insanity meets their death.

5.6.6 The man who perceives his heart as solid, accompanied by pain and constant burning, and who becomes emaciated due to heart disease, approaches his end. 5.6.7 He who perspires excessively, suffers from itching, indulges in incompatible foods, and has a tendency toward non-evacuation perishes from leprosy (kuṣṭha).
Furthermore, that person who is delicate by nature, who indulges in fats and meat, and who sleeps excessively during the day, perishes as a sufferer of prameha. 5.6.8

5.6.9 A creature whose limbs are withered, whose skin is rough even when perspiring, and who sits down with his anus gaping, is killed by diarrhea. 5.6.10 That embodied being whose digestive fire and strength do not diminish, even though his blood and flesh are wasted away, is just like a corpse.
He whose head suddenly appears red or yellow, or is tawny with singed hair, is just like a corpse.
5.6.12 He whose eyes, forehead, face, nose, and eyebrows become distorted by the wind is just like a corpse.
5.6.13 He whose tongue appears dark, thorny, and parched, and whose eyes and nails are also dark, is just like a corpse.
The wise man should declare that person to be dead whose throat is ruptured, who faints, cries out loudly, and exhibits external convulsions.

5.6.15 When a new and severe disease arises in the upper part of the body of a man who is otherwise strong, it is difficult to treat; likewise, one should declare that such a person is about to die. 5.6.16 Furthermore, that man who has the odor of a muskrat, or who perceives even golden trees as such, perishes.

A wise man who desires his own well-being should not undertake [medical treatment] for one described by these and other such signs of morbid transformation (vikāra). Thus spoke the Blessed Ātreya. Thus ends the sixth chapter on the *Indriya* [section] in the Bheḷa-saṃhitā. **The Seventh Chapter** "Now, therefore, we shall explain the *Indriyāṇīka-indriya*," so said the Blessed Ātreya.
5.7.1 Listen to me as I explain how a physician, desiring to know the measure of a person’s lifespan, should specifically examine their sense organs.
5.7.2 One should examine them through food and drink, as well as by means of vision and other faculties; for the knowledge of the objects of the senses is beyond the reach of the senses themselves.
When the knowledge dependent upon the sense organs of one who is otherwise healthy becomes disordered without any apparent cause, that is indeed a sign of death.
5.7.4 Thus has the correct definition of the arising of inauspiciousness regarding the senses been stated. Listen again to that very same matter from me in further detail.
5.7.5 Seeing the sky as if it were solidified, or seeing the earth as if it were [the sky], one who perceives both of these in such a distorted manner meets with death.
For one who sees the wind moving in the sky, yet fire does not come forth even when kindled, for that person also one should predict destruction.
5.7.7 Even in clear water, a man perceives a net where there is no net; seeing [this] whether it remains still or moves, he is deprived of his life.
5.7.8 He who, while awake, sees ghosts, various kinds of *rakṣas* demons, or any other marvel whatsoever—such a person does not live.
That man who sees the fire as being of its natural color yet devoid of luster— whether it appears blue, black, or even white— that person does not live.
5.7.10 A man does not live if he sees rays in a cloudless sky, or clouds in a cloudless sky, or lightning without clouds.
5.7.11 Or if he sees the sun as if it were a clay vessel, or blackened with excrement, or like a half-moon, he perishes quickly.
5.7.11–12: Seeing the sun at night, the moon during the day, smoke rising from fire, or a lusterless fire at night, one should predict death.

5.7.13 Those who wish to destroy one's state of being perceive people as lacking luster or as lusterless due to their power; they see beings whose characteristics are distorted, and they perceive objects through their own diminished power. 5.7.14 Furthermore, due to the exhaustion of their lifespan, they perceive colors that have been clearly defined yet appear increased by incorrect numbers, and they see signs and forms that are ill-omened.
5.7.14–15 But he who sees the invisible, or he who does not see the visible— both of them go swiftly to the abode of Yama, without a doubt.

5.7.16 One who hears what is soundless, and one who does not perceive sound— both of these should be known by the wise as being like those already dead. 5.7.17 One who perceives odors in reverse order, or indeed does not perceive them at all from every side— he should be known as one whose life has departed.
5.7.17–18 Those who do not truly know the taste, or whether it is properly cooked or not— yet perceive what is uncooked as cooked— are called "skilled" by wise men.
5.7.19 Having touched objects that are hot, cold, rough, smooth, soft, or even harsh— whether they are tangible or otherwise— one who desires death perceives them as such.
5.7.20 Without intense austerity or disciplined yoga performed according to the rules, one who perceives objects through the senses beyond their proper measure meets with death.
No man whatsoever who perceives objects of the senses through the senses— apart from [perceiving] the faults born of food— without seeing the Self, does not live.

5.7.22 Those who, though otherwise healthy, repeatedly perceive distortions in the objects of the senses due to reversals of their wisdom—for them one should predict death. 5.7.23 And he who correctly perceives this very knowledge regarding both death and life—he is fit to be known as a physician. Thus spoke the Blessed Ātreya. Thus ends the seventh chapter on the Senses in the Bheḷa-saṃhitā. Chapter Eight: Now we shall explain the chapter on the Messenger (Dūta). Thus said the Blessed Ātreya.
When a messenger for a patient cuts grass or his own nails while inquiring after a physician, such a messenger is to be rejected. 5.8.1.

5.8.2 Furthermore, when a messenger speaks incoherently and yet inquires after the physician, such a messenger of the patient should be rejected. 5.8.3 When a messenger of the patient is breaking wood with wood, or clods of earth with clods of earth, or is walking on the ground [in a distracted manner], such a messenger should be rejected.
When a messenger touches his own limbs or those of children while inquiring after the physician, such a messenger of the patient should be rejected.

5.8.5 When a messenger covers his navel with his hand while inquiring after the physician, such a messenger of the patient is to be rejected. 5.8.6 When a messenger of the patient breaks a potsherd, a pebble, or even a charcoal ember, such a messenger is to be rejected.
When a messenger sits exhausted on the ground, or wanders about while clutching his own limbs, such a messenger belonging to the patient must be rejected.

5.8.8 The wise do not grieve for what is lost, dead, or gone beyond; indeed, when a messenger speaks thus regarding a patient, he should certainly be rejected. 5.8.9 When a messenger grasps his own hand with [the physician’s] hand, or strikes the hand with his hand, such a messenger regarding a patient must likewise be rejected.
If a messenger for a patient bites his lips or his tongue, or uses his teeth to bite his nails, he should be rejected as such.
5.8.11 When a physician has arrived at the house of a patient, yet that patient is being cut or pierced [by another], such a case is to be rejected.
5.8.12 When a messenger for a patient turns back after filling a water-pot and asks a Brahmin [for advice], such a messenger is to be rejected.
A vulture, a jackal, a crow, an owl, or a raven— if these cry out on the right side of a sick person, that person shall not survive.

5.8.14 One wearing dyed garments, or one who is shaven-headed, or one with matted hair, or even one who is naked; or one covered in skins, or one like a common laborer in a great workshop— 5.8.15 One smeared with oil, or one whose nose is cut off, or one who is eloquent yet insane; or one with broken lips, or one with a donkey’s bray—such a person is not recommended as a messenger.

5.8.15–16 Thus has the conduct of messengers for those who are ill been proclaimed. He who knows this skillfully and desires success is indeed a physician. So said the Blessed Ātreya. Thus ends the eighth chapter in the Indriya section of the Bheḷa [Saṃhitā]. The Ninth Chapter. Now, therefore, we shall explain the powder of cow dung; so said the Blessed Ātreya. 5.8.16

5.9.1 That person on whose head the powder appears like dried cow dung, even though he is oily, shall abandon his body within a month. 5.9.2 For one who is emaciated by a phlegm disease (kapharoga) and whose phlegm is depleted, if both ears and the mouth become red, he will not survive beyond two months.
5.9.2–3 He whose water appears blood-red when seen upon his palate, and who has diminished blood and flesh, does not survive beyond a month. 5.9.3
5.9.4 But if a mortal does not see Arundhatī situated in the assembly of the Seven Sages, he will quickly be deprived of his life within eight months.
5.9.5 And if the mouth, the tongue, and the palate are covered with tiny black spots and completely severed on all sides, such a person does not live.
One who suffers from a headache, as well as one afflicted by diseases of phlegm (śleṣman), in whom hiccups flow forth profusely— one should declare that such a person does not survive.

5.9.7 If the body hairs and head hair of an embodied being seem as if they are being scorched, or if they appear as if bristling with excitement, such a person does not live. 5.9.8 If at another time his teeth appear blood-red, or if they are lusterless or smeared [with a coating], such a person does not live.
If the body of a person appears as if smeared with alkaline ash, and remains the same whether in heat or cold, such a person does not live.

5.9.10 He upon whose limbs, which have the color of a donkey, droplets of water float even though his body is not anointed— that person does not live. 5.9.11 He upon whose limb there appears a sore that bleeds red blood, shaped like a ball at its base, his life has departed.
Furthermore,
that man who passes urine that is pale-yellow and honey-like will indeed meet his death within five days.

5.9.13 He in whom restlessness, indigestion, emaciation, and weakness are observed— that person does not live. 5.9.14 But he who is dejected or helpless, or who loses his strength, and who suffers from a breaking pain as if afflicted by disease— he is just like a dead man.
5.9.14–15 Just as a living being who is completely overwhelmed by bile becomes one whose speech is confused, so too does he become like a dead person. 5.9.15

5.9.16 That man who finds no pleasure in his seat or his bed, and who eats with tears in his eyes, quickly meets his end. 5.9.17 But those men who are skilled in dreams say that he who, having mounted a monkey, does not perceive his resolve, is destined for the next world.
For that embodied being whose fever does not depart even after a full year— whether it be hot or cold— he is just like one who is dead.
5.9.19 If a person suffering from *prameha* develops pale pustules accompanied by complications such as centipedes, he is like a corpse.
5.9.20 He in whom the wind moves upward, whose hearing fails, and whose [sense organs] all become impaired— he is indeed like a corpse.

"O Hero, having seen a man endowed with these very characteristics, a physician should clearly refrain from undertaking treatment, thereby protecting his own reputation. Thus spoke the Blessed Ātreya. This concludes the ninth chapter on the *indriyas* in the Bheḷa-saṃhitā. The Tenth Chapter. Now, therefore, we shall expound the chapter on *chāyā* (complexion/omens). Thus said the Blessed Ātreya. 5.9.21.

5.10.1 A person whose shadow is absent, or whose shadow is solid yet lacks definition, or whose shadow is fragmented— such a person does not live. 5.10.2 That man who sees a shadow in the cloudless sky like lightning, or whose head appears to emit smoke, is known as one who has no [remaining] life.
5.10.2–3 One who perceives the earth as if it were a cloth dyed with lac, or perceives the sky as red, will be overcome by rakta-pitta (blood-bile).
5.10.4 A man whose hair stands on end, who is afflicted by cough and phlegm, and whose throat is covered with filaments— such a person they recognize as one who has no [more life].
5.10.5 He from whose temples the flesh has fallen away, whose eyes are likewise sunken and dark, and for whom a powder-like coating has formed in the mouth— his life has departed.
5.10.5–6: If the flesh should fall from the hand of a leper and be seen, then that man, even if not yet separated from life, shall not live.

5.10.7 Whether the food consumed is undigested or digested, if one afflicted by cough, dyspnea, and fever continues to eat, there is no cure for him. 5.10.8 If, after bathing, a person first experiences a wind blowing into the heart, his life does not extend beyond half a month.
But that man who, afflicted by labored breathing (ūrdhvaśvāsa), vomits blood, or experiences pain as if his abdominal cavity were ruptured— that person does not survive. (5.10.9)
5.10.10 He who has an internal burning while suffering from cold on the outside, or who perceives the sky as completely full, does not live.
5.10.11 He whose two lips are both parched, blue like the fruit of the jambu tree, and whose head is swollen— his life has departed.
He whose middle is distended while both shoulders are likewise emaciated, and who, having been purged, swells up again, is just like a corpse.

5.10.13 “The best of physicians, who correctly perceives this sensory cognition of life and death among men, shall know [the patient’s fate]. Thus spoke the Blessed Ātreya. Thus ends the tenth chapter on the Senses in the Bheḷa-saṃhitā. Chapter Eleven. Now, therefore, we shall explain the chapter on the Flowering (Puṣpīya). Thus said the Blessed Ātreya.
5.11.1 “He who sees a red-colored wind in his head or limb, or even a single-colored [wind] for the duration of a ghaṭikā, is said here to be ‘flowering’ (puṣpita).”
5.11.1–2 He who perceives the world as a well-constructed chessboard (aṣṭāpada) is called a man in "flower" (puṣpita), for he is devoid of true vision.
5.11.3 He who, while sleeping in a closed room, sees only the sky and chews his cud with his teeth, is said here to be "in flower" (puṣpita).
5.11.4 He who, with his hair standing on end, perceives the sky, the earth, and the forests as if they were ablaze, is said here to be "in flower."
If one does not smear oneself with [impurities] as if one were a living body, nor treat a corpse as if it were such, and if flies do not swarm around one, then one is said here to be "in bloom."
5.11.6 A woman who dwells in a dream with an unknown man, and says to him, "Go toward the southern direction," he does not live.
5.11.7 He who in a dream has disheveled hair, acts perversely, and sets out toward the southern direction— he, being such, does not live there.
5.11.7–8 He who sees himself in a dream with his limbs rooted as if by *kuśa* grass, or who perceives the sky filled with smoke— he does not live.

5.11.9 He who, having climbed a tree in a dream, does not protect his household from disease; or he who, with disheveled hair and matted locks, climbs onto a fire and weeps. 5.11.10 Or that man who in a dream ascends a palace supported by a single pillar, or dances in the mud—that man shall not live.
5.11.10–11. That man who, having ascended a great golden palace in a dream, indulges in dancing, singing, drinking, and eating, does not live.

5.11.12 If one traveling on an elephant or a camel should see the southern direction, a sick person shall live for seven days, while one who is healthy shall live for a hundred autumns. 5.11.13 He who goes toward the southern direction during a stormy day, or even in a dream, and awakens right there— such a person does not survive.
Whatever fruit of yoga one obtains during the day from [the practice of] peacocks, excellent boars, dogs, buffaloes, and horses, that same fruit shall be obtained in a dream at the source [of yoga].

5.11.15 When one sees in a dream both a tumor and a rhinoceros while eating, or even one with disheveled hair, such a person does not live. 5.11.16 A man who in a dream approaches Death (Kāla), or yellow clothing, or even sings while remaining motionless, such a person does not live.
5.11.16–17: He who, even when his desires have subsided in sleep, drinks the *vāruṇī* liquor, or even one whose throat possesses the quality of being variegated— such a person does not live.
5.11.18 A man who in a dream plunges into a river with turbulent waters will live for seven days if he is diseased, but for a hundred autumns if he is free from disease.
5.11.19 But that man whose cosmetic paste, after he has bathed and been anointed, falls off his body in a dream, perishes here by the sword.

"The wise man who correctly perceives this cognition of the senses shall understand both life and death among men. Thus spoke the Blessed Ātreya. Thus ends the eleventh chapter on the Senses in the Bheḷa-saṃhitā. Chapter Twelve: Now, therefore, we shall explain the section on the downward-moving [senses]. Thus said the Blessed Ātreya. 5.11.20
5.12.1 If one's shadow is cast downwards or slanted, or if it appears diminished, and if the two eyes are asymmetrical, his life has departed.
5.12.2 If the eyelashes of an embodied being droop and do not close, or if the eyes are as if burning, his life has departed.
If one's two eyebrows should be seen bending down and meeting at the top of the head, the sick person shall live for three days, while one free from disease shall live for six months.
5.12.4 When his hair is being pulled out, he experiences extreme pain; having ceased from both pleasure and pain, his life has departed.
5.12.5 In a patient whose mouth is seen to have a carbuncle or a disfigurement never seen before, his life has departed.
If the bridge of the nose withers and becomes broadened due to wind in one afflicted by coughing, his life has departed.
5.12.7 If one perceives his hands and feet as being excessively hot, or excessively cold, or stiff, or even flaccid, his life has departed. 5.12.8 He who,
having descended into a full river, sees a net in the water, or whose body appears smeared with water— of him they know that he shall not remain.
If a man repeatedly shakes his head with his mind [disturbed], and his forehead does not perspire, there is no cure for him.
5.12.10 He suffers from fever or cough, and likewise breathes with great difficulty; he is overcome and faints just like one who is dead.
5.12.11 His abdomen is distended and its outline is clearly visible; his stool is broken and there is thirst—he is just like one who is dead.
One should avoid that embodied being in whose house bell-metal breaks incessantly; one should avoid him for whom the moon appears sharp and the sun appears soft.
5.12.13 Whether he be of low or high birth, healthy or afflicted by disease, one who breathes like sandalwood does not live long.
5.12.14 One who has a goiter arising from the *yūthikā* plant, or who breathes like a path, or who breathes without food even in childhood— such a person does not live.
He who forms friendships with enemies, who acts unkindly toward those who are dear, and who becomes angry without cause— his life has already departed.
By these and other such signs as appropriate, a wise physician should not undertake the treatment of a patient who is thus afflicted.

5.12.17 "The physician who understands this knowledge of the foremost physicians, who knows the science of life as it has been taught—he is a physician skilled in the treatise. Thus spoke the Blessed Ātreya. Thus ends the twelfth chapter in the *Indriya* section of the *Bhela*. Thus ends the *Indriyasthāna* in the *Bhelasaṃhitā*. [The *Cikitsāsthāna*] First Chapter. Now, therefore, we shall expound the [chapter on] the eleven preparations of ghee (*ekādaśasarpiṣka*). So said the Blessed Ātreya. 5.12.17

6.1.1 Formerly, Dakṣa did not consider [Śiva] a limb of the sacrifice for the wielder of the trident; therefore, Śaṅkara caused Dakṣa’s sacrifice to perish. 6.1.2 And while he was destroying that sacrifice out of a desire to do what was pleasing to the Goddess, a fever spread through those worlds as he hissed hotly in anger.
6.1.2–3 This very [fever] causes distress to the entire world, both the stationary and the moving; and at the time of the destruction of beings, there is no other cause besides fever.
6.1.4 All other diseases that are enumerated as afflictions of embodied beings may take a year to kill, but fever takes away life instantly.
6.1.5 Fever is proclaimed to be the king of the entire host of diseases; because it causes all living beings to burn with heat, it is traditionally known as *jvara*.
Among all diseases, both physical and mental, fever is the foremost. Therefore, I shall first explain its treatment.
6.1.7 Eight types of fevers arising from the aforementioned forms have been proclaimed; briefly, fever is of two kinds: constant coldness and constant heat.

6.1.8 For that which consists of wind and phlegm (vāta-śleṣmātmaka), the physician should apply hot treatment to the cold state; for that of pure bile (ekānta-pitta), he should apply cold treatment to the hot state.
6.1.8–6.1.9 Vāyu, first drawing forth the heat from the stomach (āmāśaya), reaches the skin and, having entered the body hair, causes a person to experience horripilation. 6.1.9

6.1.10 But that phlegm (śleṣmā), when cooked by the heat associated with bile (pitta), undergoes dissolution, just as a cloud dissolves through its connection with [the sun's] radiance. 6.1.11 When the cold has subsided, the person again experiences a burning sensation due to the bile; the fire, having the bile as its fuel, consumes the body.
Once its momentum has subsided, the wind (vāyu), subsequently matured by heat (ūṣman), returns to its own place and attains its natural state of harmony.
6.1.13 Thus one contracts fever, and in this very same way one is liberated from it. This has been declared as the treatment for the wise in brief.
6.1.14 But those possessed of wisdom are rare; therefore, I shall explain the treatment for those afflicted by fever in detail, according to its eleven varieties.
6.1.14–15 One should know that ghee is the eleventh; hear from me that in detail: the prepared sudations, decoctions, linctuses, and digestive formulations.
6.1.16 Powders, medicinal pastes, affusions, boluses, electuaries, milk, clarified butter— and the eleventh is said to be prepared or even unprepared.
6.1.17 I shall describe their application and their individual potencies, which, having conquered phlegm and wind, [subdue] the bile of embodied beings.

Because it produces heat (*ūṣman*), one is called "feverish" (*jvarita*). Either the *vāyu* combined with *pitta*, or the *śleṣman* overwhelmed by *pitta*. 6.1.18: [The fever arises when] the *vāyu* is conjoined with *pitta*, or the *śleṣman* is suffused with *pitta*.
6.1.19 Since it produces internal heat (*ūṣman*), one should therefore treat the *pitta*. To one who is thirsty, warm water should be given, which promotes the digestion of the *doṣas*.
6.1.20 It is a fever-alleviator, a digestive stimulant (*dīpanīya*), and it removes *kapha*, *pitta*, and *vāta*. It purifies the channels (*srotas*) and provides appetite and perspiration for men.
For when the bodily fire is kindled, phlegm and wind are pacified; and because these two are moving in their natural direction, bile also subsides.

6.1.22 Therefore, they say that warm water is the best to drink in the case of a new fever (navajvara). 6.1.23 For cold water, when drunk, provokes phlegm (kapha) and wind (māruta); it further causes weakness of the digestive fire (agni), a sense of stiffness (staimitya), and loss of appetite (aruci).

However, that which is prepared with bitter herbs may be taken at will, either as a decoction cooled after boiling or as a cold infusion; for those who are accustomed to drinking them raw or those who prefer exclusively cold drinks, this is beneficial.

6.1.25 Indeed, for one who is hungry, liquid gruel (*peyā*) should be given for six nights for the purpose of nourishment. It removes hunger and thirst, is wholesome, and eliminates feces, urine, and flatus. 6.1.26 Due to its heat, it subdues *vāta* and *kapha*, and due to its lightness, it acts even further; when prepared according to the rules, it alleviates cardiac pain and induces perspiration.
Therefore, in all types of fevers and in a person who has been freed from fever, one should cause them to drink peyas (gruels) prepared according to the rules with the appropriate medicinal herbs.
6.1.28 Thus has been described the complete therapeutic treatment for the alleviation of fever caused by cold (*śītajvara*). Hereafter, I shall explain in detail what may and may not be eaten.
6.1.29 *Śāli* rice, *ṣaṣṭika* rice, wild *nīvāra* grain, along with *pramodaka*, and preparations of barley (*yava*)—these are always beneficial for consumption.
6.1.29–30: Kapiñjala partridges, hariṇa deer, vartaka quails, kālapucchaka birds, eṇa antelopes, and vārtīka birds— these wild meats are beneficial for one suffering from fever.

6.1.31 Well-prepared soups made from mung beans, āḍhakī, masūra, and likewise satīna, as well as meat broths (yūṣa), are praised for destroying fever. 6.1.32 A person suffering from fever should avoid hot grains such as vrīhi and barley, as well as roasted flour (saktu), citraka, black gram (māṣa), and sesame seeds, all of which possess a hot potency.
One should avoid the meat of domestic, marshy, and aquatic animals, as well as both cow and buffalo products, goat, sheep, and boar meat, and soured curd.

6.1.34 A person suffering from fever should avoid all flour-based foods, various kinds of vegetables, and those that are burning in digestion and hot in potency. 6.1.35 A person suffering from fever should avoid these five types of scratching birds (viṣkira)— the peacock, the partridge, the crane, the pigeon, and the cock— as they are hot in nature.
The times for emesis, purgation, oleation, and likewise for fasting in a patient suffering from fever have been explained by me in detail in the Sūtrasthāna.
6.1.37 Ministers, as well as counselors and friends who are instructive, who know his inclinations, are endowed with intelligence, and are experts in the knowledge of the sciences;
6.1.38 they should tell him various stories connected with virtue (*dharma*), pleasure (*kāma*), and wealth (*artha*), for the sake of diverting the sick man and destroying his lethargy and grief.
6.1.38–39 One should avoid conversations that are harsh, unpleasant, and not conducive to increasing joy, as well as those concerning those afflicted by bile-related diseases. 6.1.39
6.1.40 The physician should generate enthusiasm in the patient; for medicine administered to one who is spirited conduces to immortality.
6.1.41 Furthermore, for the sake of destroying pain and exhaustion, he should attend upon women with moon-like faces, full breasts, fragrant, and dressed in white garments.
One suffering from fever should always avoid overeating, standing for too long, and excessive walking; one should protect the vital breaths by every possible means. (6.1.41–42)
6.1.43 Anger, women, walking about, sleeping during the day, excessive talking, heavy burdens, travel on a road, strenuous exercise,

and the suppression of natural urges [are causes of fever]. 6.1.44 When the wind (māruta) is vitiated, drinking at night and staying awake at night are the causes for the recurrence of a fever that has already subsided.
One should never suddenly bathe this person when he is emaciated by fever; for the fever will return again to his body once it has become vitiated.
