6.1.46 Fever is said by the great seers to be born from the wrath of Maheśvara; therefore, for the sake of liberation from fever, one should worship the Bull-bannered Lord. 6.1.47 Baths, propitiatory rites, burnt offerings, vows, observances, restraints, and desired ritual acts prescribed in the Vedas are commended as destroyers of fever.
6.1.47–48: Jvara is the sovereign of diseases, possessed of fierce power; he is the progenitor of all ailments. Jvara is known as the terrible end-maker of all beings, having the nature of fire.

6.1.49 An affliction resulting from evil deeds that persists and is difficult for physicians to treat should be warded off by means of mantras and fire-offerings (homa) prescribed in the Vedas. 6.1.50 Furthermore, for a fever arising from the science of spirits (bhūtavidyā) and characterized by violent symptoms, one should perform the rite for dispelling fever using a physician of spirits; thus the fever shall not enter [the patient] again.

"This treatment for chronic fever should be administered by a physician who is a devotee of Rudra, pure, ascetic, and self-restrained. Thus spoke the venerable Ātreya. This concludes the first chapter of the Cikitsā-sthāna in the Bheḷa-saṃhitā. **The Second Chapter** Now, therefore, we shall expound the treatment of intermittent fevers (viṣamajvara). Thus spoke the venerable Ātreya. 6.1.51

6.2.1 Some physicians declare that irregular fever (viṣamajvara) is of the nature of wind (vātātmaka); some say it arises from the derangement of all three humors (sannipāta), while others say it originates from bile (pitta). 6.2.2 Still others say it is born of phlegm (śleṣma), while others say it arises from malevolent spirits (bhūta); and other diviners attribute it to afflictions caused by one's birth star (janmanakṣatra).
Furthermore, the opinions of the authors of the treatises are of various kinds; however, I shall explain this [condition] arising from the combination [of humors] by means of logical reasons.
6.2.4 For the wind (vāyu) situated in the colon (pakvāśaya), as well as that which has entered the bones and marrow, when aggravated, quickly provokes both phlegm (śleṣman) and bile (pitta).
6.2.5 Depending on its origin and the three locations [of the channels], it may be profound; it produces quotidian, tertian, or even quartan fevers.
On the first day, it vitiates the marrow, bone, and fat; when the second day arrives, it vitiates the muscle and blood.

6.2.7 Then, on the third day, it vitiates phlegm and wind; thereafter, having approached, it vitiates bile on the fourth day. 6.2.8 This fever in the bodies of living beings is thus fierce and belongs to Maheśvara; therefore, a wise person should strive for its pacification.
Arising from deep-seated locations and corrupted by the mixing of the bodily constituents (*dhātu*), the quartan fever (*caturthaka*) is therefore considered the most difficult to treat.

6.2.10 This dreadful irregular fever (viṣamajvara) causes the wasting away of living beings; therefore, one should treat it with measures that alleviate wasting (śoṣa). 6.2.11 A wise physician should oleate the patient according to the prescribed method with ghee prepared with a decoction of triphalā, or with vṛṣaghṛta through proper application.
One should cause that [medicine] to flow downward according to the strength or weakness of the disease. When the doshas are located in the stomach (āmāśaya), the physician should administer emesis.

6.2.13 One should administer both non-unctuous enemas (*āsthāpana*) and unctuous enemas (*anuvāsana*). This is the celebrated "Great Five Products of the Cow" (*mahāpañcagavya*), the most excellent clarified butter (*sarpir-uttama*).

6.2.14 When combined with the power of mantras, it liberates one from quartan fever (*caturthaka*), as well as from swelling (*śvayathu*), anemia (*pāṇḍuroga*), splenic enlargement (*plīhā*), and fistula-in-ano (*bhagaṇḍara*).
6.2.14–15 It likewise draws away abdominal enlargements, tumors, and jaundice.

6.2.16 One should cause [the patient] to drink the five products of the cow (*pañcagavya*): the essence of dung, milk, urine, curd, and ghee. This *pañcagavya* pacifies swelling (*śvayathu*), anemia (*pāṇḍutā*), and fever (*jvara*).
6.2.17 Having taken one hundred parts of *vṛṣa* (erectus) including its roots, leaves, and branches, it should be boiled in one *droṇa* of water until reduced to one-eighth.
One should cook one āḍhaka of vṛṣapuṣpa flowers with ghee in the presence of a pregnant woman. Once prepared, it should be administered in the proper manner, combined with a quarter part of honey.
6.2.19 Vṛṣasarpiḥ (bull-ghee) cures cough, dyspnea, anemia, tertian and quartan fevers, internal hemorrhaging, and consumption.
6.2.20 One should cook one prastha of ghee with one-pala portions each of ginger, rock salt, cavya, long pepper, alkali, and citraka.

Having combined it with one *prastha* of milk, one should cook it slowly over a mild fire. By this, abdominal tumors (*gulma*), skin diseases (*kuṣṭha*), and abdominal enlargements (*jaṭhara*) are pacified.

6.2.22 It should be drunk in cases of intermittent fever (*viṣamajvara*), as well as for those suffering from splenic enlargement, edema, and urinary disorders; it is also indicated for colic, anemia (*pāṇḍvāmaya*), and for stimulating the digestive fire (*grahaṇī*).
6.2.23 For all those who suffer from upward-moving wind (*ūrdhvavāta*), this is the supreme medicine: the three pungents (*tryūṣaṇa*), *citraka*, *hiṃsrā*, *viḍaṅga*, and *harītakī*.
Vibhītaka, āmalaka, and likewise the bark of cirabilva—these ten [substances] in equal parts, finely ground and reduced to the size of akṣa seeds.

6.2.25 One should properly cook one *prastha* of ghee with these [drugs] in six times the amount of milk. By this, the *grahaṇī* is kindled and *vātagulma* is pacified. 6.2.26 This very ghee is praised for the alleviation of hemorrhoids (*arśas*) and for swelling of the anus (*gudaśopha*); indeed, it is the most excellent ghee for upward-moving wind (*udāvarta*).
Roots of darbha and vetasa, sandalwood, madhuka, balā, phenilā, padmaka, uśīra, and both types of lotus—the white and the blue.
6.2.28 Kiṃśuka and the other [ingredients] should each be five palas in measure; these are to be boiled in one droṇa of water until reduced to one-fourth.
6.2.29 One should add jīvaka, ṛṣabhaka, medā, lodhra, lāmajjaka, kāleyaka, priyaka, and likewise keśara.
6.2.29–30: Tripuṇḍarīka, lodhra, padmaka, padmakesara, surabhi, kuṅkuma, mañjiṣṭhā, and madayantikā.
6.2.31 Equal parts of *mācīpatra* and *kuṅkuma* should be used, with *mañjiṣṭhā* four times that amount, and *sauvīra* equal to the quantity of oil.
6.2.32 One *prastha* of oil should be cooked with this decoction and half as much paste; this medicinal oil for massage destroys chronic intermittent fevers (*viṣamajvara*).
This is declared to be Mahāpadmaka, which removes all fevers; it quickly subdues fever arising from the combination of wind and bile.
Trāyamāṇā, Jayā, Vīrā, Nākulī, Gandhanākulī, Kāyasthā,
Cavikā, Jīraka, and Palāṅkaṣa; Chatrā, Aticchatrā, Jaṭilā, Sūkarī, Karkaṭī, Cāraṭī, Pūtanā, Keśī, Vacā, and Kaṭukarohiṇī.
Having ground together *mahāpuruṣadantā*, *vṛścikālī*, *kaṭambharā*, and *sthirā*, [a preparation] prepared with these is a destroyer of quartan fever.

6.2.37 This ghee, named Mahāpaiśācika, removes fever; it also expels spirits, grahas, epilepsy, and insanity. 6.2.38 With these very same groups of medicinal herbs, the physician should apply a medicinal paste (pradeha) and fumigate the one afflicted by fever; thus he becomes well.
6.2.38–39: Balis, rites for pacification (*śāntikarma*), burnt offerings (*homa*), auspicious ceremonies (*svastyayana*), ritual baths, and fasting— these pacify the quartan fever.

6.2.40 One should worship and approach the bull-bannered Lord (Śiva), the imperishable sovereign of beings (*bhūtādhipati*), who is the creator of this disease, in the cremation ground (*śmaśāna*). 6.2.41 One may destroy irregular fever (*viṣamajvara*) by means of bonds and remedies arising from the science of spirits (*bhūtavidyā*), as well as through fire-oblations (*homa*) and the offering of sacrificial food (*bali*). Thus spoke the venerable Ātreya. Thus ends the second chapter in the *Bhela-cikitsita*. **The Third Chapter** Now, therefore, we shall explain the treatment of hemoptysis (*raktapitta*). Thus said the venerable Ātreya.
In mortals, blood-bile (raktapitta) flows both upwards and downwards; therefore, the treatment for one suffering from blood-bile is said to be of two kinds. 6.3.1

6.3.2 From the consumption of excessively sour and salty food, from constant exposure to the heat of the sun, from fasting, from dizziness, from fear, and from incompatible foods, eating before the previous meal has been digested, and so forth;
6.3.3 as well as from the consumption of sesame seeds, oil-cakes, raw vegetables, flour-based preparations, all pungent (pittala) substances, fish, and the like— [the eyes become afflicted].
6.3.3–4 When the blood-bile (raktapitta) is aggravated, it flows both upwards and downwards, emerging from the nose, ears, eyes, and mouth, as well as from the anus and the penis.
6.3.5 He spits out phlegm that is mixed with blood, or it may be bitter or sour; yet when it has fallen upon the ground, ants do not eat it.
6.3.6 Or flies [do not settle on it] because of its bitterness, and dried bile is observed [in the mouth]; the throat feels as if it is being scorched and pained, and the palate becomes parched.
6.3.6–7 Furthermore, his mouth has a metallic smell and his throat smokes; one should observe these very same symptoms in the lower part of the body.

6.3.8 That which is directed upward (ūrdhvabhāga) may be curable, while that which is directed downward (adho-bhāga) is said to be palliable; however, when blood-bile (raktapitta) flows through all the channels, it is not cured. One should treat downward-directed raktapitta with emetics. Chapter Six, Section Three, Verse Eight.
6.4.1 They constantly see in their dreams trees that are withered and burnt; flies, grass, and hair fall upon their food.
6.4.1–2 His body hair and head hair grow excessively; he is habitually concealing and prone to anger arising from secret desires.

6.4.3 One who is prone to loathing, irascible, lustful for women, and has weak senses loses their natural luster, and dryness of the palate arises. 6.4.4 There is nasal discharge, catarrh, hoarseness of voice, headache, excessive perspiration of the thighs, and a decline in strength and complexion.
There is fullness of the head, and the hands and feet burn; there is loss of appetite, indigestion, fainting, dyspnea, and mild fever.

6.4.6 One with an injured chest coughs up blood-stained sputum; these are declared to be the premonitory symptoms of those afflicted by *yakṣman* (consumption). 6.4.7 One should observe those eleven symptoms in a wasting patient; he is beset by these premonitory signs and accompanied by severe complications.

One should not treat a patient suffering from consumption (viśoṣin) whose strength and flesh have been wasted, even if he is afflicted by few complications and the onset of the disease has not been long.

6.4.9 One should indeed undertake treatment for a patient who possesses wealth and is in the prime of youth, even after having previously declined him. Now, I shall first describe the treatment that he approves of.

6.4.10 Having studied this with proper application, a physician may attain fame and heaven. A person afflicted by wasting disease (*śoṣin*) who is constantly free from loathing and is of a pleasant disposition [is curable].
6.4.10–11: One who is fickle, a hater of the lowly, and a reviler of physicians and medicines— therefore, [the physician] should treat him with agreeable means and by providing reassurance.

6.4.12 The medical treatment should be administered by one who is composed and disciplined. For a patient suffering from consumption (śoṣa) who possesses strength, the fivefold purificatory therapy (pañcakarma) is prescribed.
6.4.13 That same therapy, if applied to one whose flesh is depleted, would be harmful. Once his body has been thoroughly purified, one should provide him with appropriate foods.
Kalama rice, long-awned rice, red śāli rice, and ṣaṣṭika rice; preparations of barley, as well as the meat of wild animals and birds from arid regions.
6.4.15 They praise mung beans for use in soups during meals; grain that has been stored for a year is beneficial in the diet of those suffering from consumption.
6.4.16 For meat that has been slaughtered recently is not deficient in its potency, especially the flesh of carnivorous animals and those dwelling in holes.

6.4.16–17 A patient suffering from wasting (śoṣin) should constantly consume various kinds of alcoholic liquors; for phlegm (śleṣman), even when greatly increased in the body, is driven away by the well-stimulated wind (vāyu).
6.4.18 For pitta and blood, becoming vitiated, obstruct the upward channels; these elements, mutually obstructed and impelled by the wind (pavana), [proceed further].
6.4.19 Dominated by kapha, they block all the rasa-carrying vessels (sirās). Then those rasa-carrying vessels, which convey [substances] to the heart—
When the channels no longer carry the essence of the types of food as they did before, what he has eaten does not contribute to the blood nor to the flesh.

6.4.21 Furthermore, it is not from fat, bone, or marrow that the bodies of embodied beings attain whiteness; rather, when their dhātus have not increased and are obstructed in their channels, [this occurs]. 6.4.22 Even for those embodied beings who eat wholesome foods, their limbs become diseased; by that cause they wither away, and in those who are wasting, consumption (śoṣa) sets in.
The wise declare that this is the primary nature of the Śoṣa [the Witherer]: his extreme violence toward living beings, like the action of a predatory beast in times of distress.

6.4.24 Likewise, even their meats cause the channels to expand; through their power to agitate, they cleanse the channels even when they are constricted. 6.4.25 Therefore, one who suffers from wasting diseases should habitually consume the meat of carnivorous animals according to his capacity. This secret has been taught by physicians to medical practitioners.

For those suffering from consumption, liquor and the flesh of carnivorous animals are like nectar. [The flesh of] wolves, jackals, bears, dogs, lions, tigers, and boars [is likewise beneficial]. 6.4.25–26.

6.4.27 With the word *eṇa*, one should give those prepared with various ingredients: vultures, along with swans, owls, frogs, hawks, and crows. 6.4.28 One should give peacocks with the word *barhin*, and one should certainly drink liquor. [One should also give] rats, cats, jackals, double-tongued snakes, and porcupines.
He should eat mongooses and red-crested cocks well-prepared; he should cause these meats to be served under the pretext of other meats.

6.4.30 One should vomit with disgust or remain on one's feet; therefore, one should eat these meats which have been proven effective in secret. 6.4.31 A physician should cook the meat of hole-dwelling carnivores at a rate of one *tulā* for every ten *droṇas* of water.
When one-eighth of the liquid remains, the physician should strain it; then, he should cook one *droṇa* of ghee with the *garbha* (infusion) of the *jīvanīya* (vitalizing) drugs. 6.4.31–6.4.32.
One should drink that ghee in the proper dose, and prepare meat with that same [ghee]; it cures cough, dyspnea, heart disease, fever, and even pain in the flanks (6.4.33).
It also removes swelling and hoarseness of voice for those suffering from wasting (śoṣin) (6.4.34). [The drugs used are] the great and small *pañcamūla*, *golomī*, *madhuka*, and *balā*.
One should boil [the ingredients] in one *droṇa* of water until reduced to one-fourth; that decoction, strained with water, should then be used to cook one *prastha* of ghee. 6.4.34–35.

6.4.36 One should add four times the amount of milk, along with the pastes of the *jīvanīya* (life-promoting) drugs, as well as those of *vidārī*, *āmalaka*, and sugarcane juice. 6.4.37 One should add portions equal to the quantity of ghee and cook it over a gentle fire. This is known as *rasāyanīya* ghee; it bestows strength.
For the prevention of heart disease, chest wounds, cough, and wasting diseases, one should therefore prepare *sarpirguḍa* (medicated jaggery) combined with sugar and honey.

6.4.39 Or one may also prepare sweetmeats (*modaka*) with wheat flour; for those suffering from consumption (*śoṣa*), these are like nectar for the aforementioned disorders. 6.4.40 These sweetmeats, which increase strength, should be eaten with milk as an after-drink (*anupāna*). If *kapha* is predominant in the consumption, they should be consumed with wine as an after-drink.

One should cook one *prastha* of ghee by combining with it a paste made from half a *prastha* of rice, half a *prastha* of washed rice, and half a *prastha* of crushed sesame seeds, mixed together with one *prastha* of water.
6.4.42 Then, once it is accomplished and purified, one should cook that ghee again with the meat of a carnivorous animal and with milk in its entirety.
6.4.43 One who knows the ritual procedure should [prepare] a well-prepared ball of meat from a wild animal, the size of a *bilva* fruit, which has been constantly infused with water.
6.4.43–44 Then, once it is cooked and purified, one should place it again on the fire together with a *prastha* of milk and one *āḍhaka* of sugarcane juice. 6.4.44
6.4.45 Vidārī, mudgaparṇī, māṣaparṇī, kaseruka, śṛṅgāṭaka, mṛṇāla, lotus seeds, and jīvaka; 6.4.46 Kṣīraśuklā, ṛṣabhaka, medā, madhuka, payasyā, kṣīrakākolī, and the bulb of the blue lotus.
Having mixed those pastes, measured in the quantity of an akṣa, together with *tālakadamba* into that [mixture], one should cook it all over a gentle fire while stirring.

6.4.48 Having caused that to be strained, it should be placed in a windless spot so that it becomes like nectar. Then, when it has solidified in the morning, one should churn it thoroughly with a churning-stick (khaja).
6.4.49 Then, while it is being churned, one should add fifty palas of powdered sugar, adding it in small portions and continuing to churn after each addition.
Furthermore, for the sake of fragrance, one should add a powder of *tvak* and *nāgapuṣpa*. Having been mixed into a single mass, it should then be allowed to steep for one night.
6.4.51 Likewise, *modaka* boluses should be prepared with the same size and shape as a dice (*akṣa*), made from the flour of barley and wheat, and mixed with powdered *tugākṣīrī*.
6.4.52 One should eat these *modakas* at the proper time and then drink milk. These pacify consumption (*yakṣman*) just as Indra’s thunderbolt destroys a tree.
By means of this [preparation], one should cure menorrhagia, wounds, emaciation, heart disease, irregular fever, insanity, internal hemorrhaging, and cough. (6.4.52–53)
6.4.54–55. Then, one should boil the roots of the *aśvattha* tree along with its shoots and fruits, as well as *śatāvarī*, *pṛśniparṇī*, *bṛhatī*,
*kaṇṭakārikā*, *golomī*, *śreyasī*, *kālā*, *śārivā*, and *punarnavā*, all crushed together, in ten *droṇas* of milk.

When that [mixture] has been boiled, cooled, and strained, one should churn it thoroughly with a churning-stick (*khaja*). Whatever ghee (*sarpiḥ*) is produced therein, one should extract and cook it further.
6.4.57 And medicinal substances should be ground into a paste; therein one should employ these: madhuka, madhulī, drākṣā, medā, vṛṣa, and jīraka.
6.4.58 Tālamajjā, śalāmajja, as well as puṣkarabīja, the jīvanīya group, trāyamāṇā, madhukas, and kaśeruka.
[One may take] blue lotus, white lotus, eggplant, and uccaṭā; or the fresh juice of kāśmarya, āmalaka, sugarcane, and vidārī.
6.4.60 Once that is prepared, one should cause it to be strained and placed in a firm silver pitcher. Having added half a *tulā* of sugar, one should stir it thoroughly.
6.4.61 One should also add a *prastha* of *tugākṣīrī*, a *prastha* of honey, and [the same amount] each of the seeds of *ātmaguptā*, jaggery, and black pepper.
One should cause two *prasthas* of *uccaṭā* and sugarcane juice to be added there; one should also cause the powder of cinnamon, cardamom, and *nāgapuṣpa* to be added there.

6.4.63 Having prepared *modaka* pills weighing one *pala* each, one should place them in a new earthen vessel. A person should eat one *pala* of that at night, and again one *pala* later [in the morning].
6.4.64 One should sleep on a soft bed, observing celibacy and remaining composed. By this practice, performed with discipline, one certainly casts off consumption (*yakṣmā*).
This also promotes the growth of a withered person whose sense organs are weak; it serves as an aphrodisiac for men whose semen is depleted. (6.4.64–65)
6.4.66 Those killed by women, those struck by the *bhāra* [demon], the aged, those whose youth has passed, those with wasted flesh, those with diminished strength, and those with depleted blood;

6.4.67 Those afflicted by bile disorders (*pitta-roga*), hemorrhaging (*rakta-pitta*), consumption (*śoṣa*), or fever arising from the humors (*doṣa-jvara*); those whose senses are impaired, whose semen is lost, and those known to have a constricted throat.
This yoga, which is like nectar, makes those men who are powerless, dull-witted, and whose senses have perished, become renewed once more.

6.4.69 Epilepsy, fainting, insanity, heart disease, and facial paralysis— [these afflict those] whose vital energy (*tejas*) has been stolen away by some elemental influence (*bhūtadharma*). 6.4.70 Indeed, these *modaka* boluses, when followed by a draught of milk, produce immediate nourishment for those who are agitated, those with extremely diminished bodily constituents (*dhātu*), those suffering from wasting diseases (*śoṣin*), and those of weak constitution.
Even by means of a hundred medical treatments, only suffering is treated. Therefore, when [the body] is wasting away, the physician should employ the procedure for elixirs (*rasāyana*). 6.4.70–71.
6.4.72 One should practice this for a year, a season, or a half-year. As for the *pippalī-vardhamāna* regimen, it is increased by five [berries] at a time.

6.4.73 It is recommended for nasal administration, massage, internal consumption, and enema therapy; it is effective for all wind-related disorders (*vātavyādhi*), emaciation from chest wounds (*kṣatakṣīṇa*), and stiffness of the head.

[This is indicated] in cases of pain in the flanks, urinary disorders (prameha), abdominal tumors (gulma), hemorrhoids, fistula-in-ano, for those with dislocated limbs, fractures, or physical deficiencies, as well as in cough, dyspnea, and cardiac oppression.

6.4.75 This oil is beneficial for those who are delicate and brings comfort to children and the elderly; it is indicated in cases of fever, diarrhea, loss of appetite, discoloration, and loss of voice.
6.4.76 Indeed, this is aphrodisiac, strengthening, and increases muscle mass within a month; it improves the voice and complexion, and for those suffering from consumption (śoṣa), it is like nectar.
And whatever scum (*niṣpāka*) may arise from this oil when it has been properly cooked, that too shall serve its purpose, like whey (*udaśvit*) for the sake of curd. (6.4.77)

6.4.78 Eleven and six are the complications arising from consumption; the physician should pacify them, just as one endowed with rain extinguishes fires. 6.4.79 One should cook one *prastha* of oil from pressed sesame seeds, adding one *pala* of *madhuka* as an internal ingredient and four times as much milk.
When that has been cooked until it is soft, one should cook it further with four times the amount of milk and one pala of madhuka.
6.4.81 By this same method, one should cook a hundred parts of madhuka; when it has been cooked a hundred times, it is known as *śatapāka*.
6.4.82 When used for drinking, external anointing, nasal drops, enemas, as a condiment, or in food, it is like nectar for men suffering from *rājayakṣman*.
Heart disease, dryness of the palate, pain in the flanks, erysipelas, thirst, insanity, erythema, cough, dyspnea, and menorrhagia. (6.4.82–83)
6.4.84 This [preparation], when drunk, subdues increased *raktapitta* (hemorrhagic disorders) that has spread to all parts of the body, as well as jaundice (*kāmalā*) and anemia (*pāṇḍuroga*).

6.4.85 It also cures inflammation of the mouth and eyes, deafness, earache, night-blindness (*naktāndhya*), cataracts (*timira*), opacities (*kāca*), loss of vision (*liṅganāśa*), and the proliferation of blood vessels (*sirācaya*).
Administered as a nasal medication (nastaḥ), it cures biḍālikā, putrid nose (pūtinasya), diseases of the head, and stiffness of the head; it also removes baldness and premature graying of the hair.

6.4.87–88: Enema therapy (bastikarma) is highly recommended for bleeding from the lower body, blood-pitta disorders, hemorrhoids, fistula-in-ano, and for vāta disorders that have spread throughout the entire body and originated from blood-pitta; it is also praised for women who are childless, for men with diminished semen, and for those suffering from deformities of the knees, sacrum, and so forth.

Those [plants] that cause great obstruction and are constantly used by women are considered the most aphrodisiac; when employed according to the prescribed method, they constitute an unsurpassed elixir (rasāyana).
6.4.90 One should prepare this "thousand-fold cooked" [preparation] according to this method. They declare this to be an elixir (*rasāyana*) for men that bestows a thousand-year lifespan.

6.4.91 A paste (*kalka*) consisting of *aśvagandhā*, *apāmārga*, *nākulī*, white mustard (*gaurasarṣapa*), sesame (*tila*), and *bilva* should be used there as a supreme massage for protection against evil spirits (*rakṣas*).
A man seeking long life should be devoted to auspicious customs and rites for well-being; he should daily perform ritual baths and pacificatory fire-offerings.
6.4.93 The *iṣṭis* prescribed by the Vedas are the destroyers of consumption (*rājayakṣman*). One should constantly practice these and worship the Bull-bannered Lord (Śiva).
6.4.94 Regarding those complications that remain—the six and eleven that have been mentioned—one should apply their treatment according to their respective specific treatments.

6.4.94–95. Thus has the treatment for royal consumption (rājayakṣman) been declared by the disciplined [teacher], which brings about fame and heaven, is meritorious, and is for the attainment of the goals of his disciples. Thus spoke the Blessed Ātreya. Thus ends the fourth chapter in the Cikitsita section of the Bheḷa-saṃhitā. Fifth Chapter. Now, therefore, we shall explain the treatment of abdominal tumors (gulma). Thus indeed said the Blessed Ātreya. 6.4.95.

6.5.1 Five types of gulma have been described in detail in the section on etiology (nidāna). I shall now explain their nature as gulma and their respective treatments individually. 6.5.2 The wind (vāta), aggravated within the body, obstructs the channels (srotas) in every direction; having spread throughout, it first vitiates the bile (pitta) and then the phlegm (kapha).
6.5.2–3 Then, it vitiates the blood and courses through the fat and muscle; having become a solid mass, it develops into a gulma (abdominal tumor).

6.5.4 Just as a multitude of elephants, horses, chariots, and vehicles belonging to wicked men who desire to kill others is called a *gulma* (a troop), so too— 6.5.5— the accumulation (*saṃsarga*) of the bodily constituents (*dhātu*), such as the nutrient fluid (*rasa*) and the rest, within the body is called a *gulma*; their massing together (*saṃghāta*) is also termed a *gulma*.
6.5.5–6.5.6 But the dense cluster of climbing plants, creepers, and even shrubs is called a *gahana* or a *gulma*; likewise, the mass of embodied beings is called a *gulma*.

6.5.7 For because it is formless, the wind (vāta) does not produce direct perception; having joined with bile (pitta) and phlegm (śleṣman), the wind takes on the state of a gulma. 6.5.8 Just as bees build a cluster made of beeswax, so too does the wind collect those very tissues (dhātus) within the abdominal cavities.
They describe the locations of that gulma and its relative severity. A gulma situated in the region of the stomach or the sides is said to be predominantly caused by vāta.
6.5.10 It may produce the symptoms of *vāta-gulma* according to its location; likewise, when situated in the seat of *pitta*, it displays the symptoms of *pitta*.

6.5.11 In the same way, this applies to *śleṣman*, blood, and *sannipāta* (the combination of all three). However, in the case of *sannipāta* involving all [factors], the respective symptoms of each are manifested.

6.5.11–12 An exogenous disorder (āgantu) vitiates the bodily constituent (dhātu) located at its own site; however, the treatment should be directed toward that specific site, for the disorder is more powerful there.
6.5.13 If a *vāta-gulma* reaches suppuration, it does so when located in the bladder; a *paittika-gulma* reaches suppuration in the region between the heart and the navel.

6.5.14 A *śleṣma-gulma*, however, undergoes suppuration in the heart if left untreated; likewise, a *gulma* born of blood (*śoṇita-ja*) and one arising from the combination of all three humors (*sannipāta*) also suppurate.

All types of *gulma* that are associated with two *doṣas* are extremely distressing; therefore, one should employ all therapeutic measures that cause their breaking up (*bhedanīya*). Even if a *gulma* is excessively oleated (*snihyamāna*), it may continue to increase in size.
6.5.16 Next, I shall describe the treatment for vāta-gulma (wind-type abdominal tumors). For Vāyu is the powerful lord of all beings and the master of life-force (prāṇa).
6.5.17 Harītakī, trikaṭu, vacā, kaṭukarohiṇī, sauvarcala salt, yavakṣāra, viḍaṅga, and likewise citraka.

With these quantities measured by the *akṣa*, one should cook a *prastha* of clarified butter (*ghṛta*). Once it has been cooked, one should strain it and administer it according to the patient's strength.
6.5.19 This ten-ingredient formulation destroys vāta-gulma, worms, cough, dyspnea, and even splenic enlargement; it destroys these diseases just as a thunderbolt destroys the asuras.
6.5.20 [The physician should take] the two pañcamūlas (the minor and major), suṣavī, aśvagandhā, punarnavā, kālā, chinnaruhā, rāsnā, bhārṅgī, gokṣuraka, and balā.
6.5.20–21: One should boil two palas each of śaṭī, puṣkaramūla, palāśa, and the substance known as gandha in one droṇa of water.
6.5.22 Having separately measured one *prastha* each of *kola*, *kulattha*, and *māṣa* beans together with barley, one should pour them all into that same [liquid].

6.5.23 With that [decoction] reduced to one-quarter, one should cook one *prastha* of clarified butter (*ghṛta*) along with curd and other ingredients, as well as sour gruel (*śukta*), fermented rice-water (*āranāla*), and *tuṣodaka*.

One should likewise add the juice of pomegranate and *āmrātaka*, as well as the juice of citron; to this, one should add four times the amount of curd, and into the center of these, one should pour [the medicinal paste].
6.5.25 Kāravī, trikaṭu, dantī, the three salts, hiṃsrā, rāsnā, vacā, yavānī, and amlavetasa;
6.5.26 viḍaṅga, pomegranate, asafoetida, nīlikā, and also trivṛt, the two alkalis, ajamodā, pāṭhā, and pāṣāṇabheda.
6.5.26–27 Ūṣaka, vṛṣaka, bhārṅgī, śvadaṃṣṭrā, and hapuṣā; also the seeds of trapusa and urvāru, as well as śatavīryā and upakuñcikā.

6.5.28 One should take cumin (*ajājī*), leadwort root (*citraka-mūrvā*), *tumburu*, long pepper (*gaja-pippalī*), coriander (*dhānyaka*), and *surasa*, each in a quantity equal to one *akṣa*. 6.5.29 This excellent clarified butter (*sarpir-uttama*), prepared with this internal decoction, should be administered; it destroys all types of abdominal tumors (*gulma*) except for those caused by blood (*rakta-gulma*).

In cases of disease localized in a single limb, in diseases affecting the sides, in enlargement of the spleen, in heart disease, in disorders of the *grahaṇī*, and in severe *vāta-gulma* (wind-type abdominal tumors), [this treatment is indicated]. 6.5.29–30.

6.5.31 This ghee, renowned by the name *dādhika*, possesses great therapeutic qualities; it destroys insanity, abdominal colic, and epilepsy. 6.5.32 One should add barley-alkali (*yāvaśūka*), alkali (*kṣāra*), rock salt (*saindhava*), *hastipippalī*, long pepper (*pippalī*), ginger (*śṛṅgavera*), and black pepper (*marica*) in equal proportions.
Of these six [drugs], there should be six separate portions, each weighing one *pala*. One should prepare a decoction using half-*pala* portions of these.
6.5.34 One should cook one *prastha* of ghee with half-*palas* each of the substances to be ground (*peṣya*), along with a decoction equal in quantity to the fat, and twice that amount of milk.

6.5.35 This is known as the "Six-Pala" (*ṣaṭpala*) ghee; it destroys abdominal tumors (*gulma*), as well as splenic enlargement (*plīhā*), hemorrhoids (*arśas*), and disorders of the digestive tract (*grahaṇī-doṣa*).

6.5.35–36: [The physician] removes vasti, kuṇḍala, and vardhma simply by means of drinking [medicines]. Having lubricated a patient with vāta-gulma using any of these oleaginous substances, the physician should skillfully purify him with an unctuous purgative.

6.5.37 One should cook ghee, parched grain flour (saktu), citraka, rock salt, vacā, and pippalī with milk, and then carefully remove it from the heat. 6.5.38 Thereafter, one should drink a dose the size of a cat’s paw (biḍālapadaka) with warm water, or with ghee, or with milk, or with wine, or with warm water.
This [formula] expels vāta-gulma and whatever colic pains associated with gulma there may be; it destroys splenic enlargement (plīha), udāvarta, and kapha-gulma. (6.5.38–39)
6.5.40 Mahauṣadha, devadāru, vāsā, kaṭukarohiṇī, citraka, pippalīmūla, pippalī, and hastipippalī;
6.5.41 Kuṣṭha, sarpagandhā, the five salts, the two alkalis (kṣāra), trivṛtā, dantī, dravantī, and upakuñcikā.

Of these salts, take portions of half a *pala* each; then, having thoroughly stirred together one *pala* of each salt with the powders [of the other ingredients] in half a *prastha* of curd, one should cook it.
6.5.43 One should cause one prastha each of muscle fat, oil, and ghee to be administered. Once it has ignited and subsided as prescribed, one should then remove it from the fire.
6.5.44 Thereafter, one should drink a dose the size of a cat's paw with warm water, or with ghee, milk, liquor, or sour gruel.
This is the alkaline decoction named *eṣakṣārāgada*, which destroys vāta-gulma, as well as splenic enlargement, hemorrhoids, colic, *vardhma*, upward movement of wind (*udāvarta*), and *kuṇḍala*.

6.5.46 It destroys worms along with disorders of the *grahaṇī*, poisons, Vāta and Apatānaka, the bites of snakes and rats, and tumors produced by [malevolent] spells. 6.5.47 It forcibly destroys Gulma arising from Vāta and Kapha, as well as that of a Sannipāta nature, just as the wind scatters torn clouds. A barren woman conceives a child, and it neutralizes even artificial poisons (*gara*). Furthermore, it cures epileptic seizures (*apasmāra*) and insanity (*unmāda*). The Sixth Chapter.
6.5.47 6.6.1 | Pitta becomes excessively aggravated in the body; that vitiated [pitta] then vitiates the blood, the flesh, and the embryo.
6.6.2 In that regard, many kinds of skin diseases (kuṣṭha) arise in the body. I shall describe their symptoms and their treatment in due order.
6.6.3 Indeed, when the accumulated humors (doṣas), which move through the skin, flesh, and blood, become corrupted, that condition is designated as kuṣṭha.
6.6.3–4 By consuming incompatible foods, by eating before the previous meal has been digested, and by the suppression of the urges of vomiting, urine, and feces— 6.6.4.
6.6.5 If one drinks milk after consuming the meat of domestic, marshy, or aquatic animals, leafy vegetables, green herbs, liquor, or excessively sour food;
6.6.6 Or if, having eaten a hot meal, one consumes honey and meat; or if, having drunk liquor and honey, one consumes hot food.

One who eats food that has been overcooked, one who indulges in sexual intercourse with a village woman, one who suddenly exposes himself to heat and sunlight, and one who plunges into water— these [are causes of death].
6.6.8 When its heat is obstructed, it provokes the wind (vāta). The provoked wind, in turn, agitates the accumulated humors (doṣa-saṃcaya).
6.6.9 Those humors, having entered the channels (sirā), excessively vitiate the blood. The three—wind, bile (pitta), and phlegm (kapha)—become obstructed by the blood and flesh.

These [factors] quickly produce all eighteen types of leprosy (kuṣṭha) in men; even among the etiological factors (nidāna), that which is designated as the "seven-leprosy" etiology has been specified.
6.6.11 Now I shall describe the characteristics of the eighteen types of leprosy (kuṣṭha). That leprosy which has a reddish appearance, is dark, dry, and painful;
6.6.12 which feels as if infested with ants, is rough, and arises quickly—this is the Vātika type. It becomes afflicted and is intensely burning.
In the Pitta-type [fever], the tongue becomes copper-colored, dark-brown, and aggravated, and is accompanied by fever; or, when those [symptoms] have arisen, it becomes motionless, thick, and heavy.
6.6.14 That leprosy which arises from phlegm (kapha) is pale, unctuous, and heavy; it is cracked, exudes much discharge, and is accompanied by burning, redness, and pain.

6.6.15 Listen now to my description of the premonitory symptoms (pūrvarūpa) of the type arising from the combination of all three humors (sānnipātika), as well as those involving the skin, body hair, nails, and flesh that are being torn apart.
6.6.15–16 Having observed these signs, the wise physician should apply medical treatment. Heat, burning sensations, perspiration, dryness, and discoloration [are the symptoms].
6.6.17 Sleepiness, horripilation, heaviness of the limbs, fatigue, redness, thirst, debility, burning sensations, pustules, and so forth [occur].
6.6.18 Thereafter, the skin diseases (kuṣṭha) arise; I shall describe their characteristics: sweating, the appearance of *kākaṇa* (small spots), being well-developed, and painful.
That which is cracked at the edges and dark blue is called *kākaṇa* leprosy. But that which is covered with many circular spots resembling *udumbara* fruits [is another type].

6.6.20 One should recognize that as *audumbara* when it is either free of discharge or discharging, characterized by circular patches resembling the *bandhūjīva* flower, which are elevated and burning.
6.6.21 One should recognize *maṇḍalakuṣṭha* as being accompanied by pain and a sucking sensation; one should identify *ṛśyajihva* kuṣṭha as being similar to the tongue of a *ṛśya* (antelope).
6.6.21–22 They know that *puṇḍarīka* to be having the luster of a lotus petal; *sidhma* leprosy is described as being like the *alābu* flower. 6.6.22

6.6.23 Kapālakuṣṭha is black, with circular patches and a rough surface; carmakuṣṭha, however, is extensive, resembling an elephant’s hide, and coarse. 6.6.24 Pāmā is accompanied by eruptions, burning sensations, itching, and pain; it flows profusely and is characterized by intense itching.
6.6.24–25 And that which arises and persists is proclaimed as *kiṭibha*. It is dark-brown or red, arisen, moist, and likewise exuding.

6.6.26 That which is thickened with flesh and associated [with these symptoms] should be known as *vicarcikā*. 6.6.27 Circular patches that are elevated at the edges, parched, dry, itchy, and dense—this is indeed remembered as *dadrū-kuṣṭha*. It is covered with rough, blue and red eruptions.
That which has many openings and exudes a flow is known as *śatāruṣka*. It resembles the awn of rice and has hairs that are white and red.
6.6.29 One should recognize that as *śvitra* (leucoderma) when it is pierced by various circular spots; it is corrupted by the force of the poison of fish, rats, or insects.
6.6.30 Arising from poison, it is accompanied by itching, redness, and pustules, or it is simply dark-colored; it appears on the palms, soles, big toes, and the heels.
That which is cracked and accompanied by pain and burning is known as *vaipādika*. That which has arisen with the color of an *udumbara* fruit and is accompanied by pain [is called *audumbara*].
6.6.32 That leprosy which is discolored like a peacock's plumage is called *sthūlāru*. It is surrounded by spreading eruptions (*visarpa*), is distorted, and exudes discharge.

6.6.33 This is declared to be *ekakuṣṭha*, arising from a single type of spreading eruption (*vīsarpa*). These eighteen types of leprosy have been described here according to their specific characteristics.
Nine of these are incurable, and likewise nine are treatable: namely, puṇḍarīka, śvitra, ṛṣyajihva, and sakākaṇa.

6.6.35 Udumbara, śatāruṣka, and that which is known as carmakuṣṭha; likewise, that which is called ekakuṣṭha and the vaipādika kuṣṭha— 6.6.36 These nine types of kuṣṭha are never cured. Sidhma, vicarcikā, pāmā, dadru, and kiṭibha [are the remaining five].
6.6.36–37: The wise declare that these nine types of leprosy— kapāla, kuṣṭha, sthūlārur, maṇḍala, and that which is born of poison— are curable.
Of these, nine types arise from karma and nine indeed arise from the humors (doṣas). Those born of karma are not cured, whereas the others are indeed cured.
One who possesses self-control and practices skillfully is liberated from them—namely, from leprosy arising from blood and that arising from the derangement of the humors.
Therefore, among those [diseases], venesection is prescribed first; however, for leprosy (kuṣṭha), even when it is very slight, frequent scarification is considered the proper course.

6.6.41 It is prescribed that his blood should be drawn using leeches, a gourd, or a horn. Now hear about the disorders of the blood according to their respective locations in the bodily constituents (dhātus).
6.6.42 Blood associated with Vāta is thin, frothy, reddish, and dry; blood associated with Pitta is known to be blue, yellow, black, heated, and intensely red.
One should recognize blood born from the combination of all three humors (sānnipātika) by its appearance as being slimy, pale, unctuous, and fibrous.
6.6.44 Blood that resembles the *indragopaka* insect is said to be healthy; this is also true for the blood of a man who has vomited or has just finished eating.

6.6.45 Thereafter, one should administer purification (*saṃśodhana*) to him who has been lubricated with prepared medicated ghees—namely, emesis (*vamana*), purgation (*recana*), head-evacuation (*śīrṣavirecana*), and non-unctuous enema (*āsthāpana*)—but one should not administer an unctuous enema (*anuvāsana*) to him.
A person suffering from leprosy should always consume śālī rice and ṣaṣṭika rice, as well as wild animals and birds, and various preparations of barley.
6.6.47 Village-dwelling animals, marshy and aquatic meat, sugarcane juice, sesame oil, clarified butter, liquor, curd, milk, daytime sleep, sour fruits, and sexual intercourse—
6.6.48 Radishes, preparations of flour, fat, and green vegetables— all these provoke phlegm (kapha), bile (pitta), and blood.

A person suffering from *kuṣṭha* should always avoid such foods as these, which cause excessive secretions (*abhiṣyandi*), as well as eating when the previous meal is undigested (*ajīrṇa*) or overeating (*adhyashana*). (6.6.48–49)
6.6.50 A person suffering from leprosy who requires oleation therapy should drink *dhānvantara* ghee, or the great *pañcagavya* [ghee],
or *śairīṣa* oil. 6.6.51 Or one should practice the *pippalī-vardhamāna* regimen with honey, or take *abhayāriṣṭa*, or indeed *gaṇḍīrāriṣṭa*.
One should feed a fistful of powdered *khadira* heartwood; one should drink that boiled for three days, and thereafter bathe and apply it as an ointment.
6.6.53 One should eat food prepared by him and provide him with water for drinking. One should practice this for a fortnight, a month, a season, or even six months.

6.6.54 When propitiated, the Khadira tree destroys even very severe forms of leprosy, just as the fire at the end of a Yuga, having grown great through the succession of world-ages, consumes the mountains.

Alternatively, one who eats wholesome food (pathyāśana) should lick the powder of the five "fearless" drugs (pañcābhayā) combined with trikaṭu (savyoṣa) or with jaggery (saguḍa); in this way, the pacification of leprosy (kuṣṭha) will occur before long.
6.6.56 A person suffering from leprosy (kuṣṭha) should drink either turmeric or *rasāñjana* with cow’s urine according to the prescribed method; thus he is liberated from the disease.
6.6.57 *Drākṣā*, turmeric, *mañjiṣṭhā*, the three myrobalans (*triphalā*), *devadāru*, ginger, the two types of *pañcamūla*, *mustā*, and *madhurasā*—[these should be used].
Saptaparṇa, apāmārga, picumanda, āṭarūṣaka, viḍaṅga, citraka, dantī, pippalī, and marica.

6.6.59 Of those [drugs] taken in equal parts, a patient suffering from *kuṣṭha* should drink one *pala* of the powder for a month combined with cow’s urine; thus he is liberated from *kuṣṭha*. 6.6.60 When that has been digested, the man should drink camel’s milk and subsist on a diet of milk; even *kuṣṭha* diseases accompanied by worms, as well as those from which hair and nails have fallen out, are cured.
Alternatively, even decayed flesh or camel’s milk may destroy [the disease]. These internal treatments have been declared for the eradication of *kuṣṭha*.
6.6.62 I shall now explain the external treatment; learn it from me in detail. One should apply ointments to the patient whose blood has been let.
6.6.63 Having rubbed [the skin] with surgical instruments, leaves, or even cow dung, one should then apply plasters that destroy leprosy to the leprous patches.
Svarjika, kākuṣṭha, tuthā, viḍaṅga, marica, manaḥśilā, and lodhra— this ointment is a destroyer of kuṣṭha.
6.6.65 One should grind together *avalguja* fruit, *dantī*, *śyonāka*, *gajapippalī*, the two types of *citraka*, the two types of mustard, and the two types of *haridrā*.
6.6.66 Having thoroughly mixed this with the juice of *mātuluṅga*, one should bury it. After seven nights have passed, this is the supreme ointment for skin diseases (*kuṣṭha*).
It cures ringworm, skull-like leprosy, scabies, eczema, thick eruptions, poison-born ailments, and vitiligo.
6.6.68 Karavīra, ulāṅgalikī, dantī, hiṃsrā, śukānanā, citraka, arka, trikaṭuka, triphalā,
and kaṭurohiṇī; 6.6.69 Kośātakī, bhadramustā, bṛhatī, sarṣapa, vacā, karañjabīja, sudhā, svarṇakṣīrī, and nidigdhikā.

*Picumanda*, *jātyāhva*, *pīlu*, *tilvaka*, *pallava*, *saudha*, *āmalaka* seeds, *karṇikāra*, *avalguja*, and *bhallātaka*. [End of] the Sixth Chapter. 6.6.70. [Beginning of] the Seventh Chapter. 6.7.1.

6.7.1 One should engage with a woman according to the proper method and avoid sleeping during the day. For one who is constantly bathing with decoctions (kaṣāya) and regularly uses decoction water, [these measures are beneficial]. 6.7.2 Specifically, one should treat cases of *śleṣmameha* (phlegmatic urinary disorders) using sharp [therapeutic measures] alone; however, in cases of *paittika* (bilious) disorders, one should employ bitter and decocted [substances].

6.7.2–3 One should avoid the four types of urinary disorders (meha) born of vāta that are incurable. Loss of appetite, aching in the limbs, thirst, cough, giddiness, and darkness before the eyes [are their premonitory signs].

6.7.4 Painful ulcers, pustules, and itching are the complications of urinary disorders (prameha). One should treat these complications in cases of prameha as well as in pustular eruptions by means of non-surgical measures.
6.7.5 For those suffering from prameha who are afflicted by such complications and likewise by pustules, this supreme medicinal therapy has been declared by me.

6.7.5–6.7.6: The physician should devise a treatment by means of these [therapies] individually or combined, according to their specific divisions, in accordance with the [nature of the] doshas and the strength [of the patient].

6.7.7 Having examined the symptoms of the twenty types of urinary diseases, as well as the causes arising from the combination of the *doṣas*, one should then formulate the appropriate medicinal formulations.
6.7.8 Therefore, I shall state their treatment by way of brief enumeration; furthermore, listen now to the detailed classification for the purpose of pacifying the urine.
The juice of the root of śatāvarī, taken in equal parts with honey and ghee, should be drunk for the cure of ikṣumeha and for the pacification of kapha and pitta.

6.7.10 The fresh juice of *kirātatikta*, as well as that of *paṭola* and *āruka*, taken with honey, pacifies urinary disorders (*meha*); likewise, a decoction known as "water" [prepared from these] has the same effect. 6.7.11 One should drink *pippalī*, ginger, and black pepper with lukewarm water; by this, one is liberated from thick urine (*sāndramēha*).
By consuming *cavya*, *citraka* roots, and likewise the bark of *pūtīka*, prepared in soups on the threshing floor, one becomes free from suffering. (6.7.12)

6.7.13 One who drinks ghee prepared with barley grains boiled in milk, combined with asafoetida (*hiṅgu*) and taken as an occasion arises, is liberated from *bhasmameha*. 6.7.14 One should administer the salt known as *kāca*, which is mixed with wood-apple (*kapittha*), ajamoda, and likewise black pepper (*marica*).
One who drinks [this] combined with pippalī and kaṇa, mixed with honey and sugar, along with cold water, shall conquer *lavaṇameha*.
One who suffers from urinary disorders (meha) should eat food accompanied by thick, flowing liquids. This [remedy] constantly overcomes urinary disorders arising from salt.
Cardamom, young bamboo shoots, asafoetida, and salt should be taken in equal parts. When drunk with wine or warm water, it conquers urinary disorders accompanied by gravel.
6.7.17–18: For śukla-meha (white urine), the consumption of *tumburu* seeds, the resin of *kapittha*, combined with honey, as well as the intake of barley-based food, are recommended.
6.7.19 Soups made from mung beans and horse gram, especially when prepared with liquids, as well as preparations of barley, should be eaten in cases of *śukla-meha*.
6.7.20 A person should drink milk boiled solely with the roots of *śvadaṃṣṭrā* and *darbha*, mixed with sugar; thus, one is liberated from *kṣāra-meha*.
A person should drink [the decoction] boiled with grapes, or likewise boiled with milk; thus one shall be completely liberated from both *pittameha* and *kṣārameha*.

6.7.22 One should also administer the powders of *pītā* and *mañjiṣṭhā* with honey for the treatment of *mehanā*; however, in cases of *śītameha*, these should always be taken with barley food. 6.7.23 Furthermore, one suffering from *raktameha* shall be relieved by drinking the paste of the leaves of *madayantī* mixed with honey, as well as that of the root of *darbha*.
One should drink their milk, and thus one is liberated from *nīlameha*. One should drink milk boiled with the sprouts of milky trees (*kṣīrivṛkṣa*).

One suffering from *nīlameha* due to a pitta disorder may be cured by drinking [the decoction] with sugar. Likewise, one may drink a decoction of the stalks and stems of the *kumuda* and *utpala* lotuses along with their leaves, according to one's capacity; thus one is generally liberated from *vārimeha*. Furthermore, one should subsist on milk and eat a measured diet of barley food.
One should mix equal parts of sugar with honey; by drinking this with cold water, one is liberated from ambumeha.
6.7.28 Thus, these sixteen treatments for the destruction of prameha, each individually removing kapha and pitta, have been proclaimed by me.
6.7.29 Those arising from vāta should be known as incurable and extremely severe; because of their extreme subtlety, they penetrate deeply and flow like a stream.

Having observed a patient suffering from *majjaprameha* (urinary discharge of marrow), one should treat him frequently with well-prepared *āsthāpana* (non-unctuous enemas) and *anuvāsana* (unctuous enemas) that alleviate *vāta*. 6.7.29–30.
Every morning, one should consume only honey and ghee, especially with meals consisting of *koradūṣa* grain or barley that have been soaked overnight.

(6.7.31) In this manner, one should diligently overcome elephant-like urinary disorders (*hastimeha*) through enemas and sudation therapies. Alternatively, being diligent, one may treat wind-type urinary disorders (*vātameha*) by consuming goat urine. (6.7.32)

One should cause the elephant to drink and also make it walk [with substances] that cause fear of urinary disorders (gajameha); with these decoctions, bitter and pungent tastes, one should drink milk.

6.7.34 Then, having carefully observed this procedure as taught in the treatise and having determined [the specific case] for each individual, the wise physician should treat the types of *prameha*. 6.7.35 This treatment for *prameha* has been declared in detail, according to the facts and in proper sequence, for the sake of accomplishing the welfare of the disciples. Thus spoke the Blessed Ātreya. Thus ends the seventh chapter in the *Bhela-cikitsita*. Chapter Eight: Now we shall explain the treatment of insanity (*unmāda*). Thus spoke the Blessed Ātreya.
Five types of insanity have been fully described in the section on etiology (nidāna), along with their symptoms and origins; now hear their treatment.
For even the activity of those [faculties]—the mind, the intellect, and the senses—is directed by it. The mind is superior to all the senses; it resides within the head and the palate.
Situated there, it indeed perceives the objects of the senses, such as taste and the rest, which are close at hand, and it governs the three states of being.
6.8.3–4 Furthermore, the mind residing in the heart is the source of the *sumanas* flower, it consists of all the sense faculties, it is the cause of all cognitions, and it is the vital strength.
6.8.5 Mind is the cause of all actions, both these and others. Those with a virtuous mind follow the path of the righteous; those with a wicked mind go astray.

6.8.6 Having understood the mind through the intellect (*manas*), one should exert control over it from there. From that, the intellect arises, which deliberates upon what ought to be done and what ought not to be done.

For it is the intellect that is intended as the awakening when one performs both the auspicious and the inauspicious; and because of this awakening of what is to be awakened, a person is called "wise" (budha) here in this world.
6.8.8 That is the intellect (*buddhi*) and that is the supreme self (*paramātman*), which is proclaimed to reside within the body; just as a skillful artisan applies action among men.
6.8.9 These are the locations of the mind (*manas*), consciousness (*citta*), and intellect (*buddhi*), as well as their functions. Now hear further the cause for their becoming thoroughly corrupted.
When the aggravated doshas move upward and remain within the head and the palate, they quickly corrupt the mind; consequently, the consciousness becomes impaired. (6.8.10)

6.8.11 When the mind (*citta*) falls into distress, the intellect (*buddhi*) meets its destruction; consequently, when the intellect is impaired, one no longer discerns what ought to be done and what ought not to be done. 6.8.12 In this manner, the terrible disease known as insanity (*unmāda*) proceeds. Therefore, I shall explain the specific distinctions between insanity and intoxication (*mada*).
6.8.12–13: When the mind and consciousness are agitated by grief, anger, joy, or the loss of possessions, one should quickly restrain that intoxication.
6.8.14 He broods, perspires, and weeps without cause; he laughs unexpectedly, is drowsy, speaks little, and is constantly restless.
6.8.15 The embodied being is terrified, irascible, and shameless; he gazes ahead and does not act as he truly is.
6.8.15–16 Roughness of the body hairs as well as turbidity of the eyes— these symptoms in one who possesses them are proclaimed as "madah" (intoxication).

6.8.17 But when intoxication increases further, it results in insanity (*unmāda*). It exhibits symptoms arising from *vāta*, as well as those originating from *śleṣman* and *pitta*. 6.8.18 Insanity is described by the wise as being of the nature of a *sannipāta* (the combination of all three humors). This definition of insanity has been set forth according to its etymological derivation.

Listen now to their treatment as previously indicated in the *Nidāna* [section]: one should employ the fivefold therapeutic procedure (*pañcakarman*) consisting of oleation (*snehana*) and sudation (*svedana*).

6.8.20 One should drink ghee prepared with sour milk (*dādhika*), or oil from the *śirīṣa* tree, or *balā*-oil processed a hundred times, or the *mahāpaiśācika* ghee. 6.8.21 Likewise, one suffering from insanity (*unmatta*) should habitually consume the *dādhika* preparation, the great alkali (*mahākṣāra*), and that which has been declared as the medical treatment for the destruction of epilepsy (*apasmāra*).
One should apply that same [punishment] in all cases of intoxication. One should cause him to be killed with whips, or likewise bind and beat him.
6.8.23 Or else, one should terrify [the enemy] with an elephant, a horse, or a serpent; or again, one should scatter grass fires from all sides.
6.8.24 Or, having scattered burning coals of the *pāribhadraka* tree, one should then sprinkle them repeatedly with cold water.
He may cause [the victim] to be cast into a river or onto a path to perish; or he may cause him to wither from hunger by casting the man into a well.
6.8.26 Men with weapons in their hands should frighten him with unprecedented terrors; the physicians should terrify him with various kinds of alarms.
6.8.27 For intense alarms cause a derangement of the mind through fear; indeed, fear itself is said to be the greatest affliction for the mind.
One whose mind is deranged may wander about even while being threatened with weapons; followed by a troop of children, one should designate such a case as incurable.
6.8.29 One should treat insanity with sudation, collyrium, nasal drops, alkaline substances, and alkaline anti-toxins, as well as those remedies prescribed for the alleviation of epilepsy.
6.8.30 Furthermore, one should have him drink aged ghee which destroys insanity; that which has stood for a hundred years is called the "excellent Kumbhasarpi" (pot-ghee).

6.8.30–31: For those suffering from insanity, sour gruel (kāñjika) and garlic, beneficial for drinking, massage, nasal administration, and as an arrow-poison [remedy], should always be ground with goat's urine.
This application combined with aged ghee is for those suffering from insanity; the physician specializing in internal medicine (kāyacikitsaka) should employ these treatments.

6.8.33 The physician who treats those afflicted by *bhūtas* should perform propitiatory rites (*śāntikarman*) and burnt offerings (*homa*). Sacrifices (*iṣṭi*), propitiatory rites, burnt offerings, and auspicious ceremonies (*svastyayana*)—these ritual procedures prescribed in the Vedas should be performed to destroy madness. Thus spoke the Blessed Ātreya. This concludes the eighth chapter in the *Bhela-cikitsita*. The Ninth Chapter. Now, therefore, we shall explain the treatment of epilepsy (*apasmāra*). Thus spoke the Blessed Ātreya. 6.8.33
6.9.1 The complete nature and the etiology of apasmāra have been stated; now learn from me its treatment in detail.
6.9.2 From falling from an elephant, a horse, or a vehicle, from injury, from vertigo, and from the loss of a beloved object, the mind falls into delusion.
6.9.2–3 When his mind is thus wandering, his heart becomes parched; the vital air, reaching the channel that carries water, obstructs the heat.

6.9.4 Overwhelmed by intense thirst, he falls into delusion and suffers from epilepsy; the epileptic patient suffers convulsions and emits foam while trembling. 6.9.5 He should consume Śirīṣa oil, as well as Kalyāṇaka ghee, Mahāpaiśācika, Mahākṣāra, or Dādhika.
Hemp seeds, *kaiḍarya*, *cāpalūnaka*, *rūpasthā*, *vayasthā*, *capūtanā*, and *keśamāriṇī*.

6.9.7 Triphalā, tryūṣaṇa, mustā, garlic, and pāpacelikā—these taken in equal parts, along with muscle fat, oil, and ghee; 6.9.8 And likewise wool-wool (ūrṇaka), one should cook them together combined with cow’s urine. When it has been ignited and then extinguished, one should remove it from the fire.

One should drink one *biḍālapada* (cat's paw) measure of this alkali with lukewarm water; it removes epilepsy and destroys insanity, as well as hemorrhoids, abdominal tumors, urinary disorders, splenic enlargement, and diseases of the abdomen. The Tenth Chapter.
6.10.0 If diarrhea occurs due to fear or grief,
6.10.1 that diarrhea should for the most part be treated with *sāma* [purgatives]; therefore, one should treat all cases of diarrhea with fasting (*laṅghana*).

6.10.1–2 One should cause a strong person to undergo fasting and administer digestive stimulants; however, for one who is weak, one should administer a combination therapy similar to that used for one who has undergone purgation.
6.10.3 If the abdomen of a person is stiff, heavy, and as if distended, and the individual has many morbid humors (doṣas) despite being treated with digestive stimulants (dīpanīya),

[one should administer a purgative]. 6.10.4 One should cause the patient to drink a potent purgative (sraṃsana) combined with digestive stimulants, which is passed slowly and in small amounts, is suppressed, and is accompanied by pain.
When his channels have been purified and the doshas have been loosened, it is easy to effect their extraction, as well as their digestion or stabilization.
6.10.6 One should cause [the patient] to drink harītakī, trikaṭuka, hiṅgu, sauvarcala, vacā, and white ativiṣā with warm water.
6.10.7 This invariably arrests diarrhea accompanied by flatulence and pain, even when it has become greatly aggravated, just as the shore restrains the ocean.
6.10.7–6.10.8: One should cause [the patient] to drink harītakī, ativiṣā, hiṅgu, sauvarcala, vacā, and rock salt (saindhava), all ground together with warm water.
6.10.9 This formulation for the treatment of *āmātisāra* has been prescribed by physicians; it should be administered by a physician seeking fame once the decoction has been properly prepared.
6.10.10 Indeed, that *āmātisāra* which does not cease through these two formulations cannot be cured even by hundreds of other methods.
For the most part, abdominal disease arising from undigested matter (āma) and characterized by kapha occurs in men; listen now properly to its treatment.
6.10.12 Citraka, the root of pippalī, vacā, kaṭukarohiṇī, pāṭhā, seeds of vatsaka, harītakī, and mahauṣadha (ginger);
6.10.13 this [formula] certainly binds the stool in cases of diarrhea arising from undigested matter (āma), accompanied by pain, and characterized by kapha and pitta.
6.10.13–14 Pāṭhā, vacā, the three pungents (trikaṭuka), kuṣṭha, and kaṭukarohiṇī— when these are properly boiled, they destroy kapha-type diarrhea.
6.10.15 Bhallātaka, śakrayava, pāṭhā, kaṭukarohiṇī, yavānī, ajājī,
kuṣṭha, citraka, and ativiṣā; 6.10.16 śaṭī, puṣkaramūla, as well as hiṅgu, harītakī, sauvarcala, and śṛṅgavera— one should grind these with cow’s urine.
6.10.16–17 One should have those boluses, measuring the size of an *akṣa*, dried in the shade and stored away. One or two of them should be drunk with lukewarm water.

This indeed cures dysentery accompanied by pain that has arisen from undigested matter (āmaja), and it likewise expels hemorrhoids just as the sun dispels the darkness. Furthermore, those formulations proclaimed for stimulating the digestive fire (grahaṇī-dīpanīya) should be employed in cases of kapha-type dysentery, as well as alkaline preparations and sugar with alkali (kṣāraguḍa).
This treatment for those with diarrhea caused by *āma* and also for those with diarrhea caused by *kapha* has been fully described; now hear that for those with diarrhea caused by *pitta*.
6.10.21 Now, that diarrhea which arises from bile (pitta) and causes excessive evacuation— learn from me how one should properly pacify it once it has been ripened.
6.10.22 Equal parts of viḍa salt, unripe bilva fruits, tamarind, pomegranate, sauvarcala salt, dhātakī, and samaṅgā [should be used].
6.10.22–23 This paste, ground into a fine powder, should be drunk with warm water at dawn; it cures immediately a man afflicted by pitta-type diarrhea and colic.
6.10.24 One should cause [the patient] to drink *rasāñjana*, *ativiṣā*, the fruit and bark of *kuṭaja*, *dhātakī*, and *śṛṅgavera* with rice-water. 6.10.25 Combined with honey,
this dispels severe *pitta*-type diarrhea, kindles the dull digestive fire, and quickly alleviates colic pain.
6.10.25–26 Pāṭhā, dāruharidrā, and the root of pippalī, as well as the fruit and bark of vatsaka, and likewise śṛṅgavera.
6.10.27 One should have these— ambaṣṭhakī, śilodbheda, dhātakī, and amlavetasa— ground into a paste and administered with rice-water.
6.10.28 [Likewise, one may administer] uśīra, bāla, hrībera, the bark of the pomegranate, mahauṣadha, the fruit of the jambū, the pulp of the kapittha, and the tender fruit of the bilva.
One should have these same [drugs] administered with equal parts in rice-water mixed with honey; this dispels the symptoms of Pitta-type diarrhea.
One should destroy *parikartikā* (cutting pain) along with its wind and its root by using *samaṅgā*, *nicula*, *lodhra*, *dhātakī*, and likewise *madhuka*. Furthermore,
one may use the sprouts of the *vaṭa* tree and *lodhra*, the fruit and bark of the pomegranate, *māṣaparṇī*, *śilodbheda*, and also *sāmbaṣṭhaka*.
In cases of diarrhea caused by pitta, one should administer a mixture of *samaṅgā*, *dhātakī* flowers, and *ambaṣṭhaka*, combined with rice-water.

6.10.33 In cases of *pittātisāra* (bilious diarrhea), a person should drink lotus (*padma*) with rice-water; or [the blood of] a rabbit or a deer, along with *madhuka* and black clay. 6.10.34 In *pittātisāra*, these should be administered mixed with rice-water. When *pittātisāra* is vitiated and has taken refuge in the deep-seated locations (*gambhīrasthāna*), it must be treated thus.
When blood is discharged excessively, that is the blood-born type of dysentery (*raktaja-atīsāra*). [The remedy consists of] blue lotus (*nīlotpala*), *bilva*, sesame, *madhuka*, jaggery, and sugar.

6.10.36 The filaments of the white lotus (*puṇḍarīka*), the water lily (*kumuda*), and honey, when drunk with goat’s milk, destroy bloody diarrhea (*raktātīsāra*). [Nirvāhi... 6.10.37 Furthermore, for one suffering from diarrhea who has a stimulated digestive fire (*dīptāgni*) but diminished muscle mass (*kṣīṇamāṃsa*) and is accompanied by pain (*saśūla*), one should administer the *anuyukti* treatment that generates fecal matter (*varcojananī*).

From the middle of the large goat, [one should take] the omentum along with blood; this, prepared with curd and barley-gruel (*yāvaka*), and combined with jaggery and the three pungents (*trikaṭuka*).
6.10.39 With that, one should feed the person at the proper time once their body has been well-steamed with mild heat. By this same method, one should prepare the meat of the boar and the curlew.
6.10.40 And by this very same method, one should prepare the cock, the partridge, the tortoise, the lizard, the peacock, and the francolin as well.
6.10.40–41 This treatment has been described for those suffering from vāta-type diarrhea; in cases of vāta-type diarrhea, all the treatments prescribed for hemorrhoids (arśas) should also be applied.
6.10.42 Whether it arises from fear or from grief, whichever *doṣa* becomes aggravated when diarrhea occurs, one should treat that specific *doṣa*.
6.10.43 Wise friends should constantly console him and gladden his mind; then he will become well.
One whose entire body is stiff, who is discolored and motionless, and who does not perceive pain— one such as this should be abandoned.

6.10.45 He whose hair falls out, whose strength and complexion diminish, and whose mouth is parched— one such as this does not survive. 6.10.46 He who lies writhing, tossing all his limbs about, with stiffened limbs and unable to move— such a person should be abandoned.
One who repeatedly gnaws at the jaw, does not feel pain when it is struck, and excessively licks the tongue— such a person should be declared to have reached the end of his life.
6.10.48 A wise man, while guarding his reputation, should not associate with one who destroys wealth and reputation; he should not perform any action that ruins either wealth or fame.
6.10.49 He who acts after discerning what is achievable and what is unachievable succeeds; he receives great honor and shines resplendent among the learned.

6.10.49–50: Now I shall describe the symptoms and the medical treatment of *viṣūcī* (cholera-like dysentery), [which occurs] in those who consume incompatible foods, heavy meals, flour-based foods, vegetables, and dry meat broths.

6.10.51 In those who constantly eat while suffering from indigestion, three bodily constituents (dhātus) become aggravated. The strength of that [aggravated] humor, having arisen, is further increased by the wind (vāyu). 6.10.52 It obstructs the channels (srotas) below, above, and across; and when the channels are obstructed by the wind, it further blocks those very channels.
When these [channels] are overwhelmed by the humors (doṣas) and by the vitiated essence of food, its movement occurs with great difficulty, both upward and downward.

6.10.54 They censure that lingering *viṣūcikā*, which is like poison, in proportion as the humor (*rasa*) produced in the bodies has resorted to the poison. 6.10.55 Having thrown the channels (*nāḍī*) into disorder, it increases the *balāsaka* (phlegm); its symptoms are cough, fever, fainting, aversion to food, and discoloration.
6.10.55–56: Exhaustion, indigestion, excessive secretion of phlegm, dysentery, oppression in the chest, as well as heart disease and rumbling in the intestines.
6.10.57 Obstruction and wasting of the limbs—this is the terrible disease called alasaka (intestinal torpor). It is characterized by nausea, trembling, vomiting, burning heat, cramps, and fever.
6.10.58 There is labored breathing, flatulence, diarrhea, an aversion to food, excessive coughing with phlegm, yawning, and a gripping pain in the heart.
Likewise, dyspnea, cough, accompanied by pain in the flanks and head, as well as perspiration and coldness of the limbs, are the premonitory symptoms of *viṣūcī*.

6.10.60 Eructation, heaviness of the stomach, and retention of urine, flatus, and feces— these five are declared to be the symptoms of *annavibhrama* (disturbance of digestion). 6.10.61 In that case, one should administer the entire treatment prescribed for those suffering from *āmātisāra* (diarrhea caused by undigested matter), as well as the complications previously mentioned regarding *viṣūcī* and *āmasa*.
The physician should treat them properly with their respective therapeutic measures. This has been declared as the treatment for visūcī in brief. (6.10.61–62)
6.10.63 Because this disease is so severe, I shall speak further in detail regarding the premonitory symptoms of *viṣūcī*, so that the physician, having understood them, may act.
6.10.64 One should promptly induce emesis with warm saline water; until the patient remains free from it, there is no comfort other than its expulsion.
A decoction made from *kāraka* or prepared with *arjuna*, when drunk as a decoction, acts as an emetic and immediately destroys cholera (*viṣūcikā*).

6.10.66 Likewise, a paste (kalka) consisting of mustā and other ingredients, combined with a paste of pippalī, when drunk with warm water, quickly destroys viṣūcikā. 6.10.67 For incompatible tastes, once consumed and corrupted by the vāta and other doṣas, become like poison within the bodies, having first increased in the receptacle of waste (malāśaya).

Therefore, one should quickly employ all treatments that are equal in potency to poison: medicinal smokes (dhūma), decoctions (kaṣāya), suppositories (varti), as well as ointments (pradeha) and rubbing-pastes (utsādana).

6.10.69 For *viṣūcī* (cholera-like dysentery), one should administer the following treatments: squeezing (*avapīḍana*), blowing [medicinal smoke] (*pradhamana*), cauterization (*agnikarman*), poultices (*upanāhana*), tactile therapies (*saṃsparśa*), and various other supportive measures (*upacāra*).

6.10.70 [The following substances are used for these purposes: *bhallātaka*, the three pungents (*trikaṭuka*), *pūtika*, *kṣavaka*, *balā*, *phaṇijja*, garlic (*laśuna*), *kuṣṭha*, and the fruits of *karañja*.

6.10.70. The king should always protect his own self by means of his ministers, his ministers by means of his treasury, and the treasury by means of his army. For one who has neither self nor ministers, how can there be a treasury or an army? And for one who lacks these four, where is the kingdom? Therefore, a king should constantly exert himself to protect these four. For it is said: "The self is protected by means of the ministers, the ministers by means of the treasury, and the treasury by means of the army; thus, through the protection of these four, the kingdom is secured. Furthermore: "A king who protects his subjects with righteousness, as a father protects his sons, attains both worlds and is honored by the virtuous. Moreover: "One should protect the weak by means of the strong, and the strong by means of the weak; for a king who knows the proper time and place secures the entire earth. Thus ends the section on the protection of the self and the like.

6.10.71 One should grind together triphalā, yavānī, and the fruits of kuṭaja; this beneficial suppository, named Śivā, should be prepared with goat’s urine. (Bhṣ 6.10.2.1) When the jawbones are locked, the patient speaks indistinctly; or even when the jaws are well-joined, he cannot utter anything at all. (Bhṣ 6.10.2.2) The drinking of fats, nasal medication (nasya), fomentations (sveda), wholesome diets, poultices (upanāha), and enemas (vasti) are recommended and beneficial for facial paralysis (ardita). (Bhṣ 6.10.2.3–4) In one droṇa of curd and sour gruel (āranāla), or half a droṇa of fat (vasā) as available, along with the meat of marshy and aquatic animals as available, sesame seeds, horse gram (kuluttha), black gram (māṣa), jujube (badara), barley, balā, the two groups of five roots (pañcamūla), rāsnā, śatamūlā, and śatāvarī—having collected all these, one should cook them over a gentle fire. With the steam rising from that, one should apply fomentation by means of a tube (nāḍīsveda). (Bhṣ 6.10.2.5–7) One should also cook oil with these same ingredients and use it for massage and internal consumption. One should also prepare a poultice using this very same collection of materials. Whatever treatment has been described for the destruction of wind-diseases (vātavyādhi), all of that in its entirety should be applied for cases of facial paralysis as well. (Bhṣ 6.10.2.8–9) One should employ Mahāsneha, Balā-taila, or Śirīṣa-taila for drinking, massage, nasal medication, or enema. One should mince the meat of marshy animals into a paste (veśavāra) and, with that not too oily preparation, apply a poultice to the patient. (Bhṣ 6.10.2.10–12) When the wind (vāyu) is obstructed by phlegm (śleṣman) in this condition, dryness arises in the temples, the head, and the cheeks. The person becomes mute, overcome by sleep, breathes heavily through the throat, is excessively covered in saliva, and his tongue becomes crooked. (Bhṣ 6.10.2.13) Such a case of facial paralysis is declared to be "obstructed by phlegm" (śleṣmopaṣṭabdha). For him, one should administer an unctuous enema (anuvāsana) as well as head-purgatives (śīrṣavirecana). (Bhṣ 6.10.2.14–15) He should be purged with Tilvaka or with Bindu-ghee; or he may drink old clarified butter (sarpis) or consume sharp medicinal smoke (dhūma). Once the phlegm has subsided, his treatment should consist of nourishing therapies (bṛṃhaṇa), and one should also carry out the treatment for wind-diseases as previously stated. In that state, the phlegm is situated in its own place while the wind is considered an "invader" (āgantuka); therefore, having observed their movement, one should perform wind-alleviating treatments. Thus said the venerable Ātreya. Thus ends the twenty-sixth chapter [of the sixth section] in the Bheḷa-saṃhitā. Chapter Eleven: Now we shall explain the treatment of malabsorption syndrome (grahaṇī). Thus said the venerable Ātreya.
Fire, wind, and the vital breaths of human beings are established therein; strength, health, and lifespan, as well as pleasure and pain, have that as their support.

6.11.2 For one dies when the fire is extinguished, and one lives when the heat is joined [with it]. Therefore, one should know that for embodied beings, the vital breath (*prāṇa*) and life itself are rooted in the fire. 6.11.3 That fire distributes well-eaten food downward for the sake of the nutrient essence (*rasa*); by means of that, a person obtains strength of the senses, nourishment, and complexion.
6.11.3–4 Fire digests food in four ways: equally, sharply, gently, and irregularly. Among these, that fire which is equal is praised.

6.11.5 For those who constantly indulge in heavy and dry food, as well as in sleeping during the day; for those who do not sleep at night, or who suppress their natural urges; 6.11.6 For those who eat before the previous meal is digested, those who have undergone excessive oleation or purgation, and likewise for those suffering from fever due to addiction to alcohol or the consumption of unwholesome things.
6.11.6–7 From the constant consumption of sweet foods and milk, as well as from frequenting water-sports, and from the habitual eating of flour-based foods, curd, and unpalatable vegetables;
6.11.8 By the habitual consumption of such things, the *grahaṇī* of a person becomes vitiated; it becomes provoked in three ways—as sluggish, sharp, or excessively irregular.
6.11.9 Likewise, diseases arising from the disorder of the *grahaṇī* manifest in men: fever, cough, anemia (*pāṇḍuroga*), edema, and cutting pain in the rectum (*parikartikā*).
Loss of appetite, indigestion, abdominal tumors, hemorrhoids, fistula-in-ano, diarrhea, skin diseases, colic, alasaka, and vertigo.

6.11.11 These and other diseases may arise in this person who eats in excess; or, the *grahaṇī* of the creature being vitiated, it destroys the *sāma* (digestive heat). 6.11.12 For one who eats sweet foods, when the bodily fire (*kāyāgni*) is overwhelmed by phlegm (*śleṣman*), food is not digested in due time; he is known as having weak digestion (*mandāgni*).
When the digestive fire is weak due to kapha, food consumed is not digested quickly; further weakened by the consumption of heavy foods, it becomes even more sluggish.

6.11.14 When such symptoms appear and the patient is aged, yet the kapha does not subside, this condition is called the irregular *grahaṇī-doṣa*. 6.11.15 In one whose digestive fire (*agni*) becomes excessively provoked due to the depletion of *soma*, whatever is eaten is digested, yet it does not lead to health, complexion, or strength.
