Even after eating and eating, hunger arises for him and he does not thrive; one should know that as *atyagni*, and it is considered the most painful [of all]. 6.11.16
6.11.17 Thus, this threefold disease localized in the *grahaṇī* has been described by me; now learn from me its treatment in detail.
6.11.18 One should drink either *dhānvantara* ghee or *prājāpatya* ghee; thereafter, one should administer emesis to him, and after that, purgation.
Or one should drink the *pippalī-vardhamāna* formulation, or even alkaline substances and astringents; one may also drink buttermilk for a month, or indeed the *gaṇḍīra-ariṣṭa*.

6.11.20 One should drink ghee mixed with curd (*dādhika*), or oil from the *śirīṣa* tree, or the great *pañcagavya*. Chapter Sixteen, Verse 20. 6.12.1 In cases of urinary obstruction (*mūtrāghāta*), one should administer a decoction of *tālapattrī*; a meal consisting of the meat of a crane (*krauñca*) is recommended for urinary obstructions.
Having ground his bone, one should have it drunk with milk; this pacifies dysuria and even breaks up urinary calculi.

6.12.3 If, however, the gravel (śarkarā) is not relieved by these applications, a surgeon who is highly learned and experienced in practice should extract it. 6.12.4 Listen now to the treatment for one whose difficulty in urination occurs due to the obstruction of the organ, accompanied by non-suppurating pain (anusanna-śūla).
One who has been well-anointed with *balā*-oil and fomented with warm water should be administered an *āsthāpana* enema using a digestive (*pācana*) formulation beginning with *mustā*.
6.12.6 When the enema has returned, one should feed him prepared rice with thin mung bean soup or with the meat broth of wild animals.
6.12.7 Thereafter, he should lie down together with a woman who has bathed and anointed herself, who wears clean garments, who is beloved, and who possesses auspicious qualities.
When the path of the semen is purified, the vital air (māruta) becomes functional; once the vital air has reached its own proper place, his painful condition ceases.

6.12.9 This treatment for the eight types of dysuria (mūtrakṛcchra), as well as the symptoms of all of them, has been declared for the benefit of the disciples. Thus spoke the Blessed Ātreya. Thus ends the twelfth chapter of the Bhela [Saṃhitā]. Chapter Thirteen: Now, therefore, we shall explain the treatment of abdominal enlargements (udara). Thus said the Blessed Ātreya.
6.13.1 In one whose body is afflicted by heavy burdens and who consumes pungent and bitter substances, the Vāyu situated throughout the entire body becomes vitiated and strikes the vessels (sirāḥ).
For by going [to eat], one fills the stomach and likewise causes flatulence; the abdomen becomes distended all around like a leather bag.
6.13.3 One should recognize this as *vātodara* (wind-belly), accompanied by these symptoms: it is bound with black streaks and likewise covered with black hair.
6.13.4 A person who, tormented by heat, consumes burning foods; or one who, having ceased physical exercise, drinks water while exhausted; [develops this condition].
In his body, the deranged *kapha* has entered the *kapha*-carrying vessels; having increased and become vitiated, it has taken refuge within the internal cavity (*koṣṭha*).
6.13.6 It causes the entire abdominal cavity to distend and produces pain; it is covered with white streaks like lotus fibers and likewise overspread with white hair.

6.13.7 His limbs become flaccid and salivation occurs from the mouth; foul odor of the mouth, lethargy, and phlegm—these are the characteristics of the patient with *udararoga* (abdominal enlargement).
6.13.7–8 For one who consumes all types of tastes and engages in improper diet and lifestyle, his abdomen appears excessively distended, as if it were half-filled by another person.
6.13.9 And likewise, the abdomen in the *sānnipātika* type is bound by various membranes, covered with various hairs, and filled with various channels (*vedanā*).
6.13.10 They declare that when a woman’s pregnancy is caused by her own [past] actions, there is an obstruction of the ears, as well as whiteness of the tongue and dirt on the nails.
6.13.10–11: Human fat, body hair, the menstrual blood of women, and feces— when these are administered, it results in *bhakta-duṣṭodara* (stomach disorder caused by contaminated food).
6.13.12 A condition known as *dūṣyodara* arises in men due to the derangement of all three humors (*sānnipātika*); it is bound by veins of all colors and possesses a bluish-yellow luster.
6.13.13 In that case, body ache, cough, dyspnea, and hiccups arise; furthermore, excessive sleep, lethargy, laziness, and a burning sensation throughout the limbs occur.
There is a sinking of all the limbs, emaciation, and a pale complexion; furthermore, whatever symptoms arise from drinking poison, those also manifest in this condition.
6.13.15 Thus, by these symptoms, one with *dūṣyodara* (vitiated abdominal enlargement) meets death. He who, having risen in the morning, always drinks water without having eaten;
6.13.16 and he who drinks excessive water during the rainy season and the winter—his abdomen suffers great pain, and other complications arise as well.
A sense of sitting down, horripilation, coldness of the digestive fire, stiffness of the head, as well as a glossy appearance and being covered with oily body hair.

6.13.18–19: By all these symptoms combined, one should recognize that water-accumulation (*udakodara*) has occurred in men. When the intestine is perforated by a *śaṅku* (a sharp probe), by the piercing of a tendon, or by the spines of fish; or when it is pierced by undigested dung, the tips of grass, or other such objects, then food and drink will flow out through that opening into the interior of the abdomen.
From that, the abdomen becomes elevated all around; furthermore, long veins appear in the four regions adjacent to the belly. 6.13.20

6.13.21 The symptoms for a distended abdomen with discharge have been fully described. When a man jumps, leaps, or exerts himself excessively, 6.13.22 his intestines are thereby pierced and twisted together;
likewise, having eaten muñja grass and hair, the intestine becomes entangled.
By that [wind], the rectum of men becomes constricted due to the compression of the intestines; likewise, the abdomen becomes distended and the penis becomes contracted.
6.13.24 One whose eyes, testicles, and hands are swollen, as well as whose feet and anus are swollen, and even one whose limbs are numb, is born [with these afflictions].
6.13.25 A man who eats and consumes raw grains and barley may become one whose belly is bound [by disease], being uneven with depressions and elevations.
Having eaten the fruit with its filaments, one should drink water; and immediately after eating, one may employ elephants, horses, chariots, and vehicles.
6.13.27–28: The physician [should take] mahauṣadha, black pepper, the two alkalis (kṣāra), triphalā, vacā, yavānī, kuñcikā, asafoetida (hiṅgu), tamarind (tintriṇīkā), and amlavetasa;
dhānyaka, ajagandhā, trāyantī, pomegranate (dāḍima), and yavāsaka; and kaṭukā, seeds of kuṭaja, and rock salt (saindhava)—all in equal parts.

6.13.28–29 Trivṛt, saptalā, dantī, kampilla, nīlikā, abhayā, and suvarṇakṣīrī— these should all be powdered together, with each subsequent ingredient being double the quantity of the preceding one. 6.13.29
6.13.30 Having steeped it for seven days in cow’s milk or urine, one should add double the amount of sugar here; one should drink this with *tryaṅgula*.
6.13.31 The powder of *suvarṇasamaka*—an antidote for the pain of all diseases—is to be taken with cow’s urine, *triphalā*, alkaline liquids, wines, or lukewarm water.
It destroys all types of abdominal enlargements, splenic disorders, consumption, abdominal tumors, and heart disease; it also cures Vātāṣṭhīlā, constipation, and swelling affecting all the limbs.
6.13.33 One should conquer *halīmaka*, *āmila*, *pāṇḍu*, and *prameha* accompanied by fever; having placed one's life in jeopardy, the consumer of the stomach (*jaṭharī*) should drink poison.
6.13.34 Or else, one should have him bitten by an enraged black cobra on either a cucumber, a gourd, or a radish; the consumer of the stomach should then eat those.
Having opened the abdomen with a measuring instrument and inspected the cavity of the intestine, one should then cause an ant-bite to be applied to the opening within the intestine.

6.13.36 Once the intestines have been drawn out through the opening, the physician should then sew up the abdominal wall; in this manner, the doctor should treat a case of *chidrodara* (intestinal perforation) for the patient who underwent surgery.

6.13.37 Likewise, one who is learned in the science of surgery (*śalya-śāstra*) should incise a case of *baddhaguda* (intestinal obstruction); having extracted the obstructing material such as *muñja* grass or hair, the physician should then sew the anus closed.
For the stomachs of those who do not engage in physical activity are full of fluids; therefore, one skilled in the application of surgical instruments should cause pain within them.
6.13.39 Leaving four finger-breadths below the left side of the abdomen, or from the navel, the physician should insert the instrument with the proper measure.
6.13.40 The physician should drain the abdomen of the patient afflicted by disease, massage the belly, and then wrap it with a bandage.
Furthermore, the wind does not cause his abdomen, though wrapped [with a bandage], to become distended. Thereafter, he should drink gruel that is free from salt and unctuous substances.
Thereafter, one should treat [the patient] with milk for half a month; then, for three months, the physician should administer a gruel of barley with milk.
From that point, one should eat a light meal without salt for three months; thereafter, it is said that salt may be added to the food, even when the condition has shifted to the abdomen.

Some authorities maintain that salt should be administered to those suffering from abdominal tumors (*ketūdarāṇām*) because it acts as a *yogavāha* (a vehicle for other substances); however, certain physicians state that the application of fire (*agnikarma*) is indicated for the abdomen.

6.13.45 When the abdomen has not yet produced fluid and is caused by the accumulation of wind (vāta) and phlegm (kapha), the digestive fire (agni) destroys the enlargement of the spleen (plīhodara); therefore, one should especially conquer it [at that stage].

6.13.46 Cessation [of treatment] has been described; therein, for one suffering from ascites (salilodara), [treatment continues] as long as the thin gruel (peyā) is effective against the abdominal swelling.
6.13.46–47 That which is formed as a circular swelling, soft to the touch, not producing a sound when struck, and not covered with moving streaks [is a *maṇḍala*]. 6.13.47

6.13.48 When being stepped upon at the navel, [the patient] glides away only gently; from that, one should indicate the emergence of fluid through slight emissions. One should also observe all the functions of the embodied beings, both those involving action and those involving effort.

6.13.49 Here, there should be one *āṭhaka* of *bhallātaka* fruits that have been struck by the wind and fallen from their stalks. Having rubbed them with fine particles of brick powder and washed them, one should release them into a strong breeze.

Once it is dried, one should again crush it into pieces and throw it into four times as much water. When reduced to one-fourth, it should be strained and cooled; then one should cook it again with an equal amount of milk. 6.13.50

6.13.51 Having soaked it with half that amount of sugar and mixed it with the powder of *lohābhaya*, *vyoṣa*, and *kaca*, one should then add an equal amount of sugar and a quarter-part of sugar, stir it with a churning-stick (*khaja*), and set it aside. 6.13.52 Then, with two *prasthas* of *āmalaka* juice, once it has cooled, one should cook it again with *dhānya*. After seven nights, having acquired its potency, it surpasses even the essence of nectar (*sudhārasa*).

To those who have purified their bodies in the morning, one should administer the dose appropriate for their own physical constitution. There is no need to avoid food or drink, nor heat, wind, travel, or sexual intercourse.
A living being may become utterly like Narasiṃha, and a man may become as substantial as a heap of gold; even decayed teeth grow back again, and white hair becomes black once more.

6.13.55 Even one whose ears, fingers, and nose are shattered, even one who has come within the reach of the teeth of Death, even a leper—even he gradually grows back, like a tree with branches of limbs and fingers when sprinkled with water. [He] conquers great peacocks by his voice, elephants by his strength, and horses by his speed. [His] power of mindfulness and intelligence is [unfailing]. The Fourteenth Chapter.
6.13.55 (repeated)
6.14.1 Vaṃśaka, naktamāla, mūrvā, kaṭukarohiṇī, tarkārī, pragraha, pīlus,
and niculas; 6.14.2 Asana, saptaparṇa, triphalā, and maricas— one should prepare a decoction from these in equal parts.
6.14.2–3 A person should drink these very powders with honey; or one should eat boiled rice prepared with this same decoction.
6.14.4 The roots of *picumanda*, *citraka*, and *hastipippalī*; the bark, leaves, fruit, and root of *karañja*, as well as *sarṣapa*—
6.14.5 all these taken in equal parts, together with earth from an anthill, ground finely with cow’s urine, constitute an excellent unguent for rubbing the body.
6.14.5–6 Rāsnā, vacā, arka root, hiṃsrā, and likewise dantī; śatapuṣpā, kuṣṭha, the two types of haridrā, and punarnavā.
6.14.7 Apāmārga, śārivā, naktamālikā, and ant-hill earth— this mixture with horse urine is an excellent unguent for rubbing the body.
6.14.8 Karaja, surasa, bilva, devadāru, vacā, arjuna, tarkārī, meṣaśṛṅgī, śobhāñjanaka, and āraṇī.

6.14.8–9: With both *bṛhatī* [species], *śyonāka*, *śvadaṃṣṭrā*, *khadira*, and *asanā*— these being equal in their efficacy when prepared in water— one should perform a sprinkling with this decoction (*kaṣāya*).
6.14.10 One should apply a plaster made of these same drugs ground with milk. By this method, ūrustambha (stiffness of the thighs) is quickly pacified.
6.14.11 [The following are used:
the two *pañcamūlas*, *triphalā*, *citraka*, *devadāru*, *ekāṣṭhīlā*, *apāmārga*, *śreyasī*, *vāyasī*, and *sudhā*.
6.14.11–12 Kālā, bhārṅgī, pṛthakparṇī, suvahā, madayantikā, kāśmarī, viśalyā, hiṃsrā, and hemavidārikā.
6.14.13 Cirabilva, aśoka, balā, aṃśumatī, vayasthā, pīlaparṇī, pāṭhā, and śatāvarī—
[these are the ingredients]. 6.14.14 One should cook one āḍhaka of oil with five-pala portions of each of these in seven droṇas of water, until eight parts remain, over a gentle fire.
Kuṣṭha, śatapuṣpā, citraka, and tryūṣaṇa, as well as devadāru, excellent aguru, viḍaṅga, and musta.
6.14.16 Aśvagandhā, pāṭhā, mūrvā, and śyonāka, along with pippalī, śṛṅgavera, dantī, hiṅgu, and amlavetasa—
6.14.17 With this as the internal ingredient, the physician should properly prepare a decoction. Once it is cooked, strained, and cooled, he should mix it with honey and ghee.
One should give this to him for drinking, as well as for use in massages and other applications; chronic ūrustambha (stiffness of the thighs) is pacified by this oil.

6.14.19 It destroys elephantiasis (ślīpada), āṭhyavāta, and khuḍavāta; or one may take *pippalīvardhamāna* with honey or with water. 6.14.20 For stiffness of the thighs (ūrustambha), they recommend *gaṇḍīrāriṣṭa*, as well as various types of alkaline preparations (*kṣāra*), alkaline antidotes (*kṣārāgada*), and diverse non-unctuous enemas (*nirūha*).
6.14.20–21 Alternatively,
the administration of *harītakī* is recommended for *ūrustambha*, because when it is being attenuated, the patient’s muscle mass and strength become diminished.

For the sake of protecting the body, one should eat and even consume nourishing foods. One should eat aged *ṣaṣṭika* rice and ancient *śāli* rice. One who is afflicted by *ūrustambha* (stiffness of the thighs) should, when the *vāta* is predominant, consume the meat of wild animals and birds.

This entire treatment for *ūrustambha* has been correctly explained. Thus spoke the venerable Ātreya. Thus ends the fourteenth chapter of the Bhela [Saṃhitā]. Chapter Fifteen. Now, therefore, we shall expound upon *visarpa*, *vātaśoṇita*, and [related disorders]. Thus spoke the venerable Ātreya. 6.14.24.
6.15.1 Five types of visarpa (erysipelas) are described as arising from vāta, pitta, kapha, their combination (sannipāta), and from two [doshas] together; I shall now state their characteristics.
6.15.2 In one who constantly consumes astringent, pungent, and dry substances, the vāyu becomes aggravated and affects the skin, blood, and flesh.
6.15.2–3 Furthermore, a strong [dosha], having taken hold of the vessels (sirās), produces visarpa; one perceives it as ants crawling, even when [the patient] is immersed in ghee.

6.15.4 Yawning, dryness of the palate, pain in the flanks, convulsions, and fever; as well as a terrible swelling that has the appearance of a reddish or even black color—6.15.5 this is vātavīsarpa (wind-erysipelas). Hear now the prescribed procedure for its treatment: one should perform cooling measures and sprinkle the area with milk.

6.15.5–6 After drinking the *tailvaka* ghee, one should administer a purgative of *harītakī*, and for the purpose of eating, one should provide foods that do not cause a burning sensation (*avidāhin*).
6.15.7 One should prepare milk, barley flour, and ghee here, combined with yaṣṭīmadhuka; this is an excellent external application (ālepana).
6.15.8 Cow’s urine, cow’s milk, or even the liquid from cow dung, along with water boiled with the five roots (pañcamūlī), is recommended for sprinkling (seka).
One should grind rāsnā and madhuka with curd-whey; this poultice, applied after being anointed with ghee, is recommended for vāta-vīsarpa (erysipelas caused by vāta).

6.15.10 The tips of milky trees (*kṣīrivṛkṣa*), *madhuka*, and blue lotus (*nīlotpala*), boiled in milk and applied lukewarm, destroy vāta-type erysipelas (*vātavīsarpa*). 6.15.11 One should apply a plaster made of all these same medicinal herbs ground with milk; when applied lukewarm for vāta-type erysipelas, one thus attains comfort.
Alternatively, in cases of visarpa caused by vāta, they sprinkle the area with whey, or with oil, milk, or ghee, all made lukewarm.

6.15.13 For one who consumes pungent, sour, salty, alkaline, sharp, and hot foods, the *pitta* becomes aggravated; residing in the channels, flesh, and skin, it mingles with the blood. 6.15.14 Enveloping the entire body, it first kindles a fever that resembles the blazing crest of a fire.
It produces a severe and dreadful spreading erysipelas (visarpa) originating from pitta; eruptions arise upon it as if fanned by fire. 6.15.15
6.15.16 Wherever eruptions arise, they dissolve there; it repeatedly discharges a yellow, green, or black discharge from its pustules.
6.15.17 This visarpa, resembling fire and caused by pitta, destroys the body; the physician should perform treatment for it only after informing the patient that it is incurable.
6.15.17–18 The physician should administer a purgative mixed with unctuous substances to him, and he should also perform affusions with milk or sugarcane juice.
6.15.19 One should sprinkle [the area] frequently with water that is like snow, or with decoctions of milk-exuding trees, or with decoctions of *madhuka*.
6.15.20 One should apply a poultice to it using this ghee processed a hundred times, or one should smear it with a paste of *madhuka* and blue lotus ground with milk.
6.15.20–21 Mañjiṣṭhā, padmaka, padma, candana, blue utpala, madhūka, madhuka, drākṣā, lāmajjaka, and kaseruka. 6.15.21

6.15.22 Mṛṇāla, vidārī, samudrāntā, śatāvarī, sahasravīryā, nalada, balā, dantī, and madhūlikā—[these should be used]. 6.15.23 These, in equal parts, should be boiled in one droṇa of water; with these very decoctions, once they have been ground into a paste, one should cook [the medicine].

An unguent of ghee is beneficial for one afflicted by *visarpa* (erysipelas) arising from *pitta*. Likewise, [an ointment] made from *nyagrodha*, *udumbara*, *aśvattha*, *plakṣa*, and *vetasa* [is recommended].

6.15.25 Five pastes ground with milk are recommended for application as a plaster. When a person afflicted by *kapha* consumes food and drink that increases *kapha*, 6.15.26 the provoked *kapha* of that embodied being remains within the blood; from this, a *śleṣmavīsarpa* (Kapha-type erysipelas) arises, characterized by mild pain.
6.15.26–27. Furthermore, eruptions (sphoṭa) arise on his body, as well as swelling and a pale complexion. He also suffers from drowsiness, excessive sleep, fever, cough, and stiffness of the head.
6.15.28 A visarpa arising from phlegm (śleṣman) takes a long time to suppurate; one should administer emesis and purgation to such a patient according to their strength.
6.15.29 Or one should drink Tailvaka ghee, or aged clarified butter (purāṇa-ghṛta), or [a preparation of] Sarja, Aśvakarṇa, Sustā, Sallakī, and Somavalkala.
The two types of *karañja*, the bark of *kapittha*, *śirīṣa*, *uśīra*, and *sārivā*; the tender shoots of milk-exuding trees (*kṣīrivṛkṣa*), the bark of *kuṭaja*, and *dhanañjaya*.

6.15.31 One should prepare a decoction of dhava, palāśa, syonāka, khadira, vetasa, and asana; this should be used lukewarm for irrigation. 6.15.32 One should apply a plaster made from these same drugs ground into a paste with goat’s milk. Then, one should cook one prastha of oil with these same drugs, both as a decoction and as a ground paste.
6.15.32–33. By means of this unguent, the kapha-type visarpa is pacified. One should apply a poultice (upanāha) to the visarpa using pieces of warm beef.

6.15.34 One should prepare an oil massage (*abhyaṅga*) with the marrow of wild animals; one should also apply a meat poultice (*upanāha*) in cases of the *kapha*-type or even the *vāta*-type [of swelling]. 6.15.35 When the three aggravated *doṣas* have taken refuge in the skin and flesh, [one should treat them] with the meat of wild animals, or with beef, peacock, chicken, or goat meat.
When [the doshas] are mixed with blood and manifest in specific regions of the body, a circular patch (maṇḍala) arises there that is either dusky or black.

6.15.37 Then, spreading with pain to the edges of the skin, it becomes red; fever, thirst, burning sensations, vomiting, fainting, and likewise vertigo arise. 6.15.38 Whatever part of the body is touched by it, heat does not leave that spot; and when the blood is burnt, the limb becomes like a dried gourd.
6.15.38–39 | One should administer there either *sukumāra*, *balā-taila*, or *śairīṣa-taila*, or even *dhānvantara-ghṛta*, in cases of *vāta-śoṇita*. 6.15.39
6.15.40 One afflicted by vātaśoṇita (gout) should consume either *pippalīvardhamāna*, or *takrāsava*, or [an infusion of] *khadira*.

6.15.41 One should regularly administer an enema (*āsthāpana*) to this patient using the *mustādi* group of drugs; alternatively, one should have him drink [medicines] via enemas prepared with *āmalaka*, honey, and oil.
Whatever treatment has been described for erysipelas (visarpa) arising from vāta, all of that should be performed in the case of vātarakta when blood (śoṇita) predominates.

6.15.43 If blood is involved in deep *vāta-śoṇita*, one should treat it like *vāta* with the administration of fats (*sneha*) by way of internal potions and oil enemas (*anuvāsana*). 6.15.44 The fat and marrow of peacock, curlew, and lapwing are recommended for drinking, massage, and enema, as is *balā-taila*.

Whether by non-therapeutic measures or by therapeutic measures, if the *vāta-śoṇita* (blood disorder) remains undigested, the practitioner who knows the application of remedies should perform incision after careful deliberation. Thus spoke the venerable Ātreya. Thus ends the fifteenth chapter of the Bheḷa-saṃhitā. Chapter Sixteen: Now, therefore, we shall explain the treatment of hemorrhoids (*arśas*). Thus spoke the venerable Ātreya. 6.15.45

6.16.1 There are six types of hemorrhoids (arśas) for embodied beings: those arising from wind (vāta), bile (pitta), phlegm (kapha), and likewise from their combination (sannipāta); those congenital (sahaja), and those arising from blood (rakta).
6.16.2 I shall describe their etiology (nidāna) and treatment (cikitsā) in due order, as it has been taught for both the invisible and the visible [hemorrhoids].

6.16.2–3 For those who consume foods that are burning-hot, heavy, and dry, and who indulge in the products of marshy and aquatic regions, as well as curd, milk, molasses, and the like, and eat meat— 6.16.3.

6.16.4 From the consumption of contaminated barley and water, from constantly eating indigestible food, and from the suppression of natural urges; 6.16.5 From excessive straining, from overindulgence in sexual intercourse, from addiction to harmful drinks, and from the pressure of a stiff back.

6.16.5–6 Due to the excessive administration of a nirūha enema, from the misapplication of enemas, from the improper consumption of oleaginous substances, from the defects of alcohol, from exhaustion, and from wasting (kṣaya),
[the following occurs].
6.16.7 By these means, the three humors—Vāta, Pitta, and Kapha—become aggravated, either individually, collectively, or in pairs, or together with the blood.
6.16.8 Having taken refuge in the rectum, they quickly cause a morbid moisture (abhiṣyanda) of the anus; therein, polyps (kīla) arise that resemble tiny mustard seeds.
6.16.8–9 They are like barley, mung beans, niṣpāva beans, jujube fruits, or badara fruits; they are the size of a thumb-joint on the body, copper-colored, and resemble cow’s udders.
6.16.10 Those firmly established splinters (kīla) in the rectum cause severe constriction of the anus; having seized the rectum, they further bind the root of the channels.
6.16.11 Due to the obstruction of those channels, the humors (doṣas), having arisen upwards and corrupted each [organ] individually, produce diseases in their respective locations (āśaya).
6.16.11 6.12. Disruption of the stool, discoloration, colic, and likewise diarrhea; tearing pain, thirst, burning sensation in the anus and back, loss of fat, and fever.
6.16.13 Loss of appetite, indigestion, emaciation of the limbs, loss of strength, paleness, pain in the joints, and swelling of the eyelids;

6.16.14 Lassitude, loss of sexual vigor, prolapse of the rectum, and constriction of the anus—these resemble the symptoms of hemorrhoids (arśas); their distinct characteristics will now be described separately.
The stool is black, dry, and slightly frothy; it is always hard, yet there is frequent breaking up of the feces.
6.16.16 Constantly seizing the thighs, back, and waist, it causes extreme weakness; there arises pain in the joints, earache, thirst, and vertigo.
6.16.17 The wind (vāyu), having provoked hemorrhoids and the liver, may also cause enlargement of the abdomen; moreover, colic pains and flatulence arise in him again and again.
When the *grahaṇī* is vitiated and wind (*anila*) arises in the form of dysentery (*durnāman*), discoloration occurs, as well as pains in the heart, the flanks, and the abdomen. (6.16.18)

6.16.19 In cases of hemorrhoids caused by pitta (pittārśas), one passes stools that are accompanied by fever, pustules, thirst, intense urgency, and blood; they are hot, liquid, and characterized by a burning sensation. 6.16.20 The patient becomes pale in complexion and appears yellowish; the anus is excessively burned, and inflammation of the anus (gudapāka) occurs.
In hemorrhoids born of phlegm (kaphaja), the stool passes with sliminess and a white coating; mixed with phlegm, it is evacuated little by little and accompanied by pain.
6.16.22 He remains seated for a long time and is unable to move from his seat; his penis, scrotum, bladder, and anus become swollen.
6.16.23 There is loss of appetite and indigestion, yet he does not purge the digested matter; furthermore, swelling sets in, particularly around the orbital regions of the eyes.

6.16.23–24 This is said to be the form of hemorrhoids arising from phlegm (kapha). One should recognize those arising from the combination of all three humors (sannipāta) by their complete set of symptoms.

6.16.25 The blood is clotted, has a fleshy odor, or is mixed with bile; its discharge occurs slowly or at times becomes persistent. 6.16.26 Then the bleeding hemorrhoids, being congested, release blood; they flow with a stream of blood like a vein that has been pierced and remains open.
Like a young woman in her menses, she repeatedly discharges blood; she eats mudga beans, liquor, danti, kakubha,
and mayūraka.
6.16.28 One should then employ the urine of cows and female buffaloes; having reduced that alkaline substance to ashes, one should skillfully administer it with wine.
6.16.29 This pacifies phlegmatic hemorrhoids, as well as swelling and jaundice. As for the treatment prescribed for Vata-type hemorrhoids:

For those with hemorrhoids caused by phlegm (śleṣman), one should perform the same treatment as before, excluding the use of oleation (sneha). In hemorrhoids arising from blood (rakta) as well, goat’s milk is recommended.
6.16.31 One should drink [this] for a season, or for a half-year, or even for a month. [The ingredients are: *balā*, *bilva* shoots, *triphalā*, and *hastipippalī*.
6.16.32 With the pastes (*kalka*) of these—*karañja*, honey, *pālāśa*, *madhuka*, blue lotus (*utpala*), and *tinduka*—each weighing one *akṣa*, one should cook one *prastha* of ghee.
6.16.32–33 One should drink this, prepared with ten times as much goat’s milk, in the appropriate dose. Indeed, it cures those [diseases] arising from blood as well as those born of pitta.

Lodhra, dāruharidrā, and the marrow of the bibhītaka tree quickly destroy hemorrhoids, just as the wind scatters scattered clouds. (6.16.34) Drinking a decoction of these with rice-water and honey destroys hemorrhoids. Lākṣā, haridrā, mañjiṣṭhā, madhuka, and blue utpala [are also used for this purpose]. (6.16.35)
6.16.35–36. Taken with goat’s milk, the flowers of the śirīṣa, the kuṭaja, and the kakubha destroy diseases born of blood.
6.16.37 One should cause the patient to drink the pastes of dārvī, haridrā, lodhra, dhātakī, kaṭphala, and vṛṣa with rice-water, according to the prescribed method.
6.16.38 Combined with honey, these [pastes] indeed pacify hemorrhoids born of blood and bile (raktapitta). [Likewise, one may use] madhuka, badara, drākṣā, and the roots of kuśa and kāśa.
6.16.38–39: Drinking rice-water mixed with honey destroys hemorrhoids. [One should also use] the [bark or leaves] of Nyagrodha, Udumbara, Aśvattha, Badarī, Plakṣa, and Vetasa.
One should collect eight *palas* each of fresh sprouts of *avākpuṣpī* and likewise of *dārvī*.
One should add two *palas* each of *śāliparṇī* and *pṛśniparṇī*, and two *palas* of *rālaśāka*; all of this should be combined.
6.16.41–42 Two *droṇas* of water should be boiled down until one-eighth remains; then, one *āḍhaka* of ghee should be prepared with this decoction and lukewarm water.
The fresh juice extracted from *cāṅgerī* and *amlīkā*, mixed with an equal quantity of oil, along with *devadāru*, *abhayā*, *mustā*, *citraka*, and the pulp of *bilva*;
6.16.43–44 *kaṭphala*, *śṛṅgavera*, *pippalī*, and *candana*; as well as *sauvīra* collyrium, the root of *pippalī*, and *tiktarohiṇī*.
Jaggery, priyaṅgu flowers, that which is called the down of the śālmalī tree, the seeds of vatsaka, as well as ativiṣā and vacā.
6.16.46 Having given these equal parts separately, one should cook them together. This prepared ghee, when used appropriately, will indeed destroy hemorrhoids with bleeding (raktārśas).
6.16.47 It also cures bile-born abdominal tumors (pittagulma), diarrhea, colic, fever, loss of appetite, severe menorrhagia in women, internal hemorrhaging (raktapitta), and dysentery (pravāhikā).
It removes anemia, poison, cough, and worms; it is the destroyer of disorders born of phlegm and is the supreme stimulator of the digestive fire.
6.16.49 This Cāṅgerī-ghṛta is renowned as being like nectar for those who are barren and for those suffering from consumption; it destroys hemorrhoids (arśas).
6.16.50 It bestows strength and complexion, removes blood-born abdominal tumors (raktagulma), and is beneficial even in cases of hemorrhoids caused by pitta and those born of blood.

In all cases arising from the combination of the humors (sannipāta), this [treatment] is honored; however, for congenital hemorrhoids (sahaja-arśas), one should act according to their specific constitution (prakṛti).
6.16.52 Having personally determined the treatment through one's own intellect according to one's capacity, [one should take] three *palas* of ginger and a fourth part (*pala*) of black pepper.
6.16.53 Half a *kuḍava* of long pepper, one *pala* of *cavya*, one *pala* of *tālīśapatra*, and half a *pala* of *kesara*.
Two palas of pippalī root, one pala of citraka, as well as one karṣa each of cinnamon bark and leaves, and one karṣa of fine cardamom.
6.16.55 One should prepare these powders with thirty palas of purified jaggery; then, pills the size of an *akṣa* fruit are made, renowned as "Life-Givers" (*prāṇadā*).
6.16.56 These same pills are also proclaimed as "Tālīsapatra-vaṭakas"; one should consume them according to one's strength, either before or after a meal.
6.16.56–57 One should also feed [the patient] with wines, meat soups, vegetable broths, and milks. By this means, one destroys hemorrhoids born of phlegm as well as those that are congenital.

6.16.58 Diseases arising from vāta and pitta, those born of blood, and others [such as those caused by phlegm], in cases of alcoholism (madātyaya), dysuria (mūtrakṛcchra), urinary disorders (prameha), and cardiac oppression (hṛdayagraha);

6.16.59 In fevers caused by poison, pain in the flanks (pārśvaśūla), chest wounds, emaciation, and after purgation; likewise for those with weak digestion, irregular digestion, and those with intestinal worms (kṛmikoṣṭhin).

6.16.59–60 For those afflicted by *śūla* and *gulma*, as well as those suffering from vomiting and diarrhea, those with heart disease, jaundice, consumption (*śoṣa*), and upward-moving wind (*ūrdhvavāta*).
6.16.61 For those afflicted by cough and dyspnea, auspicious *vaṭaka* pills are to be used; indeed, these native formulations here greatly alleviate the suffering of the embodied being.
6.16.62 Therefore, one should treat that [condition] with the therapeutic measures prescribed for consumption (*śoṣa*). This is proclaimed as the supreme instruction for the entire host of diseases.
Therefore, the physician should treat hemorrhoids in detail; for them, there is excision with a surgical instrument as well as cauterization with alkali.
6.16.64 A surgeon who has witnessed the practice of treatment should employ that medical therapy which is to be applied by one who knows Āyurveda.
6.16.65 Listen now to the procedure for medicinal plasters, massage, and sudation; having anointed the navel, the abdomen, the bladder, the scrotum, and likewise the anus—
6.16.65–66 One should sprinkle [the patient] with sour liquids, milk, and warm urine, as well as with boiled young radishes and *gṛñjanaka*.
6.16.67 One should skillfully apply fomentation with lukewarm oil-cakes (piṇyāka) or cow dung. [One should also use] rāṭha, the root of eraṇḍa, madhūka, and devadāru.
6.16.68 Having mixed these with barley flour and stirred them in milk, one should have the patient drink it. With that, one should prepare a poultice (upanāha) and apply fomentation again and again.
6.16.68–69 Hemorrhoids are pacified and pain ceases through [the use of] vṛṣa, arka, naktamāla, kāśmarya, and the two daṇḍas. 6.16.69
One should apply fomentation with decoctions of leaves and have the patient sit upon that [bed]. [The ingredients are: *mahānimba*, ginger, *kuṣṭha*, and *kāsīsa*;
6.16.71 rock salt, *citraka*, *dantī*, oleander, and *śilā-kaṇā*; *pūtika*, the bark of *varuṇa*, *vidārī*, and *lāṅgalāhvaya*.
One should grind viḍaṅga, hemadugdhā, and haritāla; with this as the internal medicinal ingredient (garbha), one should cook oil with four times the amount of urine.
In this case, one *kuḍava* each of the milks of *snuhī* and *arka* should be used. This application, when properly administered, is a supreme remedy for pacifying hemorrhoids (*arśas*).
Indeed, it performs the action of cauterization (*kṣāra-karma*) yet does not injure the rectum. [The paste consists of: *kulīraśṛṅgī*, elephant bone, *balā*, and *lāṅgalikī*.
Asafoetida, costus, blue vitriol, wood-apple, and marking-nut— this should be applied as an ointment for hemorrhoids repeatedly over a period of seven nights.
6.16.76 Śirīṣa seeds, the two types of alkali (kṣāra), kaṅkolī, and rock salt—these, ground with the milky sap of snuhī, should be saturated with the bile of cows.
6.16.77 One should repeatedly smear the hemorrhoids with this for seven nights. By this, the hemorrhoids are destroyed; of this there is no doubt.
Śigru [and other ingredients]—having combined all these together, one should grind them with the milky sap of *snuhī*.
6.16.79 Karavīra, anavadya, mālatī, and svarṇayūthikā—this decoction used for washing is said to be beneficial for hemorrhoids.
6.16.80 An ointment of fresh butter mixed with honey heals wounds; after seven nights, [the ulcer] is consumed by healing, and virility does not perish.
One should grind *saurmika*, *bida*, *daṅgā*, *śātrikaṭuka*, and *snuhī* latex together.
6.16.82 This excellent ointment will destroy hemorrhoids (*durnāmāna*). [One should take] *svarṇakṣīrī*...
*tsaka*. 6.16.83 One should grind the excrement of a cock with the milk of *snuhī*; this excellent ointment is equal to alkali (*kṣāra*) for hemorrhoids.
Hemorrhoids are burnt away within seven days, and virility is not destroyed, by means of barley, white mustard, marking-nut (*bhallātaka*), and fat.
6.16.85 Sandalwood, kuṣṭha, the heartwood of śiṃśapā, cow dung, and boar dung, [placed] upon leaves of vāriṣṭa and śigru;
6.16.86 mixed with ghee, these are praised as the best fumigation for hemorrhoids. Milk enemas are recommended for those arising from blood and bile (raktapitta).

6.16.86–87: Pungent treatments [are indicated] for those arising from *kapha*, and oil enemas (*anuvāsana*) for those of *vāta* origin. Those which arise from the combination of all three humors (*sannipāta*), as well as those that have been long-standing, are incurable here. Those born of blood (*raktaja*) and congenital (*sahaja*) swellings are palliable; the other three types are curable. Thus spoke the venerable Ātreya. Thus ends the sixteenth chapter of the Bheḷa-saṃhitā. The seventeenth chapter: Now, therefore, we shall explain the treatment of swelling (*śvayathu*). Thus said the venerable Ātreya. 6.16.87
6.17.1 One who has wasted muscle mass, weak digestion, is afflicted by disease, and is extremely debilitated, yet excessively indulges in heavy foods and those that cause acid bile (amlapitta);
6.17.2 Or one who, having recently vomited or been purged, consumes heavy foods; or one who, after fasting excessively, subsists on vegetables, roots, and fruits.

6.17.2–3 The man who eats fish, curd, and milk; who indulges in sleeping during the day; who consumes unwholesome food while suffering from indigestion; and who practices excessive physical exercise—[suffers these consequences].
6.17.4 And he who excessively consumes substances that are bitter, astringent, alkaline, sour, or pungent—especially those that are light and dry;
6.17.5 his vāta becomes aggravated and enters the external vessels (śirās); it quickly provokes the pitta, as well as the blood and the kapha.
6.17.5–6 Those vessels, filled with the humors (doṣas), spread forth dreadfully, either converging in a single region or again throughout all the limbs.
6.17.7 Thus, that disease known as *śvayathu* (edema) becomes severe. When those *doṣas* are located in the *pakvāśaya* (large intestine), that edema occurs in the lower part of the body.

6.17.8 Edema originating in the feet destroys the life-force (*asus*) of men; when it arises in the face of women, it does so as well; and when it arises in the private parts of either sex, it likewise destroys life.
In this world, swelling (śopha) most frequently arises from a combination of all the doṣas; however, whichever among them is predominant will indeed manifest its own specific characteristics.

6.17.10 Vata-type swelling is dry, black in color, and painful; when pressed, it becomes indented and subsides without apparent cause. 6.17.11 Pitta-type swelling is blue, red, or yellow; it is accompanied by pain and burning, suppurates quickly, and is associated with fever.
A swelling caused by *kapha* is characterized by a white appearance, is thick, whitish-yellow, stable, persistent, and difficult to cure. It is also extremely swollen.

6.17.13 The symptoms of the combined (sānnipātika) swelling arising from wind, bile, and phlegm are as follows: that which is incurable, accompanied by complications (upasarga), and that which is spreading (prasṛta). 6.17.14 If, in a swelling, a blue, yellow, or reddish glow is seen, and it exudes a small amount of watery fluid, one should designate that as incurable.
6.17.14–15: From the blows of weapons or staffs, from falling, or from the breaking of bones, swelling (śvayathu) is observed as the fifth [type]; it is most frequently caused by blood (raktaja).
6.17.16 Due to trauma, the flesh and bone of those [injuries] become afflicted; it quickly vitiates the vessels (*sirā*), and thereafter the blood becomes vitiated.

6.17.17 It increases, characterized by burning sensations and redness, and is accompanied by intense pain. The physician should apply the treatment prescribed for *kṣatavaisarpa* (traumatic erysipelas) to that [condition].
6.17.17–18 These characteristics of swellings have been described according to the rules; I shall now explain their treatment in due order and as it truly is.

6.17.19 One should drink *kalyāṇaka* ghee or even *mahātiktaka* ghee; or else, one should purify the person with the great *pañcagavya*. 6.17.20 Or one should have them lick *harītakī* together with *madhuka* and honey; or one should lick *pippalī* (*kṛṣṇā*) with honey, or drink it with milk.
Harītakī, śṛṅgavera, and devadāru in equal parts— this, when drunk with warm water, is a remedy for swellings.
6.17.22 Iron, *ajaśṛṅgī*, *kaṭuka*, *trivṛt*, and *tiktarohiṇī*, when drunk with the juice of *triphalā*, are a remedy for swellings (*śvayathu*).
6.17.23 *Mahauṣadha* (ginger), *devadāru*, *sudhā*, and *varṣābhū*— milk boiled with these in equal parts is an excellent destroyer of swellings.
Alternatively, the use of cow urine is excellent for destroying swelling; one may drink either buffalo urine mixed with milk, or buffalo urine alone.

6.17.25 One should drink camel urine or even camel milk, according to one's strength and according to the specific humor (doṣa); this is excellent for destroying swelling (śvayathu). 6.17.26 A person suffering from wind (anila) should eat prepared radishes; furthermore, one should perform a sprinkling (pariṣecana) with the juice of radishes.
A decoction of the roots of *naktamāla*, *arka*, *vṛṣa*, and *āragvadha*, when applied as a wash, is a remedy for swellings.
6.17.28 Suvarcalā, vyāghranakha, kuṣṭha, kaṭukarohiṇī, kākamācī, ṛṣabhaka, rāsnā, mūrvā, and punarnavā;
6.17.29 Vārtākī, the root of nicula, triphalā, citraka, vacā, kuṭheraka, the two types of haridrā, śyāmā, and mūṣakaparṇikā.
Viḍaṅga, the bark of śigru, naktamāla, and mahauṣadha, ground with cow’s urine, constitute an excellent medicinal unguent for swelling.

6.17.31–32. Danti, viḍaṅga, triphalā, the three pungents (trikaṭu), kaṭurohiṇī, citraka, devadāru, trivṛt, and hastipippalī—these powders should be taken in equal parts, with iron filings added in double that amount. When stirred with milk and drunk, this is the best remedy for the destruction of swelling (śvayathu).
6.17.32–33. One *kuḍava* of the three myrobalans (*triphalā*), one *kuḍava* of long pepper (*pippalī*), and two *palas* each of *viḍaṅga* and black pepper are prescribed.
6.17.34 One should take one *pala* each of *dantī* and *citraka*, one *pala* of *pippalīmūla*, and likewise one *pala* of *tuṣṭa*.
6.17.35 Two *palas* of *śṛṅgavera* and five *palas* of cow's [milk]; now learn from me which of the remaining ingredients are half-*pala* portions.
6.17.35–36 Rāsnā, balā, gokṣuraka, madhuka, and devadāru; vacā, ativiṣā, pāṭhā, mustā, and kaṭurohiṇī.
6.17.37 Kaṭphala, the two types of sārivā, śyāmā, bhallātaka, punarnavā, tejohvā, cinnamon bark, śatāvarī leaf,
6.17.38 nidigdhikā, vyāghranakha, mañjiṣṭhā, kuśa, śambhalī, triphalā, trivṛtā, bhārṅgī, and the fruit and bark of kuṭaja.

Having gathered these ingredients, one should prepare a paste twice the size of an egg; having mixed it into a single consistency by means of a skillful method, one should have the patient lick it with honey and clarified butter.

6.17.40 One who consumes milk while abstaining from other food should drink milk as a post-digestive draught (anupāna) according to the proper method. This is known as *ayoraja* (iron powder), a celebrated perfected elixir (*siddharasāyana*).
6.17.41 By using it for one year, a person lives for a hundred years; by using it for two years, a human being shall live for two hundred autumns.
It destroys even a terrible swelling as Indra’s thunderbolt strikes down a tree; it also cures anemia, hemorrhoids, weak digestion, and even worms.

6.17.43 Fistula-in-ano, jaundice, skin diseases, abdominal enlargements, as well as splenic disorders, epilepsy, colic, and cutting pain; 6.17.44 diarrhea, urinary disorders, chest wounds, cough, and consumption— in whichever disease this formulation is employed, [it proves effective].
It destroys each respective disease just as Keśava slays the enemies of the gods; the secondary application consists of parched grain flour mixed with roasted grains and honey.

This electuary is to be taken with milk for five or seven days in cases of hemorrhoids, internal hemorrhaging, and diarrhea; it is also the prescribed treatment for cutting pains. Likewise, in cases of wasting coughs and irregular fevers, even swelling that has persisted for a year is pacified by this within a month.

And by the application of rejuvenative therapies (*rasāyana*) as previously described according to the rules, one should likewise consume fresh *śāli* rice, *ṣaṣṭika* rice, and various new food preparations.
One should always avoid alkaline, sour, and salty substances, as well as smoke; whether the swelling is exogenous (āgantuka) or arises from the bodily humors (doṣaja).

6.17.50. [The complications of swelling] are known to be fever due to indigestion, vomiting, debility, cutting pain in the rectum, dyspnea, diarrhea, and hiccup; these are pacified by fasting, medicinal plasters, and bloodletting. Thus said the venerable Ātreya. This concludes the seventeenth chapter of the Bhela [Saṃhitā]. Chapter Eighteen: Now, therefore, we shall explain the treatment of Udāvarta (upward-moving wind disorders). Thus said the venerable Ātreya. 6.17.50.
6.18.1 But he who, by nature having a vāta constitution, consumes dry foods, constantly uses astringent and pungent tastes, and partakes of bitter flavors; 6.18.2 [and eats] jujubes,
wood-apples, breadfruit, jackfruit, pigeon-peas, bhavya fruits, and whatever other fruit is of this kind.
He consumes fermented gruel, dried meat, oil-cake, and kodrava rice; he partakes of substances that cause excessive secretions, pungent foods, and the vegetable of vetra reeds.

6.18.4–5. Due to the suppression of flatus, urine, and feces, as well as sexual intercourse, and by these and other such heavy causes, the aggravated *vāyu* (wind) pervades the entire body and seizes the anal sphincter. Remaining there, it intensely dries up the body while causing its emaciation.
The wind (pavana) violently obstructs the downward-flowing channels, as well as those carrying bile (pitta) and phlegm (śleṣman), and those conveying urine, food,
and waste.

6.18.7 Those [vātas], corrupted by wind and moving upward while remaining in the locations of the undigested (āmāśaya) and digested (pakvāśaya) tracts, cause most dreadful insanity. 6.18.8 When the apāna-vāyu reaches the upper region and unites with the udāna, it is called udāvarta; it is caused by weapons, serpents, and poisons.
6.18.8–9 Now, there are sharp pains, burning, fainting, and discoloration; the root of the bladder swells, and there is likewise severe retention of urine.
6.18.10 Then, in the flanks, the abdomen, the heart, the sides, and likewise the belly, the patient, enveloped by the *deva-nābhi* [vayu], becomes unconscious and trembles repeatedly.
6.18.11 He sighs, faints, suffers from thirst, and hiccups. Listen now to the treatment for these complications arising from *udāvarta*.
6.18.11–12 Having thoroughly anointed this [patient] with oil and salt, one should then foment him on a bed of mixed materials or in a wooden tub.

6.18.13 Thereafter, having lubricated his anus, the physician should administer a non-unctuous enema (nirūha), either once or twice, as long as he deems it appropriate. 6.18.14 Once he knows the enema has been properly retained, the patient should be sprinkled with lukewarm water and should eat soft rice with warm water as a post-drink (anupāna).
6.18.14–15 One should eat with the leaf-vegetable of *snuhā* or with the vegetable of *trivṛt*, or with the soup made from those two, or with any other excellent purgative food.

6.18.16 One should constantly treat him with foods that cause loose stools; in this way, the wind (vāyu) will not further dry up his feces. Chapter Nineteen 6.19.1 All these symptoms are seen in one afflicted by a disease of the vital points (marmans). Arising from the derangement of all three humors (sannipāta), this condition cannot be cured by medical treatment.
6.19.1–2 The divine affliction pierces, burns the vital points, and causes pain; it consists of aversion to food, fever, fainting, dyspnea, and a pervasive burning sensation.

6.19.3 Furthermore, when the complexion becomes discolored, one is dejected, and itching arises in the heart, this is declared to be heart disease caused by parasites (*krimija*); it is the fifth type and is difficult to conquer.
6.19.4 Three types of heart disease—those consisting of *vāta*, *pitta*, and *kapha*—are curable. Two among them are considered incurable; now hear the treatment for those that are curable.

Having administered oleation to one suffering from heart disease (hṛdroga), one should pacify it or likewise cleanse it. One should employ fasting for a recent onset of heart disease, except in cases caused by vāta.
6.19.6 Harītakī, vacā, rāsnā, the two types of pippalī, and viśvabheṣaja; śaṭhī and puṣkaramūla—this powder destroys heart disease.
6.19.7 Pāṭhā, vacā, yavakṣāra, abhayā, and amlavetasa; durālabhā, citraka, the three pungents (tryūṣaṇa), and the three salts.
One should prepare a fine powder of śaṭī, puṣkaramūla, tintriṇīka, pomegranate, and the seeds of mātuluṅgī. 6.19.7–8.
6.19.9 One should have these powders drunk with warm water or with wines; they dispel hemorrhoids, colic, heart disease, and abdominal tumors.
6.19.10 Sauvarcala salt, ginger, pomegranate, sour vetasa, and asafoetida as the fifth—this [mixture] pacifies asthma and heart disease.
One should cook one prastha of the best ghee with fifty palas of abhayā paste and one pala of sauvarcala salt in four times the amount of water.
6.19.12 This is the supreme ghee for living beings, named Vallabhaka; it was created as an equal to nectar, destroying dyspnea and heart disease.
6.19.13 One should drink Kalyāṇaka ghee, or even Dhānvantara ghee; one should also drink the juice of mātuluṅga along with alkali and astringents.
One afflicted by heart disease should always use these oils: *balā* oil processed a hundred times, *śairīṣa* oil, and *sukumāraka* oil. (6.19.13–14)
One should drink rejuvenative ghee, milks, and even jaggery, as well as the ghee-balls (*ghṛtamodaka*) mentioned for pacifying heart disease caused by *pitta*. [Also beneficial are:
*jīvaka*, *ṛṣabhaka*, grapes, sugar, *śreyasī*, *balā*, the two types of *medā*, the two types of *kākolī*, dates, white lotus, and blue lotus.
6.19.16–17 A physician should cook one *prastha* of buffalo ghee with these [herbs] in equal parts and four times as much milk; it should be drunk according to the prescribed method.

In cases of heart disease arising from the provocation of *vāta* and *pitta*, this is the supreme remedy for its destruction. Fat (*vasā*) and marrow (*majjā*) are equal [in measure] to oil and clarified butter (*ghṛta*).
One should provide these as they are available, or else take four times the amount. [The other ingredients are] *vacā*, the three pungents (*trikaṭuka*), *rāsnā*, *jīvantī*, *jīvaka*, and *balā*.
Having observed the patient's strength, one should administer a medicated oil (mahāsneha) prepared with *nidigdhikā*, *aṃśumatī*, *nīlī*, *bhārṅgī*, and *punarnavā*.

6.19.21 Unctuous therapy (sneha) immediately cures heart disease caused by Vāta. A physician should personally deliberate with his own intellect regarding the medicinal treatment for heart disease. 6.19.22 In heart disease caused by Pitta, [medicines] that are sweet, unctuous, and hot are used; in that caused by Vāta, they should be unctuous and hot. As for the remaining three types [of heart disease], one should treat them with sharp and hot remedies.

6.19.22–23. The treatment for those with worms in the abdomen (*kṛmikoṣṭhin*), which has been described in detail, includes [the application of] alkalies (*kṣāra*), anti-toxic alkalies (*kṣārāgada*), emetics, and purgatives.

6.19.24 That same [treatment] should be administered without malice in the case of *krimi-hṛdroga* (heart disease caused by worms). Meat from aquatic and marshy animals, curd, milk, molasses, and fruit juices— 6.19.25 All these, though they cause secretions (*abhiṣyanda*), destroy heart disease caused by *vāta*. However, one should avoid these very things in the remaining types of heart disease. Light foods and drinks are always recommended for those conditions. Thus spoke the venerable Ātreya. Thus ends the nineteenth chapter in the Bheḷa [Saṃhitā]. Chapter Twenty. Now, therefore, we shall explain the treatment of cough (*kāsa-cikitsita*). So said the venerable Ātreya.

6.19.25–6.20.1 Five types of cough have been described: those caused by vāta, pitta, and kapha, as well as that born of injury (kṣataja) and that born of wasting (kṣayaja). I shall now state their characteristics.

6.20.2–3. From upward movement of the *udāvarta*, from injury, from over-exertion, and from emaciation; from eating together [with others], from sleeping during the day, from drinking too quickly, and from hanging [the head];
and for those emaciated by diseases, from the depletion caused by unwholesome factors (*asātmya*), and from the consumption of sharp, hot, and heavy substances—these types of coughs arise in men.
6.20.3–4 I shall describe their symptoms and their various treatments. From [an excess of] wind (māruta), one coughs dryly, as if the throat were filled with awns.
6.20.5 He spits out dry phlegm, and when it is released, he does not cough; he becomes exhausted while coughing, and his heart is as if being pulled out.
6.20.6 His sides are excessively pained, and he makes a gurgling sound due to labored breathing; pain arises in the temples, and likewise there is a parching of the palate.
6.20.6–7: In one afflicted by vāta, the eyes appear dark-brown, the natural complexion changes, the digestive tract is especially empty, and the person coughs.

6.20.8–9: From the consumption of sour, dry foods and drinks, physical exercise, and hot things; and from the consumption of pungent, alkaline, dry foods, and strong liquor—pitta-type cough arises, accompanied by burning sensations and fever. Such a person expectorates excessively phlegm that is yellowish, pungent, and hot.
A bitter taste arises in the mouth and thirst is produced; furthermore, the eyes of one suffering from pitta-type cough appear yellowish.
In one who consumes food that is excessively moistening, heavy, unctuous, cold, and fatty; who is habituated to sleeping during the day;
and who suppresses the natural urges, there arises a cough accompanied by excessive salivation due to *kapha*, as well as extreme heaviness of the head and sweetness in the mouth.
From kapha, the heart feels heavy and there is a lack of desire for food; stiffness and indigestion are the characteristics of cough caused by kapha.
6.20.14 He whose chest is struck by physical exertion, carrying heavy loads, or the restraint of horses and elephants, is said to suffer from *kṣatakāsa* (chest-wound cough).
6.20.15 Afflicted by this cough, he spits out phlegm mixed with blood, resembling putrid pus, knotted and accumulated with the bodily humors (*doṣas*); he suffers from fever and diarrhea.
6.20.15–16 He feels as if his chest is being split open and he breathes heavily; he becomes exhausted while coughing, and there is thirst and dryness of the mouth.
6.20.17 The throat repeatedly becomes constricted and hoarseness of voice arises; one also coughs with a resonant sound that is distorted and broken in pitch.
6.20.18 Furthermore, in the case of *kṣatakāsa* (cough due to injury), one emits foul-smelling eructations. And from the combination of all [three doshas], *kṣayakāsa* (consumptive cough) sets in.
He suffers from fever, pain in the sides, and a burning sensation in the hands and feet; while coughing, he expectorates phlegm mixed with blood.
6.20.20 His strength and complexion diminish, and his body wastes away; he finds no pleasure in food, and what he does eat is not properly digested.
6.20.21 Diarrhea, fever, vomiting, and fainting arise in him; this is declared to be wasting cough (kṣayakāsa), and it is proclaimed to be incurable.

Cough due to chest injury (kṣatakāsa), however, is palliable; now listen to the treatment for those [types of cough] that are curable. One should treat a strong patient who has been oleated with purification therapies (śodhana).

Once he has been purified, one should feed him aged *śāli* rice and *ṣaṣṭika* rice, and he should consume the meat of wild animals and birds. He should avoid the heavy meats of aquatic and marsh-dwelling creatures. Alternatively, he may take *kalyāṇaka* ghee prepared with the ten medicinal pastes (*daśakalka*).

6.20.24–25 One should employ rejuvenative therapy (rasāyana), as well as ghee, honeyed ghees (sarpirguḍa), or the formulation of ghee boluses (sarpirmodaka), and likewise follow the prescribed regimen for rejuvenation.

6.20.26 One should apply that which was previously stated regarding blood [disorders] to cases of cough as well. Long pepper (*pippalī*), emblic myrobalan (*āmalaka*), grapes (*drākṣā*), bamboo manna (*tugākṣīrī*), and sugar (*śarkarā*)— 6.20.27 parched grain (*lāja*), ghee, and honey, taken as a linctus (*leha*), destroy cough. A linctus of long pepper, emblic myrobalan, and *rāsnā*, combined with honey, likewise destroys cough.
The powder of *harītakī* together with *pippalī*, combined with honey, should be made into a linctus; likewise, honey and ghee may be used, or honey combined with sugar.

6.20.29 One should prepare a fine powder of the three pungents (tryūṣaṇa), the three myrobalans (triphalā), padmaka, devadāru, rāsnā, balā, and viḍaṅga. 6.20.30 This powder, combined with sugar, should be licked with honey and ghee; this electuary dispels the five types of cough that have arisen.
6.20.30–31. One should powder together equal parts of barley alkali, viḍaṅga, asafoetida, bhārṅgī, ginger, rock salt, long pepper, and rāsnā.

One should drink this powder mixed with a measure of ghee to destroy cough; it also removes weak digestion, asthma, and hiccups. (6.20.32) One should pound kaṇṭakārī together with its roots, fruits, and branches, and boil it in one droṇa of water until reduced to one-fourth. (6.20.33)
Having strained that decoction, one should place it back on the fire; ghee should be added judiciously, and these medicinal pastes (kalkas) should be administered.

6.20.35–36 Durālabhā, chinnaruhā, the three pungents (tryūṣaṇa), citraka, rāsnā, karkaṭaka, and pippalīmūla— each of these [should be] half a pala. Having added twenty palas of treacle and sugar, one should extract that thickened electuary (leha).
In the cold season, one should administer a measured *kuḍava* of powdered *pippalī*, a *kuḍava* of *tugākṣīrī*, and likewise a *kuḍava* of honey.
One should lick this electuary in the proper dose; it destroys the five types of cough and removes heart disease, hiccups, and dyspnea.
Just as a snake does not transgress a consecrated mantra uttered against it, so too this electuary leaves no room for cough to persist in embodied beings.
6.20.39–40: Daśamūlī, apāmārga, śaṅkhapuṣpī, śaṭhī, vacā, citraka, ātmaguptā, and pippalīmūla— these [should be used].
6.20.41 One should take two *pala*s each of *balā*, *puṣkaramūla*, and likewise *gajapippalī*, along with one hundred fresh *abhayā* fruits.

6.20.42 Together with these, one should boil one *āḍhaka* of barley in five *āḍhakas* of water; having removed it from the heat once the barley is cooked, one should extract the *harītakī* fruits [from the decoction].

6.20.42–43. A splitting [of the swelling] should then be performed upon them using a bamboo splinter. This is the twenty-first chapter. This ointment should be applied for the destruction of *śaṅkhaka* (temporal headache). One should, however, prepare a decoction (*kaṣāya*) from all these very same ingredients. 6.20.43.

6.21.1 One should perform frequent sprinkling with that cold [water]. 6.21.2 Due to the constant suppression of natural urges and from eating before the previous meal has been digested, the blood and wind become aggravated and take their seat in the head.
That wind, having reached the head and coalescing with the blood in one place at the rising of the sun, becomes corrupted by the conjunction with the rays of the sun.

6.21.4 It produces intense pain in the temples, the head, and the cheeks; it seizes the head excessively as if striking it, and one repeatedly grasps it with the hand. 6.21.5 Cold brain-matter flows out, stirred up by the heat of the sun; thus, as the sun rises higher, the headache increases.
With his head intact, he passes away at the end of the day; for this reason, the sages call it *sūryāvarta*.

6.21.7 One afflicted by *sūryāvarta* should drink *kalyāṇaka* ghee; a purgative should also be administered, and in that condition, head-purgation (*śīrṣavirecana*) is required. 6.21.8 Likewise, one should perform nasal therapy (*nasyakarma*), as well as oleation (*sneha*) after meals; furthermore, head-enemas (*śīrṣavasti*) should be maintained using ghee, oil, or muscle fat.
One should cook peacocks, cocks, and quails with milk; then, one should extract the butter produced by churning that milk.

6.21.10 It should be prepared with six times its quantity of milk along with the life-promoting (jīvanīya) medicinal herbs; from this, a nasal drop (nasya) should be administered to destroy sūryāvarta.
6.21.11 Bilva, aṃśumatī, rāsnā, sahadevā, punarnavā, kālā, guḍūcī, suṣavī, padmaka, madhuka, and balā.
These [substances], prepared with goat’s milk and used for sprinkling, as well as ghee prepared with these very same herbs, shall destroy [the affliction].

6.21.13 One should prepare a poultice (*upanāhana*) using the meat of wild animals (*jāṅgala*). By this, his most terrible disease, *sūryāvarta*, is pacified. 6.21.14 For one who indulges in minced meat, curd, fish, flour-based preparations, milk, and daytime sleep, the three humors (*dhātu*) become aggravated.
6.21.14–15 Furthermore,
the manyāpāśa and atyaghāṭā [vātas] cause intense pain in the neck; moreover, when it arises from there, it remains as a sharp [pain] in the eyebrows and the eyes.

6.21.16 It causes the sides of the cheeks to throb and remains seizing the jaw; it produces diseases of the eyes and strikes the temples with pain. 6.21.17 This extremely severe disease of the head is called Anantavāta; it arises from the derangement of the three humors (sannipāta), and I shall now describe its treatment.
6.21.17–18 One should pierce the vein located on the forehead and administer the drinking of medicated fats (sneha). One should purge his body and also purge his head.

6.21.19 The treatment prescribed for Sūryāvarta and Śirograha should also be applied in the case of Anantavāta; then it will result in well-being. 6.21.20 [Anantavāta is caused] by overeating, sleeping during the day, the suppression of vomiting and sneezing, physical trauma, exposure to heat, and the retention of natural urges.
6.21.20–21: Both Kapha and Vāta, having violently seized the channels carrying to the head, remain there tearing apart half the head and the root of the temples.
Swelling arises in the cheek and the eye likewise becomes discolored; this is the disease of the head known as *ardhāvabhedaka*, which is very difficult to overcome.

One should administer head-purgatives (*śiro-virecana*) and nasal therapy (*nasya-karma*). Furthermore, depending on availability, one should appropriately apply all types of muscle fat (*vasā*), clarified butter (*ghṛta*), and oil.
One should administer a large dose of that very [substance], and by it one succeeds. [One may also use] cotton seeds, black gram, wheat, mustard, and barley. (6.21.23–24)
6.21.25 One should prepare two types of *pañcamūla* together with milk; by means of that [mixture], which retains its heat, one should administer fomentation through a tube (*nāḍīsveda*).

6.21.26 And with those [substances] boiled in milk while still warm, one should apply a poultice (*upanāhana*) to the patient. [The ingredients are: *karañja*, seeds of *śigru*, bark, leaf, and sugar.
This head-purgative (śīrṣavirecana) is for all diseases of the head; it should be applied at the back of the head, at the edge of the forehead, and as far as the temples.
One may also cauterize with the stalk of *manyā* or *pippalī*. By that same procedure, one should treat *ardhāvabhedaka* as well.

Cauterization is indicated for diseases of the head caused by *vāta* and also for those caused by *śleṣman*; therefore, a wise physician should apply it when these head diseases have become excessively aggravated.
Alternatively, one may cauterize with wild pippalī fruits or again with the stalk; this is for those who constantly consume dry food as well as for those suffering from udāvarta.

6.21.31 When the wind (pavana) moves upward and causes shaking of the head, one should administer mild unctuous substances (sneha), or even *balā-taila*. 6.21.32 For one who consumes all types of tastes, nasal therapy (nasya-karma), drinking unctuous substances, and daily oil enemas (anuvāsana) [are beneficial], even when there is indigestion from overeating.
When the three doshas are provoked together, they cause swelling at the head; in such a case, one should first venesection the veins and likewise drink aged ghee.

6.21.34 Purification by smoking and the evacuation of the head— this is the summary of treatments proclaimed for diseases of the head. 6.21.35 I shall now describe the diseases located within the throat along with their treatments, [caused] by loud speaking, agitation, excessive eating, and so forth.
6.21.35–36. By the consumption of dry foods and drinks, the wind (pavana) becomes excessively aggravated; his throat smokes, and likewise it makes a wheezing sound.
6.21.37 His heart is distressed and his voice becomes hoarse due to the wind (māruta); in such cases, nasal therapy (nasya) and the internal administration of *balā-taila* are recommended.

6.21.38 When there is a predominance of phlegm and wind (*kapha-vāta*), gargles (*kavalagraha*) should likewise be employed; these consist of long pepper (*pippalī*), long pepper root (*pippalīmūla*), black pepper (*marica*), and chebulic myrobalan (*harītakī*).
6.21.38–39 Ginger, barley alkali, lodhra, and likewise tejovatī— these, taken in equal parts as a powder, together with honey.

6.21.40 For anorexia caused by phlegm (śleṣman), mouth-washing is the primary treatment. [One should use] long pepper (pippalī), licorice (madhuka), mūrvā, sandalwood (candana), lotus (kamala), and blue water-lily (utpala).
6.21.41 Likewise, uśīra, padmaka, lodhra, cardamom (elā), and lāmajjaka—these should be prepared in equal parts with honey.
In cases of anorexia caused by pitta, one should administer double the amount of sugar along with cumin, black pepper, costus, wood-apple, and sochal salt.
6.21.43 For disorders caused by Vāta, a mouth-rinse consisting of madhuka, sugar, and oil is recommended. [Also used are] jambu, the tender leaves of āmra, lodhra, triphalā, cavya, and ciktraka.
6.21.44 Paṭola, naktamāla, śirīṣa, khadira, asana, dārvī, haridrā, mustā, tejohvā, madhuka, and balā [are likewise employed].
One should prepare a decoction from these [drugs] in equal parts; this gargle (kavalagrāha) should be administered mixed with honey. 6.21.45
6.21.46 Fresh *kapittha* fruit, combined with *vyoṣa*, honey, and sugar, is recommended for all types of loss of appetite; it should be held in the mouth.
6.21.47 Cumin, black pepper, grapes, *tintriṇīka*, pomegranate, *sauvarcala* salt, and *kāravī*, combined with jaggery and honey [are also beneficial].
[The gargle] made with *drākṣā* (grapes) and *ghautaka* [is] a cleanser of the mouth; it is the best gargle, recommended for all types of anorexia.

6.21.49 Three doshas arise in the throat, causing a swelling that obstructs the passage; they increase the terrible *galaśuṇḍī*, which spreads throughout the throat. 6.21.50 Venesection, the internal administration of fats (*sneha*), strong head-purgatives (*śīrṣavirecana*), the application of surgical instruments, and medicated smoking will destroy *galaśuṇḍikā*.
Earache caused by Vāta, as well as ear-wind (karṇavāta), are Vāta-originated; deafness is likewise declared to arise from both Vāta and Śleṣman.

6.21.52 The drinking of medicated fats (*sneha*), nasal drops (*nasya*), tubular fomentation (*nāḍīsveda*), and poultices (*upanāhana*), as well as the muscle fat (*vasā*) and marrow (*majjā*) of marshy animals, are recommended for filling the ears (*karṇapūraṇa*). 6.21.53 Long pepper (*pippalī*), bilva root, costus (*kuṣṭha*), licorice (*madhuka*), *lodhra*, tiger-claw (*vyāghranakha*), spikenard (*māṃsī*), small cardamom (*sūkṣmailā*), and deodar (*devadāru*).
6.21.53–54 One should cook one *prastha* of oil with this *garbha* over a mild fire, along with equal amounts of the juices of radish and ginger. 6.21.54
6.21.55 One should apply a cotton wick (*picu*) soaked in that [oil] into the ear and administer nasal therapy (*nasya*). By this means, even the most agonizing earache is quickly pacified.
6.21.56 Śirīṣa-oil processed a hundred times, as well as *balā*-oil and *miśraka*-oil, when applied to the ear, swiftly remove earache and deafness.
One should cook the flesh of goats, snakes, peacocks, crocodiles, and porcupines in seven *droṇas* of milk on an equal scale.
6.21.58 When one-quarter remains, it should be cooled, strained, and churned; the butter that arises therefrom should be cooked with these [substances] in equal parts:
6.21.59 Kṣava, phaṇijjaka, saindhava salt, balā, vacā, vyāghranakha, māṃsī, devadāru, and likewise agaru.
6.21.59–60 Jīvaka, ṛṣabhaka, medā, śṛṅgī, and karkaṭakasya; ātmaguptā fruit, drākṣā, tvak, patra, and vāluka.

6.21.61 Having caused all of that to flow out, one should have it stored securely; then one should administer picu, anointment, potions, and enema therapy. 6.21.62 By this, diseases of the head, whatever earaches there may be, ear discharges, and diseases located above the clavicle (jatrugatāḥ) are pacified.
This treatment for earache caused by an excess of vāta has been declared. Hereafter, I shall explain that which arises from blood and that which arises from worms.
6.21.64 When vitiated *pitta* and blood flow specifically toward the ear, swelling, redness, and earache arise.
6.21.65 One should venesect the vein at the forehead and administer purgation to him; likewise, one should prescribe nasal medication (*nasya*) and head-purgation (*śirovirecana*).
Whether by non-treatment or by treatments, one brings the ear to suppuration; for that, one should apply a poultice (upanāha) and wound-oil (vraṇataila) for healing.
6.21.67 Likewise, one should clear ear-discharge (*karṇasrāva*) with ear-picks (*karṇaśalākā*). Trikaṭu, rock salt (*saindhava*), kuṣṭha, mañjiṣṭhā, and madhuka;
6.21.68 rāsnā, haridrā, tejohvā, varāṅga, the bark of *tilvaka*, lac (*lākṣā*), *mūrvā*, *eraṇḍa*, *karka*, *kesara*, *āsana*, and *vīraṇa*.
6.21.68–69: *Sūkṣmailā*, *tagara*, *patra*, *tvak*, *vyāghranakha*, *āragvadha*, *mālatī*, sesame seeds, *māṣa* beans, the knot of *bhūrja* bark, and *nidigdhikā*.
6.21.70 One should cook one *prastha* of oil with these ingredients in equal parts, adding the fat (*vasā*) of a snake, as well as the flesh of a brown mongoose and a donkey.
6.21.71 With this [oil], one should fill the ear and let it remain for a *muhūrta*; it cures ear discharge, earache, deafness, and ear pain.
This oil cures all diseases of the head, as well as obstructions in the ear canals, the palate, and likewise the skull.

6.21.73 Intense pain arises, along with a burning sensation, pricking, and dizziness; these, according to the wise, are the symptoms of earache caused by worms. 6.21.74 They say that when all these symptoms are present, it is declared here to be incurable. Moths, centipedes, as well as insects and ants—
Entering the auditory canals, they indeed cause intense pain; his ears feel as if they are being pierced, and likewise there is a gurgling sound.

6.21.76 When a worm moves within the ear, there is sharp pain; when it is motionless, there is no pain. One should fill the ear with honey, sour gruel (*śukta*), milk, wine (*surā*), or *āsava*, and warm it. After a short while, one should tilt the head downward. Once the worm has emerged, if ear discharge (*karṇasrāva*) occurs, one should perform the treatment for ear discharge as previously described. [End of Chapter Twenty-Two]

Just as food eaten by men during the day does not cause disorder when there is indigestion from the previous meal, yet that which remains overnight may indeed cause disorder, understand from me the reason for this.
6.22.2. For one who exerts himself, moves about, or whose mind is distracted, as well as when the secretion of digestive juices (rasa) is sluggish, eating during the day does not cause harm. 6.22.3.
They say the heart resembles a lotus; it becomes closed and opened by the rays of the sun at the end of the day.
When his heart has awakened and his channels have opened, those [impurities] originating in his heart flow out through the open channels during the day.

6.22.5 By this means, his bodily constituents (*dhātavaḥ*) do not undergo moisture during the day; likewise, even for one who is satiated by a morning meal, [the food] does not become moist while the previous meal is undigested. 6.22.6 Furthermore, by this method, the evening meal does not become spoiled; yet, if it remains overnight, it becomes corrupted and may even give rise to diseases.
6.22.6–7. Thus, even when the passages are closed, wind and fire within embodied beings digest food here at night, even without physical exertion.
6.22. When the heart is languid, during the night, when there is nausea, and when the channels are constricted, one should not engage in physical exercise.
Because of the remnants of food remaining in the heart and in the stomach (āmāśaya), his body becomes flaccid due to that undigested matter failing to reach proper digestion.

When the heart is afflicted and obstructed, when his feces and urine are suppressed at the end of the night, and when the essence of food has arrived, there arises a condition born from pitta and kapha.
When the wind (māruta) is obstructed by a mass of food and ascends upward, it causes a seizing pain in the heart, nausea, a sense of fullness in the limbs,
and from that residue of food, it produces fainting, thirst, fever, vomiting, diarrhea, hiccups, and a loss of appetite for food.
If one stays awake after a meal has not been digested, it produces these diseases which are like poison. Therefore, staying awake after a meal during indigestion is forbidden. Chapter Twenty-three.

6.23.1 Learn from me of sleep, excessive sleep, and fainting. For when one is overcome by *tamas* at the end of the day, the quality of *sattva* [diminishes]. 6.23.2 Then his senses gradually withdraw from their functions, as the food he has eaten is being digested by the phlegm located in the heart.
When the channels carrying sight and hearing are obstructed by that which has increased [in intensity], living beings are severed from their activities during the day by the rays of the sun.

6.23.4 Attacked by those various physical and mental [afflictions] thus described, lassitude—which is characterized by a lack of activity and loss of appetite—enters one through the quality of darkness (tamas).
6.23.5 In this way, that which is called sleep arises in all beings; ordained of old by Brahmā, it removes anxiety, grief, and fatigue.
While he is sleeping, the prāṇa and apāna breaths, together with heat, remain awake within this body; joined with the individual soul (jīva), he does not perish.
6.23.7 When the mind is withdrawn along with the withdrawal of the senses, yet it still frequents their respective objects, know that state to be called "dreaming.
6.23.8 When it engages in conversation with ancestors, gods, and humans, and attains other [experiences], that indeed is a variety of dream; for it is not [the nature] of the Self.
Excessive sleep occurs in living beings when phlegm (śleṣman) increases; however, for those in whom wind (vāta) is predominant, sleep invariably comes to an end.
6.23.10 Enemas, drinks of medicated fats, the meat broths of domestic, marshy, and aquatic animals, and the drinking of jaggery and milk are supreme inducers of sleep.
6.23.11 Massage, dry powder massage, bathing, wine, and likewise ghee; mental clarity and tranquility are the remedies for one whose sleep has been lost.
One should avoid smoking, purgation, as well as emesis and head-purgation (errhines), fasting, and excessive sleep. 6.23.11–12.
6.23.13 Traveling by improper means, excessive physical exertion, and deep reflection on hidden matters—these, along with a constant diet of barley and attachment to sleep, one should abandon.
6.23.14 Clarity of the senses depends upon the palate and the mind; the *citta* (mind-stuff) resides in the heart, while the intellect (*buddhi*) is the support of all the senses.
When the blood and the three humors (doṣas) have converged and become vitiated, they afflict the hearts of men here and even cause them to wither away.

When the heart is parched, one indeed becomes deluded through negligence; and when the heart is oppressed, it causes the mind and consciousness to be bewildered. From the sinking of the consciousness and the mind, one falls into a state of unconsciousness. Chapter Twenty-Four: [The Section on] Being Afflicted by Fever.
