This oil dispels eighty diseases arising from *vāta*, including facial paralysis, tingling in the feet, pain in the sides, fever, wasting, scrotal hernia, intestinal obstruction, dysuria, cardiac oppression, and exhaustion of the limbs; as well as those originating from the combination of all three humors (*sannipāta*), those caused by two combined humors, and those arising from a single humor.
6.24.2–3 It cures disorders of the female reproductive tract, sterility, and excessive menstrual discharge; it bestows strength and complexion, and overcomes cough and consumption.
6.24.4 One hundred palas each of balā roots, daśamūla, śatāvarī, guḍūcī, rāsnā, madhuka, and devadāru;
6.24.5 And ten-pala portions each of kulattha, badara, yava, and māṣa— these should be boiled in five droṇas of water.
One should cook the decoction remaining after one *droṇa*, combined with one *āḍhaka* of oil, one *prastha* of ghee, and one *droṇa* of milk.
6.24.7 The physician should indeed administer these substances to be ground into a paste: tagara, uśīra, vālaka, kuṣṭha, dhānyaka, musta, elā, vacā, aguru, and candana.
6.24.8 [He should also give] paripelava, kālīya, māṃsī, śrīveṣṭaka, rasa, kunduruṣka, takkola, sarala, nalikā, and nakha.
6.24.8–9 Spṛkkā, saffron, camphor, the fruit of jasmine and *tinduka*, the leaves of *coraka* and *nāgāhvaya*, *śatāhvā*, and *hareṇukā*.

6.24.10–11. One should cook oil with equal parts of *saturuṣka*, the *jīvanīya* group, *priyaṅgu*, *hapuṣā*, *sthauṇeyaka*, *uśīra*, and *śaileya*, using these ground into a paste. This oil removes diseases caused by *vāta*; it should be employed for drinking, massage, nasal administration (*nasya*), and enema (*basti*).
"Punarvasu declared that it is appropriate to apply treatments for the suppression of those vātas which reside in the entire body, whether they are combined or arise individually. (6.24.11–12)

6.24.13 A man who is constantly and according to rule satiated with this oil is abandoned by all diseases, just as deer avoid the dwelling place of a lion. 6.24.14 One should take a well-grounded *tulā* of *balā* that has yielded its essence, and boil it in four *droṇas* of water until one-fourth remains.
One should cause ten *palas* of powdered *balā* to be added there, and one should give two *āḍhakas* of oil from plucked sesame seeds. 6.24.15

One should cook that [medicinal paste] with four times its quantity of milk over a gentle fire. It is recommended for all wind-related diseases (vātavyādhi), as well as for internal hemorrhage (raktapitta), chest wounds, and wasting (kṣatakṣaya).

It is also beneficial for disorders of the female reproductive tract (yonivyāpad), for the loss of semen, and for dryness of the palate, thirst, burning sensations, pain in the flanks, and menorrhagia.
It cures consumption, epilepsy, erysipelas, and stiffness of the head; Balā oil is said to promote longevity and complexion, and to increase progeny.
6.24.19 One should take two hundred palas of the root of *rāsnā* and one hundred palas each of *balā*, *śatāvarī*, *guḍūcī*, and *varaṇa*. 6.24.20 Furthermore,
one should add five palas each of *āḍhakī*, *śigru*, *airaṇḍa*, *śirīṣa*, *āragvadha*, *śvadaṃṣṭrā*, and *bhūtikā*.
6.24.20–21 One should cook finely ground [medicinal substances] in ten *droṇas* of water until one *droṇa* remains; into that decoction, one should then boil half a *maṇa* of oil.
6.24.22 Ten *droṇas* of milk and half a *ḍhaka* of clarified butter should likewise be boiled together; into this mixture, one should cook the embryo.
6.24.23 [One should add] *madhuka*, *mālatī* flowers, *mañjiṣṭhā*, *madayantikā*, *kāśmarya*, *ajamodā*, *śṛṅgī*, and yellow *mustaka*.
Ātmaguptā, āḍhakī, mūrvā, vārtākā, madhūlikā, sahadevā, eraṇḍā, rohiṣa, and navamālikā.
Phañjikā, madhūka, vīrā, nīra, and kadamba; the fruit of pīlu and palāśa, as well as kumārī, aśvattha, and tainduka;
hrībera, pippalī, kuṣṭha, drākṣā, kaṭukarohiṇī, kāyasthā, vayasthā, madhuparṇī, and citraka.
6.24.26–27 And [he prepared] the *mahāpuruṣadantā*, the *modakī*, and the *sallakī*; the finest *devadāru* and *aguru*, as well as *candana* and *paripelava*.

6.24.28 One should cook an equal amount of oil with these ingredients ground together in one-pala portions: blue lotus (*nīlotpala*), fragrant root (*uśīra*), grapes (*mṛdvīkā*), and sour vetasa (*amlavetasa*).

6.24.29 It is recommended for use in food, as an ointment, for drinking, as an enema (*vasti*), and as nasal drops (*nasya*), in all diseases of Vata, in wasting due to chest injury (*kṣatakṣīṇa*), and in headaches.
In cases of loss of voice, internal hemorrhaging (raktapitta), hiccup, dyspnea, menorrhagia, and when vāta is combined with pitta or combined with blood.

6.24.31 This Rāsnā oil is excellent for irregular fever, heart disease, trembling of the limbs, epilepsy, blood-born tumors (raktagulma), and for men whose semen has been depleted. 6.24.32 It increases strength and muscle mass. [One should take] one hundred palas of Sahacara root, along with its leaves and branches.
One should prepare [the paste] by finely grinding [the ingredients] in four *droṇas* of water; when reduced to one *droṇa* and strained, one should slowly cook one *āḍhaka* of oil in it.

6.24.34 One should apply a poultice (upanāha) to his head using the flesh of aquatic animals and those from marshy lands; one should also perform nasal therapy (nasya) and apply a medicinal wick (picu) to the crown of the head.
6.24.35 One should open his mouth comfortably with a forceps (sandaṃśa), and likewise administer unctuous meat broth through a vessel (bhṛṅgāra).
Likewise, when the wind has reached the stomach (āmāśaya), the physician should not treat with unctuous substances a patient who, while opening his teeth, cannot bring them together.

6.24.37 One should prescribe fasting for him, as well as purification therapies (*saṃśodhana*). Vāyu located in its own site, having been provoked by the coating of undigested matter (*āma*), increases when treated with unctuous substances (*sneha*) and meat broths. Therefore, his diet should consist of dry and pungent foods. 6.24.38 [One should avoid] unctuous substances and meat broths; rather, he should be treated with drying measures. 6.24.39 [The physician should prescribe] bitter, astringent, and pungent [substances], as well as those that are light and cold. 6.24.40 [He should also prescribe] decoctions of *kaṣāya* [taste], *virecana* (purgatives), and *laṅghana* (fasting); likewise, one should employ *dhūma* (fumigation) and *nastaḥkarma* (nasal therapy). 6.24.41 [One should apply] *pradehas* (poultices), *pariṣekas* (affusions), and *upanāhas* (poultices for counter-irritation); furthermore, one should employ *śirovirecana* (head-purgatives) and *vamanas* (emetics). 6.24.42 [One should prescribe] *vyoṣa* (the three pungents), *lavaṇas* (salts), *yavānī* (Trachyspermum ammi), *hiṅgu* (Asafoetida), *sauvarcala* (black salt), *rāmaṭha* (another form of Asafoetida), and *cavya* (Piper chaba). 6.24.43 [One should prescribe] *viḍa* (black salt), *saindhava* (rock salt), *pippalī* (long pepper), *dāru* (Cedrus deodara), *śigrubīja* (seeds of *Shigru*), *ajājī* (cumin), and *jīraka* (caraway). 6.24.44 [One should prescribe] *śuṇṭhī* (dry ginger), *bhūtīka* (Cymbopogon citratus), *vacā* (Acorus calamus), *hiṅgu*, *sauvarcala*, *rāmaṭha*, and *cavya*. 6.24.45 [One should prescribe] *viḍa*, *saindhava*, *pippalī*, *dāru*, *śigrubīja*, *ajājī*, and *jīraka*. 6.24.46 [One should prescribe] *śuṇṭhī*, *bhūtīka*, *vacā*, *hiṅgu*, *sauvarcala*, *rāmaṭha*, and *cavya*. 6.24.47 [One should prescribe] *viḍa*, *saindhava*, *pippalī*, *dāru*, prescribe] *viḍa*, *saindhava*, *pippalī*, *dāru*, *śigrubīja*, *ajājī*, and *jīraka*. 6.24.54 [One should prescribe] *śuṇṭhī*, *bhūtīka*, *vacā*, *hiṅgu*, *sauvarcala*, *rāmaṭha*, and *cavya*. 6.24.55 [One should prescribe] *viḍa*, *saindhava*, *pippalī*, *dāru*, *śigrubīja*, *ajājī*, and *jīraka*. 6.24.56 [One should prescribe] *śuṇṭhī*, *bhūtīka*, *vacā*, *hiṅgu*, *sauvarcala*, *rāmaṭha*, 6.24.38–39 A physician skilled in the scriptures should administer [therapies] for the purpose of food or medicine. When [the poison] is located in the stomach (āmāśaya), one should prescribe emesis, alkalis (kṣāra), and likewise alkali-sugar confections (kṣāraguḍa).

6.24.40 Non-poisonous *śīdhu* liquors, beneficial meat from wild animals, *śyāmāka* millet, *koradūṣa* grain, mung beans, and red *śāli* rice; 6.24.41 Fomentation and barley-based food are beneficial when the *vāyu* has entered the stomach (*āmāśaya*). When the *vāyu* produces its symptoms having entered the large intestine (*pakvāśaya*), [the following remedies are indicated].

6.24.41–42 Whether [the poison] has reached the channels, all the limbs, the marrow, or even the bones, one should administer treatment after having examined the symptoms of that person who has been freed from the [poisonous] form.

6.24.43 The entire treatment for wind-diseases (*vātavyādhi*) that has been taught applies when the wind has reached the site of the blood; however, the treatment previously mentioned [for blood disorders] should be applied when the wind has entered the blood (*vātaśoṇitaka*). 6.24.44 In the case of *gṛdhrasī* (sciatica) that has arisen, *balā-taila* is recommended.
Root-plant oil (mūlaka-taila) or the oil of *sahacara* is excellent; likewise, enemas, internal oleation drinks, and massages with unctuous substances [are beneficial].

In the *gṛdhrasī* (sciatica), the letting of blood is highly recommended. Regarding the eighty diseases born of *vāta* that were previously enumerated, this is their treatment within the seven locations of *vāyu*. This applies to both those diseases arising from *māruta* that are curable and those that are incurable.
Then they leap up and stand still within the seven locations of the vital air (vāyu). There occurs a breaking of the bones and marrow, trembling, and the withering of the limbs.

6.24.49–50 Māruta (Vāta) causes hemiplegia, epilepsy, insanity, facial paralysis, lockjaw, clubbed hands, kyphosis, deformity of the fingers, and dislocation of the joints; it also produces other wind-related diseases. One should treat those conditions that are curable according to their specific locations and in the proper sequence.
6.24.50–51 Thus has this treatment for those afflicted by wind-diseases been described in detail. For wind is the cause of life for living beings, as well as the cause of its end.

6.24.52 He constantly causes the sun and the moon to move in continuous succession; likewise, he brings rain through the wind in the world and provides protection. 6.24.53 The wind carries the celestial chariots of all the inhabitants of heaven in every direction; it establishes the shoreline in the ocean and even creates the clouds.
The dispersal of clouds occurs through the wind, and lightning arises from the wind. The wind sustains the three worlds; everything proceeds from the wind.

The wind brings forth flowers and fruits, sustains the waters, and causes the falling of meteors, earthquakes, and the supporting of the earth. Endowed with exceeding strength, the wind can even hold up the Gaṅgā in the sky; such are the many manifestations of the qualities of the wind.

6.24.56–57 Therefore, the best of physicians should diligently perform its treatment according to the scriptures; in this way, he shall attain success. Thus spoke the venerable Ātreya. Thus ends the twenty-fourth chapter in the Bheḷa [Saṃhitā]. Chapter Twenty-five: Now, therefore, we shall explain the treatment of splenic enlargement (plīha) and halīmaka. Thus said the venerable Ātreya. 6.24.57

6.25.1 If a man eats excessively foods that cause secretions to flow, or if he engages in physical exercise after having undergone fasting or purgation; 6.25.2 Or if, after eating and drinking water, he suddenly runs, or travels rapidly in a carriage on his back, or swims, or suffers from the improper administration of oleation therapy;
For embodied beings who are afflicted by other diseases and are weak, the spleen may enlarge from its natural site; hear from me its symptoms.
6.25.4 It causes softness of the spleen and pain that is both sharp and hard; this enlargement of the spleen (plīhā) arises from vāta and involves a great accumulation [of tissue].
6.25.5 Accompanied by fever and thirst, characterized by sweating and intense pain, yellowish in color, and with stiffened limbs—such is the spleen (plīhā) caused by pitta.

One who constantly fails to maintain a store of food, who is perpetually afflicted by upward-moving wind (udāvarta), and who is overwhelmed by pain, is considered to have a spleen disorder (plīha) characterized by phlegm (śleṣmātmaka).

6.25.7 Where a physician perceives the symptoms of all three doshas, he should know that splenic enlargement (plīhā) caused by the combination of all three (sānnipātika) is incurable. 6.25.8 That which is the size of a fist is easily curable; one should treat it with the utmost care. However, when it has increased to an excessive size, it cannot be cured by any means whatsoever.
In all these cases, there is debility, a sense of heaviness, exhaustion of the limbs, lack of relish for food, indigestion, retention of feces and urine, and fever.

6.25.10 One should drink grape wine (*mārdvīka*) with moderation, or the *gaṇḍīra-ariṣṭa* liquor; or one should have the patient drink *candraprabha* or sugarcane-based liquor (*śārkara*) in cases of *halīmaka*.

6.25.11 One should administer the *rasāyana* known as *ayorajīya* with milk; or, being self-controlled and pure, one should consume the electuary (*leha*) of *agastya* and *abhaya*. Thus spoke the venerable Ātreya. Thus ends the twenty-fifth chapter in the Bheḷa-saṃhitā. The Twenty-sixth Chapter: Now, therefore, we shall explain the treatment of *apatantraka* (convulsions), so said the venerable Ātreya.
6.25.11–6.26.1 By the consumption of dry food and drink, by the suppression of natural urges, and likewise by excessive physical exertion in one who has already been emaciated; 6.26.1

6.26.2 In one who has undergone purgation and medicated nasal therapy, who has been emaciated by enemas, who has skipped a meal, or who has overeaten; 6.26.3 the Vāyu (bodily wind), having become aggravated and moving into the colon (*pakvāśaya*), becomes purified and, having afflicted the heart, remains pervading the ten vessels (*dhamanī*).
6.26.3–4 Filling the channels upward, it rushes into the head and the temples; by its convulsions, his limbs are bent like a bow.
6.26.5 With eyes closed or fixed, or breathless, he writhes; with difficulty he draws breath like a crawling snake, and he moans like a pigeon.
6.26.6 When the heart is released from the wind, he regains his composure; yet again he lies down with drooping eyes, as if unconscious and lacking self-control.
A terrible wind-born disease, localized in the arteries and the heart, arises from the complete obstruction of the channels and from the forceful suppression of natural urges.
6.26.8 Due to the agitation of the channels, apatantraka occurs constantly; a wise physician should neither induce emesis nor purgation in this patient.
6.26.9 One should not administer non-unctuous enemas (āsthāpana) to him, nor should one cause him to fast; [the treatment consists of] long pepper, viḍaṅga, drumstick seeds, and black pepper.

6.26.9–10 One should prepare these [substances] finely ground as a head-purgative (śīrṣavirecana) for one who is suffering from labored breathing and an increase of both phlegm (śleṣman) and wind (māruta).

When that phlegm is overcome, consciousness returns. Sauvarcala salt, pomegranate, asafoetida, and amlavetasa, as well as mahauṣadha (ginger) when drunk, destroy apatantraka. Likewise, asafoetida, puṣkaramūla, tumburu, and harītakī [are effective].
This should be administered with water decocted from barley and three types of salt; it cures heart disease, pain in the flanks, and severe convulsive disorders (apatantra).

This formulation quickly pacifies colic and Vata-type abdominal tumors (gulma). One should prepare a fine powder of *vibhītaka*, *ativiṣā*, *bhadramustā*, *pippalī*, *bhārgī*, and *śṛṅgavera*. These powders should be drunk with wine or warm water.
Harītakī, vacā, rāsnā, rock salt (saindhava), and sour vetasa quickly destroy asthma, cough, and apatanaka in men. (6.26.15–16)

6.26.17–18: Combined with a measured dose of ghee, this destroys apatānaka (hemiplegia). The physician should cook equal parts of śukanāsā, mahāvallī, the two types of bṛhatī, mahauṣadha, nicula, bhārṅgī, kālikā, and punarnavā, each in the measure of one akṣa.
6.26.18–19 One should cause [the patient] to drink one prastha of ghee prepared with one āḍhaka of water; this also cures dyspnea, cough, severe hiccups, heart disease, and apatantraka.
6.26.20 One should not transgress this clarified butter (sarpir) as the great ocean does not overstep its shore. Kākādanī, balālambā, the two types of bṛhatī, and mahauṣadha;
6.26.21 kadambapuṣpī, kālā, candravallī, and likewise vṛṣā; ādārī, vidārī, suvahā, and keśavatī as well.
One should boil two-pala portions of each of these in one droṇa of water; with these same [herbs] in the measure of one akṣa each, one should cook one prastha of ghee. 6.26.21–22.

One who drinks this [medicinal ghee] prepared with a decoction of twice the quantity, according to the proper method, overcomes even incurable and severe hiccup as well as dyspnea. One should cook one *prastha* of ghee with two *palas* of *harītakī*, two *palas* of *sauvarcala* salt, and twice the amount of milk.
This ghee cures apatanaka, heart disease, and urinary disorders; it also immediately treats even advanced cases of hiccups and dyspnea.

6.26.26 This therapeutic treatment has been described for the purpose of destroying *atapānaka*. Now I shall describe the symptoms and the treatment for those afflicted by *ardita* (facial paralysis).
6.26.27 [It arises] from blows with weapons or wood, from excessive indulgence in sexual intercourse, from vomiting, from the drinking of wine, and from the drawing of a bow.

For those who habitually engage in constant physical exercise, for one who has fallen from a height or has leaped over a distance, for one whose food intake is unrestrained, and for one emaciated by disease— (these are the conditions for which [the following applies]).
6.26.29 When the wind (vāyu) becomes aggravated in a person, it moves only upward; it afflicts the root of the jaw, the head, and even the neck.
6.26.30 It causes his face and eyes to become distorted; his head and neck tremble, and even his nose becomes crooked.
His eyes are closed and motionless, yet he stares intensely upward; his gaze is askance, with eyes that are squinted and distorted.

6.26.32 His lips become swollen, his chin is bent, he spits excessively, and his speech becomes faltering. Chapter Twenty-Seven: [Remedies] for the Destruction of Ulcers 6.27.1 Observing the stage of the ulcer, one should then apply the appropriate treatment: namely, incision (*bhedana*), ripening (*pācana*), stabilization (*stambhana*), and drying (*śoṣaṇa*).
6.27.1–2 One should perform the procedures of draining and healing on a wound using the following: uditā, karṇamoṭa, rāsnā, and mūlakaparṇikā.
6.27.3 Śukanāsā, sugandhā, samaṅgā, kuṣṭhaka, kāleyaka, balā, dantī, pāṭhā, śatapadī, and sthirā— 6.27.4 This paste,
to be applied as a compress, destroys swelling in wounds. Udumbara, śirīṣa, madhuka, candana, and sesame seeds [are also used].
Indukānta, samudrāntā, and likewise śatāvarī; nīlotpala, padmaka, the two types of bark (tvac), and the two types of sārivā.
6.27.6 This paste—ground sesame mixed with madhuka and the paste of picumanda—destroys inflammation and wounds.
6.27.7 When combined with the two previous ingredients and ghee, it heals wounds in ulcerated areas. Triphalā, dhātakī, lodhra, samaṅgā, madhuka, and balā [are used for this].
The two *bṛhatī* plants, *samudrāntā*, and likewise *śatāvarī*; blue lotus, *kaṭphala*, jasmine, and golden *yūthikā*.

Oil prepared with equal parts of the pastes of these [plants] serves as a healer of wounds. The tender leaves of *nimba*, mango, and *āmalakī*, along with *madhuka* and *balā*—oil cooked with these in the juice of cow dung destroys wounds. [Likewise, oil may be prepared with] *nyagrodha*, *udumbara*, *aśvattha*, *plakṣa*, *pāṭhā*, *varuṇa*, and *arjuna*.
6.27.10–11. Decoctions made from *śamī*, *badarī*, and these [other] plants are for washing wounds. Barley-based food, red *śāli* rice, mung beans, *nīvāra*, and *ṣaṣṭika* rice [are beneficial].

6.27.12 A person with an ulcer should always consume the meat of wild animals (*jāṅgala*). He should also avoid sour substances, curd, leafy vegetables, and the meat of marshy or aquatic animals (*ānūpa* and *vārija*).
6.27.13 A person with an ulcer should strictly avoid milk and heavy foods. A physician specializing in internal medicine (*kāyacikitsaka*) should apply these therapeutic measures to the ulcer.
6.27.13–14 Furthermore,
one should perform scarification on the ulcer, as well as the remaining therapeutic procedures: excision, incision, scraping, suturing, and scarification.

6.27.15 Whatever else may be equal to that which promotes digestion, as well as the twelve defects of wounds and the sixfold examination; 6.27.16 And the thirty-six determined therapeutic measures for those caused by foreign bodies (śalya)— the physician treating internal medicine (kāyacikitsaka) should perform these procedures according to their general description.
Triphalā, madhuka, lodhra, mañjiṣṭhā, bilva, śuṇṭhikā, samaṅgā, dhātakī, lākṣā, and the resin of the śālmali tree.

6.27.18 The resin of the *pālāśa* and the resin of the *kakubha*: these fine powders are the supreme healers for wounds. 6.27.19 The resins of *guggulu*, *sallakī*, *sarja*, and *tiniśa* are said to be healers of wounds, whether used together or individually.

"The procedures for fumigation regarding wounds and those actions to be performed during the immediate aftermath—this remainder of the work of the surgeon must be carried out by one who has witnessed the practice. Thus spoke the venerable Ātreya. This concludes the twenty-seventh chapter on surgery (bheḷa). Chapter Twenty-Eight: Now, therefore, we shall explain the treatment of alcoholism (pānātyaya); so said the venerable Ātreya. 6.27.20

6.28.1 All tastes, with the exception of salt, are established in wine; it is sharp, hot, subtle, quick-acting, and pervasive. 6.28.2 It is digestive, pleasing to the heart, beneficial to all beings, light, a remover of anxiety, grief, and fatigue, and an increaser of sexual pleasure and joy.
6.28.2–3 It produces joy in a situation that calls for joy and removes fear in a situation that causes fear; it generates pleasure and recreation, and is the supreme bestower of splendor and valor.

6.28.4 It pervades all the limbs of the body, even down to the subtlest parts; due to its sharpness it deludes the mind, and due to its heat it produces *pitta*. 6.28.5 Because of its clarity it is pleasing to the heart; because of its dryness it provokes *vāta*; because of its sharpness it destroys *śleṣman* (phlegm); and because of its exhilarating nature it is said to be aphrodisiac (*vṛṣya*).
6.28.5–6 Due to the excessive consumption of intoxicants, the provoked pitta and vāta dry up the rasa-carrying vessels, as well as the kloman and the palate.
6.28.7 Overcome by thirst, he excessively delights in drink alone; yet as he drinks again and again, the fire and wind in his body dry up his frame.
6.28.8 It quickly reaches old age in the body, like water on sand; therefore, even for one who drinks day and night, being devoted to drink, [the body wastes away].
Thirst does not subside, and the drink is quickly digested; moreover, in one who has been intoxicated by liquor, the *pitta* and *vāyu* of that embodied being become agitated.
6.28.10 When the mind and intellect are deprived [of their faculties], they afflict the intelligence; consequently, one weeps, strikes out, emits [semen], and runs about excessively.

6.28.11 One falls down and leaps up, strikes, speaks much that is incoherent, goes to other women who should not be approached, and no longer discerns what ought to be done from what ought not to be done.
Likewise, he falls into a pit and lies down like one who is dead; naked, he enters a state of unconsciousness and wanders about devoid of awareness.

"Even such a person as this might have his senses overwhelmed by drinking from me; therefore, a wise man should drink wine in moderation and not indulge in it excessively. When consumed with proper method, that drinking is called nectar; it makes one's appetite for food exceedingly keen."
A physician who produces excitement in women for the sake of sexual intercourse treats the resulting disease with drink alone; there is no other treatment for it.

Therefore, one should partake of wine and auspicious words; one should consume light foods and the meat of wild animals and birds. Having bathed with fragrant bathing powders and applied unguents to the body, one should listen to pleasant sounds together with dear kinsmen.

6.28.17–18 Indeed, in a home of extreme happiness, one should perform this [practice] starting from a *prastha* and increasing progressively. [Therein are] beloved women of middle age, slender-waisted and fair-smiling. 6.28.18-19 Indeed, in a home of extreme happiness, one should perform this [practice] starting from a *prastha* and increasing progressively. [Therein are] beloved women of middle age, slender-waisted and fair-smiling.
Delighted by the rays of the moon, wearing variegated garlands, garments, and wreaths, those clever women— clad in silken robes and adorned with pearls and gems—
had their limbs anointed with red sandalwood paste; these incomparable women, beautiful with jeweled girdles, lay embracing one another upon the bed.
6.28.20–21 Women are indeed primarily characterized by a cold touch by their very nature; and by their very nature, women increase the joy of men.

For the *soma* element, which is cooling, increases in the heart through joy; therefore, during an excess of intoxication (*madātyaya*), one should quickly attend to a woman who generates great delight, through conversation, playful talk, massages, and diversions. There, the sounds of songs and musical instruments, as well as friends intoxicated with wine, [should be employed].
Those who follow one's wishes should sing and bring joy during the onset of intoxication; likewise, faultless wines mixed with cool water [should be used].
6.28.25 One should have him drink various refreshing drinks with wholesome meats as side dishes, along with excellent syrups (*pānaka*), *ṣāḍava* preparations, and satiating juices.
6.28.26 In cases of alcoholism (*madātyaya*), he should consume *takṣīrī* and *cukrī*, as well as buttermilk, grape juice, *sīdhu* liquor, *taittirīka* meat broth, and honey.
Fermented rice-gruel (*āranāla*), semen, the juices of jujube and pomegranate, parched grain (*lāja*) which is nourishing, and fine barley-meal which is also nourishing.
6.28.28 One should drink this satiating potion like a beverage with cold water, consisting of sauvarcala, ajājī, and likewise rock salt (saindhava).
6.28.29 Taken with a garnish of mātuluṅga, it destroys alcoholism (pānātyaya) in men; [it may also be prepared with] lac juice, taittirīka, pomegranate juice, and honey.

6.28.29–30 When the complication of intoxication has arisen, one should drink according to the previous procedure. One should prepare a well-ground measure (prastha) of *karkandhu* and *badara* fruits.
6.28.31 Having strained it seven times repeatedly in water weighing two *prasthas*, one should place it well-protected in an earthen vessel.

6.28.32 One should add two *palas* of jaggery (*guḍa*), likewise one *pala* of sugar (*śarkarā*), one *karṣa* of fine black pepper (*marica*), and a fourth part [of a *karṣa*] of saffron filaments (*kesara*).
One should have two karṣas each of cinnamon bark and cinnamon leaves, one karṣa of small cardamom, and half a karṣa of lotus stalks ground into a fine powder. 6.28.33–33.1.

6.28.34 A refreshing drink (pānaka) prepared with the appropriate spices (jātī), when consumed during the complications of drinking, quickly destroys the effects of over-drinking, just as the wind disperses scattered clouds. 6.28.35 This [preparation] cures vomiting, thirst, burning sensations, diarrhea, dysentery, loss of appetite, and difficulty in urination, as well as alcoholism (pānātyaya) in men.
Having crushed kāśmarya, pomegranate, grapes, madhuka, parūṣaka, and kuṭaja fruits, one should throw them into one āḍhaka of water.
6.28.37 One should administer fine powders of *sūkṣmailā*, *madhuka*, *lodhra*, *mañjiṣṭhā*, and likewise *pippalī*, in appropriate measures according to the requirements.

6.28.38 *Kesaraka* and the flower of the blue lotus (*nīlotpala*) should also be added here; this [mixture] is to be given in cases of alcoholism (*pānātyaya*) and serves to alleviate thirst and vomiting.
6.28.38–39: Two palas of *guḍūcī*, two palas of *balā*, and likewise two palas each of *lāmajjaka*, *mṛṇāla*, *madhuka*, and *utpala*.
6.28.40 These [ingredients] should be crushed and placed in a new vessel containing one āḍhaka of water; one should add eight palas of jaggery and likewise blue lotus (nīlotpala).
6.28.41 This drink, combined with saffron filaments (kesara), should be administered in cases of alcoholism (pānātyaya); it destroys fever, burning sensations, thirst, dyspnea, vomiting, and hiccups.
6.28.41–42. If the disorder of intoxication (pānavibhrama) is not pacified by these palliative measures, one should skillfully administer the powder of *trivṛt* mixed with wine.
6.28.43 One should drink a purgative powder or even a great nourishing (mahātarpaṇa) preparation; or, having consumed the previously mentioned boluses (modakas), one should drink wine (surā).
6.28.44 When the physician perceives that [the patient] is fit for emesis, he should induce vomiting with powders combined with wine, as well as with digestive (pācana) agents.

The physician should treat that patient with a compound containing barley-alkali (*yavakṣāra*). Indeed, liquid gruels (*peyā*) are not recommended for humans suffering from intoxication (*madātyaya*).
6.28.46 In cases of intoxication (madātyaya), barley-gruel and barley-meal are not recommended as they destroy the [digestive] fire; moreover, once drunk, they generate a further urge to drink.
6.28.47 That residual liquor, having increased, may produce terrible complications. Therefore, in the case of excessive drinking (pānātyaya), unwholesome fats and even gruels should be consumed.
Alcohol pursues the subtle channels of the body; it remains even in other irregular channels throughout the various parts of the body.

6.28.49–50: When held in all directions within the visceral cavities, they agitate the bodily humors, beginning with vāta. These tissues (dhātus), having become rough, increased, and corrupted by drinking, combine with the drink and produce many diseases. Indeed, wine has been specifically described by the wise as being "pervasive" (vyavāyi).
But those who indeed pursue objects such as wine and other subtle things— no other flavor is capable of sustaining them against those objects.
Therefore, for those suffering from intoxication (pānātyaya), liquor itself is the supreme medicine. For it is its own source; when drunk and absorbed, it reaches the stomach.
Having been brought under control through effort, it enters the great channel (mahāsrotas). Even medicinal substances combined with liquor are effective in every way for one who is afflicted.
When the effects of alcohol have subsided, one should perform all cooling treatments; furthermore, for embodied beings, these should indeed be combined with wine as nourishing restoratives.

6.28.55 These [medicines] should be administered to one who has been excessively purged, for the purpose of cleansing the channels, because of their heat, sharpness, expansiveness, pervasiveness, and dryness. 6.28.56 For poison and wine are said to be equal in terms of their taste and potency; therefore, one should apply all those respective therapeutic measures in the same manner as one would for poison.
6.28.56–57 Moistening, sharp, and hot, as well as caustic collyrium and nasal drops— therefore, one should avoid hot water, sudation, fumigation, and the drinking of ghee.
6.28.58 One suffering from *pāṇu* disease should avoid the flame of fire, as well as barley gruel (*yavāgū*), curd, milk, vegetables, and the meat of domestic, marshy, and aquatic animals.

6.28.59 Furthermore, one suffering from *pāṇu* disease should avoid preparations made from sesame flour; however, he may consume *śāli* rice, *ṣaṣṭika* rice, mung beans, and the meat of wild animals and birds.
Physicians praise [alcohol] in cases of intoxication from drinking and during meals; now hear from me regarding its use when the humors are in equilibrium and when they are isolated.
6.28.61 When excessive drinking aggravates the *vāyu*, one should observe the symptoms of the *vātika* disorder and apply its appropriate treatment.
6.28.62 Wine combined with *sauvarcala* salt and *vyoṣa*, mixed with honey, or combined with *cukra* and pomegranate, is beneficial for the condition of excessive drinking that provokes *vāta*.
Water, wine, fermented gruel (*śukta*), curd, sour *kāñjika*, and honey— this nourishing mixture is beneficial for the condition of wind-induced fainting (*vātapānātyaya*).

6.28.64 One should habitually practice oil massage, rubbing, bathing, and drinking half-watered liquids; one should also consume meat soups clearly seasoned with sour agents and the three pungents (vyoṣa), as well as rice.
6.28.65 For men suffering from the complications of vāta, the meat of goats, partridges, cranes, cocks, and peacocks is beneficial for food.
Mango, hog-plum, *bhavya*, wood-apple, and *karamardaka* should be drunk as a beverage according to the previously described method for those suffering from wind disorders (*vāta*).

One should cause [the patient] to drink *cavya*, *sauvarcala* salt, asafoetida (*hiṅgu*), *mātuluṅga*, *mahauṣadha* (ginger), and the powder of *ajamoda* together with wine. In the case of intoxication caused by *pitta*, one should drink a refreshing beverage (*pānaka*) mixed with sugar, combined with honey, and diluted with half as much water.

Some, however, condemn the administration of liquids to men suffering from the complications of pitta-type alcoholism (*madyātyaya*), arguing that it cannot be treated by any other means if wine is not used.
Indeed, even wine should be consumed when combined with substances that pacify *pitta*, along with the juices of *vidārī* and *āmalaka*, or with sugarcane juice.

(6.28.70) One should prepare a refreshing drink (*pānaka*) combined with wine using *madhūka*, *madhuka*, *kāśmarya*, dates, and blue lotus (*nīlotpala*), following the same method as previously described. (6.28.71)
6.28.71–72 Clad in moist linen garments, adorned with pearls and gems, dark-complexioned, and their limbs anointed with sandalwood paste, one should sleep embracing women.
One should drink wine with the paste of dates or with sugarcane juice; likewise, one may drink boiled *pīlu* juice or even the juice of eggplant (*vārtākī*).
Juice from grapes and *vidārī*, wine, sugarcane juice, and honey—this drink is beneficial for men suffering from the complications of *pitta*-dominated alcoholism.

One suffering from the complications of excessive consumption of bile (pitta-pānātyaya) should sleep embracing a leather water-bag filled with cold water and adorned with perfumes and garlands within the house.

6.28.76 Lakes and rows of forests with lotuses and blooming lilies; and a bed made of lotus leaves, sprinkled with sandalwood paste— 6.28.77 Embracing lotus stalks and white water-lilies, one should lie down, fanned by fans moistened with water.
In cases of alcoholism caused by pitta, which is comparable to a weapon, a thunderbolt, or poison, one should feed the patient red *śāli* rice along with meat from wild animals mixed with ghee.
6.28.79 Or, one may eat a soft meal with cooled mung bean soup; or one may drink a decoction of triphalā mixed with wine.
6.28.80 Or again, one may take sugarcane juice with honey, or with the paste of trivṛt; or [one may take] the bark of triphalā, madhūka, padmaka, and lotus filaments.
Blue lotus, lotus stalks, nalada, sandalwood, and balā— this decoction prepared with these [ingredients], cooled, and combined with sugar and honey.
6.28.82 A small amount mixed with wine is beneficial in cases of excessive drinking caused by *pitta*. Grapes, ripe *pīlu* fruits, dates, and *parūṣaka*;
6.28.83 *bhavya*, the marrow of the jackfruit (*panasa*), and the marrow of the palm fruit (*tāla*); having crushed all these in one-pala portions with one *āḍhaka* of water—
When one-fourth remains, one should pour it into a new jar, having added eight palas of sugar and one pala of blue lotus.

One afflicted by *pitta*-related alcoholism (*pānātyaya*) should drink that beverage (*pānaka*) according to the proper method. In cases of alcoholism caused by *kapha*, emesis induced with wine (*madya*) is beneficial.
*Paṭola*, *picumanda*, the sprouts of *madana*, *guḍūcī*, *āṭarūṣa*, *triphalā*, and *pāribhadraka* [are used for this purpose].
One should drink this decoction cooled and mixed with honey; one should constantly consume bitter, astringent, and pungent substances.

One should consume the meat of wild animals and birds, and drink the powder of *kuṭannaṭā* combined with the juice of *triphalā*. One should constantly employ digestive-stimulating formulations with one's drink; indeed, wine is most beneficial in disorders of *śleṣman*.
Therefore, we declare that alcohol is [therapeutic] in cases of *pānātyaya* caused by *śleṣman*. This treatment for *śleṣma-pānātyaya* has been declared according to the *vimāna* (classification).
6.28.91 However, when there is a total collapse of the humors (sannipāta), one should always administer treatment. For seven or eight days in men, this is prescribed for alcoholism (pānātyaya).
6.28.92 For once the alcohol has been digested, it resorts to wrong pathways; by the passage of this much time, whatever disease does not subside [should be treated].
Having prepared the drink in the proper sequence, one should administer its treatment for all diseases that have arisen, such as hiccup, dyspnea, and others.

6.28.94 One should apply their treatment according to their respective [standard] treatments. Thus has been described in detail the treatment for those suffering from intoxication (pānātyaya). 6.28.95 This has been proclaimed for the welfare of all beings and for the accomplishment of the purpose of his disciples. Thus spoke the Blessed Ātreya. Thus ends the twenty-eighth chapter of the Bhela [Saṃhitā]. Thus ends the Section on Therapeutics (Cikitsāsthāna) in the Bhela Saṃhitā. [Section on Pharmaceutics (Kalpasthāna)] Chapter One. Now, therefore, we shall explain the pharmaceutical preparations of madana; thus said the Blessed Ātreya.
7.1.1 Listen as I describe to you the three *piṇḍītaka* groups mentioned in the compendium; both the black and the white varieties— these three together are known as *madana*.

7.1.2 Of all fruits, however, the madana is the most effective for purification; it should be employed for emesis and non-unctuous enemas (āsthāpana), as well as for unctuous enemas (anuvāsana). 7.1.3 When those fruits are not fully developed and have not yet matured, but are nonetheless filled with juice, the physician should then extract them.
7.1.3–4 Likewise, having soaked these for seven nights in a heap of barley and then again in a heap of husks, together with the bark of *saṃkuñcita* fruit, [one should proceed].

7.1.5 Having recognized that they have been well-cultivated and have become soft, the expert in the science [of medicine] should purify them in two or three ways, and having thoroughly purified them, he should add them [to the formulation]. 7.1.6 After keeping them among grains for a month, he should smear them with clay and place them in a house that is closed with doors, free from smoke, and sheltered from the wind.
7.1.6–7.1.7 One should place [the vessel] in the air so that sweat does not form. From these marrow-fraught [substances], one should take a handful including the flesh and nails.
7.1.8 Having crushed [the ingredients], one should let them soak in a stone mortar or a vessel for one night with a decoction of *madhuka*.
7.1.9 Then, having risen in the forenoon and washed one's hands, one should massage [the paste]; and having heated it, one should strain it while adding salt and honey.

One should cause the patient to drink [the preparation] after he has been oleated; by that means, one should properly induce emesis. By this very same method, one may also use the fruits of *jīmūtaka*.

7.1.11 One should also prepare [a decoction] with *ikṣvāku*, *kuṭaja*, and the salts, as well as with *kṛtavedha*, *hastiparṇī*, and the fruits of *dhāmārgava*. 7.1.12 With these, one should prepare a decoction and saturate the seeds of the fruit; by this method, the physician should administer it according to the patient's strength.
7.1.12–13 The physician should extract the seeds of the Madana fruit so that they are neither too pale nor too green.
7.1.14 When the fruits are fully developed, ripe, and have attained their full flavor, the physician should pierce them all around with a needle or with thorns.
7.1.15 Then, the physician should soak them for three nights in a decoction of *madana* fruits; one should follow this same procedure with the fruits of *jīmūtaka* as well.

Furthermore, with the fruits of *dhāmārgava*, as well as *kṛtavedha* and *hāstiparṇa* from the *ikṣvāku* and *kuṭaja* families, one should induce vomiting by means of that excellent preparation. (7.1.15–16)

7.1.17 Furthermore, according to this same method, the physician should administer a very unctuous enema using the decoction of each of the following individually—kuśa grass, *varuṇa*, *kākodumbarikā*, and likewise that called *kuṣṭha*—after having carefully considered the patient's strength and weakness. The Third Chapter. Thus spoke the venerable Ātreya: 7.3.1 The wise man should extract the *ikṣvāku* fruits in spring as well as in autumn, when they have flowered and emit a honey-like fragrance.

7.3.1–2 We shall now describe the procedure for those [patients] according to the rule for the Ikṣvākus: milk prepared by the Ikṣvākus should be used by the physician to induce emesis in that very manner. 7.3.2
7.3.3 Or, having prepared curd from milk, one should have him drink it according to his strength; or, having churned it, one should administer fresh butter to the monkey.
7.3.4 This procedure prescribed for the Ikṣvākus has been fully described by me; taking fresh stalks, one should place them within molasses.
7.3.4–5 Having stayed elsewhere for one night, one should wash the hands and then massage [the area], having heated the strained liquid mixed with salt and honey. 7.3.5

7.3.6 One should cause the patient to drink [the preparation] after he has been lubricated; by that means, he will be successfully treated. By this very same method, one should prepare it with sugarcane, *darbha*, and sugarcane water.
7.3.7 Likewise, one should prepare it with the juice of *poṭagala* and sugarcane, saturated with broth; or else, mixed with the leaves of *kovidāra*.
7.3.7–8 One should steam the shoots of *ikṣvāku* over a fire of cow dung; having removed them once they are steamed, one should crush them in a mortar.
7.3.9 Then, having thoroughly sprinkled it with the decoction of *phalaka* and having mixed it well, one should cause it to be placed in this decoction for one night, well-protected.
7.3.10 One should administer it according to its strength by means of the previously described procedure; furthermore, one should have a *prasṛta* measure of *ikṣvāku* seeds made into a fine powder.
7.3.10–11 The physician should have pills prepared with a decoction of *kovidāra*. Having dissolved those very pills in this same decoction, [he should administer them].

7.3.12 One should cause him to drink [the decoction] according to his strength and induce vomiting with it properly; by this same method, one should use *kuśa* grass and *tagara*. 7.3.13 With the decoction of either of these, the physician should cause the well-anointed patient to vomit; he should induce vomiting with it properly, according to his strength and as prescribed.
One should have the patient drink milk prepared with *ikṣvāku* according to their strength. This procedure for emesis using *ikṣvāku* has been proclaimed.

7.3.15 "Gentle [therapies] are effective when practiced with regularity and should be applied according to place and time," so said the venerable Ātreya. Thus ends the third chapter in the Kalpasthāna of the Bheḷa-saṃhitā. The Fourth Chapter. Now, therefore, we shall explain the pharmaceutical preparation of *dhāmārgava*. So said the venerable Ātreya. 7.4.1 One should uproot the *dhāmārgava* plants either in spring or in autumn, when they are in full bloom and shine with a honey-like fragrance.
7.4.1–2 On this level ground, prepared with *kuśa* grass and *rohiṣa* grass, which has the luster of black clay or even golden earth—

7.4.3 In the heat of the sun, on a riverbank, or likewise in a pit or an anthill; [fruits that are] fully developed, ripe, and have attained their full flavor— 7.4.4 the wise physician, having extracted them, should place them in a heap of barley, or the steadfast one should place them in a heap of chaff for seven nights.
Having recognized that they have been well-cultivated and have become soft, the knower of the treatise should crush them upon a stone and pour them into vessels to extract [the essence].
7.4.6 One should cause it to soak for one night in a decoction of *kovidāra*. Then, having risen in the forenoon and washed his hands, he should massage [the patient’s body].
7.4.7 Having strained it, mixed with salt and honey, and warmed it, one should have the patient—who has been treated with unctuous therapy—drink it; by this means, he will properly induce vomiting.
7.4.7–8 Having gathered a fistful of these *dhāmārgava* fruits, including the nails, and having crushed them on a grinding stone, one should administer them in vessels.
7.4.9 One should have [the patient] steeped for one night in a decoction of *kovidāra* and then induce vomiting according to strength, using the same procedure as previously described.
7.4.10 One should cause [the patient] to vomit with a decoction of *nalada*, *tālīsa*, and *śatapuṣpā*, or with *kuṣṭha*, *mūrvā*, and *pāṭhā*, following the previous method.
7.4.10–11 One should have a full añjali-measure of dhāmārgava made into a fine powder; having cast it into a decoction of śyāmāka, one should leave it for one night according to the prescribed rule.

7.4.12 Likewise, one should steep it in a decoction of *phalakaṣāya* produced by the Ikṣvākus, and then saturate it in a decoction of *jīmūtaka* and *hastiparṇa*. 7.4.13 Then, having removed it and dried it thoroughly, one should have it made into fine powders; mixed with this, one should have the man drink *kṛsarā* that is not too hot.
Blue lotus, white lotus, nalada, and likewise kumuda—one should cause him to smell these after having touched him with that powder.
7.4.15 It is said that [the poison] reaches the heart via the vessels as far as the *miśraka* [nerve-center]. One should quickly cause him to smell those flowers.
7.4.16 Having repeatedly powdered the middle [portion], one should have him smell it again and again; by this very method, the person vomits easily.
One should have a full añjali-measure of *dhāmārgava* seeds ground into a fine powder. Having divided it into three parts, the wise man should store them in a well-concealed place.
7.4.18 Then the physician should cause two parts to drip [into the liquid] using a decoction of *bilva*. Once the decoction has dripped out and is clear, he should store it in a well-protected place.

7.4.19 One part [of this] should be made into pills the size of a jujube fruit (*kola*) or a *karkandhu* plum. Using a decoction of *kovidāra*, one should induce vomiting according to the previously described procedure.
Having prepared pills from *karkandhu*, *badara*, or *kola* fruits with *sīdhu* wine according to the prescribed method, he should then induce vomiting effectively by means of that.

7.4.21 One should induce vomiting easily with the juice of the rohita fish, the karkaṭaka, and aquatic birds. 7.4.22 According to this very method, having prepared pills with sour substances, honey, and sīdhu wine, one should administer them duly according to the patient's strength. Thus spoke the venerable Ātreya. Thus ends the fourth chapter in the Bheḷa [Saṃhitā]. Fifth Chapter. Now, therefore, we shall explain the pharmaceutical preparation of *kuṭaja*; thus said the venerable Ātreya.
7.5.1 In either spring or autumn, the physician— pure, clean, and having bathed his head— should collect the *kuṭaja* flowers under the asterism of Puṣya or Aśvayuja.
7.5.2 In a clean place prepared with *kuśa* grass and *rohiṣa* grass, or one with the luster of black clay, or likewise one with golden clay;
7.5.3 Nor in the heat of the sun, nor on a riverbank, nor likewise in a chasm or an anthill; [nor those that are] completely full, overripe, or whose juice has already been extracted.
7.5.3–4 Then, having taken a fistful of these *kuṭaja* fruits along with their nails, one should let them soak for one night in a decoction of *kovidāra*.

7.5.5 Then, having risen in the forenoon and washed his hands, he should massage [the patient]. Having heated the strained liquid mixed with salt and honey, 7.5.5 7.5.6 he should cause the patient—who has been lubricated—to drink it; by this, he will be properly induced to vomit. According to this very same procedure, the physician should prepare a decoction (kaṣāya).
And with the seeds of the *kovidāra*, the *nīpa*, and the *vidula*, as well as those of the *gulūcī*, the *suṣvī*, the *paṭola*, and the *picumanda*.

7.5.8 Having prepared a decoction of *madhūlikā*, one should induce vomiting with it; or, having taken a handful of these very fruits along with their nails... 7.5.9 One should rub that powder with a decoction of *madhuka*.

7.5.9–10 One should have pills made from that [mixture], resembling the size of *karkandhu* or *badara* fruits. One should induce vomiting with a decoction of *kovidāra* using the previously mentioned procedure.

7.5.11 One should induce vomiting by that [medication] according to one's strength and as prescribed; thus, this procedure for *kṛtavedhana* has been declared in the detailed exposition on emetics. 7.5.12 Only he who understands this in such a manner is fit to act for kings. Thus spoke the Blessed Ātreya. Thus ends the fifth chapter in the Section on Formulas (*Kalpasthāna*) of the *Bhela-saṃhitā*. The Sixth Chapter. Now, therefore, we shall explain the formula for *caturaṅgulī*; thus said the Blessed Ātreya.
But that which is grown in a pleasant location and measures four finger-breadths in size—one should collect a handful of its fruit and then have it ground into powder.

7.6.2 Having reduced that to powder, one should divide it into three parts and set aside one part. The other two parts, having been thoroughly purified, should then be stirred well. 7.6.3 Having strained it by dripping and filtered it until it is perfectly clear and undisturbed, one should add the reserved portion back into it and cook it over a fire of cow-dung.
7.6.3–7.6.4 While it is being infused in that manner, one should cause these subtle substances to be added: the fruits of *harītakī*, *āmalaka*, and *vibhītaka*.
7.6.5 Having added a portion of *madhūka*, one should prepare that ointment; then, a palmful of powder should be licked, by which one is purged.
7.6.6 By this same procedure, having extracted the juice from the fruits of *kaṇṭakārī*, one should drink the resulting linctus mixed with wine.

Alternatively, a well-prepared gruel (peyā) prepared with four fingers’ measure [of the drug] should be administered; by this, one is properly purged, without either insufficient action (āyoga) or excessive action (atiyogitā).

7.6.8 One should cook half a *tulā* of sugar with one *droṇa* of the juice of *dhātrī* (myrobalan) fruits. When cooked, four *palas* of ghee should be added, along with half a *pala* each of the following:
7.6.9 *Nata*, *vela*, the four aromatics (*caturjāta*), *yaṣṭi*, rock salt (*saindhava*), cumin (*jīraka*), *palāśa*, ginger (*viśva*), black pepper (*marica*), and four *palas* of *mṛdvīkā*.
Seven karṣas each of Pippalī and Trivṛt, along with honey, constitute that preparation known as Tatkhaṇḍāmalaka; it destroys anemia, edema, and jaundice.

7.6.11 The whirling of the head (śirobhramaṇa) overcomes insanity and disorders of acid bile (amlapitta). 7.6.12 One āḍhaka measure of bhallātaka fruits that have been struck by the wind and fallen from their stalks should be ground with fine particles of brick powder, washed, and then dried in a strong breeze.

When that [mixture] has dried, it should again be split into pieces and placed in four times as much water. When reduced to one-fourth, it should be strained, cooled, and cooked again with an equal quantity of milk. 7.6.13

7.6.14 One should boil that [mixture] again once it has cooled, adding an equal amount of ghee; it should then be thoroughly saturated with half as much sugar and mixed with the powder of *lohābhayā* (iron pyrites) and *vyoṣa*. 7.6.15 Having stirred this with a churning stick (*khaja*) and added an equal amount of sugar along with a quarter-part [of the previous ingredients], one should set it aside. Then, after two *prasthas* of *āmalaka* juice have been added while it is cool, one should boil it again with *dhānya* (coriander).

After those seven nights, having acquired potency, it surpasses even the essence of nectar (*sudhārasa*). One should take a dose appropriate for one's own body by those who have purified their bodies in the morning.

7.6.17 There is no avoidance of food and drink, nor of heat, wind, travel, or sexual intercourse. A living being who practices this shall become like a lion among men; he shall become a man as bright as a heap of gold.

7.6.18 Decayed teeth grow back again, and white hair becomes black once more. Even one whose ears, fingers, and nose are shattered, who is tormented by worms, whose throat is split, or who suffers from leprosy—[shall be restored].

Like a tree whose branches are his fingers and limbs that grows gradually when watered by moisture, he surpassed great peacocks with his voice, elephants with his strength, and horses with his speed. (7.6.19)
7.6.20 One should saturate [the powder] with the milky sap of the *sudhā* plant. One should drink that according to one's capacity; by this, one is properly purged.
7.6.21 *Dantī*, *akṣatā*, *tejohvā*, *tarkārī*, and *sudurālabhā*—one should mix this decoction of astringent herbs with the milky sap of the *sudhā* plant.
One should drink that according to one's strength, for by it one is properly purged. One should mix cow’s milk with the milky sap of the *sudhā* plant in a single vessel.
One should drink that according to one's capacity; by this, one is properly purged once the urine and feces have been eliminated and the wind (vāta) has been set in its downward course.

7.6.24 First, for one whose bowels have been lubricated and who has undergone sudation according to the prescribed method, these formulations should be administered when the time of twilight has passed and the sun is clear, during the *maitra* muhūrta when it is fully manifest. Thus said the venerable Ātreya. Thus ends the sixth chapter in the Kalpasthāna of the Bheḷasaṃhitā. The Seventh Chapter. Now, therefore, we shall explain the pharmaceutical preparation of *dantī* fruit. So said the venerable Ātreya. [... repeated text ... 7.6.24

7.7.1 The wise physician, having divided [the mixture] into three parts, should cause it to be stored securely. He should then pour two portions of *āmalaka* juice into it. 7.7.2 Once the strained decoction has become clear, he should place it on the fire for further boiling (*pariyoga*). While it is being cooked in that manner, he should add the medicinal powder to it.
One should add an equal measure of powdered triphalā mixed with honey; once it has become a thick paste (leha), one should then remove it from the heat.

7.7.4 The powder of its palm-leaf should be licked; by that, one is purged. Having made fine powders from the roots of these very plants, 7.7.5 one should cook ghee, having stirred it with a decoction of *śyāmāka* grain. One should know when it is cooked, and then one should remove it from the fire.
7.7.5–6 One should pour that [mixture] into a new, firm jar smeared with honey; having well-smeared it with fine clay, one should cause it to be placed in a secure location. 7.7.6

7.7.7 One should have the patient drink a handful (prasṛta) of this; by it, one is properly purged. Having made powders from all these roots in their entirety, 7.7.8 one should prepare pills with them mixed with the juice of *bṛhatī*. Having prepared the pills, they should be the size of a *karkandhu* or a *badara* fruit.
Then, having stirred it with a decoction of *śyāmāka* grain, one should administer two or even three doses to that man who has been treated with oleation and sudation, according to his capacity.

7.7.10 By this [procedure], one is properly purged; there is neither deficient application nor excessive application. Since emesis and purgation are rooted in oleation and the like, purification does not succeed for one whose gastrointestinal tract has not been lubricated. Thus said the venerable Ātreya. Thus ends the seventh chapter in the Kalpasthāna of the Bheḷa-saṃhitā. Chapter Eight: Now, therefore, we shall explain the procedure for *śaṅkhinī*. So said the venerable Ātreya. 7.7.10

7.8.1 During the interval between the months of Caitra and Vaiśākha, while the collection of barley is taking place, the physician, remaining unperturbed, should uproot the fully ripened fruits of the *śaṅkhinī* plant.
7.8.2 [He should do so] in a field that is not saline, free from drainage issues, scorched by the sun, or one that has the luster of black clay or golden soil.
7.8.2–3 It should not be in a place that is uneven, nor at an anthill, nor even one covered with grass; rather, it should be a very level plot of ground where the *śaṅkhinī* plant grows.

7.8.4 Having poured that [mixture] into a *droṇa* measure of that vessel which has been prepared with the binding [substance], and having let it soak for a night in barley leaves, one should remove it and set it aside.
7.8.5 Having covered it completely for seven nights or half a month, one should have it dried in the sun and reduced to a fine powder.
7.8.5–6. Furthermore, the physician should have two parts of these fruits prepared; having placed sesame as the third part, he should grind them together in a mortar. 7.8.6

7.8.7 Having crushed [the plant] on a smooth grinding stone, one should extract the oil from it; then, one should add an *akṣa*-measure of *śaṅkhinī* or even the paste of *trivṛt*. 7.8.8 Into that oil, the physician should add four times as much milk; having thoroughly mixed all these together, one should cook it over a gentle fire.
7.8.8–9 Having brought the cooked [mixture] and strained it, one should have it stored in a well-protected place. One should administer of it either an añjali, a prakunca, or even a prasṛta.

By that wholesome [preparation], one is purged; there is neither deficient nor excessive application. Then, one *prasṛta* measure of the very fine powder of *śaṅkhinī*, boiled with a vessel of milk, should be placed on the fire for cooking (*adhiśrayet*). Having thus cooked it, strained it, and cooled it, one should stir it vigorously (*abhimanthayet*).
In that case, whatever fresh butter (navanīta) there may be, one should extract it and cook it with the paste of *śaṅkhinī* fruits, along with milk and water.
7.8.13 One should drink that [mixture] according to one's strength; by this, one is properly purged. One should grind the paste of *śaṅkhinī* fruit thoroughly on a stone slab.
7.8.14 Having stirred it with cow’s milk, one should drink it; by this, one is purged. And by this very same method, one should cause [the patient] to drink it with camel’s milk.
In goat’s milk, in sheep’s milk, or again in buffalo milk; or else in cow urine, in camel urine, or again in goat urine.
Alternatively, one may drink it with elephant urine, by which one is purged. Then, while crushing grapes, one should have them placed in a solution of treacle (phāṇita).
Having fried *śaṅkhinī* in oil, one should place the decoction over the fire and add half-parts of the powders of long pepper (*pippalī*) and chebulic myrobalan (*harītakī*).
Therefore, having licked the palm of the hand, one is properly purged by that; likewise, the kernels of the *śaṅkhinī* fruit should be given along with salt.

7.8.19 The physician should fry [the seeds] in *śaṅkhinī* oil and then mix them with molasses; having mixed them with wheat flour and clarified butter, he should have sweetmeat balls (*modaka*) prepared. 7.8.20 By consuming three or two of these, one is then properly purged. [The following are suitable for this: wine, *sauvīraka* vinegar, buttermilk, curd-scum, and *tuṣodaka*.
Or one may drink *kaṭvara*, *kola-sīdhu*, or likewise *dadhi-pakva-rasa*; or the fermented liquor (*sīdhu*) of *karkandhu* and *badara* fruits, or that of *pīlu* and *priyāla*.

7.8.22 One should cause [the patient] to drink either the juice of *bhavya* and *pārāvata*, or grape-wine (*mṛdvīkā-madya*), or the juices of *bilva*, *śigru*, and *kapittha*. 7.8.23 For this procedure for *śaṅkhinī* has been fully described by me; he who understands it thus is fit to perform it for kings. Thus spoke the Blessed Ātreya. Thus ends the eighth chapter in the Section on Formulas (*Kalpasthāna*) of the Bheḷa-saṃhitā. Ninth Chapter. Now, therefore, we shall explain the formula for *śyāmā-trivṛt*. Thus said the Blessed Ātreya.
The physician should extract the roots of the *śyāmā* plant along with its threefold fibers from a field of auspicious soil, having prepared them with *kuśa* grass and *rohiṣa*.
7.9.2 Alternatively, one may take these roots from black earth or even from golden soil; having collected them, one should have them reduced to a fine powder.

7.9.3 Having mixed this with a decoction of *sthirā*, one should administer it according to the patient's strength. By this, the patient is properly purged; there is neither deficient action nor excessive action.

Having stirred it with just the juice of the three myrobalans (triphalā), or with the juice of grapes (drākṣā) and *pīlu*, or even with milk or clarified butter (sarpiḥ), one should have the patient drink it.

7.9.5 One should administer the meat-juice of the deer, the nyanku, and the buffalo; or that of the rhinoceros, the sparrow, the partridge, and the common quail. 7.9.6 One should cause a man who has been well-anointed with oil and fomented to drink one of these juices combined with trivṛt and śyāmā, according to his strength.
Having finely ground the powders of *śyāmā* and *trivṛt*, one should divide them into three parts and deposit one part oneself in a hidden place.

7.9.8 The physician should cause two parts of the juice of *priyaṅgu* to drip into a vessel, having strained it until it is very clear and free from impurities. 7.9.9 Having placed this decoction over the fire, he should cook it with a gentle flame; while it is being cooked in that manner, he should cause these powders to be added to it.
Priyaṅgu, tagara, tālīsa, nalada, as well as hībera, mustā, balā, and kālānusārivā.
7.9.11–12 One should mix the powders of *aśoka* flowers, *padma*, *saugandhika*, *nalina*, *puṇḍarīka*,
and the root of *pippalī* with honey, and lick a dose measured by the palm of the hand, being well-oiled and having digested one's meal, according to the scriptures and according to one's strength.
By that [application], one is properly purged; there is neither lack of application nor excessive application. Likewise, sandalwood, *padmaka*, *nīpa*, *sāla*, and *saptacchada* [are used].
7.9.14 Punarnavā, the tuberous root, kirātatikta, or indeed tikta itself, as well as other bitter and sweet tastes previously mentioned—
7.9.15 with the decoctions (kaṣāya) of these, a purgative should be administered for those afflicted by pitta. [One may also use] the flesh of pigeons, doves, cranes, peacocks, and wild cocks.
Kuraṅgas, hariṇas, eṇas, and green kālapucchakas; vartakas, tittiris, śaśas, lāvakas, and piñjalas.
7.9.17 One should administer purgatives for a patient with a pitta-dominant constitution using those juices, as well as heartwoods, fruits, powders, leaves, and milks.
7.9.18 These include the stationary substances previously mentioned, as well as the meat-juices of wild animals and birds, and liquid preparations such as decoctions of fruits and medicinal extracts.
7.9.18–19 One should prepare for them various linctuses, foods, and edibles; [specifically] the juice of *parūṣaka* and grapes, mixed with honey and sugar.
7.9.20 Having drunk *trivṛt* combined with *akṣa*, one is properly purged. The physician should administer it mixed with sugar and honey as well.
7.9.21 When that [mixture] has cooled, one should add *trivṛt* powder according to the patient's digestive capacity (*koṣṭha*), and then the powder of *kampillaka* and two parts of *tinduka*.
Likewise, middle-sized fruits of *āragvadha* in the measure of an *akṣa*, one *dharaṇa* of *trivṛt* powder, sugar, *madhuka*, and honey. (7.9.22)

7.9.23 The physician should prepare a bolus (modaka) by combining all of these finely powdered ingredients: black pepper (marica), *nāgapuṣpa*, and cinnamon bark and leaves (*tvakpatra*). 7.9.24 Alternatively, one may prepare an electuary (leha) with these; by this means, one is properly purged. [One should take] one *kuḍava* of grape juice (*drākṣārasa*) and one *kuḍava* of *parūṣaka* juice.
Half a *kuḍava* of honey and one *pala* of sugar, combined with the powder of *trivṛt*, form a linctus by which one is effectively purged. (7.9.25)
7.9.26 This is the purgative for lords whose humors have been diminished: sugar-candies, sugar-balls, or balls of jaggery and black gram.
7.9.27 By this method, one should administer purgatives for those with a predominance of pitta: powders of trivṛt, long pepper, and the fruits of āragvadha.
7.9.27–28 A wise person should drink these as a paste (*kalka*) in the quantity of one *akṣa* as a purgative; [specifically] one *dharaṇa* of *trivṛt* powder, along with sugar, *madhuka*, and honey.

7.9.29 Having drunk this mixed with *akṣa*, one is properly purged. One should lick the powders of *trivṛt*, *pippalī*, *yavakṣāra*, and *mahauṣadha* for the purpose of pacifying the provocation of *śleṣman*; by that, one is purged. [One may also use] the urine of a sheep, a goat, a camel, and a buffalo.
7.9.30–31: One should employ these eight—the urine of a deer, cow, donkey, and elephant—either individually or all together. 7.9.31
7.9.32 One should lick [these] mixed with the powder of *trivṛt* along with honey, or likewise those sharp, non-fermented wines at night.

7.9.33 Having drunk them mixed with the powder of *trivṛt*, one is properly purged; a person of phlegmatic constitution (*ślaiṣmika*) should drink the powder of *trivṛt* according to the state of their digestive tract (*koṣṭha*).
With the decoction of trivṛt, mixed with honey and sour vetasa; or else with whey (dadhimaṇḍa) or with the juice of jujube fruits (kolaka).
7.9.35 Or one should drink [the gruel] with soups of *kulattha* and *mudga*, along with *satīna* and *cirabilva*; or with a soup of *yava* and *kola*, or even with a soup of *kaulattha*.
7.9.36 Or it may be taken with a soup prepared with *taṇḍulīyaka*, sour vetasa, and pomegranate; or with a soup of *śigru*, *kola*, *āhvā*, and radish, or with their juice.
Or with the juice of *āmalaka* fruits, or of *bījapūra* and *ārjaka*, or with the scum of *kapittha* juice, or with the juice of *karamarda*. (7.9.36–37)
7.9.38 Whatever other fruit is also known as sour, one should drink it with its own juices or with the decoction of the five roots (pañcamūlī). 7.9.39 Or,
mixed with a paste of *kaṭu* [drugs] and combined with barley-alkali (yavakṣāra), one should prepare a linctus for the purpose of licking using a paste of the fruit of *mṛdvīkā*.
The physician should cause the fresh juice to be extracted from each of the previously mentioned fruits when they are well-formed and fully ripe.
7.9.41 When it has become sour and salty, one should add rock salt (*saindhava*). To this electuary (*leha*), one should add the powder of *trivṛt* according to the patient's digestive capacity.

7.9.42 One may likewise lick it with honey or with jaggery, or similarly with pungent spices (*kaṭuka*). By this same method, one should prepare boluses (*modaka*), six-flavored preparations (*ṣāḍava*), and meat juices (*rasa*).
Acidic fruit drinks, along with prepared foods that are both chewed and swallowed— this is declared to be the purgative regimen for kings and lords. (7.9.42–43)
7.9.44 The physician should thus employ this procedure, as well as another: [a powder] of *śāṇa* and *āmalaka*, and the fruits of *vibhītaka*.
7.9.45 *Tilvaka*, *saptalā*, *dantī*, *śaṅkhinī*, *caturaṅgula*, one part of *harītakī*, and indeed *yavakṣāra*.
There should be one śāṇa of pippalī and likewise one śāṇa of viḍaṅga; there should be three śāṇas of trivṛt powder— one should sprinkle all of that [over the patient].

7.9.47 These powders, taken with honey, clarified butter, or jaggery, or as a linctus according to the prescribed method... [End of Section] ...Siddhisthāna, First Chapter. 8.1.1 In one whose stomach is empty, the *vāta* becomes aggravated during emesis; the spleen (*plīhā*) moves from its place, and consequently, the humors destroy the vital breaths (*asūn*).

8.1.1–2 Thereafter, on an auspicious lunar day, at a favorable moment, and under a propitious constellation and division (*karana*), he should drink thin gruel or a scum of boiled rice, well-oleated and seasoned with salt. 8.1.2

8.1.3 Having become pure and wearing white garments, and having honored the twice-born, one should then administer the emetic to him after paying homage to the best of physicians. 8.1.4 It should be drunk while facing the east, in a pleasant shelter protected from the wind; one should not cause him physical exertion, and a thin gruel (maṇḍa) is recommended as food.
This procedure should be performed for both emesis and purgation. Three *prastha*s of decoction [are used], while three *māgadhā*s are used in the minor [dose].

8.1.6 However, for a person of superior constitution (*jyeṣṭha*), the emetic dose should be superior; it should not be given to one of inferior constitution (*kanīyasa*). For a person of medium constitution (*madhyama*), it should be four *prasthas*; for the superior, those [four] would be nine *prasthas*.
8.1.7 The inferior, medium, and superior doses are each of three distinct types, according to whether the emetic or even the purgative has been previously administered by the patient.
8.1.7–8.1.8 A wise person should also examine it by its smallest measure: three palas is declared the best, while one pala would be the minimum. 8.1.8

8.1.9 One should know that "medium" consists of two *pala*s; this is my settled opinion. Those who have been afflicted by poison or leprosy, and those oppressed by cough and dyspnea— 8.1.10 If they are young and strong, one should cause them to vomit with the best [emetic]; if they are in the middle stage of life, one should employ the medium [emetic] in that case.

8.1.10–11 But if one applies [the treatment] in such a way that it is increasingly milder as the vital breath becomes weaker, yet employs it in the reverse manner, one will not overcome diseases. 8.1.11

8.1.12 One should either cause complications to arise or bring about the patient's destruction; for this purpose, one should properly administer a decoction of *aṅkola* or *nimba*. 8.1.13 Having ground the fruit of *madana* together with the fruits of *devadālī*, one should apply it with ghee and these medicinal substances, either lukewarm or cold.
Fresh neem leaves, rock salt, and black pepper, or again, [the powder] combined with rock salt, taken with buttermilk or the scum of buttermilk.

8.1.15 Bandhujīva, pippalī, madana, and ghee— combined with a decoction of these, this is a preeminent emetic medicine. 8.1.16 Madana, bandhujīva, śatapuṣpā, and śukānanā, combined with rock salt (saindhava), is a preeminent emetic medicine.
8.1.16–17 The leaves, flowers, and fruits of the *madana* tree, as well as rock salt (*saindhava*), *bandhujīva*, and *rājakośātaka*.

8.1.18 Thus, the practice of induced vomiting (*pracchardana-yoga*) is the primary emetic medicine; it is the best for those afflicted by poisons and is highly esteemed in cases of cough and asthma. 8.1.19 But when a person who has drunk an emetic does not vomit, what medicine should be applied there, and how should the physician proceed?
The physician should show him separately the preserved powders of flies and hair, and he should apply that to the broth. 8.1.20
By this procedure, a person is quickly made to vomit; this treatment has been fully described, especially for those who are weak.
8.1.21–22 A person should press the region of the heart and the back and then vomit; for by this method, what was drunk from its place of residence is moved.
For one first vomits phlegm (kapha), then bile (pitta) immediately thereafter; when bile has ended, wind (vāta) arises, and then one vomits blood.
8.1.24 I shall now describe the signs of one who has properly vomited: lightness in the stomach, purity, clarity of the heart, and freedom from lethargy.
8.1.25 Hunger and thirst at the proper time, cleanliness of the channels, restoration of the digestive fire, and the cessation of all diseases caused by phlegm (kapha).
Furthermore, a bitter taste in the mouth is not a sign of proper emesis; rather, nausea, irritation of the vessels, and a tearing sensation in the neck and throat occur.
8.1.27 Excessive belching, darkness of vision, cough, hiccup, dyspnea, loss of voice, vāta-fever, dry vomiting, thirst, colic, and indeed insomnia;
8.1.28 Dryness of the mouth and heart, as well as the discharge of blood from a wound, the sense organs become obstructed, and fainting arises for him.

Jaw-lock (hanustambha) and tremors occur when one has vomited excessively; as do upward hemorrhaging, urinary disorders (prameha), abdominal tumors (gulma), hemorrhoids, and fistula-in-ano (bhagandara).
8.1.30 One suffering from abdominal enlargement, anemia, heart disease, intestinal worms, epilepsy, or poisoning; one afflicted by swelling and stiffness caused by Vāta;
8.1.31 One with irregular fever, erysipelas, or gout; one with hemorrhoids, extremely weak digestion, or afflicted by skin diseases and edema.

One suffering from upward-moving wind (udāvarta), as well as one with insanity (unmāda), afflicted by skin spots (piplu) and freckles (vyaṅga), and those whose bodily constituents (dhātus) are agitated by the arising of bile (pitta) and phlegm (śleṣman).

8.1.33 Women who have disorders arising from the combination of humors (*sannipāta*), those with vitiated reproductive tracts (*yoniduṣṭā*), those afflicted by colic, those suffering from uterine tumors (*raktagulminī*), and those oppressed by *saumya* [disorders] [should be treated].

8.1.34 When there is unctuousness, redness of the limbs, lightness, softness of the body, purity of the heart, eructations, and urine, and the downward movement of *vāta*, [the treatment is successful].
Clarity of voice and complexion, the presence of hunger, and the subsiding of disease, along with the natural return of phlegm to its own site, are the signs of one who has been properly purged.

8.1.36 The abdomen becomes distended with wind, there is the appearance of itching and circular patches (maṇḍala), pustules arise on the limbs, and there is dizziness along with an overwhelming fever. 8.1.37 Constriction of the heart, impairment of the digestive fire, heaviness in the belly, and difficulty in the passage of feces, urine, and flatus are the signs of one who has been improperly purged.

Pain in the flanks, prolapse of the rectum, convulsions involving the contraction of the limbs, enlargement of the scrotum, loss of consciousness, pain in the anus, thirst, and exhaustion [are the symptoms].

8.1.39 Emptiness, a state of being worn out, and a tingling sensation [in the abdomen] arise; in those who have been excessively purged, pain and swelling occur. 8.1.40 In one who has been purged and feels heavy, whatever remains undigested should be induced to vomit. However, medicine that is wholesome to the patient should be drunk as a non-unctuous enema (nirūha) for those with hard stools.

The physician should overcome the excessive symptoms [of the disease] by means of milk, ghee, and other substances; likewise, he should conquer them with oleation therapies, poultices, and massages. Chapter Two. 8.1.41: [The physician should overcome the excessive symptoms of the disease] by means of milk, ghee, and other substances; likewise, he should conquer them with oleation therapies, poultices, and massages. Chapter Two.

8.2.1 They say that nasal therapy (*nasya*) is fourfold: *avapīḍa*, *anuvāsa*, *dhūma*, and *pradhamana*. Listen now to me as I explain each of them separately. 8.2.2 Throat obstruction (*galagraha*), *rohiṇikā*, *śaṅkhaka*, *ardhāvabhedaka*, catarrh (*pratiśyāya*), cough (*kāsa*), asthma (*śvāsa*), hiccups (*hikkā*), and *biḍālikā* [are conditions for which these therapies are indicated].
8.2.2–3 Indeed, diseases of the mouth, epilepsy, abscesses of the teeth and palate, dental swellings, and likewise putrid nose and mouth [are described]. 8.2.3

8.2.4 Furthermore, there are four types of *abhiṣyanda* (ophthalmia), as well as those arising from the eyes such as *tandrā*, *sārbuda*, *adhīmantha*, nasal polyps (*nāsārśas*), and fistula-in-ano (*bhagaṃdara*). 8.2.5 For *upajihvā* (ranula), *galagranthi* (goiter), *kaṇṭhaśālūka* (tonsillitis), *galaśuṇṭhikā*, and *alasaka*, head-purgation (*śīrṣavirecana*) should be administered.
8.2.5–6 Long pepper, *vilanga*, long pepper, and *phaṇijjaka*; *kṣavaka*, *yavānī*, and the seeds of *śigru*, as well as *mayūraka*.
8.2.7 Asafoetida, black salt, bhārṅgī, fruits of naktamāla, jyotiṣmatī, ginger, and the seeds of śirīṣa—
8.2.8 one should employ these for the purpose of head-evacuation (avapīḍana) in the aforementioned diseases, either as a nasal drop, as an inhalation, or in combination, or even all together.
8.2.8–9 A wise physician should cook oil with these very groups of herbs, combined with sheep’s urine; this is the best remedy for head-purgation (śīrṣavirecana).

8.2.10 One should inhale the smoke of all fragrant substances, excluding nata and kuṣṭha, in the form of a medicinal wick (dhūmavarti); this is the best head-purgative (śīrṣavirecana). 8.2.11 By means of purging the head, the ears, tongue, eyes, and nose are purified according to their respective humors (doṣa), as are the channels of the mouth and nose.
