8.2.11–12 When the head has been properly purified, there is clear discharge from the orifices, no excess phlegm is secreted, and the pain subsides. 8.2.12

8.2.13 In cases of disease, there is a breaking and powdering of the channels (*srotas*), as well as their complete purification; likewise, when the channels are excessively purified, the head becomes strained. 8.2.14 [These treatments are indicated] in cases of loosening of the teeth, lockjaw (*hanustambha*), stiffness of the neck (*manyāstambha*), headache, deafness, earache, and tearing pain at the base of the ear.
When there is drooping of the eyelids, falling out of the hair, lack of consciousness, wandering of the gaze, hiccupping, watering of the eyes and mouth, hoarseness of voice, or loss of speech;

8.2.16 In cases of swelling of the cheeks, lips, and face; in disorders of the eyes; in blindness (timira); in foul odors from the mouth and nose; and also in premature graying of the hair (pālitya), [nasal therapy is indicated]. 8.2.17 For those diseases described as being located above the clavicle (ūrdhvajatrugata), nasal therapy (nasyakarma) is beneficial, using either oil or clarified butter (sarpis).
Jīvaka, ṛṣabhaka, drākṣā, pippalī, madhuka, balā, prapauṇḍarīka, medā, sugar, and blue lotus (nīlotpala).

8.2.19 Nidigdhikā, aṃśumatī, nīlikā, saindhava, vacā, rāsnā, śvadaṃṣṭrā, mañjiṣṭhā, bṛhatī, and punarnavā— [each] one pala [in measure]. 8.2.20 Oil or ghee prepared with these [drugs], along with four times as much milk, is declared to be the supreme nasal medication (nasya).
By drinking oil as a nasal medication, a man becomes free of black hair, possesses firm sense organs, and is rid of wrinkles, graying hair, and freckles; he becomes endowed with keen vision.

8.2.22 By saturating the ears, eyes, nose, and mouth with unctuous substances, one achieves the freedom from obstruction of the sense organs, clarity of voice and complexion, and the purification of the channels;
these are to be known as the signs of proper oleation. Dryness of the channels and their emptiness, on the other hand, are the signs of insufficient oleation.
Heaviness and pain in the head, the channels being filled with oil, and a coating on the ears and palate are the signs of excessive unctuousness from nasal therapy (nasya). 8.2.24

8.2.25 One should not administer [an enema] to one who has indigestion, nor to one whose head is wet, nor to one desiring to travel on a road, nor to one who has just drunk water, nor to one suffering from fever. 8.2.26 Nor should it be given to one who has engaged in sexual intercourse, nor to one who has consumed intoxicants, nor to one who has overeaten, nor to one who has not undergone oleation and sudation, nor likewise to one who has not attained relief.
When [the enema] has been properly administered, the pain and swelling subside completely; for, by means of the urine and feces, his vāta is indeed expelled.
8.2.28 The physician should recognize that as *anirūḍha* (insufficiently purged); its symptoms are likewise: the disease [remains], flatulence, colic, and suppression of feces and urine.

8.2.29 A fullness of the abdomen and abdominal distension (*ānāha*) are the symptoms of one who is *durnirūḍha* (badly purged). Furthermore, in one who has been properly purged (*nirūḍha*), the blood becomes vitiated.
But when [the obstruction] is excessively chronic and devoid of feces, the wind (māruta), enveloping the abdomen with sharp pain (śūla), afflicts all the limbs. (8.2.30)

8.2.31 Thus, the fivefold [procedure] has been stated and explained; one who understands the application of the five therapies (pañcakarma) is called a physician worthy of a king. So said the Blessed Ātreya. Thus ends the second chapter in the Bheḷa [Saṃhitā]. **The Fourth Chapter** Now, therefore, we shall explain the successful administration of emesis and purgation regarding the ten complications. So said the Blessed Ātreya. 8.4.1 A wise physician should diligently prepare downward-acting and upward-acting medicines, which are indeed like poison or a weapon.
8.4.1–2 Those that are pungent, bitter, and astringent; those that cause a burning sensation and others; those that are subtle, hot, sharp, liquefying, and heavy.
8.4.3 Having reached those [channels], they enter the heart-vessels (*hṛdaya-dhamanī*) and cause the humors (*doṣa*) to flow sideways, upwards, and downwards.
8.4.4 Due to their subtlety, they follow even the subtlest parts of the body and cause the bodily constituents (*dhātu*) to leak away, even through the wrong channels in embodied beings.

8.4.4–5 Those [emetics] which arise from the upper part of the body draw those excessively aggravated doshas toward the heart as if leading them there; likewise, having filled the stomach (āmāśaya), they act upon the upper portion.

In this very way, having filled the stomach with secretions, they flow downward in the various morbidities of embodied beings here. As long as the humors (doṣas) remain within embodied beings, they cause them to overflow; thereafter, they purify [the body] either upward or downward.

But for those [therapies] that are improperly applied, misdirected, or administered while the patient is running about, ten complications arise due to either non-application (ayoga) or excessive application (atiyoga).
8.4.9 Excessive discharge, flatulence, constipation, prolapse of the rectum, heart disease, colic, and likewise cutting pain; 8.4.10 Hemorrhage,
headache, and tenthly, dysentery— learn from me the successful management for each of these complications.

Now, if the emetic has been drunk and yet it does not act, one should drink a stronger dose; with appropriate after-drinks and food, the purification will be achieved, and then one should administer an enema to the person.

8.4.12 Even if purgation is not fully accomplished, one should administer an unctuous enema (anuvāsana) again. If it still does not reach its effect, after three days have passed, one should drink clarified butter (ghṛta).
8.4.13 Having been treated with oleation and sudation, and having been fed a light meal, a person should drink a stronger dose of either a purgative or an emetic.
8.4.13–14 When a purgative, having been drunk, results in emesis, the same procedure as for emesis is prescribed; this is also recorded as the case for a purgative. 8.4.14

8.4.15 Furthermore, if a person who has been freed from oleation and sudation but possesses a hard bowel (krūrakoṣṭha) drinks medicine while suffering from indigestion, it causes him distress. 8.4.16 In one who has undergone fasting therapy, or who has eaten excessively, or who is dry, or who has fasted, or who has undergone scarification (parikartana), or who has undergone purgation (parisrāva), or who has applied an ointment (pralepa), or who has not undergone sudation, [the medicine causes distress].
8.4.16–17: In a person who has been freed from oleation and sudation and whose bowels have become soft, the remaining morbid humors (doṣas) give rise to dysentery (pravāhikā).
8.4.18 From excessive roughness, excessive heat, or the improper preparation of medicines, colic arises in men, as well as a severe prolapse of the rectum.
8.4.19 When emesis or purgation has been drunk [as a medicine] but its urges are suppressed, the aggravated vāta, pitta, and kapha cause a seizing pain in the heart.
His limbs sink, and there is exhaustion and severe pain; there is stiffness of the head, distress in the abdomen, and he may even become unconscious.
8.4.21 For one who has undergone sudation, whose bowels are softened, and who has been treated with oleation, a purgative taken in an excessive dose may lead to the loss of life.
8.4.22 Such a person may discharge semen along with feces that are black or even red, or it may be the color of the Lodhra flower or resemble the Bhaṇḍī flower.
When one who has been excessively heated resorts to cooling treatments, seeks out cool shelters, and partakes of cold water; 8.4.23.
8.4.24 When the aggravated *vāyu* obstructs the channels and remains there, it becomes harsh; consequently, the bodily humors (*doṣas*) of that embodied being overflow.
8.4.25 The non-passage of flatus, urine, and feces, along with thirst and fever—this is described by physicians as "obstruction" (*vibandha*), arising from a confusion of their understanding.
when a physician administers a dry medicine that is not unctuous, the provoked *māruta* (vāta) seizes all the limbs of that patient.
8.4.27 When the vital air (vāyu) enters the hips, back, head, neck, and heart, then one falls into delusion and the loss of consciousness.
8.4.28 These ten complications have been described individually with their various characteristics; one should apply treatment for them according to the instruction of Ātreya.
In that case, having anointed the non-yogin with oil and salt, one should treat him with either *saṅkara-prastara-sveda* (mixed-bed fomentation) or *nāḍī-sveda* (tube fomentation).

8.4.30 Having thoroughly established [the enema] and allowed it to rest, one should sprinkle the patient with lukewarm water and feed him soft rice with the meat broth of wild animals (*jāṅgala*). 8.4.31 Then, one should administer an unctuous enema (*anuvāsana*) with lukewarm oil extracted from fruits; by this, flatulence, cutting pain, and discharge are pacified.
8.4.31–32 Sāla, rubūka, triphalā, dantī, and citraka— ghee cooked with these should be administered according to the patient's strength.

8.4.33 To one who has been saturated by that oil, well-lubricated, and prepared with sudation therapy (sveda), one should administer a sharp emetic or purgative medicine. 8.4.34 By this, heart disease, horripilation, stiffness of the head and shoulders, as well as constipation, cutting pain, and colic are pacified.
When the discharge from a fissure (parisrāva) is not subsiding according to its true nature, one should administer a decoction enema (kaṣāya-vasti) or even a slimy enema (picchā-vasti).

One should administer a milk enema (kṣīravasti) with boiled honey and ghee, or with ghee processed with the *jīvanīya* group of drugs; one should also perform an oil enema (anuvāsana) with that same ghee.
One should give milk boiled with castor root, the three myrobalans (*triphalā*), grapes, and *kāśmarya*, mixed with various other substances.
8.4.37–38: Yāvaśūka, kṣāra, rock salt (saindhava), sour vetasa, asafoetida (hiṅgu), the essence of pomegranate, long pepper (pippalī), and ginger (viśvabheṣaja).
8.4.39 When drunk with clarified butter (*sarpiṣ*), milk, wine, or even hot water, it will alleviate severe colic (*śūla*) and cutting pain (*parikartikā*).
8.4.40 One should cook oil with these: *devadāru*, *bilva*, *rāsnā*, *karkaṭa* (the so-called crab-tree), *eraṇḍa*, and *pūti*.
One should administer an unctuous enema (anuvāsana) with that [oil] at that time; thus it becomes comfortable, and the stiffness of the limbs, the pain, and the cutting sensation are pacified.
8.4.42 If the pacification of these complications is not achieved, one should apply their respective specific treatments according to each individual case.
8.4.43 Thus has the treatment for deficient administration been described by me in detail; now I shall speak of the treatment for complications arising from excessive administration.
In the event of excessive emesis, one should administer purgation; and if purgation is excessively applied, the physician should cause the patient to drink an emetic. 8.4.44

8.4.45 However, if emesis is excessively administered, an *āsthāpana* enema should be performed; if both [emesis and purgation] are excessive, a styptic (*stambhana*) treatment is said to be beneficial.
8.4.46 That person should scrape [the tongue] with rice-water mixed with honey, and he should sprinkle his feet and hands, or likewise immerse them in water.
One should rub all the limbs with *lāmajjaka*, lotus stalks, and *candana* along with *padmaka*, and one should sprinkle them with decoctions (*kaṣāya*). 8.4.46–47.

8.4.48 Dhātakī, madhuka, lodhra, padma, mocarasa, as well as nīlotpala, samaṅgā, kaṭphala, and padmakesara— 8.4.49 With these, one should prepare a lukewarm peyā (gruel) from red śāli rice; when it has become very cool, one should drink it mixed with honey. This is the supreme *sthāpana* (stabilizing treatment) for him.
Lākṣā, lodhra, samaṅgā, honey, and the lotuses kamala and utpala, when drunk with goat’s milk, are said to arrest hemorrhaging. (8.4.49–50)

One should cause the patient to drink the juice of *kapittha* leaves mixed with honey; likewise, a person should drink the juice of jujube (*bādara*) with milk, or grape juice with honey. (8.4.51) The juices of wild animals should be served clearly seasoned with the essence of pomegranate; furthermore, milk enemas (*kṣīravasti*) combined with ghee and pomegranate should be administered. (8.4.52)
But when the blood has flowed excessively, one should administer an enema of blood itself, using the meat of hare, antelope, sheep, goat, or buffalo.

8.4.54 One should drink boiled rice that has been softened with milk, strained, and mixed with honey; or alternatively, one may soften the rice again with sugarcane juice. 8.4.55 Likewise, a gruel prepared with the horns of the *nyagrodha*, *udumbara*, *plakṣa*, *vetasa*, and *aśvattha* trees, along with their milk, is the supreme restorative treatment (*sthāpana*).
Padmaka, the exudation of the śālmali tree, samaṅgā, and dhātakī; likewise jambū- and āmra-sāra, madhuka, parched grain (lāja), lac (lākṣā), and priyaṅgu.

8.4.57 Milk boiled with these [drugs] should be drunk, or one should also have the patient drink gruel (yavāgū) prepared with them; alternatively, one may drink them mixed with rice-water along with honey.
8.4.58 Boiled rice made from *koradūṣa* grains, combined with honey and *sasyaka*, and joined with *palaṅkaṣā*, will cure diarrhea (*atisāra*).
Curd mixed with sesame oil and kept for seven nights, when served with a meal of *koradūṣa* grain, destroys diarrhea. (8.4.59)
8.4.60 After buttermilk has stood for seven nights, the physician should prepare a decoction of radish with it; this, when served with a meal of *koradūṣa* grain, destroys diarrhea.
8.4.61 *Vaṭāṅkura*, *mocarasa*, *lodhra*, the pith of mango stones, young *bilva* fruits, and the flowers of *dhātakī* [are also used].
When the buttermilk has stood for five nights, one should prepare a soup with these [herbs]; it should be served with *koradūṣa* rice, as this destroys diarrhea.

8.4.63 One should cook milk with blue lotus (*nīlotpala*), blue sesame (*nīlatila*), *samaṅgā*, and *lodhra*; this destroys diarrhea. 8.4.64 Likewise, one should cook sesame oil with *lodhra* and goat’s milk; by this, dysentery (*pravāhikā*) and prolapse of the rectum (*gudabhraṃśa*) are entirely pacified.
One should boil milk with *balā*, *atibalā*, *bilva*, *eraṇḍa*, and *coraka*; this destroys *kapha* and *pitta*.
In cases of lockjaw (hanustambha) and severe pain from hemorrhoids (arśas), one should drink this [mixture]. Furthermore, with this very paste, one should apply a plaster over the head.
By this, fainting and vertigo are pacified for embodied beings; as for whatever other complications may arise, they should be treated according to their respective cures.
One should likewise cook milk with these—sugar, padmaka, uśīra, nyagrodha, and udumbara; this destroys thirst and burning sensations.
8.4.69 One should administer a milk enema (kṣīravasti) or even a slimy enema (picchāvasti); in cases of excessive action, cold medicated ghee enemas (ghṛtavasti) are recommended.

8.4.70 Whatever was previously described regarding the treatment for hemorrhoids (jīvādāna), that should be performed in the case of prolapse of the rectum (gudabhraṃśa); thus it will result in well-being.

When wind-pain (vāta-śūla) has arisen, one should apply fomentations such as those using a mixture of materials or a bed of heated grains, as well as poultices, to those who have been properly anointed with oil.
One should administer an asthāpana (non-unctuous enema) prepared with vacā, śvadaṃṣṭrā, pūtīka, and the five roots (pañcamūlī), or a sukhoṣṇa (lukewarm) anuvāsana (unctuous enema).

One should treat the patient with alkaline preparations and alkaline ghees that alleviate colic, or one should have them drink an appropriate dose of the six-pala ghee (ṣaṭpala-ghṛta) mixed with curd.
In the same way, the physician should apply the procedure even in cases of obstruction; and those complications which occur after emesis and purgation [should likewise be treated]. 8.4.73–74.
8.4.75 A wise physician should treat these according to their respective medical protocols. Even one who is well-oiled (lubricated) should consume the meat of domestic or aquatic animals.

8.4.76 When phlegm (kapha) has increased, purgation or emesis should be administered to him immediately. Furthermore, medicine should not be drunk during indigestion, whether in small or large quantities.
When there is excessive nausea, upward movement of wind (udāvarta), or when the medicine has been improperly administered, a purgative taken in this manner results in emesis.

8.4.78 Emesis should not be administered to one who is emaciated, or parched, or even to one who is delicate or very robust, nor to a person whose *kapha* has not yet accumulated, nor to one who is un-oleated (*asnigdha*).

8.4.79 Alternatively, if the emetic has been retained or causes agitation, one should administer a purgative. Regarding this, some authorities say that a liquid vehicle (*anupāna*) is appropriate, while others say it is improper.
For medicine that is administered in excess indeed leads to the taking away of life. After ten days have passed, [the patient] should be treated with oleation and sudation.

8.4.81 One should cause this very sharp medicine, prepared according to the [prescribed] method, to be administered. This success regarding purgation and emesis has been proclaimed, as well as the complications and their treatments, in due order and correctly. Thus spoke the Blessed Ātreya. Thus ends the fourth chapter in the Section on Success (*Siddhisthāna*) of the *Bhela-saṃhitā*. Chapter Five. Now, therefore, we shall explain the success regarding the measures for enemas (*vastimātrīyasiddhi*). Thus indeed said the Blessed Ātreya. 8.4.81

8.5.1 Physicians recommend the administration of enemas (basti) when the meal has been mixed with food; other doctors [recommend it] after purgation (virikta), while still others [recommend it] after a non-unctuous enema (nirūḍha). 8.5.2 Wise authorities say that these three are inferior and do not praise them. I shall thoroughly refute their opinion with logical arguments.
However, in one who has been repeatedly purged, the digestive fire becomes cold; likewise, the channels residing in the heart and those residing in the rectum and abdomen become cold.
8.5.4 When the *māruta* (vata) is aggravated, it flows into the receptacle of the digested food (*pakvādhāna*). It cools the bodily fire (*kāyāgni*) and diminishes his strength.
8.5.5 If an enema (*vasti*) is administered when the channels (*srotas*) are either purified or unpurified, it enters deeply into the body and does not return at all.
8.5.5–6 It may cause vomiting, thirst, heart disease, pallor, and likewise edema; therefore, one who has been purged by emetics should certainly not be given an oil enema.
8.5.7 For an embodied being whose food has become mixed and who has again developed a disorder, oil therapy (sneha) is useless when the channels are smeared with impurities.
8.5.8 For an embodied being who has been treated with a non-sharp (mild) non-unctuous enema (nirūha), an unctuous enema (snehavasti) is not recommended while the humors (doṣas) remain agitated.
Furthermore, some who have a perception that the bodily humors (doṣas) have been pacified after the body has remained overnight [with oil] praise the practice of non-unctuous enema (anuvāsana).

8.5.10 Now hear from me the procedure for the administration of enemas (basti), which is free from complications, for one who has been properly oleated and has undergone purgation according to the prescribed method. 8.5.11 Likewise, for one who has consumed a mixed meal and has again been oleated, one should administer an unctuous enema (anuvāsana) after five nights have passed.
8.5.11–12 An oil enema (anuvāsana) should not be administered to one whose digestive tract is excessively dry above; for his wind (vāta), being forced upward, settles in the heart.
8.5.13 One should feed [the patient] even half the usual amount of food, along with thin mung-bean soup or the broth of wild game.
8.5.14 Having eaten and being comforted, and having voided excrement and urine, the man should lie down on his left side upon a level bed.
He should contract his right thigh and extend the left; the man should place a pillow under his head.
8.5.16 Then one should comfortably introduce the enema (vasti) for him, following along the spinal column, according to the strength of the procedure, neither too quickly nor too slowly.

8.5.17 An enema that is free from defects, gentle, and has removed the wind (vāyu) is recommended; however, one in which the wind is excessively bound or obstructed is not praised for the administration of the enema.
8.5.17–18 Having placed the nozzle at the opening of the bladder, one should press it firmly with one hand and hold the other hand steady, without allowing the hands to tremble. 8.5.18
8.5.19 First, having lubricated the anus, the instrument, and the hands, the practitioner should insert it; then he should place the patient supine and extend his legs.

8.5.20 Once the enema has been administered, one should not hold it back for more than a muhūrta, but allow it to pass as comfortably as possible. Thereafter, one should not suppress the urges that have arisen.
A non-obstructive enema containing oil and feces succeeds even when there is no wind. Furthermore, for one whose oil enema returns immediately after being administered, [it is successful].

8.5.22 He is not said to be a performer of his duty who causes another to administer it. Thus, being thirsty during the night, he should drink warm water in the morning. 8.5.23 An enema should be administered at intervals of one day for men, and never continuously; likewise, massage, rubbing, and the pouring of lukewarm water [should be applied].

8.5.23–24 And the administration of warm water as an after-drink is recommended during the enema procedure; the physician should administer it four, three, or as many times as is required until lubrication is achieved again.

8.5.25 After the unctuous enemas (snehavasti) have been administered, one should then perform the non-unctuous enema (āsthāpana), once the channels have been moistened by the prescribed unctuous substance.

8.5.26 For the purification of the channels, one should comfortably administer nirūha enemas according to the proper method; for if the internal organ (koṣṭha) is impure and fouled, an unctuous enema applied [without prior purification]— [...would be ineffective.]
[The author] demonstrates the superiority of the white [variety]; it should be applied during the parvan [periods], and the administration of purgation and enema therapy should be performed.

8.5.28 One should avoid the administration of gruel as a post-therapeutic drink during the procedure of enema (*basti*). There are twenty-four types of *nirūha* enemas, including those with oil-massage (*anuvāsana*). 8.5.29 A skilled physician should administer this prescribed treatment for upward-moving wind (*ūrdhvavāta*) in mild, moderate, and severe diseases.

8.5.29–30 One should administer mild, moderate, and sharp enema therapies (basti-karma). [The diet should consist of] the meat of domestic, marshy, and aquatic animals, flour-based foods, minced meat, and curd.

8.5.31 One should avoid preparations of sour vegetables and various kinds of solid foods, as well as the drinking of cold water and immersion in cold baths. 8.5.32 In the administration of enemas (basti), one should avoid heavy foods and drinks; instead, one should provide *śāli* rice, *ṣaṣṭika* rice, and mung beans for the purpose of eating.

8.5.32–33. Hares, partridges, and quails should be provided for the sake of flavoring. One who possesses knowledge, who consumes well-measured food, who is devoted to serving the physician, and who attends to the enema—such a person shall live for a hundred autumns. Thus said the venerable Ātreya. Thus ends the fifth chapter in the Section on Success (Siddhisthāna) of the Bheḷa-saṃhitā. The Sixth Chapter. Now, therefore, we shall expound the "Success in Preparations" (Upakalpasiddhi). Thus said the venerable Ātreya. 8.5.33.
8.6.1 Listen to me regarding the bladder (vasti), its accessories, the oil, and all [related matters], as well as the method of their application, the procedure, and the clinical action.
8.6.2 Enema therapy (basti-karma) is recommended for children, the elderly, the young, and those of middle age, as well as for the healthy and for the diseased.
Wise men say that the materials for the eyes [of the image] are gold, silver, copper, bell-metal, lead, iron, horn, bamboo, bone, and the tips of reeds.
8.6.4 Now, these primary and secondary [parts] should be applied respectively among superior, inferior, and middling men.
8.6.5 The mouth of the pellet should be the eye, measuring no less than twelve finger-breadths; the dwelling of the pericarp is one finger-breadth, and one should insert that into the anus.
In that regard, the gift is praised when it has the shape of a cow’s tail, is very smooth, possesses a comfortable *karṇika* (handle), and has a circumference equal to the forefinger.

8.6.7 There, having remained for one hundred *mātrās*, it returns by itself if it is wine prepared with meat and fresh fats, even when taken at an improper time. 8.6.8 And if it is withdrawn before the proper time, it does not purge because of its rapid action; therefore, in that case, it may be considered moderate, as it might return after three hundred *mātrās*.
8.6.8–9 Thus, for one who has passed the [proper] time and whose enema does not return, it will quickly be brought back by means of a sharp non-unctuous enema (āsthāpana). 8.6.9

8.6.10 Therefore, one should prepare a stronger enema beforehand; for a severe obstruction is not recommended when maintaining the vital breaths (*prāṇa*). 8.6.11 Therefore, he who knows the proper time, the disease, the strength and weakness [of the patient], and the full form [of the treatment] regarding decoction enemas (*nirūha*), does not fall into delusion.
For neither a thunderbolt nor fire can kill in such a manner as a poorly administered enema might instantly deprive one of life. (8.6.12)

8.6.13 An enema that is properly administered and directed toward the vital breath (*prāṇa*) is praised as an immediate remover of disease. For when it has been correctly withdrawn, it destroys the multitude of diseases; however, if not withdrawn, it takes away life. 8.6.14 When it is withdrawn with force, it leads the humors (*doṣa*) situated in the deep [seats] back to their proper path, and those situated on the path, being out of alignment, it brings into their natural course.
8.6.14–15: The force of the enema destroys Vāta, just as the wind destroys a rain-cloud. Indeed, all disorders of Kapha and Pitta follow the influence of Vāta.

There are eighty diseases caused by vāta, forty born of pitta, and twenty arising from kapha; these do not include those resulting from the combination of humors. Indeed, among all these diseases, enema (basti) is always the foremost refuge for beings afflicted by them.
For all these [diseases] originate from Vāyu and are dependent upon the bladder; therefore, it is said that the enema (vasti) constitutes half, or even the whole, of medical treatment.

8.6.19 But the man who always employs the enema (*vasti*) for four months—diseases shall avoid him, just as elephants avoid the dwelling of a lion. 8.6.20 These specific qualities have been explained regarding the procedure of the enema; now hear from me the efficacy and the method of administration of this *nirūha* [non-unctuous enema].
In cases of perspiration, stale digestion, or when food is fully digested, one should administer a strong purgative; for it draws out his urine, feces, and phlegm.

8.6.22 It promotes the downward movement of Vāta and generates strength; it also eliminates the stable poison and the power of the Doshas that are situated within the channels (nāḍīs). 8.6.23 When administered, this Nirūha purges all of that; indeed, there is nothing else equal to it for the entire host of diseases.
Just as one parts the hair that is disheveled, so too, by means of a non-unctuous enema (nirūha), there should be the clearing away of the excessively disordered humors (doṣas).
8.6.25 For a Nirūha enema, when properly administered with balanced qualities and full potency, swiftly eradicates diseases, just as merit uplifts a man endowed with it.

8.6.26 [It is indicated] for those with difficult urination or defecation, those suffering from colic, those with Vāta-type Gulma, those with downward reversal of the bodily winds (Udāvarta), heart disease, and pain in the flanks.
In cases of abdominal enlargements, urinary disorders, skin diseases, and intestinal worms, when [the blood] is conjoined with phlegm and vitiated by blood; 8.6.27.

8.6.28 For all combined disorders and those arising from the simultaneous aggravation of the three humors (sannipāta), as well as for those that are deep-seated or have reached the fundamental tissues (dhātu), non-unctuous enema (nirūhaṇa) is the best treatment. 8.6.29 When phlegm (kapha) is expelled, appearing like a conch shell or crystal, and free from urine and feces, that is the characteristic sign of a successful nirūha enema.

One should administer an oil enema (anuvāsana) to a patient who has been well-purified by a decoction enema (nirūha), who has not remained fasting for too long, who has rested comfortably, who is fully recovered, and who has been fed.

8.6.31 On one side are the enema treatments (*basti-karma*), and on the other side is all other medical therapy; when properly administered, the enema treatment acts as nectar for the sake of immortality.
8.6.32 The semen of a person who has many sexual restraints does not undergo depletion; however, men whose semen is diminished may suffer from excessive indulgence with women.

8.6.32–33: "By the application of enemas (*vasti*), even a eunuch becomes a man in every respect; it is also traditionally taught that this brings about the growth of flesh even for emaciated mortals. Thus spoke the venerable Ātreya. Thus ends the sixth chapter in the Section on Success (*Siddhisthāna*) of the *Bhela-saṃhitā*. The Seventh Chapter: Now, therefore, we shall explain the success regarding the dosage of fruits (*phalamātrāsiddhi*). Thus said the venerable Ātreya. 8.6.33.

8.7.1 Wise men say that among non-unctuous enemas (nirūhas), the fruit alone is the best; however, physicians declare that among those fruits, *madana* is the most excellent. 8.7.2 Some praise *jīmūtaka*, others likewise *dhāmārgava*; some say *kṛtavedhana*, and others say *kuṭaja*.
8.7.2–3 All these aforementioned doctrines are considered individually to be censurable; however, a combination of medicinal drugs is highly recommended for decoction enemas (nirūha).

8.7.4 We shall now explain, according to the proper method, the non-unctuous enemas (nirūha) for wind, bile, phlegm, and fire, as well as those which are beneficial for the combination of all three (sannipāta), in their respective order. 8.7.5 One should boil two *pañcamūla* groups, along with *kola*, *nīla*, *nalada*, and dried radish— two *pala* of each of these— in one *droṇa* of water.
When one-eighth of the decoction remains, one should remove it from the heat; then, one should add these medicinal drugs that are to be ground into a paste.
8.7.7 Nikuñjikā, kharapuṣpā, pippalī, saindhava, vacā, the seeds of trapusa and urvāru, śatapuṣpā, and yavānikā;
8.7.8 Kuṣṭha, tagara, and yaṣṭīmadhuka— this is proclaimed as being prepared with milk, decoction, and cow’s urine.
This non-unctuous enema (nirūha), containing oil, destroys diseases of vāta. [One should take] the leaves and roots of paṭola, picumanda, and śatāvarī.
8.7.10 Trāyamāṇā, balā, rāsnā, bṛhatī, kaṇṭakārikā, guḍūcī, triphalā, śyāmā, sārivā, and bamboo bark—
8.7.11 taking two-pala portions of each of these separately, one should prepare them according to the previously mentioned method; [adding] madhuka, bamboo fruit, śatapuṣpā, and durālabhā.
8.7.11–12 One should prepare the paste (kalka) of mahāsahā and maṃśumatī separately with milk, as well as with a decoction (kaṣāya), ghee, and honey. 8.7.12
8.7.13 A well-prepared *nirūha* enema mixed with these [decoctions] destroys *pitta*. [The ingredients are: *daśamūlī*, the two types of *karañja*, *dantī*, and *citraka*;
8.7.14 *ekāṣṭhīlā*, *turaṅgī*, *triphalā*, *devadāru*, *pūtika*, *rauhiṣa*, *śyāmā*, *mūrvā*, and *rājatṛṇa*.

One who knows all the pharmaceutical preparations should prepare these five [substances] separately, each weighing five palas, by properly combining them with drugs that act as purgatives and emetics.
8.7.16 This non-unctuous enema (nirūha), combined with urine and oil, is excellent for destroying kapha. [One should take] ashwagandha, bala, rasna, shvadamstra, along with punarnava;
8.7.17 as well as patola, the two types of panchamula, bharangi, shyama, shatavari, guduchi, triphala, shigru, and the fruits of karṇikā.
The physician should cut these five *pala* measures each—*uśīra*, *rajanī*, *patra*, *pūtika*, and *kattṛṇa*—into small pieces separately.
8.7.19 One *droṇa* of water should be boiled down until one-eighth remains, along with *madhuka*, *śatapuṣpā*, rock salt (*saindhava*), mustard seeds, and jaggery.
8.7.20 [Add] *hapuṣā*, *ajamodā*, the fruits of *madana*, *vacā*, the seeds of *aśoka*, long pepper (*pippalī*), and *kuṣṭha*.
8.7.20–21 These medicinal drugs, to be ground into a paste individually, combined with milk and oil, and mixed with ghee and urine— 8.7.21.
8.7.22 That Nirūha enema is praised when churned with a churning-stick (khaja) and strained; it may be prepared with one, two, or three [drugs], according to the excessive measure required.

8.7.23 Having ascertained the strength or weakness of the disease, one should administer it with a quantity slightly less or more than that; for a person of twenty years of age, the standard measure is one Prastha.
Now, one should administer half a *prastha* for twelve years, and for six years, one should administer a *kuḍava* of decoction here. 8.7.24

8.7.25 The physician should administer a decoction enema (kaṣāya-vasti) mixed with salt, oil, milk, and honey; due to its heating nature (sveda), it should consist of two *prasṛta* measures. 8.7.26 For a medium-strength enema, one should use one *prasṛta*, and for the weakest, half a *prasṛta*. One should prepare the decoction so that it is neither too cold nor too hot.
Vāyu becomes aggravated by coldness, whereas excessive heat would burn the rectum. When it is excessively thick and knotted due to the *doṣa*, it faints (becomes obstructed).

8.7.28 An excessive rush of intoxication occurs and complications arise for him; or else, if a mild decoction (kaṣāya) is administered to one who is emaciated, 8.7.29 it removes only a small amount of the morbid humor (doṣa) and does not cleanse the rectum; moreover, it produces cutting pain, colic, and dysentery (pravāhikā).

If administered in excessive sweetness, it causes a burning sensation; if improperly digested (vidagdha), it may cause stiffness of the limbs, disorders of the duodenum (grahaṇī), hemorrhoids, anemia, and fistula-in-ano.

8.7.31 However, an enema that is too strong or improperly administered is quickly expelled; it does not eliminate the morbid humors (doṣas), but rather causes fever and fainting. 8.7.32 For a person who is feverish, burning with heat, or fainting, one should administer milk enemas (kṣīravasti) combined with cold substances and sweet tastes.
Now, if a salted non-unctuous enema (nirūha) produces pitta-type pains in the abdomen, it should be ground with warm water; then a sweet non-unctuous enema should be administered.

8.7.34 If a patient’s kapha would be aggravated by a sweet non-unctuous enema (nirūha), one should administer a nirūha containing pungent and astringent substances; however, for a patient whose vāta [would be aggravated], [one should use] that which pacifies vāta.
8.7.35 In that case, vāta-pacifying enemas might become excessively aggravated; therefore, the substances should be combined with salt and be sweet.

8.7.35–36b: The physician should not administer [enemas] that are cold or hot indiscriminately; rather, he should distinguish between them. In the case of pitta, the nirūha enema should be cold, whereas it should be hot for kapha and vāta.

8.7.37 In cases of excessive phlegm or when there is a strong wind, a warm non-unctuous enema (āsthāpana) should be administered. One should prepare it by grinding the fruit of *madana* with clear oil.
8.7.38 Physicians praise this "fruit-oil" (*phalataila*) for use in a non-unctuous enema (*nirūha*). This fruit-oil enema should be combined with cow's urine.
One should prepare a salted *nirūha* enema, which is excellent for breaking up abdominal distension (*ānāha*). Alternatively, one should cook two *prastha*s of *bilva* and *eraṇḍa* fruits.
8.7.40 One should prepare a sour and salty decoction, boiling it down until one-eighth remains; to this decoction, one should add *pīlu* fruits as a paste to be ground.

8.7.41 An enema combined with fruit-oil (*phalataila*) should be administered to break up abdominal distension (*ānāha*). This [enema] also breaks up all types of upward-moving wind (*udāvarta*), as well as swellings and abdominal tumors (*gulma*).
Now, this enema will destroy flatulence and upward movement of wind (udāvarta). [One should use] the powder of oṣṭhajihva, pṛṣṭhacūrṇa, bṛhatī, and kaṇṭakārikā.
